t: Comparison of macrophage and liver transcriptomes indicates that peritoneal macrophages, not the liver, are the primary local producers of many complement and coagulation system components.
Peritoneal macrophages showed high RNA-seq expression of all three C1q genes, while the Ampliseq platform detected mainly C1qB.
Liver transcriptome showed no or very low expression of serum amyloids Saa3/Saa1, C1qA/B/C, properdin, or ficolin, contrasting with high expression of these genes in peritoneal macrophages.

Liver transcriptome analysis indicated the liver is the main producer of most complement (C3, factor H, C4b, C4bp, C8g, factor 5, CRP, C1r, C1qbp) and coagulation factors (fibrinogen, thrombin/F2, factors V, VII, X, XII, XIII), with lower levels of factors IX, XI, and VIII.

Unlike peritoneal macrophages, human peripheral blood monocytes did not express C1q, C4a, C4b, or complement factor H, and lacked expression of all coagulation components, despite both cell types expressing properdin and ficolin.
Peritoneal macrophages express approximately 25-fold higher levels of fibronectin transcript than the liver, suggesting macrophages are important local producers of this connective tissue protein.

Some individual human monocyte donors showed almost total absence of HLA-B and/or HLA-C expression, suggesting a reduced MHC class I repertoire that could affect susceptibility to intracellular pathogens.
RNA-seq data indicated peritoneal macrophages exclusively express M-lysozyme (Lyz1) and not P-lysozyme (Lyz2), while the Ampliseq method could not distinguish the two paralogs.

PAD-4, essential for histone citrullination and NET formation, was expressed at much higher levels in peritoneal macrophages than in human monocytes, suggesting differing capacities to form extracellular DNA traps.
GATA-6 was the only GATA transcription factor expressed at significant levels in mouse peritoneal macrophages, whereas human blood monocytes were negative for all GATA factors.

Large peritoneal macrophages showed low steady-state MHC class II expression and require activation to become antigen-presenting cells, whereas human monocytes constitutively expressed high MHC class II and were ready to present antigen without prior activation.

Peritoneal macrophages expressed high levels of connective tissue components lubricin, syndecan-3, and extracellular matrix protein 1, all of which were essentially absent in human blood monocytes, indicating major differences in connective tissue homeostasis roles between the two cell types.
Both mouse peritoneal macrophages and human monocytes expressed high levels of the IgG transport receptor FcRN, a previously unreported finding in these cell populations.
Intracolonic infusion of fecal supernatant from IBS-D patients into mice increased mucosal serotonin (5-HT) levels compared with healthy control fecal supernatant.
Mucosal serotonin reuptake transporter (SERT) expression was reduced by approximately 50% following intracolonic infusion of IBS-D fecal supernatant compared with healthy control fecal supernatant.
Mast cell stabilizers, cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) inhibitors, and a PGE2 receptor antagonist each prevented the SERT downregulation caused by IBS-D fecal supernatant.
In mast cell-deficient (W/Wv) mice, IBS-D fecal supernatant infusion failed to reduce SERT expression, indicating mast cells are required for the SERT downregulation effect.

Downregulation of SERT expression evoked by IBS fecal supernatant was prevented by a bacterial LPS antagonist (LPS from Rhodobacter sphaeroides) and a bacterial trypsin inhibitor, implicating fecal LPS and trypsin activity in the mechanism.
In vitro LPS treatment of cultured mouse mast cells caused increased COX-2 expression and PGE2 release.
Intracolonic infusion of IBS-D fecal supernatant in mice reduced colonic transit, increased fecal water content, and increased visceromotor responses to colorectal distension.
The 5-HT3 receptor antagonist ondansetron prevented the reduced colonic transit, increased fecal water content, and increased visceromotor responses induced by IBS-D fecal supernatant.
Ondansetron, a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist, prevented the reduction in colonic transit, increase in fecal water content, and increased visceromotor responses induced by IBS-D fecal supernatant.

A bacterial trypsin inhibitor, together with an LPS antagonist, prevented the downregulation of SERT expression evoked by IBS-D fecal supernatant, implicating fecal trypsin activity alongside LPS in the mast cell-mediated pathway.
EphrinB2/ephB2 was specifically expressed in colonic nerves and was upregulated in colonic tissue from IBS patients compared to controls, correlating with pain severity.
EphrinB2/ephB2 expression was upregulated in colonic tissue of Trichinella spiralis-infected IBS rats compared to controls.
Functional synaptic plasticity, visceral sensitivity to colorectal distention, and colonic mesenteric afferent activity to mechanical and chemical stimuli were all enhanced in IBS rats.
Treatment with ephB2-Fc, an ephB2 receptor blocker, reversed the enhanced synaptic plasticity, visceral sensitivity, and mesenteric afferent activity seen in IBS rats.
Ifenprodil, a selective NR2B antagonist, blocked the enhanced synaptic plasticity, visceral sensitivity, and mesenteric afferent activity in IBS rats.
EphrinB2-Fc, an ephB2 receptor activator, promoted phosphorylation of NR2B in IBS rats and in longitudinal muscle-myenteric plexus (LMMP) cultures.
EphrinB2-Fc mediated sustained enteric neural activation via increased intracellular calcium levels in myenteric neuron cultures.
EphrinB2-Fc raised expression of the synaptic plasticity-related immediate early genes c-fos and arc in enteric neuron cultures.
EphrinB2-Fc treatment increased phosphorylation of the NR2B subunit of NMDA receptors in colonic tissue from IBS rats and in LMMP cultures.
EphrinB2-Fc induced sustained neural activation associated with increased intracellular calcium levels in primary myenteric neuron and LMMP cultures.
EphrinB2-Fc treatment raised expression of the immediate early gene c-fos, an indicator of synaptic plasticity, in enteric neuronal cultures.
EphrinB2-Fc treatment raised expression of the immediate early gene arc, consistent with induction of synaptic plasticity in enteric neurons.

EphrinB2-Fc (an ephB2 receptor activator) applied to LMMP cultures and primary myenteric neuron cultures directly induced enteric synaptic plasticity, demonstrating a causal cellular mechanism for the receptor system.

The authors conclude that ephrinB2/ephB2-mediated NR2B synaptic potentiation in the enteric nervous system represents a novel mechanistic explanation and potential therapeutic target for sustained visceral pain hypersensitivity in IBS.
Peripheral blood qRT-PCR showed elevated expression of the neuropeptides SP, CGRP, and VIP in asthma patients, with SP showing the most pronounced increase.
Serum ELISA confirmed a significant increase in SP expression in patients with allergic rhinitis.
Analysis of the GSE75011 dataset showed MyD88 was highly expressed in AR patients.
GSVA quantification of the MyD88-independent TLR4 cascade pathway activity across GSE75011 samples showed the pathway was activated in both asthma and AR patients.
Peripheral blood cytokine profiling in asthma patients showed elevated IL-6, IL-17A, IL-23, and TGF-β with decreased IL-2 and IL-10.
Serum ELISA in AR patients showed decreased IL-10 and elevated IL-6, IL-17A, IL-23, and TGF-β compared with normal participants.
Dose-dependent SP treatment of the LAD2 mast cell line increased secretion of IL-6, IL-17A, IL-23, and TGF-β while decreasing IL-10 secretion in the cell supernatant.
SP treatment of BEAS-2B bronchial epithelial cells upregulated mRNA expression of MyD88, IRAK4, TRAF6, and MKK3, with NFKB1 also elevated but not reaching significance.

Western blotting showed no significant change in p65 or phosphorylated p65 (NF-κB pathway) expression in BEAS-2B cells after SP treatment, suggesting NF-κB is not involved in SP-induced cytokine regulation.
Western blotting showed dose-dependent elevation of p38 and phosphorylated p38 protein expression in BEAS-2B cells after SP treatment, supporting MyD88-p38 pathway activation rather than NF-κB.

Correlation analysis of GSE75011 data showed the MyD88-independent TLR4 cascade pathway activity was significantly positively correlated with expression of MyD88, NFKBIA, IKBKB, NFKB1, TAB1, IRAK1, IRAK4, and TRAF6.
Single-cell expression profiling from Tabula Muris showed MyD88 is widely expressed across bronchial cell types.

The mitochondrial protein-coding gene MT-ND6 mRNA was significantly upregulated during the rehabilitation stage of COVID-19 recovery compared to earlier stages, while remaining stable during treatment and convalescence.
Aside from MT-ND6, none of the canonical mitochondrial genes (13 protein-coding genes, tRNAs, rRNAs) showed significant differential expression across the three COVID-19 recovery stages.
Three selected mitochondrial long non-coding RNAs (mt-lncRNAs) showed a stable transcriptional profile with no significant differences across the three COVID-19 clinical recovery stages.

Although the MT-ND6 locus encodes both a canonical mRNA and a non-canonical lncRNA, only the canonical MT-ND6 mRNA was differentially expressed across recovery stages, indicating that SARS-CoV-2 infection affects different classes of mitochondrial RNA from the same locus independently.

PCA of mitochondrial small RNA (mt-sRNA) expression showed patients clustered together during treatment and convalescence but separated distinctly during the rehabilitation stage, with 8 of 12 individuals separating along the first principal component (31% variance).

Among 75 analyzed mt-sRNA clusters, differential expression analysis found 9 differentially expressed between treatment and convalescence, 33 between treatment and rehabilitation, and 43 between convalescence and rehabilitation stages.
Comparing males and females, 19 mt-sRNA clusters were significantly differentially expressed, though this may be confounded by differing age distributions between sexes in the cohort.

mtRNA1, a 33-nt small RNA encoded within mt-tRNA-Glutamic acid, showed a consistent decreasing trend from treatment (highest) to convalescence (intermediate) to rehabilitation (lowest), suggesting persistent suppression even after infection clearance.
mtRNA2, a 32-nt small RNA encoded within mt-rRNA 12S, showed similar expression during treatment and convalescence but was upregulated during the rehabilitation stage, opposite to mtRNA1's pattern.

mtRNA8 and mtRNA9, isoforms differing by 3 nucleotides both encoded within mt-tRNA-Serine 2 (AGU/C), both showed downregulation specifically during convalescence and reached highest expression at rehabilitation.
mtRNA16 and mtRNA57, encoded within mt-tRNA-Lysine and mt-COX2 respectively, were relatively stable during treatment and convalescence but became upregulated during the rehabilitation stage.

Some mt-sRNA clusters, including mtRNA144, mtRNA57, and mtRNA104 (upregulated during rehabilitation) and mtRNA1 (downregulated), were significantly enriched in expression in one sex, suggesting sex-specific expression of certain small mitochondrial RNAs.
Comparing mt-sRNA cluster expression across COVID-19 severity groups (mild, moderate, serious) and across different patient ages did not yield any significant differences.

In an independent plasma-based small RNA dataset comparing 10 COVID-19-positive versus 10 age-matched COVID-19-negative individuals, PCA showed no clustering by infection status and no small mitochondrial RNAs were significantly differentially expressed.

Three of the six previously identified differentially expressed mt-sRNAs were absent in plasma samples entirely, while the remaining three were detected at thousands of copies, suggesting tissue-specific regulation of mitochondrial small RNA expression.

Overall, the analyses suggest SARS-CoV-2 infection does not broadly affect general mitochondrial transcription but rather disrupts the biogenesis of specific non-canonical mitochondrial products, an effect more pronounced for small RNAs than for longer RNAs.
Overall perceived fatigue measured by the FIS-40 questionnaire improved significantly after 8 weeks of CoQ10 plus selenium supplementation compared with baseline.
Physical fatigue perception improved significantly after supplementation compared with baseline.
Cognitive fatigue perception improved significantly after supplementation compared with baseline.
Global quality of life (SF-36) score improved significantly after 8 weeks of CoQ10 plus selenium supplementation.
SF-36 bodily pain, emotional role functioning, and mental health domains improved significantly from baseline after supplementation.
Sleep quality measured by the PSQI did not change significantly after 8 weeks of CoQ10 plus selenium supplementation.
Plasma total antioxidant capacity (TAC) increased significantly after 8 weeks of CoQ10 plus selenium supplementation compared with baseline.
Plasma lipid peroxidation (MDA/TBARS) decreased significantly after 8 weeks of CoQ10 plus selenium supplementation compared with baseline.
Circulating inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, and TNF-α) decreased significantly after 8 weeks of CoQ10 plus selenium supplementation.
Blood CRP levels did not change significantly after 8 weeks of CoQ10 plus selenium supplementation.
LDL cholesterol levels decreased significantly after CoQ10 plus selenium supplementation.
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and free T4 levels changed significantly after CoQ10 plus selenium supplementation.
Plasma FGF21 levels were not significantly different after 8 weeks of CoQ10 plus selenium supplementation.
Plasma NT-proBNP levels were not significantly different after 8 weeks of CoQ10 plus selenium supplementation.
No adverse effects were observed during the 8-week CoQ10 plus selenium supplementation trial in ME/CFS patients.

The rationale for combining selenium with CoQ10 is that the selenium-dependent enzyme thioredoxin reductase is required to reduce CoQ10 to its active ubiquinol form, so selenium deficiency could limit cells' ability to obtain optimal ubiquinol concentrations.
ME/CFS prevalence is estimated at 0.2-2%, with peak onset in adolescence and the 30s-40s, and a 3:1 to 4:1 female-to-male predominance.

In ME/CFS, resting-state BOLD signal was generally lower than controls before exercise, but after exercise ME/CFS showed elevated activation of the anterior default mode network node in the medial prefrontal cortex compared to both pre-exercise and controls.
In GWI, there was no difference from controls before exercise during a simple 0-back task, but following exercise GWI showed increased activation of the anterior default mode network.

During a difficult 2-back working memory task, postexercise BOLD activation in the dorsal midbrain, right middle insula, and left Rolandic operculum significantly increased in ME/CFS but significantly decreased in GWI, despite equivalent baseline activation across groups.

Incremental exercise-induced BOLD change (ΔBOLD) was significantly greater/more positive in ME/CFS than in GWI (which showed negative change) across midline PAG, VTA, DR, MR, bilateral PBC, PO, PTN, and right locus coeruleus, while controls showed no net change.

A GWI 'START' subgroup with normal heart rate response before exercise but new-onset postural tachycardia after exercise (transient, lasting 1-3 days) showed a unique decrease in BOLD activation in right locus coeruleus and bilateral parabrachial complex following exercise.
Post-traumatic stress disorder was present in 45% of the GWI sample discussed in this research program.

Dolorimeter-based pressure pain testing showed GWI women had exquisite tenderness and ME/CFS women had intermediate pain sensitivity compared to controls, consistent with sexual dimorphism of midbrain nociceptive/anti-nociceptive circuits.

Cerebral blood flow is reduced in ME/CFS during head-up tilt and during exercise, which may reduce oxygen supply to the metabolically demanding inferior colliculus and contribute to dorsal midbrain dysfunction.
MRI studies have shown brainstem atrophy in GWI and brainstem dysfunction in ME/CFS.
ME/CFS has been reported to have deficient pyruvate metabolism, which the authors hypothesize may impair conversion of ethanol to acetate and contribute to alcohol intolerance/aversion in ME/CFS.
GWI veteran subsets defined by postural tachycardia and exercise-induced changes showed different patterns of cerebellar vermis and hemisphere activation after exercise.

POTS was operationally defined in this research program as a heart rate increase of ≥30 beats per minute upon standing that does not change with exercise, distinguishing it from the transient 'START' postural tachycardia phenotype seen in GWI.

EPA supplementation has shown some benefit for anxiety and PTSD but only small, non-clinically-significant effects compared to placebo for depression, providing rationale cited for testing EPA in ME/CFS.

Migraine is common in both ME/CFS and GWI, whereas cluster headache is uncommon in these conditions, a pattern the authors interpret via distinct sickness-behavior/interoceptive versus exteroceptive-pain mechanisms.

The authors propose that CGRP antagonists, used therapeutically for migraine, may also have therapeutic benefit for malaise, hyperalgesia, and related complaints that are diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS and GWI, based on CGRP-expressing parabrachial complex neurons implicated in threat/malaise signaling.

Factor analysis of the DePaul Symptom Questionnaire's 54-item inventory in an international ME/CFS sample identified seven symptom domains, including post-exertional malaise, cognitive dysfunction, and sleep dysfunction.
Contrary to many existing ME/CFS case criteria that list pain as a core domain, the empirical factor analysis did not identify pain as an independent symptom factor.

Comparison of the empirically-derived factor solution against the Canadian Consensus Criteria (CCC), ME-ICC, and IOM criteria found that the CCC was best supported, though the authors still recommend revisions to it.
A CDC multicentre assessment study found that about 75% of ME/CFS patients (mean illness duration 14.3 years) were not working due to their illness.
A systematic review estimated that fewer than one-third of ME/CFS patients resume employment within three years of diagnosis.
Men, older patients, and those ill for longer periods were more likely to have stopped working because of ME/CFS.
An influential systematic review (Cairns and Hotopf) reported that only about 5% of adult ME/CFS patients recover spontaneously.

In the PACE trial (n=641), employment loss remained unchanged after CBT (84%) and increased after GET (83% to 86%), while unemployment, disability, and private disability benefit uptake increased after both CBT and GET.

In Prins et al. (n=278), there was no statistically significant difference in hours worked between CBT and no-treatment groups at 8 and 14 months, and actometer data published 9 years later showed CBT did not produce objective improvement.
O'Dowd et al. found no statistically significant differences in work status between CBT/GET treatment and control groups over 6-14 months follow-up.
In Huibers et al., more patients returned to work without treatment at 4 and 12 months than patients treated with CBT by their general practitioner.
An evaluation of CBT in the Netherlands found patients worked 5 hours per week less after treatment, and the percentage working decreased from 41% to 31%.
Van Berkel et al. found that 12 months of GET had no effect on work status at 3 and 12 months, with very high true dropout rates (up to 80% by 12 months when all dropouts were included).
Evaluation of the official Belgian CFS clinics (n=655) found the percentage working decreased from 18.3% to 14.9% after CBT/GET, while incapacity benefit receipt increased from 54% to 57%.
Evaluation of official English CFS clinics (n=952) found the percentage of patients able to work decreased from 30% to 18% after CBT/GET.

Reanalysis of the Stevelink et al. London CFS clinic data (n=508, 62% follow-up) showed that the reported 9% return-to-work rate overstated benefit, since 6% who were working at baseline became unable to work, leaving a true net return-to-work rate of only 3%.

In the Stevelink et al. cohort, cognitive-behavioural targets (fear-avoidance, catastrophizing, symptom focusing, all-or-nothing behaviour), fatigue severity, and anxiety caseness did not change after an average of 16.5 CBT/GET treatment sessions, and physical functioning changed only marginally.

An Oxford Brookes University patient survey (n=2274) conducted for the NICE guideline revision found that symptoms worsened after treatment in 58.3% of CBT and 81.1% of GET patients, and the proportion who became bedridden and dependent on others increased substantially after both treatments.

A reanalysis of Adamson et al. data from the same London clinic as Stevelink et al. found that patients who dropped out had substantially lower physical functioning scores than those who completed treatment.

A study by Shor found that a subgroup of ME/CFS patients in a Lyme-endemic environment had symptom perpetuation driven by persistent, seronegative Borrelia burgdorferi infection, and that treatment with appropriately directed antimicrobials improved outcomes.
A large international web-based survey found that 75% of long COVID respondents reported post-exertional symptom exacerbation, the hallmark feature of ME/CFS.
A reanalysis of the PACE trial found that 13.3% of participants already met the trial's own recovery criteria at baseline, before receiving any treatment.

In the Stevelink et al. London clinic cohort, 23% (53/229) of patients classified as 'not working' at baseline were already well enough to work before receiving any treatment, inflating apparent treatment benefit.

The authors propose that post-exertional malaise/exertion intolerance in ME/CFS reflects an underlying sickness-response mechanism involving disrupted aerobic cellular energy production, supported by multiple studies showing objective exercise-related physical abnormalities not seen in sedentary healthy controls.

The updated NICE ME/CFS guideline concluded that CBT and GET are not effective and do not lead to recovery, that GET is harmful and should not be used, and that CBT should only be offered as a supplementary treatment for comorbid anxiety or depression.
Among 236 ME/CFS patients with a history of mold exposure, 92.4% tested positive for at least one Aspergillus-derived mycotoxin (OTA, AF, or GT) in urinalysis.
Ochratoxin A was the most prevalent mycotoxin detected in urinalysis, present in 80.9% of the ME/CFS sample.
Aflatoxin was the least prevalent mycotoxin detected, present in 29.6% of the ME/CFS sample.
Gliotoxin was detected in 39.8% of the ME/CFS sample, the second most prevalent mycotoxin after OTA.

The text reports conflicting figures for co-positivity: one statement gives 54.2% of patients positive for all three mycotoxins, while a later statement in the same paper gives 19.92% positive for all three and 54.24% positive for only one mycotoxin.

Mycotoxin prevalence patterns (OTA > GT > AF) were graphically comparable between female (91.8% overall; OTA 81.3%, AF 30.8%, GT 37.9%) and male (94.4% overall; OTA 79.6%, AF 25.9%, GT 46.3%) ME/CFS patients despite the large sample-size disparity.

Patients diagnosed at a younger age (<65 years, n=187) showed higher overall mycotoxin prevalence (93%) and higher individual toxin prevalence (OTA 66.5%, AF 18.2%, GT 26.2%) than those diagnosed at >65 years (n=49; overall 89.8%, OTA 14.4%, AF 11.4%, GT 13.6%), attributed to longer reported duration of mycotoxin exposure prior to ME/CFS onset in the younger group.
Urinary OTA concentrations in ME/CFS patients averaged 12.371 ± 12.183 ppb and were significantly right-skewed and non-normally distributed (Kolmogorov-Smirnov p<0.001).
Urinary AF concentrations averaged 0.787 ± 1.717 ppb and showed a right-skewed, non-normal distribution similar to OTA and GT (p<0.001).
Urinary GT concentrations averaged 126.063 ± 584.604 ppb and showed a right-skewed, non-normal distribution (p<0.001).

Age at diagnosis in the mold-exposed ME/CFS cohort had a mean of 53 years with a bimodal distribution peaking around 40 years and again at 55-65 years, and this age distribution passed a Kolmogorov-Smirnov normality test (p=0.007).

Prevalence of OTA and AF in this ME/CFS cohort was reported as similar to a prior study by Brewer et al. (2013) comparing 107 ME/CFS patients to healthy controls in Kansas City, though the current study could not assess statistical significance due to lack of a control group.
The paper cites prior clinical management in which administering glutathione to ME/CFS patients was reported to significantly reduce post-exertional malaise (PEM) symptoms.
A study within this Research Topic (Sørland et al.) found endothelial dysfunction at baseline in ME/CFS patients, which persisted after cyclophosphamide treatment regardless of clinical response.
The Sørland et al. study reported a significant correlation between high SDMA levels and low flow-mediated dilation values in ME/CFS patients.
Autoantibodies directed against vasoregulatory receptors are increasingly implicated as contributors to vascular dysregulation in ME/CFS.
Herpesviruses and other viral pathogens have long been recognized as potential triggers implicated in ME/CFS pathology, with follow-up studies showing multiple viruses can elicit the disease.
Studies published within and referenced by this Research Topic provide evidence that some long-COVID patients develop ME/CFS, including reported cases of ME/CFS six months after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Chronic fatigue syndrome, dyspareunia, and bowel disorders were confirmed as among the main symptoms reported by patients with endometriosis.
Urinary disorders and chronic pelvic pain, though typically considered hallmark symptoms of endometriosis, were found to occur at a low frequency in this cohort.
Symptom incidence increased progressively from the 25-29 year age group up to 40-44 years, followed by a significant decrease in the 55-59 year age group.
Across all symptoms analyzed, higher symptom incidence was found among patients who were employers, graduates, or freelancers compared with other occupational groups.
A higher number of gestations was associated with a protective effect against chronic fatigue syndrome among endometriosis patients.

Anatomic double-bundle ACL reconstruction using autologous hamstring tendon hybrid grafts (reinforced with polyester tape) in an 18-year-old male with hypermobile EDS resulted in markedly improved anterior knee laxity at 36 months postoperatively.

Second-look arthroscopy at 30 months postoperatively showed the ACL graft in this hEDS patient had no laceration and excellent synovial coverage, indicating graft integrity and incorporation despite the connective tissue disorder.

The author, a tall thin male, experienced two spontaneous pneumothoraces (40% and 80% lung collapse) at ages 15 and 16, initially attributed to body habitus before later genetic diagnosis of classical EDS.
Spontaneous pneumothorax has been reported in vascular EDS (vEDS) patients at a prevalence of up to 18% in some studies, with 81% of pneumothoraces preceding vEDS diagnosis.

The author's untreated GERD was severe, with a 24-hour ambulatory DeMeester score of 110 (>100 indicates severe GERD) and Barrett's esophagitis limited to the gastroesophageal junction found on endoscopy.
PPI regimen for 8 weeks produced initial symptom improvement in the author's GERD but symptoms recurred, indicating refractory disease requiring further investigation.

Laparoscopic magnetic sphincter augmentation reduced the author's DeMeester score from 110 preoperatively to 15 postoperatively, with regression of Barrett's epithelium noted on follow-up endoscopy at age 21.

GERD has been characterized as a common manifestation of hypermobile EDS (hEDS), occurring in up to 50% of patients in some studies and often refractory to high-dose PPIs combined with H2-blockers and acid neutralizers.

The author experienced lifelong physical-activity-related fatigue, poor conditioning, and lightheadedness during exertion, which was only later recognized as a symptom of EDS rather than personal deconditioning.

Chronic fatigue in cEDS and hEDS is hypothesized to arise from poor postural control, nocturnal skeletal pain, and cardiovascular dysautonomia contributing to exercise intolerance/muscle weakness, unrefreshing sleep, and post-exertional malaise, phenotypes that may be indistinguishable from chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS).
EDS cardiovascular disease, most common in vEDS and hEDS, presents as abdominal aortic aneurysm in up to 32% and mitral valve prolapse in up to 6% of EDS patients.
Up to one-quarter of EDS patients show aneurysmal disease, most commonly of the descending thoracic or abdominal aorta, though aortic root dilation can also occur.

Qualitative interviews with EDS patients revealed common psychosocial themes including delayed diagnosis and treatment, physical restrictions, and restructuring of leisure/social relationships, with most patients reporting delay in diagnosis and being labeled a 'hypochondriac.'

The author carries a genetic mutation indicative of classical EDS but does not meet full clinical diagnostic criteria, illustrating that genetic abnormality may not correspond to overt clinical symptoms.
Adults with ASD had significantly higher adjusted odds of generalised joint hypermobility (GJH) as measured by the Beighton Scoring System compared to non-ASD controls.

Adults with ASD had a stronger, higher adjusted odds ratio for symptomatic GJH (GJH plus musculoskeletal/skin symptoms suggestive of HSD/hEDS) compared to non-ASD controls, than for non-specified GJH.
Symptomatic GJH as defined by the self-reported 5-part questionnaire (5PQ) also demonstrated a stronger association with ASD than non-specified 5PQ-defined GJH.
Prevalence of GJH (BSS cut-off ≥4/9) was significantly higher in women with ASD than non-ASD female controls, and similarly higher in men with ASD than non-ASD male controls.
Prevalence of symptomatic GJH was substantially higher in both women and men with ASD compared to non-ASD controls.

All four self-reported items suggestive of symptomatic GJH (back/joint pain, skin hyperelasticity, velvety skin, recurrent dislocation) were significantly more common among ASD participants than controls, with two-thirds reporting frequent pain, three-fold more frequent dislocation, and more than twice the rate of skin abnormalities.
In subgroup analysis of ASD patients without comorbid ADHD (n=61), a significant association between ASD and GJH emerged only for symptomatic GJH, not for non-specified GJH.
69% of participants with ASD in this cohort were also diagnosed with ADHD, a comorbidity rate the authors attribute to recruitment from psychiatric clinics.

Including comorbid anxiety disorder as a covariate in sensitivity analysis did not significantly affect GJH in any regression model, and the ASD-GJH association remained significant, supporting an association independent of anxiety.
Country of origin (proxy for ethnicity) had no significant influence on GJH in the regression models, confirmed in a sensitivity analysis with more detailed origin data.
The ASD-GJH association remained significant in a sensitivity analysis excluding age as a covariate, indicating the finding was robust to age adjustment.
Among non-ASD control participants, the prevalence of GJH by BSS was 11% for females and 4.7% for males, lower than prevalence rates reported in a comparable North American university student sample.
The association between ASD and GJH was slightly weaker than the previously reported association between adult ADHD (without comorbid ASD) and GJH using the same control group and methodology.

Classical EDS is caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in COL5A1 or COL5A2, leading to a decreased amount of functional type V collagen in the extracellular matrix and abnormal collagen fibril morphology.
Vascular EDS is caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in COL3A1 encoding the pro-α1-chain of type III collagen, which regulates collagen fibril assembly and diameter.
Vascular EDS patients have a median survival of 51 years, with 17% experiencing a first vascular complication by age 20 and about 70% by age 40, most deaths resulting from arterial rupture.
Arthrochalasia EDS results from heterozygous deletion of exon 6 of COL1A1 or COL1A2, which removes the N-propeptide cleavage site and causes retention of the N-propeptide in collagen fibrils.

Dermatosparaxis EDS is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in ADAMTS2, the type I procollagen N-proteinase, leading to incomplete N-propeptide cleavage of both pro-α chains and a hieroglyphic collagen fibril appearance.
Cardiac-valvular EDS results from biallelic COL1A2 loss-of-function variants causing unstable mRNA and complete absence of pro-α2(I)-chains, forcing formation of α1(I) homotrimers.

A specific arginine-to-cysteine substitution in the COL1A1 triple helical region produces α1(I) dimers and dermal collagen fibrils with variable diameters and irregular interfibrillar spaces, causing a phenotype overlapping cEDS and vEDS.

Kyphoscoliotic EDS-PLOD1 is caused by biallelic PLOD1 variants causing lysyl hydroxylase 1 deficiency and reduced hydroxylysine content in dermal collagen, resulting in abnormal crosslink formation and mechanically unstable tissue.

Biallelic FKBP14 variants cause a kyphoscoliotic-EDS-overlapping phenotype through loss of the collagen chaperone FKBP22, causing ER enlargement and altered in vitro ECM assembly in patient dermal fibroblasts.
Classical-like EDS type 1 is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in TNXB leading to tenascin-X deficiency and a phenotype similar to type V collagen defects.

In a subset of individuals with generalized joint hypermobility, heterozygous TNXB variants causing TNXB haploinsufficiency were identified, linking partial TNX deficiency to joint hypermobility outside classic clEDS1.

Myopathic EDS results from biallelic or heterozygous COL12A1 defects affecting type XII collagen, which forms flexible bridges between collagen fibrils and other ECM molecules; patient fibroblasts show increased interfibrillar space.

Classical-like EDS type 2 is caused by biallelic AEBP1 variants; AEBP1 binds type I, III and V collagen and aids collagen polymerization, and patient fibroblasts show dermal collagen fibrils with variable diameters and irregular contours.

Spondylodysplastic EDS is caused by biallelic defects in B4GALT7 or B3GALT6, encoding enzymes that form the tetrasaccharide proteoglycan linker region, resulting in variable reduction of heparan, chondroitin and dermatan sulfate content on proteoglycans.

Musculocontractural EDS is caused by biallelic CHST14 or DSE variants causing D4ST1 or DS-epi1 deficiency, leading to complete replacement of dermatan sulfate by chondroitin sulfate or severely reduced dermatan sulfate, impairing decorin function in collagen fibrillogenesis.

spEDS-SLC39A13 is caused by biallelic variants in SLC39A13 encoding the zinc transporter ZIP13; deficiency causes uniform underhydroxylation of collagen lysine/proline residues and abnormal crosslinking, possibly via zinc-iron cofactor competition.

Brittle cornea syndrome is caused by biallelic variants in ZNF469 or PRDM5; dermal fibroblasts from affected patients show altered ECM-related gene expression and altered deposition of collagen and fibronectin.

Periodontal EDS is associated with heterozygous gain-of-function variants in C1R and C1S, causing intracellular and extracellular activation of C1r/C1s and consequent classical complement cascade activation.
An 8.9 kb duplication of exons 10-16 is the most common pathogenic variant in PLOD1, found in approximately 30% of kEDS-PLOD1 cases, and is detectable by specific PCR or MLPA.
Urinary LP/HP crosslink ratio is a reliable diagnostic test for LH1 deficiency: normal individuals have a ratio of 0.2, whereas kEDS-PLOD1 patients show ratios of 2 to 9.
Absence of urinary dermatan sulfate disaccharides on anion-exchange chromatography is specific for musculocontractural EDS caused by D4ST1 or DS-epi1 deficiency.
Qualitative or quantitative alterations in type III (pro)collagen detected by SDS-PAGE can identify about 95% of vEDS patients.
Western blot analysis of serum bikunin showed significantly decreased bikunin-CS and increased GAG-free bikunin in patients with spEDS caused by B4GALT7 or B3GALT6 defects.

Generalized joint hypermobility in the general population is reported with a prevalence of 6% to 57% in females and 2% to 35% in males, reflecting the influence of age, ethnicity, sex and environmental factors.
Spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in approximately 10% of individuals with vascular EDS.

Transcriptome-wide analysis of classical EDS dermal fibroblasts revealed dysregulation of genes involved in ECM remodeling and wound healing, along with altered endoplasmic reticulum homeostasis and autophagy.

Transcriptome profiling of dermal fibroblasts from vEDS patients revealed differential expression of genes encoding ECM molecules and genes involved in ER homeostasis, along with thinner dermis and dilated ER on ultrastructural analysis.
Heterozygous Col3a1+/G182R knock-in mice showed markedly increased spontaneous mortality compared with wild-type littermates by 24 weeks of age.
Homozygous Col3a1G182R/G182R mice showed a significant genotype deficit at weaning, indicating partial embryonic/perinatal lethality.
Surviving homozygous Col3a1G182R/G182R mice had markedly higher mortality than heterozygous mice by 24 weeks.
Male Col3a1+/G182R mice out of breeding had substantially higher spontaneous mortality than female mice, mirroring a possible sex effect seen in humans.
Breeding female Col3a1+/G182R mice showed increasing mortality across successive lactation periods, largely due to aortic rupture.
Surviving Col3a1+/G182R mice had lower systolic blood pressure than wild-type littermates at 24 weeks of age.
Col3a1+/G182R mice were significantly lighter than wild-type littermates, reflecting the low body weight commonly observed in vEDS patients.
Nearly all mortality in Col3a1+/G182R mice was due to thoracic aortic rupture, as confirmed by autopsy.
Aortic echography showed no aortic dilation preceding rupture in Col3a1+/G182R mice, contrasting with Marfan syndrome models where aneurysm precedes rupture.
Thoracic aortas of Col3a1+/G182R mice had a significantly smaller total area, mainly due to a thinner adventitia, with preserved intima-media thickness.
Collagen fiber density in the aortic wall (especially the intima-media) was reduced in Col3a1+/G182R mice compared to wild-type.
Electron microscopy revealed abnormal heterogeneity of collagen fiber diameters and lower fiber density in the aortic wall of Col3a1+/G182R mice.

Adventitial fibroblasts in Col3a1+/G182R mice showed abnormal morphology with dilated endoplasmic reticulum, consistent with retention of misfolded collagen, while smooth muscle and endothelial cells appeared normal.
HSP47, a collagen-specific ER chaperone, was upregulated in thoracic aortas of Col3a1+/G182R mice, supporting activation of unfolded protein response machinery.
ATF6, an ER transmembrane transcription factor sensitive to misfolded proteins, was upregulated in Col3a1+/G182R thoracic aorta, indicating UPR activation.
Autophagy genes ATG5 and ATG7 were upregulated in Col3a1+/G182R thoracic aorta, suggesting activation of autophagic degradation of misfolded collagen.

Digital droplet PCR showed no difference in total Col3a1 mRNA levels between genotypes, and WT and mutant alleles were expressed equally in heterozygous mice, indicating the phenotype is not due to reduced transcription.
Western blot showed a trend for increased procollagen III protein amount in arteries of Col3a1+/G182R mice compared to wild-type, contrary to expectation.

Immunofluorescence showed a drastic reduction in mature (native conformation) collagen III and a lower collagen III/collagen I ratio in Col3a1+/G182R aortic adventitia, likely reflecting antibody non-recognition of misfolded mature collagen III.

RNA-seq of thoracic aortas identified 210 differentially expressed genes in Col3a1+/G182R mice, with gene set enrichment analysis showing upregulation of inflammatory (TNFα/NFκB, inflammatory response) and cell stress (hypoxia, UV response) pathways.
In contrast to another vEDS knock-in model, PLC/IP3/PKC/ERK (MAPK) pathway activation was not observed at either transcript or protein level in Col3a1+/G182R mice.
TGFβR1 protein showed only a non-significant trend toward higher expression in Col3a1+/G182R mice, with no significant differences in p-ERK or p-PKC by western blot.
Bio-Plex assay showed no significant difference in TGFβ1, TGFβ2 or TGFβ3 protein ligand levels between genotypes, consistent with transcriptomic data.
Propranolol significantly lowered heart rate but not systolic blood pressure and provided no survival benefit in Col3a1+/G182R mice.
Celiprolol at a therapeutic-equivalent plasma concentration did not change SBP, HR, or mortality in Col3a1+/G182R mice, despite its established human benefit in vEDS.
Amlodipine lowered SBP but showed no survival benefit and a trend toward worsened mortality at 15 weeks in Col3a1+/G182R mice.
Thoracic aortas from Col3a1+/G182R mice showed increased expression of the collagen-specific chaperone HSP47 compared to wild-type mice.
ATF6, an ER transmembrane transcription factor activated by misfolded proteins, was also upregulated in Col3a1+/G182R aortas.
Increased expression of autophagy genes ATG5 and ATG7 in Col3a1+/G182R aortas supports activation of autophagic degradation of misfolded collagen.
Digital droplet PCR showed no difference in total Col3a1 mRNA between genotypes, and WT and mutant allele transcript levels were equivalent within Col3a1+/G182R mice.
Western blot showed a trend for increased procollagen type III protein in arteries of Col3a1+/G182R mice compared to wild-type littermates.

Immunofluorescence showed drastically reduced mature collagen III detection and a lower collagen III/collagen I ratio in Col3a1+/G182R aortic adventitia, likely reflecting misfolded collagen III rather than a quantitative deficit.
RNA sequencing of Col3a1+/G182R thoracic aortas identified 210 differentially expressed genes (140 downregulated, 70 upregulated) compared to wild-type.

GSEA Hallmark analysis found gene sets related to TNFα signaling via NFκB, inflammatory response, and cell stress (hypoxia, UV response down) were differentially enriched in Col3a1+/G182R aortas, mostly upregulated inflammation/stress pathways with one gene set downregulated.

Among 223 MAPK pathway genes analyzed, Dusp10, Hspa1a, Hspa1b, and Rps6Ka5 were upregulated and Map2k3 was downregulated in Col3a1+/G182R mice, but the overall MAPK pathway enrichment was not statistically significant.

Comparing with genes reported in the Col3a1G938D/+ vEDS model, Hspa1a and Hspa1b were similarly upregulated in Col3a1+/G182R mice, but Ldlr and Wwp2 were downregulated here whereas they had been reported as upregulated in the other model, indicating partial discordance in PLC/IP3/PKC/ERK pathway gene expression between vEDS mouse models.

Western blot showed no significant difference in p-ERK or p-PKC protein levels between genotypes, while TGFβR1 was only slightly higher (non-significant trend) in Col3a1+/G182R mice, arguing against major PLC/IP3/PKC/ERK pathway activation in this model.
Bio-Plex quantification of TGF-β1, TGF-β2, and TGF-β3 ligand levels in thoracic aorta showed no significant differences between Col3a1+/G182R and wild-type mice.
Propranolol lowered heart rate but did not reduce systolic blood pressure (even increased it at 24 weeks) and provided no benefit on 24-week mortality in Col3a1+/G182R mice.

At a dose achieving therapeutic plasma levels, celiprolol did not change SBP or HR and provided no benefit on 24-week mortality in Col3a1+/G182R mice, in contrast to its established benefit in human vEDS patients.
Amlodipine lowered SBP but did not improve, and trended toward worsening, mortality in Col3a1+/G182R mice, possibly via reflex sympathetic activation.

Adding propranolol to amlodipine significantly reduced SBP and HR compared to amlodipine alone and reversed the early (15-week) mortality increase seen with amlodipine alone, but did not significantly improve overall 24-week mortality versus amlodipine monotherapy.

Hydralazine increased heart rate without lowering SBP, and produced only a non-significant decrease in 24-week mortality in Col3a1+/G182R mice, failing to reach the benefit reported in a different vEDS knock-in model.
Combining celiprolol with hydralazine produced no additional effect on SBP/HR and no mortality benefit compared to hydralazine alone or untreated mice.

Losartan started during breeding markedly lowered SBP and reduced 24-week mortality in Col3a1+/G182R mice, but the benefit reversed and mortality rose back to control levels after stopping the drug at 24 weeks.

Losartan initiated at weaning (4 weeks of age) also significantly lowered SBP without affecting HR and markedly reduced 24-week mortality compared to untreated mice, confirming the benefit occurs independent of prenatal/neonatal treatment timing.

Of six renin-angiotensin system genes identified in the transcriptomic dataset, none was significantly upregulated in Col3a1+/G182R aortas, suggesting losartan's benefit is not explained by baseline RAS gene overexpression.

Subcutaneous Angiotensin II infusion at a dose with minimal effect on SBP caused rapid and near-universal mortality from aortic rupture in Col3a1+/G182R mice compared to a much lower rate in wild-type mice, implicating AT1 receptor signaling in vascular fragility.

A 50-year-old male with childhood-diagnosed Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome and long-standing fatigue, daytime somnolence, and snoring was found on polysomnography to have severe obstructive sleep apnea with an AHI of 107 and oxygen saturation below 90% for 16% of sleep time.

A meta-analysis found that OSA prevalence among EDS/Marfan syndrome patients was 39.4%, and these patients were on average 6 times more likely to have a diagnosis of OSA compared to the general population.
A parallel cohort study of 100 EDS patients matched to healthy controls found that 23% of EDS patients suffered from symptomatic OSA syndrome compared to 3% of healthy controls.

Sleep-disordered breathing was found to be common not only in EDS patients referred to a sleep clinic but also in EDS patients presenting for routine internal medicine care, many of whom had unrecognized fatigue, poor sleep, and daytime sleepiness never evaluated for SDB.
Nasal CPAP treatment led to improvement of complaints (fatigue, poor sleep, daytime sleepiness) in EDS patients with sleep-disordered breathing according to the cited study.

Craniofacial and cartilaginous abnormalities in EDS (nasal/maxillary cartilage defects, mandibular retrognathia, high arched palate, increased pharyngeal collapsibility, scoliosis/kyphosis, vocal cord abnormalities) are proposed as mechanisms increasing the risk of sleep-disordered breathing, suggesting EDS may serve as a genetic model for OSA.

Fatigue, daytime sleepiness, joint pain, dislocation, recurrent injuries, dizziness, chronic pain, anxiety, dysautonomia, and phobic states are common symptoms of EDS that are considered by some to overlap with chronic fatigue syndrome and are also frequent in sleep-disordered breathing.

Catheter ablation for postinfarct ventricular tachycardia was successfully and safely performed in a patient with mild-phenotype Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, with no access site or procedural complications.

The authors advise avoiding invasive procedures, particularly arterial/transarterial access, in patients with more severe (vascular, type 4) EDS phenotypes, whereas milder phenotypes may tolerate intervention with careful planning.
Vascular (type 4) EDS is a rare subtype (approximately 1 in 90,000) associated with poor prognosis, with 50% mortality by age 48, largely due to vascular dissection and hollow organ rupture.
Cardiovascular manifestations of EDS include mitral valve prolapse and aortic root dilatation, particularly relevant in classic (type 1) and vascular (type 4) subtypes.
A cited case-control study of 33 EDS patients found no significant echocardiographic difference between EDS patients and controls.

A previously reported EDS patient with recurrent VT and syncope experienced multiple procedural complications, including femoral hematoma during coronary angiography and delayed lead perforation with pericardial effusion after transvenous ICD implantation, requiring sternotomy for device explant.

A prior case report described successful, uncomplicated slow pathway ablation in a patient with vascular (type 4) EDS using a single-catheter magnetic navigation (stereotaxis) approach with a softer catheter tip to minimize venous access and intracardiac instrumentation.

Autonomic dysfunction, including postural dysregulation and vasovagal syncope, is commonly encountered in EDS patients and should be excluded as a cause of syncope before considering cardiac device implantation.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS type IV) is caused by heterozygous mutations in the COL3A1 gene, which affect type III collagen production.

A 34-year-old primigravida with previously undiagnosed vascular EDS experienced a spontaneous 9 cm 'open book' uterine rupture at 36 weeks gestation during labor, requiring emergency cesarean section with major hemoperitoneum.

The patient exhibited characteristic vascular EDS phenotypic features including thin translucent skin with visible veins, distinctive facial morphology, spontaneous hematomas, dystrophic scarring from poor wound healing, and small-joint hyperlaxity with frequent non-traumatic dislocations.

Family history revealed sudden unexplained death of the patient's mother at age 39 and death of her sister from abdominal aortic rupture at age 35, consistent with autosomal dominant transmission of vascular EDS.

In a series of 220 patients with vascular EDS (81 obstetrical patients, 167 deliveries), maternal mortality rate was 11.5%, with uterine rupture during labor, vascular rupture during labor, and vascular rupture within two weeks postpartum as causes.
In a review of 50 pregnancies among 26 vascular EDS patients (Lurie et al.), maternal mortality was 38.5%, with 23% of patients experiencing postpartum hemorrhage.

In a series of 13 vascular EDS patients (27 pregnancies, Dubruc et al.), most deliveries (78.3%) occurred vaginally, and 33% of vaginal deliveries were complicated by perineal tears; 8.7% of patients experienced a major complication (mitral valve rupture or cecal rupture), with no deaths.

Fetal complications of pregnancies affected by vascular EDS include a 50% risk of disease transmission to offspring, plus risks of prematurity from premature membrane rupture or cervical incompetence, and intrauterine growth retardation.

Long-term treatment with celiprolol at maximum tolerated doses (ideally 400 mg/day) is recommended for prevention of arterial accidents in vascular EDS during pregnancy, with monitoring of fetal growth and utero-placental blood flow.

There is no consensus on optimal delivery route for vascular EDS patients: vaginal delivery risks uterine rupture, vaginal wall tearing, and difficult-to-suture perineal lesions, while cesarean section carries increased risk of vascular or digestive complications, postpartum hemorrhage, and difficult suturing of fragile, large uterine scar tissue.
Wound healing is markedly slower in patients with vascular EDS than in the general population, requiring wide, tension-free sutures left in place two to three times longer than usual.

Whole exome sequencing and Sanger sequencing identified a homozygous synonymous PLOD1 variant c.1095C>T (p.Gly365=) in the proband, with both parents as heterozygous carriers, consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

In silico splicing prediction tools (NetGene2 and ASSP) both predicted that the c.1095C>T variant disrupts normal splicing, causing premature termination of exon 10, with NetGene2 reporting a confidence score of 0.95.

RT-PCR on patient lymphocyte-derived cDNA confirmed that the c.1095C>T variant causes aberrant splicing with premature termination of exon 10, altering expression of the four bases GCGC, consistent with computational predictions and Sanger sequencing.

Quantitative real-time PCR showed the proband's PLOD1 mRNA level was significantly lower than the normal control, while both heterozygous parents had mRNA levels approximately half of normal control but remained phenotypically unaffected.

Minigene splicing assay in HEK293T cells showed that the mutant-type (MT) construct produced a smaller spliced cDNA product than the wild-type (WT) construct, confirming that c.1095C>T causes a premature termination codon in exon 10.

Applying ACMG criteria (PM2, PS3, PP3, PP4), the authors reclassified c.1095C>T from variant of uncertain significance to 'likely pathogenic' based on absence in population databases, functional evidence of a damaging splicing effect, splice prediction, and a phenotype highly specific for kEDS.

The neonatal proband presented with congenital muscle weakness, excessive joint hyperlaxity (hip abduction, bipedal valgus/flexion), skin hyperextensibility, and easy bruising but no kyphoscoliosis at birth or on follow-up, meeting kEDS-PLOD1 diagnostic criteria despite absence of the classic kyphoscoliosis feature.
The proband showed markedly elevated serum creatine kinase, CK-MB, and CK-MBmass levels indicating myocardial damage.

The proband had intraventricular and subarachnoid hemorrhage without evidence of birth trauma or coagulation abnormality, which the authors attribute to vascular fragility characteristic of kEDS-PLOD1 rather than birth injury.
Prior literature cited indicates that lysyl hydroxylase 1 (LH1) activity in skin fibroblasts of kEDS patients is approximately 25% lower than in normal individuals, impairing collagen cross-linking.

Cited animal-model data indicate that PLOD1-knockout mice show high early mortality (15% died within 1-4 months) due to collagen fiber degeneration and abnormal vascular smooth muscle leading to aortic dissection.

Comparing to a previously reported 9-year-old male with the identical c.1095C>T variant who was born with kyphoscoliosis and never achieved independent ambulation, the current proband was born without kyphoscoliosis, suggesting phenotypic variability and that kyphoscoliosis may develop later in life in some patients with this variant.
Electrophysiological examination revealed multiple peripheral nerve lesions in the proband, which improved but did not fully resolve after 13 days.
Among subjects meeting the ≥8 mm threshold for first ray hypermobility, 86% had a planus foot type, while 42% of non-hypermobile subjects were also planus, indicating an association but with overlap.
Partial-weightbearing first ray mobility was significantly greater in planus feet than rectus feet, with a large effect size.
Full weightbearing first ray mobility did not differ significantly between planus and rectus foot types.
First metatarsophalangeal joint flexibility parameters did not differ significantly between planus and rectus foot types.
Arch height flexibility was significantly greater in planus feet compared to rectus feet, consistent with prior literature showing pes planus has a more flexible arch.
The first ray hypermobility group (≥8 mm) showed markedly higher partial-weightbearing first ray mobility than the non-hypermobile group, with a very large effect size.
No significant linear relationship was found between partial-weightbearing first ray mobility and arch height index while standing.
No significant linear relationship was found between first ray mobility and first MTP joint laxity, though the p-value approached significance.
No significant linear relationship was found between first ray mobility and arch height flexibility.
Stepwise linear regression found that weightbearing first ray mobility and first MTP joint laxity together predicted 38% of the variance in partial-weightbearing first ray mobility.

One study participant was excluded after presenting signs of generalized joint hypermobility (hyperextension of the little finger, thumb apposition to forearm, elbow hyperextension, and forward trunk flexion with palms to floor), consistent with Beighton-type criteria, distinguishing localized first ray hypermobility from a generalized hypermobility phenotype.
Benign joint hypermobility syndrome (BJHS) was present in 56% of female patients with carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS).
BJHS-positive CTS patients had significantly higher symptom severity scores than BJHS-negative CTS patients in both hands.
BJHS-positive CTS patients had significantly lower functional capacity scores than BJHS-negative CTS patients in both hands.
Tinel's, Phalen's, and reverse Phalen's provocation tests were significantly more often positive in the right hand of BJHS-positive CTS patients compared to BJHS-negative patients.
There was no significant difference in electrophysiological measures (distal motor latency and sensorial conduction velocity of the median nerve) between BJHS-positive and BJHS-negative CTS patients.
Body mass index was significantly higher in CTS patients with BJHS compared to those without BJHS.
Symptom duration did not differ significantly between BJHS-positive and BJHS-negative CTS patients.

Dentin dysplasia is described as an autosomal dominant hereditary disorder that can occur in isolation or as one manifestation of an underlying systemic disease, including Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, calcinosis, and brachioskeletogenital syndrome.
In the presented case of dentin dysplasia Type I, the patient showed no systemic signs or symptoms, allowing the clinicians to rule out an associated systemic disorder such as Ehlers–Danlos syndrome.

Dentin dysplasia is linked to mutation of a locus on chromosome 4q13-21 and recent research suggests mutation of the DSPP gene and dentin matrix acidic phosphoprotein gene occurring during incorporation of Hertwig's epithelial root sheath cells into the dental papilla.
Juvenile fibromyalgia affects approximately 2-6% of school-aged children and is most common among female adolescents.
Across cited skin biopsy studies, roughly half of clinically diagnosed fibromyalgia patients showed abnormal (reduced) small nerve fiber density.
Small fiber neuropathy prevalence among adults in the Netherlands was estimated at 52.95 cases per 100,000.
Pregabalin was found not to significantly improve morbidity in pediatric fibromyalgia patients.
A meta-analysis of eight studies found a pooled random-effects prevalence of small fiber pathology of 49% among adults with fibromyalgia.
In a case-control study of 15 pediatric patients, Boneparth et al found that 53% of juvenile fibromyalgia patients had reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density.

Evdokimov et al found some degree of denervation in 63% of 117 adult female fibromyalgia patients, and denervation of both lower leg and upper thigh was associated with a more severe fibromyalgia phenotype.

Fasolino et al studied 57 fibromyalgia patients (54 female), 30% of whom had small fiber pathology, but found no significant differences in clinical evaluation, quantitative sensory testing, or laser-evoked potentials between those with and without small fiber pathology.
Leinders et al found a correlation between miR-let-7d expression and small fiber pathology in fibromyalgia patients.
Evdokimov et al found differential expression of pain mediators and axon pathfinders in the skin cells of fibromyalgia patients, but this did not correlate with decreased IENFD.
In immune-mediated small fiber neuropathy causes such as Sjogren's syndrome and systemic lupus erythematosus, IVIg has been shown to improve morbidity in both pediatric and adult patients.
Corticosteroids have been shown to be useful in inflammatory-associated small fiber neuropathy in both adults and children.
IVIg has not been found to be useful in cases of idiopathic small fiber neuropathy in adults.
Lodahl et al found that paresthesia and peripheral autonomic dysfunction are more common in small fiber neuropathy patients compared to fibromyalgia patients.

The Besta Criteria for SFN diagnosis was reappraised and validated against the NEURODIAB Criteria in 2019, showing strict agreement between the two, with IENFD assessment identified as the most reliable diagnostic tool, followed by warm and cold QST thresholds.

Corneal denervation has been found to parallel intraepidermal denervation, suggesting corneal confocal microscopy could serve as a minimally invasive surrogate for skin biopsy in monitoring small fiber pathology.
Complete retinal thickness was significantly reduced in FM patients compared to controls in the four inner-ring ETDRS regions (temporal, superior, nasal, inferior).
RNFL thickness was significantly reduced only in the inferior inner-ring region (IN_I), with no significant difference in other regions.
GCL+ thickness (ganglion cell bodies and astrocytes) was significantly reduced in FM patients in the inner-ring regions, with the strongest discrimination in the temporal inner region.
GCL++ thickness (including horizontal, bipolar and amacrine cell bodies) was significantly reduced in FM patients across the four inner-ring ETDRS regions.
No significant differences in choroidal thickness were found between FM patients and controls in any of the nine ETDRS regions.
The four OCT-derived thickness variables with greatest discriminant capacity for FM vs. controls were highly intercorrelated, indicating redundant information across retinal layers.

An AI ensemble classifier (RUSBoosted decision trees) using two OCT-derived retinal thickness features achieved 82% accuracy, 86% sensitivity, 78% specificity, and AUC of .82 in distinguishing FM patients from controls.
Among FM patients, EQ-5D and FIQ scores were inversely correlated, indicating that greater disease impact was associated with worse quality of life.
In FM patients, age positively correlated with EQ-5D score within the depressive and biological subgroups but not overall.
No significant differences in disease duration, FIQ, or EQ-5D scores were found between the atypical, depressive, and biological FM subgroups (Giesecke classification).

Prior studies cited in this protocol reported that photobiomodulation (PBM) reduced pain, sleep disturbance, tiredness, muscle spasm, morning stiffness and tender point counts in people with fibromyalgia.
The protocol proposes that FMS patients have compromised mitochondrial respiration and decreased ATP synthesis, contributing to lack of energy and chronicity of pain and tissue tenderness.
A prior whole-body PBM trial conducted in a sports (non-FMS) population showed only short-term effects without conclusive changes.

This protocol describes a planned triple-blinded, placebo-controlled RCT delivering whole-body PBM via a NovoTHOR bed (20 min supine sessions, 3x/week for 4 weeks, 12 sessions total) versus an indistinguishable sham (placebo light/heating with blinding goggles) to FMS patients, with outcomes assessed at baseline, session 6, end of treatment, and 2 weeks, 3 and 6 months post-treatment.
Immediate reactions after COVID-19 vaccination occurred in 24 of 196 (12.2%) high-risk patients, totaling 25 events.
The incidence of immediate reactions did not differ significantly between BNT162b2 (mRNA) and Ad26.COV2-S (adenoviral vector) vaccines.
In severe immediate reactions, no significant acute tryptase elevation compared to baseline was found, and no cases met anaphylaxis criteria.
Immediate reaction incidence significantly differed by underlying diagnosis, being highest in miscellaneous-indication patients and idiopathic anaphylaxis patients and lowest in pMCD patients.
Women had a significantly higher likelihood of experiencing an immediate reaction than men.
Age and prior history of anaphylaxis were not significant predictors of immediate reaction occurrence.
No significant differences in immediate reaction incidence were observed among different pMCD subgroups (CM, MIS, pMCAS, ISM, advanced SM).
Compliance with antihistamine premedication had no statistically significant impact on immediate reaction occurrence in pMCD patients.
pMCD patients who had immediate reactions trended toward lower baseline tryptase than non-reactors, though this did not reach statistical significance.
A prior history of MCAS was more frequent among pMCD reactors than non-reactors, but this difference did not reach statistical significance, possibly due to low event numbers.
Nearly half of follow-up responders reported a late reaction (any symptom within 72 hours) after the first vaccine dose.
Late reaction occurrence did not significantly differ between BNT162b2 and Ad26.COV2-S recipients.
MCAS-like late reactions after vaccination occurred only in pMCD patients with a prior history of such symptoms, not in those without such history.
No significant differences in age, sex, baseline tryptase, or diagnostic subcategory were found between pMCD patients with versus without MCAS-like late reactions.

No cases of anaphylaxis occurred in this large cohort of primary mast cell disorder patients (including 9 children) receiving mRNA-based or adenoviral vector COVID-19 vaccines, supporting overall vaccine safety in this population.
Baseline serum tryptase in the pMCD cohort was markedly higher than that of the overall high-risk study cohort, consistent with elevated mast cell burden in mastocytosis/pMCAS.
ALA interacted with BLA and BLG to form cross-linked polymeric aggregates without generating lower-molecular-weight degradation products.

Circular dichroism showed only a slight, statistically insignificant increase in α-helix and β-sheet content of ALA-BLA/ALA-BLG compared with native proteins, indicating minimal secondary structure change.

Tertiary structure of BLA and BLG was substantially altered after ALA interaction, with UV absorbance increased 2.02-fold (BLA) and 2.23-fold (BLG) and surface hydrophobicity (ANS fluorescence) increased 3.51-fold (BLA) and 1.03-fold (BLG) relative to native proteins.
Mice sensitized with ALA-BLG showed significantly greater anaphylactic shock symptoms and reduced body temperature than BLG-sensitized mice, especially when challenged with ALA-BLG.
Similar to BLG, ALA-BLA sensitization/challenge produced increased anaphylactic symptoms and decreased body temperature compared with native BLA.
B cell activation marker B220 expression was significantly higher in mice sensitized and challenged with ALA-BLA/ALA-BLG than with native BLA/BLG.
Mice sensitized and challenged with ALA-BLA showed increased BLA-specific IgG, IgG1 and IgE levels but reduced IgG2a levels compared with cross-challenge groups.
ALA-BLG significantly increased BLG-/ALA-BLG-specific IgG and IgE levels and reduced IgG2a levels, and increased ALA-BLG-specific IgG1 compared with native BLG.
Splenocytes from mice sensitized and challenged with ALA-BLA significantly suppressed secretion of the Th1 cytokines IL-2, IFN-γ, and TNF-α compared with other groups.

IL-6 and IL-13 secretion significantly increased after antigen-specific stimulation in the ALA-BLA sensitized/challenged group compared with other groups; IL-4 and IL-5 showed no significant difference.
Th17-related IL-17A and Th9-related IL-9 production were both enhanced in mice sensitized and challenged with ALA-BLA.
IL-10 secretion was reduced in the ALA-BLA sensitized/challenged group, consistent with Treg suppression.
The percentage of FcεRI+c-kit+ peritoneal mast cells was significantly higher in mice sensitized and challenged with ALA-BLA than in BLA-sensitized groups, with similar enhancement seen with ALA-BLG.
Serum mMCP-1, a marker of allergen-induced mast cell activation, was remarkably enhanced in mice sensitized and challenged with ALA-BLA and ALA-BLG compared with native protein groups.
Plasma histamine levels were increased in mice sensitized and challenged with ALA-BLA/ALA-BLG compared with BLA/BLG groups.

The percentage of CD25+Foxp3+ Tregs within CD4+ population was significantly decreased in Peyer's patches and mesenteric lymph nodes (and non-significantly in spleen) in the ALA-BLA sensitized/challenged group compared with BLA.
Treg percentages were remarkably decreased in Peyer's patches, mesenteric lymph nodes, and spleen in the ALA-BLG sensitized/challenged group compared with BLG.
Morphological structure of the intestine and lung was damaged in mice sensitized and challenged with ALA-BLA/ALA-BLG compared with those given native BLA/BLG.

The authors concluded that ALA-BLG has a stronger potential to promote allergic sensitization and elicitation than ALA-BLA, attributed to the inherently stronger allergenicity of BLG (>75% of allergic patients have BLG-specific IgE vs ~30-35% for BLA).
LIFE dose-dependently inhibited RBL-2H3 mast cell adhesion to fibronectin-coated plates, reducing adhesion by ~70% and ~80% at 50 and 100 μg/mL respectively.
The RGD-competitive integrin inhibitor echistatin, used as positive control, reduced mast cell adhesion to fibronectin by ~12% at 0.75 nM.
LIFE decreased integrin α4 mRNA expression by ~30% and ~50% at 50 and 100 μg/mL respectively, and reduced surface integrin α4 protein by ~80% at 100 μg/mL.
LIFE at 100 μg/mL reduced surface expression of integrin β3 by ~30%, although mRNA levels were not significantly altered.
Integrin α5 mRNA and surface protein expression were not significantly changed by LIFE treatment.
LIFE at 50 μg/mL inhibited the time-dependent increase of FAK phosphorylation during mast cell adhesion to fibronectin, without altering total FAK protein.
LIFE at 100 μg/mL inhibited IgE-induced mast cell degranulation on fibronectin-coated plates by ~30%, as measured by β-hexosaminidase release.
LIFE at 100 μg/mL significantly inhibited IL-3 release from activated mast cells by ~86%.

Conditioned medium from IgE-activated mast cells decreased expression of collagen I (-45%), collagen III (-80%), fibronectin (-78%), elastin (-80%), biglycan (-59%), lumican (-33%), and fibrillin-1 (-64%) in normal human dermal fibroblasts, while FBN4 and LOX were unchanged.
Conditioned medium from activated mast cells strongly increased MMP1 expression (607% of control) and mildly increased MMP3 (37% of control) in dermal fibroblasts.
Conditioned medium from activated mast cells markedly increased CXCL8 expression (1400% of control) in dermal fibroblasts, while TNF-α was unchanged.

Unlike previous reports on early SD lesions, mast cell conditioned medium did not change α-SMA or CD26 expression in fibroblasts but increased anti-fibrotic marker CD74, and did not alter TGF-β1 or VEGF-A.
LIFE treatment restored/enhanced expression of COL1, COL3, FN1, ELN, and BGN in a dose-dependent manner in mast cell CM-treated fibroblasts, though FBN1 and LUM were not restored.
LIFE downregulated MMP-1, MMP-3, and CXCL8 expression in a dose-dependent manner at 25, 50, and 100 μg/mL in mast cell CM-treated fibroblasts.
HPLC phenolic profiling identified ellagic acid as the major compound in LIFE, present at 19.0 mg ellagic acid equivalent/g dried extract (approximately 1.90 ± 0.87% w/w).
Ellagic acid, an active component of LIFE, inhibited mast cell adhesion to fibronectin by ~70% at 200 μM.
DHC treatment reduced mast cell degranulation as measured by decreased β-hexosaminidase activity and histamine release in IgE-sensitized, antigen-stimulated RBL cells and BMMCs.
DHC reduced the morphological changes typical of MC activation, including cellular elongation and F-actin reorganization.
DHC inhibited activation of the MAPK signaling pathway in IgE-activated mast cells.
DHC inhibited activation of the NF-κB signaling pathway in IgE-activated mast cells.
DHC inhibited activation of the AP-1 transcription factor pathway in IgE-activated mast cells.
DHC attenuated IgE/antigen-induced allergic reactions in a passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) mouse model, reducing dye extravasation and ear thickening.
DHC reduced OVA challenge-induced active systemic anaphylaxis in mice, including protection against body temperature drop and reduced serum histamine and IL-4 secretion.
4-MU dose-dependently reduced β-hexosaminidase and histamine release from IgE/antigen-activated rat basophilic leukemia (RBL) mast cell-like cells.
4-MU treatment decreased IL1β, IL4, and TNFα transcript levels in IgE-activated RBL cells.
4-MU pretreatment prevented IgE-activation-induced degranulation morphology and F-actin cytoskeletal decomposition in RBL cells.
4-MU dose-dependently attenuated phosphorylation of SYK, p38, ERK, JNK, and NF-κB p65 and increased IκBα levels in FcεRI-activated RBLs, without changing total protein levels.
Combining pathway inhibitors (U0126, SP600125, SB203580, BAY 11-7082) with 4-MU did not produce synergistic inhibition of IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation beyond 4-MU alone.

4-MU (0.1–100 μM) showed no significant cytotoxicity in RBL cells or primary bone-marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs), supporting its use at 20-40 μM (RBL) or up to 100 μM (BMMC) doses in subsequent experiments.
4-MU dose-dependently reduced β-hexosaminidase and histamine release from IgE/antigen-activated primary bone-marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs).
4-MU attenuated IgE-induced increases in IL1β, IL4, and IL6 expression in BMMCs.
Topical 4-MU (50 mg/kg) reduced dye diffusion, dye extrusion, ear thickness, and edema in an IgE/antigen-induced passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) mouse model.

Systemic 4-MU (50 mg/kg i.p.), similar to the antihistamine ketotifen, attenuated the OVA-induced rectal temperature drop and suppressed the rise in serum histamine in an active systemic anaphylaxis (ASA) mouse model.
4-MU treatment reduced serum IL4 levels in OVA-challenged ASA mice.
4-MU did not affect transcription of FcεRI receptor genes (Fcer1A, Ms4a2, Fcer1G), suggesting it does not act by altering IgE-FcεRI receptor binding/expression.
LPS-challenged piglets showed higher malondialdehyde (oxidative stress marker) in jejunum and ileum compared with non-challenged controls.
Dietary 1.0% glutamate supplementation reduced jejunal MDA concentration and increased jejunal GSH levels compared with LPS-challenged pigs.

LPS challenge increased bacterial translocation to the spleen and tended to increase it in the liver compared with controls, with no effect on mesenteric lymph node translocation, and glutamate supplementation did not significantly alter translocation.

LPS-challenged pigs had lower jejunal villus height and villus height/crypt depth ratio compared with controls, while 1.0% glutamate supplementation increased jejunal villus height and ileal villus height/crypt depth ratio compared with LPS pigs.
LPS challenge reduced serum asparagine, aspartic acid, and tyrosine levels compared with controls, and dietary glutamate supplementation failed to restore these three amino acids.

Pigs fed 1.0% glutamate diet had higher serum levels of arginine, leucine, phenylalanine, methionine, valine, serine, asparagine, glutamate, glutamine, and alanine compared with non-challenged control pigs.

LPS challenge reduced claudin-1 protein expression in jejunum compared with controls, while glutamate supplementation increased claudin-1 expression in jejunum and ileum compared with LPS-challenged pigs.

LPS challenge increased intestinal mucosal mast cell numbers in the ileum compared with controls, while dietary glutamate supplementation (1.0% and 2.0%) reduced ileal mast cell numbers compared with LPS-challenged pigs.
LPS-challenged pigs had higher ileal neutrophil numbers than controls, and dietary 2.0% glutamate supplementation decreased jejunal neutrophil numbers compared with LPS-challenged pigs.
Serum cortisol concentration increased at 2 and 4 hours after LPS challenge compared with controls, and glutamate-fed pigs had lower cortisol at 4 hours than LPS pigs.
LPS challenge increased CRFR1 mRNA abundance in both jejunum and ileum compared with controls, and glutamate supplementation reduced this LPS-induced increase in both tissues.
LPS challenge increased jejunal CRF mRNA abundance compared with controls, and glutamate supplementation decreased this LPS-induced increase.
LPS challenge increased jejunal glucocorticoid receptor (GR) mRNA abundance compared with controls, and glutamate supplementation reduced this increase.
LPS challenge increased jejunal TrkA mRNA abundance compared with controls, and 2.0% glutamate supplementation decreased this increase.
LPS challenge did not significantly affect jejunal NGF mRNA abundance, but 1.0% glutamate supplementation decreased jejunal NGF mRNA compared with LPS-challenged pigs.
There was no significant difference in CRFR2 mRNA abundance in jejunum or ileum among any of the four treatment groups.
Dietary glutamate supplementation reduced jejunal tryptase mRNA abundance compared with LPS-challenged pigs, consistent with reduced mast cell activation.
LPS challenge increased TGF-β1 mRNA abundance in jejunum and ileum compared with controls, and 1.0% glutamate supplementation further increased jejunal TGF-β1 mRNA compared with LPS-challenged pigs.
LPS challenge increased EGFR mRNA abundance in jejunum and ileum compared with controls, and 2.0% glutamate supplementation decreased jejunal EGFR mRNA compared with LPS-challenged pigs.
There was no difference in IEL number between control and LPS-challenged pigs, but 1.0% glutamate supplementation increased jejunal IEL numbers compared with LPS-challenged pigs.

Electron microscopy showed that LPS challenge disrupted tight junction and desmosomal integrity (loss of membrane fusion, cytoskeleton condensation), whereas glutamate-fed pigs maintained intact tight junctions and desmosomes, though with widened intercellular space.
Reduced cardiac uptake of 123I-MIBG on scintigraphy is diagnostically useful for pure autonomic failure.
Skin biopsy of areas with decreased sweating can demonstrate Lewy pathology in peripheral autonomic nerves, aiding diagnosis of PAF.
Among more than 10,000 autopsy cases in the BBAR aging cohort in the Tokyo metropolitan suburban area, only two had a clinical diagnosis of pure autonomic failure.
Both PAF cases showed diffuse Lewy body pathology involving the peripheral autonomic nervous system, brainstem, limbic system and neocortex, with only mild loss of pigmented substantia nigra neurons.
Other age-related pathologies such as Alzheimer's disease pathology, argyrophilic grain disease, and TDP-43 proteinopathy were only mild in these PAF cases.

Neuropathological features in both PAF cases fulfilled morphological criteria of dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), pure neocortical form, suggesting dementia may be a late clinical complication of PAF.

Both PAF autopsy cases showed diffuse Lewy body pathology extending through the peripheral autonomic nervous system, brainstem, limbic system, and neocortex, with only mild loss of pigmented neurons in the substantia nigra.
Co-existing senile changes such as Alzheimer pathology, argyrophilic grain disease, and TDP-43 proteinopathy were only mild in these PAF autopsy cases.
