The neuropathological findings in the PAF cases fulfilled the morphological criteria for the pure neocortical form of dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), suggesting dementia may be a late clinical complication of PAF.

Among BBAR autopsy cases, about one third had Lewy pathology somewhere in the body, and of these, 5% had Lewy pathology restricted to the peripheral autonomic nervous system, which the authors suggest may represent the earliest stage of PAF.

Streptozotocin (STZ) injection induced severe hyperglycaemia in mice compared with controls, and the histamine H3 receptor antagonist PF0086087 did not correct this hyperglycaemic state at any dose tested.
PF0086087 administration did not significantly affect body weight gain compared with untreated STZ-induced diabetic mice.

STZ-induced diabetic mice developed significant submucosal oedema in the distal colon compared with controls, and PF0086087 reduced this oedema in a dose-dependent manner, reaching significance at the highest doses.

STZ-induced diabetic mice showed increased mucin production (PAS staining) in the distal colon compared with controls, likely reflecting goblet cell hyperplasia secondary to colon dysmotility, and PF0086087 at the highest dose suppressed this mucin overproduction back to control levels.
The total number of PGP9.5-positive (pan-neuronal marker) myenteric neurons did not differ significantly between STZ-induced diabetic mice, PF0086087-treated groups, and controls.

STZ-induced diabetic mice showed a significant decrease in the proportion of nNOS-positive myenteric neurons (nNOS/PGP9.5 ratio) compared with controls, consistent with early-phase nitrergic dysfunction without neuronal loss, and PF0086087 at 100 mg/kg prevented this STZ-induced decrease.

STZ-induced diabetic mice showed a significant increase in Substance P (SP) immunoreactivity in myenteric ganglia compared with controls, and PF0086087 at 30 and 100 mg/kg restored SP signal to control levels.
No significant changes were observed in the density or fluorescence intensity of VIP-positive nerve fibres in the myenteric plexus among control, STZ-induced diabetic, and PF0086087-treated groups.
Serum miR-483-3p levels were significantly increased in patients with newly diagnosed hypertension compared with age-matched healthy controls.
Serum miR-483-5p showed an increasing trend in newly diagnosed hypertension patients versus controls but did not reach statistical significance.
miR-483-3p levels were higher in CD31+ endothelial microparticles isolated from serum of hypertension patients than controls, suggesting endothelial origin.
Serum miR-483-3p levels were significantly lower in patients with long-term (>15-year) hypertension compared with healthy controls, opposite to the newly diagnosed cohort.
Serum nitric oxide levels were decreased and ET-1 levels increased in long-term hypertension patients compared with controls, alongside reduced FMD and increased baPWV.
Serum miR-483-3p level positively correlated with NO and FMD, and negatively correlated with ET-1 and baPWV in hypertension patients.
Angiotensin II treatment of HUVECs increased miR-483-3p levels in a dose- and time-dependent manner.
miR-483 mimic overexpression significantly decreased Ang II-induced mRNA and protein expression of ACE1, ET-1, TGF-β, and CTGF in HUVECs.
HUVEC-derived exosomes, identified by electron microscopy, NTA, and CD81/CD63 markers, were taken up by HASMCs, demonstrating an exosome-mediated EC-to-SMC communication pathway.
Exosomes from HUVECs overexpressing pre-miR-483-3p delivered elevated miR-483-3p to HASMCs, which correspondingly decreased mRNA and protein expression of ACE1, TGF-β, and CTGF in HASMCs.
Angiotensin II receptor blockers candesartan, telmisartan, and valsartan (but not losartan) increased miR-483-3p levels in HUVECs, with telmisartan showing the strongest effect.
Telmisartan treatment of spontaneously hypertensive rats for 8 weeks decreased systolic blood pressure and increased miR-483-3p levels in serum and aorta compared with saline-treated SHR.
In hypertension patients (cohort 3), serum miR-483-3p was significantly elevated after 3 months of telmisartan treatment (80 mg/day), coinciding with reduced SBP and DBP.
Plasma 1-deoxySA and 1-deoxySO levels were not significantly elevated in the overall idiopathic SFN cohort compared with healthy controls.
Higher plasma 1-deoxySA and 1-deoxySO levels correlated with lower distal intraepidermal nerve fiber density in SFN patients.
Patients in the QST-based sensory loss subgroup had significantly higher 1-deoxySA levels compared with those in the thermal hyperalgesia or healthy subgroups.
Higher 1-deoxySA and 1-deoxySO correlated with worse (lower) warm detection threshold and lower thermal pain scores on painDETECT.
Plasma 1-deoxySA and 1-deoxySO levels correlated positively with body mass index.
1-deoxySA and 1-deoxySO plasma levels were significantly higher in SFN patients with arterial hypertension.
1-deoxy-sphingolipid bases correlated positively with triglycerides and cholesterol and inversely with HDL cholesterol.
1-deoxy-sphingolipids correlated positively with plasma L-alanine and inversely with L-serine and the serine/alanine ratio, consistent with a substrate shift in serine palmitoyltransferase activity.

Next-generation sequencing screening of SPTLC1 and SPTLC2 found no pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in any of the idiopathic SFN patients, excluding a hereditary cause of elevated 1-deoxy-sphingolipids.
Serum vitamin C was significantly lower in patients with Aβ nerve fiber dysfunction compared with those with pure C/Aδ fiber neuropathy.
Patients in the sensory loss QST subgroup had significantly lower vitamin C levels than those with thermal or mechanical hyperalgesia.
Vitamin C levels were significantly lower in SFN patients with arterial hypertension.
Serum reduced glutathione levels were significantly lower in SFN patients with Aδ nerve fiber dysfunction.
Serum TGF-β was significantly lower in patients with moderately or severely reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density compared with those with normal IENFD.
Serum TNF-α was elevated in 16.7% of examined SFN patients but did not correlate with specific clinical subphenotypes or metabolic syndrome markers.
Distal intraepidermal nerve fiber density was reduced in the large majority of the idiopathic SFN cohort, with severe reduction in over a third of cases.

Compared with matched healthy controls, SFN patients showed highly significant thermal hypoesthesia (Aδ/C fiber dysfunction), mechanical hyperalgesia/allodynia, and elevated mechanical detection threshold (Aβ dysfunction), while vibration detection threshold remained normal.

There was no significant correlation between IENFD (small fiber degeneration) and QST z-values (small fiber dysfunction), suggesting that neuropathic symptoms relate more to nerve fiber dysfunction than to degeneration.
PainDETECT scores were significantly higher in patients with QST-defined C fiber dysfunction, primarily attributed to burning and pressure pain, but did not correlate with IENFD.

Sudomotor function assessed by electrochemical skin conductance (Sudoscan) was abnormal in about a quarter of tested patients, more often at the hands than the feet, and did not correlate with histological sweat gland denervation or subjective hypohidrosis.
Postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS) was a previously diagnosed comorbidity in 8% of the idiopathic small fiber neuropathy cohort.
Fibromyalgia was a concomitant diagnosis in 11% of the idiopathic small fiber neuropathy cohort, discussed as a potential overlapping condition/confounder.
Migraine was a concomitant chronic pain diagnosis in 15% of the idiopathic small fiber neuropathy cohort.
Autonomic symptoms were reported by 85% of the idiopathic SFN cohort, most commonly dizziness/impending blackouts, hyperhidrosis, and diarrhea.
Delayed gastric emptying (DGE), also termed postsurgical gastroparesis syndrome, occurs in an estimated 5-30% of patients following distal gastrectomy for gastric cancer.

In a cohort followed 5 years after pylorus-preserving distal gastrectomy, epigastric fullness occurred in 60% of patients and gastric stasis in the remnant stomach occurred in 40%, with decreased emptying of liquid and semisolid diets.
The incidence of food retention after distal gastrectomy for early gastric cancer declined over time, from 55.5% at 3 months to 31.9% at 12 months and 20.9% at 24 months post-surgery.
A prior meta-analysis found that acupuncture (with or without medication) had a significantly higher total effective rate than control acupuncture for gastrointestinal motility disorders.

The authors' own previous randomized controlled single-center study demonstrated that transcutaneous electroacupuncture (TEA) improved bowel movement and alleviated postoperative ileus after gastrectomy.
In animal models, electroacupuncture improves gastric motility, accelerates solid gastric emptying via a vagal mechanism, and ameliorates chemotherapy-induced dyspepsia.

Gastric emptying within a week after distal gastrectomy was reported to be markedly slower with Billroth-I reconstruction than Billroth-II, but no difference was found between the two reconstruction types at 3-6 months.
Delayed gastric emptying was reported to be associated with laparoscopic surgical approach and with the duration of the postoperative period.

Prior studies have indicated that transcutaneous electroacupuncture can increase vagal (parasympathetic) activity and suppress sympathetic activity, which the current protocol will assess via ECG-derived heart rate variability (LF/HF ratio).
Null mutations in SERPINF1 (encoding PEDF) cause severe type VI osteogenesis imperfecta, marked by unmineralized osteoid accumulation and a fish-scale bone lamellar pattern.
Loss of PEDF in Serpinf1 mice delays osteoblast maturation and extracellular matrix mineralization compared with wild-type osteoblasts.
Barium sulfate perfusion showed significantly increased vessel density in the tibial periosteum of Serpinf1 mice compared with wild-type littermates.
The increased bone vascularization in Serpinf1 mice correlated with an increased number of CD31+/Endomucin+ endothelial cells implicated in angiogenesis-osteogenesis coupling.
Global RNA-Seq transcriptome analysis of Serpinf1 mouse osteoblasts identified osteogenesis and angiogenesis as the biological processes most impacted by loss of PEDF.
TGF-beta signaling is activated in Serpinf1 (PEDF-null) osteoblasts, and these cells show heightened sensitivity to TGF-beta stimulation compared with wild-type osteoblasts.
TGF-beta stimulation combined with PEDF deficiency produced additive suppression of osteogenic marker transcription and additive stimulation of pro-angiogenic factor transcription.
PEDF attenuated TGF-beta-induced expression of pro-angiogenic factors, indicating a direct antagonistic effect of PEDF on TGF-beta-driven angiogenic gene expression.
The authors propose that the functional antagonism between PEDF and TGF-beta pathways could be therapeutically exploited using PEDF and/or TGF-beta-neutralizing antibodies to treat type VI OI.
The number of toluidine-blue-positive mast cells was significantly increased in the lacrimal glands of IgG4-ROD patients compared with control lacrimal glands.
Both the number of tryptase-positive cells and tryptase gene expression were markedly increased in lacrimal glands of IgG4-ROD patients compared with controls.
The number of chymase-positive cells was significantly increased in the lacrimal glands of IgG4-ROD patients compared with controls.
Chymase gene expression showed a trend toward increase in IgG4-ROD lacrimal glands compared with controls, though this did not reach the reported significance seen for cell counts.
A strong positive correlation was found between the number of mast cells and the number of tryptase-positive cells across all examined lacrimal glands.
A significant positive correlation was observed between the number of tryptase-positive cells and chymase-positive cells across all examined lacrimal glands.

Correlation analysis showed a significant positive correlation between mast cell numbers and chymase-positive cell numbers, indicating most mast cells contain both tryptase and chymase in these lacrimal glands.
Collagen-I gene expression was significantly elevated in lacrimal glands of IgG4-ROD patients compared with controls, corresponding with visible dense fibrosis on Azan Mallory staining.
The number of TGF-β1-positive cells was largely increased in lacrimal glands of IgG4-ROD patients compared with controls, localized mainly to fibroblast-like cells and some mast cells.

In serial sections, chymase-positive staining spatially overlapped with TGF-β1-positive staining within fibrotic areas, suggesting MCTC-type mast cells are a cellular source of TGF-β1 activation via chymase.

Vimentin/α-SMA double-positive myofibroblasts were densely present in fibrotic areas surrounding lymphocytic hyperplasia in IgG4-ROD lacrimal glands, whereas control glands showed vimentin-positive fibroblasts without α-SMA co-staining (no myofibroblasts).

There was no significant difference between chymase-positive and tryptase-positive cell numbers within IgG4-ROD lacrimal glands, supporting the interpretation that the increased mast cells are predominantly of the MCTC (tryptase+/chymase+) subtype.
Post-COVID-19 symptom persistence at 12 or more weeks was substantially more prevalent among patients hospitalized for acute COVID-19 than among non-hospitalized patients.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported persisting symptom, occurring in 41.5% of all symptoms reported at 12 or more weeks after COVID-19.
Physical exhaustion was the second most common persisting symptom, occurring in 40.8% of all symptoms reported at 12 or more weeks after COVID-19.
Difficulty concentrating (brain fog-type cognitive symptom) was reported in 30.6% of all symptoms occurring at 12 or more weeks after COVID-19.
Loss of the sense of taste was reported in 25.9% of all symptoms occurring at 12 or more weeks after COVID-19.
Loss of the sense of taste was reported by 25.9% of patients with symptoms persisting at 12 weeks or more after COVID-19.
Loss of the sense of smell was reported by 25.5% of patients with symptoms persisting at 12 weeks or more after COVID-19.
Patients with post-COVID-19 symptoms reported significantly impaired quality of life compared to those without persisting symptoms.
Female sex was identified as one of the strongest risk factors for developing post-COVID-19 (long COVID).
Overall severity of comorbidities was identified as one of the strongest risk factors for post-COVID-19.
Severity of acute COVID-19 was identified as one of the strongest risk factors for post-COVID-19.
86% of survey participants scored 4 or above on the Fatigue Severity Scale, indicating fatigue beyond normal levels, with no significant difference by lab-confirmation status.
Cognitive dysfunction (brain fog, poor concentration, memory problems, confusion) was one of the most common ongoing symptoms, affecting 69.2% of participants at time of survey.
Ongoing symptoms affected three or more organ systems in 83.5% of participants, demonstrating the multisystem nature of Long Covid.

Using the Post-COVID-19 Functional Status Scale, nearly a third of participants (32.3%) reported being unable to live alone without assistance at six weeks from illness onset, and only 10.3% had no or negligible functional limitations.

Hierarchical clustering identified a minority multisystem ongoing symptom cluster (OSC2, 11.2%) with more severe involvement of cardiopulmonary, neuro-cognitive, nose/throat, pain and systemic symptoms compared to the majority cluster (OSC1).
Female sex was independently associated with more than doubled odds of membership in the severe multisystem ongoing symptom cluster (OSC2).
Poor baseline health prior to COVID-19 infection was strongly associated with membership of the severe multisystem ongoing symptom cluster.
Acute multisystem symptom presentation (ASC2 membership) was associated with 2.5-fold higher odds of belonging to the severe ongoing multisystem symptom cluster.

Older age (>60 years), higher income, and sufficient rest in the first two weeks of illness were each independently associated with lower odds of belonging to the severe multisystem ongoing symptom cluster.
Women were at higher risk and older participants (>60 years) at lower risk of transitioning over time from the mild acute symptom cluster (ASC1) into the severe ongoing multisystem cluster (OSC2).
Having a lab-confirmed positive COVID-19 test was associated with reduced likelihood of transitioning into the more severe multisystem ongoing symptom cluster over time.
Long Covid substantially impaired ability to work, with 19.1% unable to work (88.3% attributing this solely to COVID-19 illness), 9.7% working reduced hours, and 37.6% reporting loss of income.

Loss or alteration of smell/taste and brain fog were significantly more common in lab-confirmed than in unconfirmed participants, whereas several other ongoing symptoms (abdominal pain, nausea, chest pain/tightness, chills, hoarse voice, sore throat, sneezing, pins and needles) were less common in lab-confirmed participants.
The authors note emerging evidence that Long Covid is linked to a weak antibody response to SARS-CoV-2, potentially implicating this in the underlying immunological process of the disease.
Mental health symptoms were common, with anxiety reported by 28% and depression by 18% of participants.

The most commonly reported triggers exacerbating or returning symptoms were physical activity (77.2%), stress (55.1%), disturbed sleep (46.9%), cognitive activity (42.2%), and domestic chores (35.0%).

Very few participants (2.3%) felt they had recovered to their pre-COVID baseline health, with the vast majority (77.7%) still experiencing symptoms at the time of survey completion (mean illness duration 7.2 months), and recovery rates were similar regardless of lab-confirmation status.
PCR test sensitivity for SARS-CoV-2 declines substantially with time from symptom onset, from 77% at 4 days to 50% by 10 days, cited as a reason many Long Covid patients lacked lab confirmation.
The majority of participants reported a fluctuating (57.7%) or relapsing/remitting (17.6%) illness course, with 72.8% experiencing symptoms daily.
A small study found that ME/CFS patients had adrenal glands roughly 50% smaller than healthy controls, mirroring the adrenal atrophy seen in prolonged critical illness.
A recent study found that ME/CFS patients' thyroid hormone panels resemble those of critical illness patients, with a significantly lower T3-to-rT3 ratio.
Studies cited show endothelial function is impaired in ME/CFS in both large vessels and the microcirculation, associated with redox imbalance.
Prior findings cited show cerebral hypoperfusion in ME/CFS patients.
Prior findings cited show intracranial hypertension occurring in ME/CFS patients.
Plasma from ME/CFS patients was found to inhibit eNOS and nitric oxide production in endothelial cells, an in-vitro finding cited as a new mechanistic lead.
Cited findings link the gut microbiome to inflammation and to fatigue symptoms in ME/CFS.

Many prior ME/CFS studies have documented dysfunctions in the hypothalamic-pituitary-somatotropic, hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid, and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axes, associated with inflammation and oxidative & nitrosative stress.
ME/CFS is reported to show increased oxidative & nitrosative stress and altered cytokine profiles, elements consistent with a proposed vicious cycle also seen in critical illness.
Mitochondrial activity may be similarly affected in ME/CFS as in critical illness, potentially reflecting an adaptive hibernation-like downregulation.
Leaky gut is described as associated with auto-immunity, which is considered an important factor in ME/CFS pathology.

Severe GH deficiency is hypothesized to relate to several typical ME/CFS symptoms including fatigue, myalgia, delayed muscle recovery, exertional malaise, neurocognitive dysfunction, and physical disability.
A cited new hypothesis proposes that endothelial senescence underpins ME/CFS by disrupting intestinal barriers and the blood-brain barrier.
At baseline before the first exercise test, over half of all measured plasma metabolites showed lower relative levels in ME/CFS patients compared with controls.
The male ME/CFS cohort showed a more pronounced and consistent skew toward lower metabolite levels versus controls than the female cohort.
Unsupervised clustering (t-SNE/PCA) of plasma metabolomic profiles grouped strongly by individual participant rather than by disease status or sex.

The number of significantly different metabolites between female ME/CFS patients and controls increased substantially across the exercise/recovery protocol, most strikingly 24 hours after the first exercise bout.
In the male cohort, significant metabolite differences (only detectable at uncorrected P<0.05) doubled during the 24-hour recovery period, whereas exercise itself did not amplify differences.
Only 7 of 1157 metabolites (0.6%) were significantly different between ME/CFS patients and controls at baseline after multiple-testing correction (q<0.05), most of them lower in patients.

1,5-anhydroglucitol, a validated blood marker of long-term glycemic control, was one of the few metabolites significantly different between ME/CFS patients and controls at baseline, implicating dysregulated glucose handling.
Nicotinate and nicotinamide metabolism, precursor pathway for NAD+/NADP+, was significantly disrupted between ME/CFS patients and controls in both KEGG and SMPDB pathway analyses.

Energy and sugar metabolism pathways, including amino sugar/nucleotide sugar metabolism, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, and pentose phosphate pathway, were significantly disrupted between ME/CFS patients and controls.

Lipid metabolism pathways including alpha-linolenic/linoleic acid metabolism, fatty acid elongation and degradation, and unsaturated fatty acid biosynthesis were significantly disrupted between ME/CFS patients and controls.
The number of metabolic pathways significantly different between ME/CFS patients and controls increased progressively across the exercise/recovery protocol.

Comparing the metabolic effect of exercise on day 1 versus day 2, female ME/CFS patients showed 14 significantly different pathways (including butyrate metabolism), whereas female controls showed no significant pathway differences, indicating an abnormal, non-reproducible metabolic response to repeated exertion in patients.

Glutamate metabolism emerged as a common node linking most of the pathways found significantly disturbed by exertion in ME/CFS patients, including butyrate, arginine/proline, lysine, glucose-alanine cycle, and urea cycle pathways.
The malate-aspartate shuttle and glucose-alanine cycle, both central to cellular energy production, were affected differently between exercise on day 1 versus day 2 specifically in ME/CFS patients.

During the 24-hour recovery period, 28 metabolic pathways were significantly different between ME/CFS patients' and controls' recovery responses, including citric acid cycle, glycolysis, glucose-alanine cycle, urea cycle, and ammonia recycling.

Chemical enrichment analysis (ChemRICH) of the female cohort at baseline found 8 significantly enriched metabolite clusters, with 7 (nucleosides, xanthines, bile pigments, carnitines, saturated/unsaturated fatty acids) decreased in patients and only hexoses increased.

The carnitines chemical cluster, decreased in ME/CFS patients relative to controls at 3 earlier time points, shifted to being increased in patients specifically at D2POST (after the second exercise/24h recovery).
The acyl-choline arachidonic acids cluster decreased in response to both exercise bouts but then increased during the 24-hour recovery period, consistently across female controls and ME/CFS patients.
Alpha-ketoglutarate, a TCA-cycle energy metabolite, increased with exercise in controls but decreased in ME/CFS patients over the same period, with the decrease most pronounced in male patients.

The 24-hour recovery period (D1POST to D2PRE) showed the largest number of significantly divergent metabolites (61) between ME/CFS patients and controls, with amino acids (43%) and short/medium-chain carnitine-containing lipids (53% of significant lipids) disproportionately enriched.

Time-series multivariate analysis (Hotelling T2/MEBA) showed lactate underwent the largest temporal changes in female controls, whereas in female ME/CFS patients malate and branched-chain amino acid catabolites (methyl-oxo derivatives) and vitamin B5 showed the greatest temporal dynamics.

An unidentified metabolite (16397) showed the strongest control-vs-patient temporal divergence of all metabolites, decreasing in 84% of ME/CFS patients during the 24-hour recovery period versus only 50% of controls.

Despite glutamate metabolism being implicated across many disturbed pathways, neither glutamate nor glutamine itself differed significantly in absolute plasma levels between ME/CFS patients and controls at any time point.

Despite extensive untargeted metabolomics across 1157 features, no single discriminatory metabolite or metabolite panel could serve as a standalone biomarker distinguishing ME/CFS patients from controls.

Metabolites of unknown chemical identity were disproportionately represented among the most statistically significant features distinguishing ME/CFS patients from controls, comprising 25-43% of significant metabolites despite being only 19% of the overall data set.

Plasma glucose was slightly elevated in ME/CFS patients in this cohort, contrasting with the same group's earlier study that found glucose reduced in patients, but consistent with their second prior study.

A 'Warburg effect' pathway (aerobic glycolysis favoring lactate production over oxidative phosphorylation, typically associated with cancer cells) was among the pathways significantly altered during the recovery period in ME/CFS patients versus controls.
Alpha-ketoglutarate increased with exercise in controls (day 1 and day 2) but decreased in ME/CFS participants over the same period, with the decrease more pronounced in male patients.

Plasma lactate showed the highest Hotelling T2 value (most temporal change) among all 1157 metabolites in the female control cohort, increasing with both maximal exercise tests and declining during the 24-hour recovery period, with a smaller rise on day 2 than day 1.

Among 11 metabolites of interest, only pyruvate, lactate, and hypoxanthine were significantly different between controls and ME/CFS patients when comparing D1PRE to D2POST, reflecting cumulative changes after two maximal exercise tests over 24 hours.

During the 24-hour recovery period (D1POST to D2PRE), short- and medium-chain carnitine species (under 12 carbons) were disproportionately represented among significantly different metabolites between ME/CFS patients and controls, while long-chain carnitines were not significant.

Pathway analysis of the 24-hour recovery period (SMPDB) identified 28 significantly different pathways between ME/CFS and controls (P<0.05), including glucose-alanine cycle, citric acid cycle, malate-aspartate shuttle, pyruvate metabolism, amino sugar metabolism, glycolysis, urea cycle, and ammonia recycling.

Pathway comparison of the effects of day 1 versus day 2 exercise in ME/CFS patients (but not in controls) revealed 14 significantly different pathways (P<0.05), including butyrate metabolism, carnitine synthesis, oxidation of branched-chain fatty acids, phytanic acid peroxisomal oxidation, malate-aspartate shuttle, and glucose-alanine cycle, indicating divergent metabolic response between the two exercise bouts specifically in patients.

The 'Warburg effect' pathway (aerobic glycolysis, preferential lactate production from glucose) was among the significantly altered pathways during the recovery period in ME/CFS patients, though the authors note hypoxia could not be assessed as a cause from this data.

Neither glutamate nor glutamine itself was statistically different in plasma between ME/CFS patients and controls at baseline or throughout the study time points, even though glutamate metabolism was a common denominator of many significantly altered pathways.

Prior ME/CFS studies report inconsistent directions of plasma glutamate change: slightly decreased in the authors' earlier female cohort and in a study by Armstrong et al. (significant reduction, women only per Fluge et al.), normal in Naviaux et al., and slightly increased in both sexes in the current dataset.

A prior neuroimaging study found glutamate/glutamine levels were not altered in the brain of ME/CFS participants compared with controls, consistent with the lack of plasma-level differences observed in this study, though plasma levels may not reflect tissue-specific abundance.

The authors' prior microbiome work found lower levels of butyrate-producing bacteria in the gut microbiome of individuals with ME/CFS, linking gut microbial metabolism to the glutamate/butyrate pathway disturbances observed in this plasma study.

The 'arachidonic acids' acylcholine cluster (oleoylcholine, arachidonoylcholine, linoleoylcholine) consistently decreased following both exercise bouts but increased during the 24-hour recovery period, in both ME/CFS and control female cohorts.

At the D2PRE and D2POST time points (24-hour recovery and after second exercise), ChemRICH analysis identified newly enriched clusters specific to those time points including pyruvates, dicarboxylic acids, deoxycholic acids, and cholic acids (bile acids), with 53% of enriched cluster metabolites higher in ME/CFS than controls at both time points.

Plasma glucose was slightly elevated in ME/CFS patients in this cohort, consistent with the authors' second prior study but contradicting their first study in which glucose appeared reduced in patients, illustrating inconsistency across studies.
No single discriminatory metabolite or group of metabolites among the 1157 assessed could serve as a standalone biomarker for ME/CFS.

In female patients, an association between post-exertional malaise and hypermetabolism was supported by a shift of newly-significant metabolites over the recovery period from being decreased (hypometabolic) to increased (hypermetabolic) relative to controls, consistent with a prior uncontrolled PEM-induction study.

Prior ME/CFS metabolomics reviews found the most reproducible altered pathways across studies to be amino acid metabolism and urea cycle, glycolysis, lipid metabolism, and redox-related pathways, though methodological differences (ranging from ~20 to 933 metabolites measured) strongly affect pathway output estimates.

Prior sex-stratified ME/CFS metabolomics studies (Naviaux et al., Nkiliza et al., Fluge et al.) report both shared and sex-specific metabolic pathway effects, while one large serum metabolomics study found patient subgroups (metabotypes) unrelated to sex, illustrating that sex-based subgrouping is not universally supported.

In the male ME/CFS cohort, statistically significant metabolic differences from controls were only detectable at the uncorrected P<0.05 threshold, with the number of significant metabolites doubling during the 24-hour recovery period while exercise itself did not amplify differences, contrasting with the female cohort pattern.

A Venn diagram analysis of significantly different metabolites across the four time points showed that 21% were common to all time points (exercise-independent) in the female cohort versus only 6% in the male cohort, and distinctive time-point-specific patterns differed by sex, with 49% of male-specific metabolome transformations occurring during the 24-hour recovery period and second exercise.

Unknown metabolites were disproportionately represented among the most statistically significant features distinguishing ME/CFS from controls, rising to 25-43% of significant hits depending on time point despite comprising only 19% of the overall dataset.
EVs bearing the B cell marker CD19 were significantly higher in severe ME/CFS participants compared to healthy controls.
EVs bearing the platelet marker CD41a were significantly higher in severe ME/CFS participants compared to healthy controls.
CD19+ EV levels were significantly higher in severe compared to mild ME/CFS cases.
CD41a+ EV levels were significantly higher in severe compared to mild ME/CFS cases.
Overall EV levels measured by flow cytometry did not differ significantly based on ME/CFS status compared to healthy controls.

By nanoparticle tracking analysis, total EV counts were slightly but not significantly lower in healthy controls compared to ME/CFS participants, and EV size did not differ significantly between clinical groups.
No significant differences were found among study groups for T cell, myeloid, exosome, activation, or neuronal EV surface markers.
Left subiculum head volume was significantly larger in ME/CFSICC patients than healthy controls, surviving multiple comparison correction.
Left presubiculum head volume was significantly larger in ME/CFSICC patients than healthy controls, surviving multiple comparison correction.
Left fimbria volume was significantly larger in ME/CFSICC patients than healthy controls, surviving multiple comparison correction.
Right CA1 body volume differed between ME/CFSFukuda patients and healthy controls only before multiple comparison correction, not after.
Left CA1 body volume was smaller in ME/CFSICC patients than healthy controls before multiple comparison correction, but this did not survive FDR correction.
CA3 head volume was smaller in ME/CFSICC patients than healthy controls before correction, but did not survive FDR correction.
CA3 body volume was smaller in ME/CFSICC patients than healthy controls before correction, but did not survive FDR correction.
Right subiculum head volume was larger in ME/CFSICC patients than healthy controls before correction, but did not survive FDR correction.
In ME/CFSFukuda patients, greater fatigue severity was positively correlated with larger left hippocampal tail volume.
In ME/CFSFukuda patients, greater fatigue severity was positively correlated with larger left parasubiculum volume.
In ME/CFSFukuda patients, greater fatigue severity was positively correlated with larger left HATA volume.
In ME/CFSFukuda patients, greater fatigue severity was positively correlated with larger left whole hippocampal head volume.
In ME/CFSFukuda patients, greater fatigue severity was positively correlated with larger left whole hippocampus volume.
In ME/CFSFukuda patients, more severe sleep disturbance was associated with smaller right CA1 body volume.
In ME/CFSICC patients, greater fatigue severity was strongly negatively correlated with left hippocampal tail volume.
In ME/CFSICC patients, more severe sleep disturbance was strongly positively correlated with larger left hippocampus tail volume.
In ME/CFSICC patients, more severe sleep disturbance was strongly positively correlated with larger right hippocampus tail volume.
In ME/CFSICC patients, more severe sleep disturbance was strongly positively correlated with larger subiculum body volume.
In ME/CFSICC patients, greater physical function score (phys_all) was negatively correlated with left dentate gyrus granule cell layer (GC-ML-DG) head volume.
In ME/CFSICC patients, greater physical function score (phys_all) was negatively correlated with left CA4 head volume.
In ME/CFSICC patients, higher pain scores were negatively correlated with left GC-ML-DG head volume.
In ME/CFSICC patients, higher pain scores were negatively correlated with left CA4 head volume.
In ME/CFSICC patients, poorer information processing score (procinfo) was strongly positively correlated with larger left subiculum head volume.
In ME/CFSICC patients, poorer information processing score was positively correlated with larger CA1 head volume.
In ME/CFS ICC patients, larger left molecular layer of the hippocampus (head) volume was strongly positively correlated with worse information processing score.
In ME/CFS ICC patients, larger left whole hippocampal head volume was strongly positively correlated with worse information processing score.
In ME/CFS ICC patients, larger right subiculum head volume showed the strongest positive correlation with worse information processing score among all subfields examined.

In the Norwegian discovery cohort, the TPPP gene region showed the strongest genetic association with ME/CFS at SNP rs115523291, but this top SNP could not be replicated in the Danish or UK Biobank cohorts.

Several other SNPs within the TPPP gene showed modest association signals with ME/CFS in the self-reported UK Biobank CFS cohort and in a combined analysis of the Norwegian and UK Biobank cohorts (rs139264145).
Across the combined genome-wide analysis of 2532 ME/CFS patients, no SNP achieved genome-wide significance, so no established ME/CFS risk loci were identified.
The authors note that TPPP is expressed in brain tissue, which they consider biologically relevant given the neurological symptoms of ME/CFS.

A ROC analysis combining baseline total DSQ score, three baseline immune markers (IL-5, IL-6, IL-13), and the severity-of-mononucleosis score at the time of IM had modest predictive value for severe ME/CFS at six months.

A refined index combining three baseline gastrointestinal DSQ symptoms (stomach pain, bloating, irritable bowel symptoms), decreased baseline IL-13 and/or IL-5, and severe gastrointestinal symptoms at the time of mononucleosis predicted severe ME/CFS with strong accuracy.
Random forest analysis identified stomach pain, bloating, and irritable bowel symptoms as the baseline clinical DSQ features most predictive of severe ME/CFS.
Decreased baseline levels of IL-5 were identified as a predictive immune feature for development of severe ME/CFS following infectious mononucleosis.

Decreased baseline levels of IL-13 were identified as a predictive immune feature for development of severe ME/CFS following infectious mononucleosis, contrasting with IL-13 overproduction seen in inflammatory bowel diseases.
Severity of mononucleosis at the time of acute infection, particularly gastrointestinal severity, was predictive of subsequent development of severe ME/CFS.
Attempts to statistically predict the development of any (non-severe) ME/CFS following IM using the same variables were not significant, so analyses focused only on severe ME/CFS outcomes.
The authors suggest gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, bloating, and vomiting may be linked to underlying autonomic dysfunction in ME/CFS.
Prior related work found that days spent in bed since infectious mononucleosis and autonomic dysfunction two months post-diagnosis were associated with postinfectious ME/CFS at six months.
ME/CFS participants had lower peak oxygen consumption (aerobic fitness) than controls, with a mean difference of 6.5 ml/kg/min.

At the gas exchange threshold (GET), ME/CFS participants had significantly lower absolute VO2, VCO2, breathing frequency, HR, chronotropic index, and Watts, and significantly higher ventilatory equivalents (VE/VO2 and VE/VCO2) compared to controls, with small-to-moderate effect sizes.
In the fitness- and age-matched subsample, significant differences at GET persisted for breathing frequency, VE/VO2, and VE/VCO2, and ME/CFS participants had higher tidal volume than controls.

ME/CFS participants had moderately and significantly lower ventilatory efficiency, shown by a higher VE/VCO2nadir and lower OUES, and lower HR performance (lower %HRR and %predicted max HR) compared with controls.
In the fitness-matched subsample, OUES and %predicted max HR differences were no longer significant, but VE/VCO2nadir and %HRR differences remained significant.

At peak exercise, ME/CFS participants had significantly lower VO2, VCO2, VE, breathing frequency, HR, oxygen pulse, chronotropic index, Watts, exercise time, and lactate, and significantly higher VE/VO2, VE/VCO2, and RPE compared to controls.
In the fitness-matched subsample at peak exercise, significant differences remained for breathing frequency, VE/VO2, VE/VCO2, and RPE, and ME/CFS demonstrated higher peak tidal volume.
There were no significant differences between ME/CFS and controls for blood lactate responses at rest, during exercise, or recovery, in either the entire sample or the fitness-matched subgroup.

Contrary to some prior reports, this large sample showed little evidence of chronotropic incompetence in ME/CFS, with participants on average achieving ≥90% predicted peak HR, ≥80% heart rate reserve, and CTI ≥0.90 throughout exercise.

Perceived exertion (RPE) was the largest observed difference during exercise, with ME/CFS participants rating exercise as requiring more effort throughout the test, and this difference persisted after matching for aerobic fitness.

In the fitness-matched subgroup, ME/CFS participants showed a unique breathing strategy characterized by reduced breathing frequency and increased tidal volume compared to controls, observed consistently across GET, peak, and dynamic exercise measures.
A larger percentage of ME/CFS participants had current comorbid illnesses (fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome, and/or migraine) compared to controls.

Controlling for current comorbid FM, IBS, or migraine did not substantially alter group differences overall, though in the fitness-matched subgroup the VE/VO2 group difference was no longer significant after this adjustment.

ME/CFS participants had markedly worse self-reported physical function (large effect size) and physical activity (moderate effect size) than controls, including meaningful (>10 point) differences on the PROMIS Physical Function T-score.

During dynamic exercise (20-100% peak VO2), ME/CFS participants had significantly lower VE, fR, HR, O2 pulse, VO2/WR, and CTI, and significantly higher VE/VO2, VE/VCO2, and RPE compared to controls; in the fitness-matched subgroup, differences remained for fR, VE/VO2, VE/VCO2, CTI, RPE, with increased VT.

Fitness matching (aerobic capacity and age) eliminated many cardiometabolic differences between ME/CFS and controls, including VE, HR, O2 pulse, OUES, and VO2/WR, indicating these are largely explained by differences in aerobic fitness rather than being disease-specific; however, ventilatory efficiency, breathing pattern, and RPE differences remained, suggesting disease-specific impairment in oxygen utilization/ventilatory efficiency rather than delivery.
Five of 14 post-COVID ME/CFS patients had peripheral endothelial dysfunction (RHI ≤1.67) versus none of the healthy controls.
Five of 16 PCS patients had peripheral endothelial dysfunction versus none of the healthy controls.
In healthy controls, RHI correlated negatively with age, consistent with typical vascular aging.
In PCS patients, RHI showed a paradoxical positive correlation with age, contrary to the typical inverse relationship seen in healthy individuals.
RHI was positively correlated with systolic blood pressure in PCS patients, an unexpected direction relative to normal physiology.
RHI was positively correlated with diastolic blood pressure in PCS patients.
RHI was positively correlated with BMI in PCS patients, opposite to the expected inverse relationship.
Serum ET-1 concentrations were significantly higher in post-COVID ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls in the initial PAT study cohort.
In an independent validation cohort, ET-1 levels were confirmed to be significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls and post-COVID reconvalescents.
ET-1 was also elevated in non-ME/CFS PCS patients compared with both healthy controls and post-COVID reconvalescents.
Serum Ang-2 levels were significantly lower in PCS patients (without ME/CFS) compared with healthy controls in the PAT study cohort.
The validation cohort confirmed significantly decreased Ang-2 levels in PCS patients compared with HCs, and also lower than in ME/CFS patients.
Ang-2 levels were also diminished in asymptomatic post-COVID reconvalescents (PCHC) compared with healthy controls, suggesting a persistent vascular change even without symptoms.
Serum ESM-1 (Endocan) concentrations did not differ significantly between ME/CFS, PCS and healthy control groups.
Median serum ACE activity did not differ significantly between ME/CFS and PCS patients, although a subset of patients in both groups had below-normal ACE levels.
Serum ACE2 levels did not differ significantly between ME/CFS, PCS and healthy controls, and did not correlate with RHI.

Elevated IL-8 levels (post-erythrocyte lysis, above the normal reference range) were found in a majority of PCS and ME/CFS patients, though median levels did not differ significantly between patient groups.
None of the measured endothelial biomarkers (ET-1, Ang-2, ESM-1, ACE, ACE2, IL-8) correlated with the RHI in any group.
PEM severity, measured by the DSQ-PEM score, was significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than in PCS patients without ME/CFS in both study cohorts.
In the validation cohort, ME/CFS patients showed significantly worse fatigue (Chalder Fatigue Scale) and physical disability (Bell Disability Scale) than PCS patients without ME/CFS.

Cardiopulmonary exercise testing studies in post-COVID syndrome (PCS) patients with mild acute infections consistently show hyperventilation during exercise with no abnormalities in blood gases or other pulmonary/cardiovascular parameters to explain it.
PCS patients increased ventilation and tidal volume as soon as exercise effort began, indicating early central respiratory stimulation rather than blood-gas-driven stimulation.
Vascular disturbances are apparent in PCS, and initial studies provide evidence of endothelial dysfunction.
Microthrombi are proposed to seriously impair microcirculation in PCS patients, independent of endothelial dysfunction.

Recovered COVID patients showed significant changes in lymphocyte stiffness, monocyte and neutrophil size/deformability, and decreased erythrocyte deformability, proposed to relate to long-term symptoms.
Leukocytes from ME/CFS patients show impedance changes in response to an osmotic challenge that inevitably activate NHE1, a response not observed in healthy controls.
Dysautonomia, characterized by abnormal heart rate variability, is present in PCS patients with fatigue.
Orthostatic symptoms and reduced cerebral blood flow are reported to be similar between PCS and ME/CFS patients.
Small fiber neuropathy, present in a subset of ME/CFS patients, is also found in patients with post-COVID syndrome.

The authors hypothesize that hyperventilation-induced respiratory alkalosis combined with intracellular acidosis from glycolytic metabolism steepens the proton gradient, strongly activating NHE1 and loading skeletal myocytes with sodium, which is proposed as a key pathophysiological mechanism in ME/CFS and PCS.

The authors propose that high intracellular sodium reverses the sarcolemmal NCX transport mode from calcium export to calcium import, causing mitochondrial calcium overload and functional/structural damage resembling ischemia-reperfusion injury, contributing to more severe and prolonged PEM.
There is some indication that respiratory training may improve the clinical situation in patients with post-COVID syndrome.
Slow deep breathing combined with hyperoxia was shown to improve autonomic dysfunction in diabetes, cited as supporting evidence for breathing-based interventions on dysautonomia.
The incidence rate of Lyme disease in the UK between 2000 and 2018 was 5.18 per 100,000 person-years, increasing from 3.15 in 2000-2004 to 7.20 in 2015-2018.
Lyme disease incidence was approximately 5-fold higher in Scotland (15.32 per 100,000 py) than in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland.
Patients with a Lyme disease diagnosis had a significantly increased crude risk of subsequent consultation for any types of fatigue compared to matched unexposed comparators.
Lyme disease patients had a markedly increased crude risk of subsequent ME/CFS diagnosis compared to matched comparators, though based on few events.
The adjusted association between Lyme disease and any subsequent fatigue was strongest for infections diagnosed in autumn and winter compared to spring or summer.
In a sensitivity analysis restricted to fatigue events recorded 6 months or more after index date, the Lyme disease-fatigue association was attenuated but remained present in winter and autumn.

After adjustment for antibiotic treatment, Lyme disease was associated with a strongly increased hazard of subsequent ME/CFS diagnosis, an effect that persisted (though attenuated) in the 6-month sensitivity analysis.
Higher healthcare utilisation frequency in the 6 months prior to index was strongly and linearly associated with subsequent fatigue, with more than 10 GP visits conferring over 7 times the risk.
History of depression and antibiotic treatment at index were associated with fatigue and appeared even more strongly associated with ME/CFS risk, although confidence intervals were wide.
Among Lyme patients, repeated infection with Borrelia burgdorferi was associated with increased incidence of any type of fatigue, though not with ME/CFS specifically.

In a post-hoc analysis restricted to patients with erythema migrans (whose index date closely reflects true infection date), the seasonal difference in the Lyme disease-fatigue association was attenuated compared to the main confirmed cohort.
The majority of Lyme disease patients (73.1%) received antibiotic treatment at diagnosis, most commonly doxycycline as a unique agent (57.7%), followed by amoxicillin alone (12.4%).
The vast majority of diagnosed Lyme disease cases were classified as Lyme borreliosis rather than neuroborreliosis or Lyme arthritis.
At baseline, 77.8% of long COVID participants met Fukoda ME/CFS diagnostic criteria on the DePaul Symptom Questionnaire Short Form.
55.5% of participants met the Canadian ME/CFS criteria at baseline.
62.9% of participants met the IOM ME/CFS criteria at baseline.
There was no significant association between prior COVID-19 hospitalisation and meeting ME/CFS diagnostic criteria under any of the three DSQ-SF algorithms.

After the 10-week SingStrong intervention, fewer participants met ME/CFS criteria across all three algorithms, with 13 instances of participants no longer meeting criteria versus 4 instances of newly meeting criteria.
Significant pre- to post-intervention improvements were observed in breathlessness at rest, during dressing, and on stairs, following the SingStrong singing and breathing retraining programme.
Fatigue significantly improved from intervention baseline to post-intervention following the SingStrong programme.
Performance of usual activities and pain/disability significantly improved post-intervention in the severity domain of the C19-YRS.
Voice quality and cognition/communication significantly improved post-intervention in the impact/disability domain of the C19-YRS.
New or worsened difficulty with concentration and short-term memory reported since COVID-19 onset were unchanged after the SingStrong intervention.
PTSD-related symptoms (unpleasant dreams, memories, avoidance) reported by participants at baseline remained largely unchanged after the SingStrong intervention.
Bowel and bladder control difficulties associated with COVID-19 were largely unchanged after the SingStrong intervention.
Participants' self-reported health severity domain scores were significantly worse at intervention baseline compared to their recalled pre-COVID health status.
The authors note that high baseline anxiety may have exacerbated physical symptoms of breathlessness, pain, and fatigue in this long COVID cohort, similar to prior COPD findings.
Serum BAFF concentrations did not differ significantly between post-giardiasis ICF/CFS patients and non-fatigued controls, though the mean was numerically lower in ICF/CFS.
Serum BAFF concentrations did not differ significantly between post-giardiasis FGID patients and controls without FGID.
Serum anti-CdtB antibody levels did not differ significantly between post-giardiasis ICF/CFS patients and non-fatigued controls.
Anti-CdtB antibody levels were not higher in post-giardiasis FGID patients, nor in IBS or IBS-D subgroups, compared to controls.
In the IBS-D subgroup, anti-CdtB antibody levels tended to be lower than in controls, contrary to prior literature reporting elevation in IBS-D.
Serum anti-flagellin antibody levels did not differ significantly between post-giardiasis ICF/CFS patients and non-fatigued controls.
Serum anti-flagellin antibody levels were similar between post-giardiasis FGID cases and controls.
Contrary to a prior report, no increase in anti-flagellin antibody levels was found in the post-giardiasis IBS or IBS-D subgroups compared to controls.

Individuals with fibromyalgia show elevated familial genetic risk scores (FGRS) not only for fibromyalgia itself but also for IBS, internalizing psychiatric disorders, pain syndromes, several autoimmune disorders (especially RA and Hashimoto's thyroiditis), and sleep disorder.

IBS and CFS patients show lower average FGRS elevations than FM but risk is still widely distributed across FSD, psychiatric, autoimmune, pain, and sleep disorder categories, with IBD showing the highest genetic risk among autoimmune disorders in IBS patients.

Compared to IBS and CFS cases, FM cases have significantly higher genetic risk for FM, major depression, anxiety disorder, RA, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, back pain, migraine, and sleep disorder (p<0.0001).
IBS and CFS FGRS profiles differ significantly only for three comparisons: each disorder's own primary FGRS, plus IBS shows higher genetic risk for inflammatory bowel disease than CFS.
The RA FGRS profile is dominated by risk for RA itself, with only modest elevations for three of four autoimmune disorders and back pain, contrasting with the broader FSD profiles.
The MD FGRS profile is more diverse than RA's, with substantial elevations for MD and anxiety disorder and more modest elevations for back pain, sleep disorder, IBS, and migraine.

Compared with RA patients, FM patients have lower genetic risk for RA and polymyalgia rheumatica but markedly higher genetic risk for FM, IBS, MD, AD, back pain, migraine, sleep disorder, and modestly higher risk for CFS.

IBS patients have higher genetic risk for inflammatory bowel disease compared to RA patients, while both IBS and CFS show markedly lower genetic risk for RA and other autoimmune disorders relative to RA cases.
IBS and CFS patients show much lower genetic risk for MD and anxiety disorder compared to MD patients, whereas FM patients show only a modest reduction in MD genetic risk and no reduction in AD risk.
Genetic risk for fibromyalgia itself was much greater comparing FM to MD patients, while no such elevated FM-specific genetic risk difference was seen for IBS or CFS versus MD.
Genetic risk for back pain, migraine, and sleep disorder was substantially higher only in FM patients compared to MD patients, not in IBS or CFS.
Genetic risk for autoimmune disorders, especially RA and Hashimoto's thyroiditis, was clearly greater in FM patients than MD patients.
Genetic risk for inflammatory bowel disease was particularly elevated in IBS patients compared to MD patients.

Latent class analysis of FM genetic risk scores across internalizing, pain, and autoimmune domains supported a three-class solution reflecting only quantitative (not qualitative) differences, with no evidence for distinct genetic subtypes of FM.

Sleep disorder aggregates in the families of FM patients even when relatives with FM themselves are excluded from analysis, supporting the hypothesis that sleep dysfunction may be a pathogenic contributor to FM rather than purely a consequence of pain.

Removing all FM cases from relatives used to construct the FGRS produced only very small reductions in genetic risk scores with no change in overall patterns, arguing against reverse causation as an explanation for the shared genetic risk profile.
Comorbidity among the three FSD was modest, with only 854 individuals in the entire cohort having both an FM and a CFS diagnosis, and the strongest overlap being between FM and CFS.
The FGRS methodology was validated against an alternative quantitative family-history score (LT-FH), showing a high correlation of +0.94 in matched Swedish samples.

The three functional somatic disorders showed strong female predominance, most marked for fibromyalgia (85.5% female), followed by irritable bowel syndrome (70.8% female) and chronic fatigue syndrome (66.8% female).

In a patient with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome who developed an intussusception-type aortic dissection after surgical repair of an intercostal artery bleed, endovascular intervention successfully rescued the failed open aortic repair.

The authors note that endovascular rescue may be a viable option for managing failed open aortic repair complications in Ehlers-Danlos patients, contributing to the limited existing literature on endovascular intervention in this population.
A young woman presenting with spontaneous ecchymoses (unexplained bruising) was subsequently diagnosed with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

The prevalence of HαT among a combined cohort of individuals with HSD, hEDS, and axial skeletal abnormalities with hypermobility was similar to that in unselected populations, indicating no association between HαT and these congenital connective tissue disorders.
In the combined hEDS and HSD cohort, individuals with HαT had a significantly higher prevalence of retained primary dentition requiring surgical extraction compared with those without HαT.
In the combined hEDS and HSD cohort, dysphagia diagnosed by barium swallow or manometry was significantly more prevalent among individuals with HαT than those without.

When all three cohorts (hEDS, HSD, and axial skeletal abnormalities with hypermobility) were combined, retained primary dentition remained significantly associated with HαT even after correction for multiple comparisons, while dysphagia did not.
Among individuals with hEDS alone, HαT was associated with an increased prevalence of retained primary dentition requiring surgical extraction.
Among individuals with HSD alone, HαT was associated with an increased prevalence of retained primary dentition and a significant association with dysphagia diagnosed by barium swallow or manometry.

Anaphylaxis and pruritus showed non-significant increased trends in prevalence among HαT-positive individuals with joint hypermobility, but these did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons.

In the axial skeletal abnormality cohort analyzed alone, no significant differences in clinical manifestations were found based on HαT status, though non-significant positive trends were observed for anaphylaxis, pruritus, and dysphagia; clinical data were only available for a subset of genotyped individuals.

The authors note that retained primary dentition was previously the only connective tissue abnormality found to be significantly associated with HαT among unselected healthy adults, consistent with the current findings.
A novel heterozygous missense mutation in C1R, c.674G>C (p.R225P), was identified as the cause of a familial case of periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

The affected individual(s) displayed pretibial hyperpigmentation and extensive periodontitis but lacked the skin extensibility and joint hypermobility typically seen in pEDS, suggesting this mutation broadens the clinical phenotype of the disorder.
Electron microscopy of the filum terminale in hEDS-associated tethered cord syndrome revealed both inherited collagen fibril abnormalities and acquired fibril damage.
Biomechanical tension testing showed the filum terminale had elastic properties in both hEDS and typical tethered cord syndrome groups, but this elasticity was impaired in the hEDS-TCS group.
Filum terminale excision led to statistically significant improvement in urinary, bowel, and neurologic symptoms at 3 and 12 months post-surgery in both the hEDS-TCS and typical TCS groups.

Intergroup comparison after filum excision showed no difference in overall outcome between hEDS-TCS and typical TCS patients, except that neurologic improvement was more pronounced in the hEDS-TCS group.
A case report describes hemothorax and bloody ascites occurring as complications of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
The report describes two cases of pulmonary vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in which hemoptysis was the main clinical manifestation.
The paper reports a case of multiple spontaneous coronary artery dissections and ruptures occurring in a patient with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
TNXB deficiency causes Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and up to 10% of CAH (21-hydroxylase deficiency) patients also have EDS, a combined entity termed CAH-X.
Chimeric CYP21A1P/CYP21A2 genes, caused by unequal crossover with the pseudogene, are found in 20-25% of CAH alleles due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency.
The CH1 TNXA/TNXB chimera carries a 120-bp deletion in exon and intron 35 derived from the TNXA pseudogene, leading to TNX haploinsufficiency.

The CH2 chimera carries a pseudogene-derived TNXB variant c.12174C>G (p.Cys4058Trp) that eliminates a critical disulfide bond in the TNX C-terminal fibrinogen-like domain, producing a dominant-negative effect rather than reduced expression.

The CH3 chimera involves a cluster of three pseudogene-derived TNXB variants, of which modeling suggests p.Arg4073His is detrimental to proper TNX protein folding while the other two variants did not significantly affect folding energy.

In Schalkwijk et al.'s 2001 study of 151 EDS patients, 168 disease controls, and 21 healthy individuals, TNX and tenascin-C protein levels were assessed by ELISA, and 4 of 5 TNX-deficient patients were found to have homozygous TNXB mutations, defining classic-like EDS (clEDS).

Among 20 heterozygous family members carrying a TNXB haploinsufficiency mutation, generalized joint hypermobility (GJH) was observed in only nine, all of whom were female, establishing an association between TNXB haploinsufficiency and hypermobility-type EDS (hEDS).

In a large NIH prospective observational study of 193 unrelated CAH patients, heterozygosity for a TNXB deletion (CAH-X syndrome) was observed in 7% of patients, establishing the association between the hypermobility phenotype and TNXB haploinsufficiency.

Of 246 CAH probands screened by Merke et al. in 2015, 14 carried the previously described CH1 chimera and 7 unrelated patients carried the novel CH2 (c.12174C>G) chimera, yielding an overall CAH-X prevalence of 8.5%; the CH2 variant did not reduce protein expression, supporting a dominant-negative mechanism distinct from CH1 haploinsufficiency.

In three patients with biallelic CAH-X, a novel dominant-negative CH3 chimera was identified, and computational modeling predicted that the p.Arg4073His variant reduces protein-folding energy by disrupting a cation-pi interaction between Arg4073 and Phe4080.

Lao et al. (2019) developed a high-throughput allele-specific PCR CAH-X screening method and found a 15.6% overall prevalence of CAH-X, rising to 29.2% among subjects with a 30-kb CYP21A2 deletion genotype, higher than previously estimated.
Gao et al. (2020) assessed a Chinese cohort of 424 patients with 21-hydroxylase deficiency and found 14% had a chimeric TNXA/TNXB gene using MLPA and Sanger sequencing.

In the authors' own cohort of 337 Argentine 21-OHD patients, TNXB gene analysis in 66 unrelated CYP21A2 30-kb deletion carriers found an overall CAH-X prevalence of 14%, and a 73% incidence of TNXA/TNXB chimeras among 30-kb deletion carriers with the junction site downstream of exon 7.

Among four biallelic CAH-X patients in the authors' cohort (two CH1/CH1, two CH1/CH2), the CH1/CH2 patients had a more severe EDS phenotype with greater skin involvement, and cardiac defects (an atrial septal defect and a mild pulmonary valve defect) were detected in these two patients.

Chen et al. reported three biallelic CAH-X patients (ages 14, 19, 29) with unique TNXB variant combinations who all had skin hyperextensibility and extreme joint hypermobility, and additionally displayed widened atrophic scarring, rectal prolapse, severe gastroesophageal reflux, high palate, elongated uvula, and mild ventricular enlargement in two patients.

Phenotype severity correlates with dosage of dominant TNXB alleles: monoallelic CAH-X is associated with the milder, more common hEDS type, while biallelic CAH-X is associated with the more severe clEDS subtype.

Gastrointestinal disorders such as chronic gastroesophageal reflux and irritable bowel syndrome, hernias, and organ prolapse are reported more frequently in patients heterozygous for the dominant-negative CAH-X CH2 chimera than in those with the haploinsufficient CH1 chimera.

CAH-X patients (with concurrent CAH) are consistently more severely affected than patients with TNX-deficient EDS without CAH, suggesting hormonal factors or chronic glucocorticoid treatment may modulate connective tissue dysplasia severity, though this mechanism is not fully understood.
The Beighton Score is presented as the most objective clinical assessment tool to measure generalized joint hypermobility in evaluating CAH-X/EDS patients.
Lao et al. reported a novel cause of CAH-X syndrome not associated with TNXA/TNXB chimeras but due to a TNXB splice donor site variant.
Arterial tortuosity syndrome in this Arab cohort is caused by a p.S81R mutation in the SLC2A10 gene, which encodes the glucose transporter GLUT10.
Electron microscopy of skin biopsies from ATS patients showed large spaces among collagen fibrils, indicating disorganization of collagen structure.
Elastin fiber content and thickness were reduced in the skin of ATS patients compared to normal.
Small muscular arteries in the skin of ATS patients showed discontinuous internal elastic lamina, lack of myofilaments, and disorganized medial smooth muscle cells with vacuolated cytoplasm.
Fibromyalgia patients showed a smaller heart rate response during the first 30 seconds of active standing compared to healthy women.
Fibromyalgia patients showed a smaller blood pressure response during the first 30 seconds of active standing compared to healthy women.
Fibromyalgia patients showed a smaller cardiac output response during the first 30 seconds of active standing compared to healthy women.
Fibromyalgia patients showed a smaller total peripheral resistance response during the first 30 seconds of active standing compared to healthy women.
Fibromyalgia patients showed a smaller pre-ejection period response during the first 30 seconds of active standing compared to healthy women.
Fibromyalgia patients showed a smaller heart rate change during the first 30 seconds of lying down compared to healthy women.
Fibromyalgia patients showed a smaller cardiac output change during the first 30 seconds of lying down compared to healthy women.
Fibromyalgia patients showed a smaller total peripheral resistance change during the first 30 seconds of lying down compared to healthy women.
The magnitude of autonomic cardiovascular adjustments to postural changes was inversely associated with the severity of clinical pain in fibromyalgia patients.
Female fibromyalgia patients had a significantly higher prevalence of abdominal pain than male patients.
Male fibromyalgia patients reported a significantly higher frequency of coexisting depressive symptoms than female patients, despite no difference on the BDI-II score.
Widespread pain index (WPI) did not differ significantly between male and female fibromyalgia patients.
Symptoms severity scale (SSS) did not differ significantly between male and female fibromyalgia patients.
Global disease impact measured by R-FIQ total score was significantly higher in women than men with fibromyalgia.
R-FIQ pain sub-score was significantly higher in women than men with fibromyalgia.
R-FIQ fatigue sub-score was significantly higher in women than men with fibromyalgia.
R-FIQ memory sub-score was significantly higher in women than men with fibromyalgia.
R-FIQ tenderness sub-score was significantly higher in women than men with fibromyalgia.
R-FIQ balance sub-score was significantly higher in women than men with fibromyalgia.
R-FIQ environmental sensitivity sub-score was significantly higher in women than men with fibromyalgia.
Beck Depression Inventory-II scores did not differ significantly between male and female fibromyalgia patients despite the difference in self-reported depressive symptom frequency.
Serum BDNF levels were significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
Male fibromyalgia patients had significantly lower serum BDNF levels than female fibromyalgia patients.
Male fibromyalgia patients had significantly lower serum BDNF levels than male healthy controls.
Female fibromyalgia patients had significantly lower serum BDNF levels than female healthy controls.
Serum BDNF levels showed no correlation with any clinical or clinimetric feature evaluated in fibromyalgia patients.
Serum BDNF showed good diagnostic performance for identifying fibromyalgia patients versus healthy controls, with an AUC of 0.89 and an optimal cut-off of <6.47 ng/ml.
An early Mexican study found stromal nerve thinning and reduced subbasal corneal nerve fiber density in fibromyalgia patients, correlating with various pain descriptors.
A detailed phenotyping study from the Netherlands found corneal nerve loss in 51% of patients with fibromyalgia, and this loss was related to central sensitization.
A study from Turkey found that reduced corneal nerve fiber length correlated with the widespread pain index in fibromyalgia patients.

In a large cohort of 117 women with fibromyalgia, multiple small fiber abnormalities were demonstrated, including a comparable reduction in intraepidermal nerve fiber density and corneal nerve fibers.
In a cohort of patients with idiopathic small fiber neuropathy, corneal nerve density and length were significantly reduced and related to sensory symptoms.

In a case-control study of 86 patients with suspected small fiber neuropathy, adding CCM and/or pain-related evoked potentials to abnormal IENFD and neurological exam increased the diagnostic yield for SFN from about 70% to 85%, while QST, QSART, and proximal IENFD contributed minimally.

In a small series of 4 patients who developed painful diabetic neuropathy during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, altered taste and smell and increased thermal thresholds were observed, suggestive of underlying small fiber neuropathy.

Corneal nerve loss and increased dendritic cell density were found 12 weeks after relatively mild COVID-19, particularly in those with neuropathic and fibromyalgia-like symptoms meeting criteria for long-COVID.
Patients with migraine showed reduced corneal nerve fiber density and length compared to controls.
Corneal nerve loss was demonstrated in patients with chronic migraine and photophobia, but not in patients without photophobia, suggesting photophobia-specific small fiber involvement.
A prior empirical study found that the strength of explosive synchronization conditions in the brain network strongly and positively correlates with chronic pain intensity in fibromyalgia patients.

In the computational brain network model, only increasing local structural connectivity (CI modulation) converted the abrupt first-order explosive synchronization transition into a gradual, second-order general synchronization transition, while decreasing connectivity or altering signal randomness did not.
CI modulation significantly decreased the positive correlation between node degree and node frequency (an ES-promoting network configuration) for most of the thirty target brain regions tested.
Connectivity-decrease (CD) modulation increased the degree-frequency correlation (an ES-promoting configuration) at several target nodes, the opposite of the desired effect.
Modulating the randomness of local node dynamics (increase, RI, or decrease, RD) largely failed to change the degree-frequency correlation, unlike connectivity-based modulation.
CI modulation significantly increased global network synchronization and signal amplitude, implying decreased responsiveness and a mitigated ES condition.

Increasing local structural connectivity centered on subcortical and cortical hub regions (e.g., putamen, pallidum, amygdala, insula, entorhinal cortex, accumbens, isthmus cingulate, hippocampus, temporal pole, caudate, precuneus) significantly decreased brain network sensitivity to external stimuli.

The degree of the targeted brain region negatively correlated with post-modulation responsivity and complexity, indicating that CI modulation of higher-degree hub nodes produced greater reductions in network sensitivity than modulation of peripheral nodes.
Randomness-based modulations (RI and RD) significantly reduced responsivity in some cases but did not produce consistent reductions in complexity, unlike CI modulation.

Prior brain imaging work (cited) found that the posterior insula and primary somatosensory/motor cortices join the brain's 'rich club' hub structure only in fibromyalgia patients with the highest clinical pain intensity, not in those with low pain intensity or in healthy controls.

The simulations identify the insula, left isthmus cingulate cortex, and right precuneus as the most effective hub target sites for connectivity-enhancing modulation to convert ES to GS and reduce network sensitivity, suggesting these as candidate noninvasive brain stimulation targets for fibromyalgia.

The authors speculate, based on prior findings that larger ES conditions in EEG networks predict larger hysteresis during loss/recovery of consciousness, that FM brains with larger ES conditions may show faster loss of consciousness and prolonged recovery during general anesthesia.
Suspicion of mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) was based purely on patient self-evaluation in 53% of the 100 patients studied, most of whom were female.

Among 100 patients with suspected MCAS, 87 different symptoms were reported, most commonly fatigue (n=57), musculoskeletal pain/weakness (n=49), and abdominal pain (n=43), with overall high disease activity and impact.
Only 2 of 79 tested patients showed an episodic increase in tryptase (>20% + 2 ng/ml) following a symptomatic episode, failing to meet the diagnostic criterion for MCAS in the vast majority.

Only 5% of patients showed a complete response to mast cell (MC)-targeted treatment as measured by patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), indicating poor treatment response in the majority of the cohort.
Depression and anxiety disorders were frequent comorbidities among patients with suspected MCAS, each affecting 23 patients, and 65 patients had pathological HADS scores.
MCAS was formally confirmed in only 2% of the 100 prospectively studied patients with suspected MCAS, indicating that mast cell activation is not the driver of symptoms in most such patients.
Elevated urinary histamine metabolite levels can help identify patients with mast cell activation who may not meet full criteria for mast cell activation syndrome.
Urinary prostaglandin D2 metabolite elevation is proposed as a biomarker that narrows diagnostic possibilities and identifies involved metabolic pathways in mast cell disorders.
Urinary leukotriene E4 metabolite elevation is proposed as a biomarker that narrows diagnostic possibilities and identifies involved metabolic pathways in mast cell disorders.

Serum tryptase has been the primary diagnostic biomarker for systemic mastocytosis and mast cell activation syndrome but requires acute and baseline samples taken at two separate visits with two venipunctures.
Hereditary alpha tryptasemia has recently been reported to cause an increased baseline tryptase level, complicating the diagnostic interpretation of elevated tryptase.
Baseline spot/random urine mediator metabolite samples can be self-collected by patients at the exact time symptoms occur, offering a practical advantage over serum tryptase testing.
Sera from 4 of 10 chlorhexidine-allergic patients induced mast cell degranulation upon challenge with alexidine, indicating IgE-mediated cross-reactivity between chlorhexidine and alexidine.
Sera from 3 of 10 chlorhexidine-allergic patients induced mast cell degranulation upon challenge with octenidine, indicating IgE-mediated cross-reactivity between chlorhexidine and octenidine.
Sera from individuals with isolated chlorhexidine-specific IgE (without clinical allergy) and from healthy controls showed no mast cell reactivity to alexidine or octenidine.
Unlike chlorhexidine, alexidine and octenidine, polyhexamethylene biguanide (PHMB) directly activated mast cells via occupation of the MRGPRX2 receptor rather than via IgE-mediated mechanisms.

PHMB-reactive sIgEs were found in some patients with isolated chlorhexidine sIgE, but these were unable to trigger PHMB-induced degranulation when MRGPRX2 was knocked down in mast cells, confirming that PHMB-induced degranulation is IgE-independent and MRGPRX2-dependent.
Luteolin inhibited FcεRI-mediated mast cell activation, including degranulation and cytokine release, in vitro.
Luteolin inhibited MRGPRX2-mediated mast cell activation, including degranulation and cytokine release, in vitro.
In a mouse model, luteolin reduced paw swelling and Evans blue dye exudation in a dose-dependent manner, indicating decreased vascular permeability associated with mast cell-mediated anaphylaxis.
Luteolin administration decreased serum concentrations of histamine, TNF-α, MCP-1, IL-8, and IL-13 in mice.
Luteolin inhibited mast cell-mediated anaphylactic reactions by suppressing the phosphorylation level of PLCγ, implicating calcium signaling regulation as the underlying mechanism.
Neonatal maternal separation plus early weaning (NMSEW) alone increased dura mater expression of the mast cell protease gene cma1 in adult female mice.
NMSEW alone increased dura mater expression of the inflammatory cytokine TNF alpha in adult female mice.
NMSEW alone did not alter sucrose preference behavior in either male or female mice.
In females, combining NMSEW with an adult mild stress (which alone had no effect in normally-handled animals) produced reduced sucrose preference, indicating a second-hit anhedonia phenotype.
In females, the combination of NMSEW and adult mild stress produced even greater increases in meningeal cma1 expression than NMSEW alone.
Systemic administration of the mast cell stabilizer ketotifen prior to adult stress prevented both the reduction in sucrose preference and the increase in cma1 expression in NMSEW females.
At baseline, female mice show higher levels of mast cell activation in the transverse sinus region of the dura mater compared to males.
In both males and females exposed to adult stress, early life adversity (NMSEW) increases the number of mast cells in the interparietal region of the dura mater.
In both males and females exposed to adult stress, early life adversity (NMSEW) increases mast cell activation levels in the sagittal sinus region of the dura mater.
D3R expression was significantly increased in ankle tissue of collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) mice compared to naive controls.
Pharmacological D3R blockade with NGB2904 and genetic D3R deletion both worsened arthritis severity (paw swelling, ankle width, arthritis score) in CIA mice.
