D3R-deficient mice exhibited significantly higher tnfa, il1b, and il6 mRNA in knee joints after CIA induction, and higher circulating serum cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-10, IL-4, IL-13) than WT mice, with no baseline difference in naive mice.

Mast cell markers FcεR1 and c-kit were significantly increased in the knee joints of CIA mice, and D3R deficiency further augmented both markers, with more mast cells visualized in D3R-/- joints by Toluidine blue staining.

The mast cell stabilizer ketotifen reduced ankle width, arthritic paw incidence, and D3R-deficiency-augmented proinflammatory cytokines in CIA mice, indicating mast cells mediate D3R's protective effects.
Conditioned medium from LPS/DA-activated mast cells significantly reduced primary chondrocyte viability, while medium from D3R agonist (7-OH)-treated mast cells restored chondrocyte viability.

D3R deficiency (via knockout BMMCs or shRNA in p815 mast cells) strongly augmented IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α expression, and neutralizing antibodies against these cytokines improved chondrocyte viability, confirming they mediate the mast cell-chondrocyte damage effect.

CIA significantly increased phosphorylation of p38, ERK, JNK, and their downstream molecules AP-1 (c-jun) and NF-κB (p65), with D3R-/- mice showing higher phosphorylation levels than WT mice; pharmacologic inhibition of each MAPK node reduced proinflammatory cytokine production in mast cells.

TLR4 protein was highly expressed in the knee joints of CIA mice and was further augmented in D3R-deficient mice; TLR4 knockdown abolished the excessive cytokine production induced by D3R shRNA in p815 mast cells.
D3R deficiency did not change tlr4 mRNA transcription levels in the CIA model, indicating D3R regulates TLR4 post-transcriptionally (via protein degradation) rather than at the transcriptional level.
The D3R agonist 7-OH significantly decreased TLR4 protein expression in the mouse knee joint in vivo, while D3R shRNA knockdown increased TLR4 staining in activated p815 mast cells in vitro.

Ubiquitin siRNA knockdown increased TLR4 expression and fully abolished the TLR4-reducing effect of D3R agonist 7-OH in mast cells, but D3R activation did not alter the amount of ubiquitin bound to TLR4, indicating ubiquitin is required for TLR4 degradation but its binding to TLR4 is not directly modulated by D3R.

The D3R agonist 7-OH increased LC3-II puncta/expression and decreased p62 in activated mast cells, and LC3 knockdown increased TLR4 expression, blocked TLR4-lysosome colocalization, and prevented 7-OH from reducing TLR4 and proinflammatory cytokines, establishing LC3-II as required for D3R-mediated TLR4 degradation.

D3R knockdown elevated phosphorylated mTOR and AKT but inhibited AMPK phosphorylation in mast cells, whereas the D3R agonist 7-OH had the opposite effect (inhibiting p-mTOR/p-AKT, promoting p-AMPK); pharmacologic modulation of AKT (GDC0068), mTOR (rapamycin), and AMPK (A769662) each reversed D3R-knockdown-induced excess TLR4 expression and proinflammatory cytokines.

GSEA showed that LRP1B mutation in HCC tumors was associated with enrichment of mast cell activation and mast cell-mediated immunity gene sets, along with humoral immune activation and negative regulation of cytokine production.

CIBERSORT immune-cell deconvolution showed that activated mast cells were significantly enriched in the LRP1B-mutant HCC group, whereas resting mast cells were significantly higher in the wild-type group.

Immune cell correlation analysis showed mast cell activation was positively correlated with dendritic cell activation and negatively correlated with resting memory CD4+ T cells, while resting mast cells positively correlated with M1 macrophage proportion.

In the retrospective clinical cohort, immunohistochemistry for mast cell tryptase showed significantly higher mast cell infiltration in tumor tissue from LRP1B-mutant patients compared to wild-type patients.
In the retrospective clinical cohort, patients with LRP1B mutation had significantly higher tumor mutation burden than those with wild-type LRP1B.
Multivariate Cox regression identified LRP1B mutation as an independent risk factor for shorter overall survival in HCC patients receiving anti-PD-1 antibody treatment.
LRP1B mutation was independently associated with shorter progression-free survival in HCC patients receiving anti-PD-1 antibody treatment, alongside treatment type.
HCC patients with LRP1B mutation had a 0% objective response rate and 45% disease control rate to ICI treatment, compared to 22% ORR and 65% DCR in wild-type patients.
LRP1B somatic mutation frequency in HCC was substantially higher in a Chinese ICGC cohort than in an American TCGA cohort.

HCC patients with high LRP1B expression (TCGA) had significantly shorter overall survival than those with low LRP1B expression, though LRP1B expression was not an independent prognostic factor on multivariate analysis.
LRP1B expression was positively correlated with infiltration of B cells, CD8+ T cells, CD4+ T cells, macrophages, neutrophils, and dendritic cells in HCC using TIMER analysis.
LRP1B methylation was significantly lower in HCC tumor tissue than normal tissue, and lower LRP1B methylation (also seen in the mutant group) was associated with shorter HCC survival.

Increasing complexity of naming-word (NW) and serial subtraction (SS) cognitive paradigms did not produce significant differences in bilateral cerebral blood flow velocity (CBFV) response at any time-point in healthy participants.
Both NW and SS paradigms induced a highly significant, temporally consistent bilateral rise in CBFV at stimulation onset, confirming that these tasks reliably evoke a neurovascular coupling response.

A significant interaction between timepoint and stimulation duration was found for the reference serial subtraction (SSREF) task in both right and left hemispheres, with significant CBFV differences across durations seen in the right hemisphere but not for the reference naming-word (NWREF) task.

Interhemispheric CBFV responses diverged by task type: left hemisphere CBFV was greater than right during R-word naming at T3, whereas right hemisphere CBFV exceeded left during serial subtraction tasks at later timepoints (T4-T5).

Varying the duration of stimulation (5s, 30s, 60s) for reference NW and SS tasks did not significantly alter the amplitude of the initial CBFV peak (T2), though only the 60s SSREF duration produced a secondary CBFV peak.
Patients with pulmonary sarcoidosis had significantly higher Small Fiber Neuropathy Screening List (SFN-SL) scores than healthy volunteers.
In patients with sarcoidosis, the most frequent clinical symptoms of SFN were impaired cardiovascular regulation (palpitations, dizziness), chest/limb pain, and blurred vision.
Skin biopsies showed intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IEND) values within normal limits but below average reference values in sarcoidosis patients.
A statistically significant negative correlation was found between intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IEND) and SFN-SL questionnaire scores in sarcoidosis patients.
Complaints typical for small fiber neuropathy were reported in 60% of sarcoidosis patients.
A US epidemiological study estimated the annual incidence of small fiber neuropathy at 1.3 per 100,000 with a prevalence of 13.3 per 100,000.
An earlier Dutch study reported a much higher minimum incidence (11.73/100,000) and prevalence (52.95/100,000) of SFN than the US estimate.

In a deep phenotyping study of idiopathic SFN patients, adding corneal confocal microscopy and/or pain-related evoked potentials to distal IENFD and neurological exam raised identification of small fiber impairment from ~70% to 85% of patients.

In subjects with impaired glucose tolerance followed over 3 years, those who progressed to type 2 diabetes showed significantly lower corneal nerve fiber density, branch density, and fiber length, whereas skin biopsy-derived IENFD and mean dendrite length did not differ from controls at baseline.
Subjects with persistent impaired glucose tolerance or those who reverted to normal glucose tolerance showed no significant change in CNFD, CNBD, CNFL, or IENFD over follow-up.

Patients with painful diabetic neuropathy showed lower corneal nerve fiber density, branch density, and fiber length, along with lower cold sensation threshold and higher warm sensation threshold, compared to those with painless diabetic neuropathy.
For diagnosing diabetic neuropathy, corneal confocal microscopy showed slightly higher sensitivity than skin biopsy (0.77 vs 0.61) with comparable specificity (0.79 vs 0.80).
In patients with sarcoidosis-related SFN, CCM detected small fiber neuropathy in a higher proportion of patients (45%) than skin biopsy (28%).
Small fiber pathology was detected via CCM in the cornea of about half of fibromyalgia patients, with four further subtypes identified based on CCM abnormalities and central sensitization.

Earlier studies of idiopathic SFN patients demonstrated decreased corneal nerve fiber density and increased nerve fiber tortuosity along with increased dendritic cells, suggesting systemic inflammation.

Brines et al. showed that CCM could differentiate metabolic (type 2 diabetes) from autoimmune (sarcoidosis) causes of SFN, with correlations between CCM variables being stronger in metabolic disease than in sarcoidosis.
Damage to thin A-delta and C-fibers in SFN is probably mediated by cytokines including TNF-alpha, IL-2, IL-6, and IL-8, though this mechanism has not been fully studied.
In some cases of idiopathic SFN, autoantibodies against potassium channels or nicotinic receptors have been detected, supporting an autoimmune etiology.

Skin biopsy studies found pro-inflammatory cytokine titers were higher in more distal body parts than proximal parts in a length-dependent manner, supporting a role for cytokine gradients in SFN pathogenesis.
Patients with autoimmune-associated SFN reportedly experienced beneficial effects from treatment with intravenous immunoglobulins or TNF-alpha inhibition.

The authors developed qpack, an open-source Python software package that automates calculation of QASAT scores (a quantitative scale combining cardiovascular reflex tests, transcranial Doppler, sudomotor testing, and skin biopsy small fiber density) to reduce calculation errors and improve reproducibility.
Among 234 lung transplant recipients treated over the study period, the incidence of persistent, symptomatic orthostatic hypotension was 5.6%.
A previously published pilot cohort from the University of Zurich found undiagnosed OH in 30% of 30 stable lung transplant recipients, with 3 symptomatic and 3 having supine hypertension.
All 13 patients with persistent orthostatic hypotension also had additional signs of autonomic dysfunction not attributable to OH alone.
Common symptoms in OH patients included dizziness (84.6%), limited ambulation (76.9%), falls (76.9%), and muscle weakness (69.3%).
Falls related to OH caused fractures in 46.2% of patients, with 38.5% requiring orthopedic surgery.
GI manifestations of autonomic dysfunction included ileus in all patients (100%), gastroparesis in 53.8%, diarrhea in 61.5%, and Ogilvie syndrome with cecal dilation >10 cm in 15.4%.
Urinary complaints (retention, dysuria, incontinence, hesitancy) occurred in 61.5% of patients with OH and autonomic dysfunction.
Tachycardia-bradycardia syndrome was observed in 15.4% of the patients with OH and autonomic dysfunction.
Labile blood glucose levels requiring frequent insulin dose adjustment occurred in 61.5% of patients with OH and autonomic dysfunction.
One patient developed sweating paroxysms with new-onset peripheral neuropathy, and another had dry mouth with oral mucosal fragility.
All 13 patients with OH developed renal insufficiency with eGFR less than 50% of baseline.
Patients with OH commonly had weight loss, with a median BMI decrease of 2.7 kg/m2 compared to pre-transplant BMI.
Among 8 male patients tested, 7 had hypogonadism, with median total testosterone 151 ng/dL, bioavailable testosterone 59 ng/dL, and free testosterone 25 pg/mL.
Three-year survival was significantly lower among lung transplant recipients with OH/autonomic dysfunction than among the remaining transplant recipients (46.2% vs 74.8%).
Persistent OH was treated with an escalating pharmacologic regimen of midodrine (100%), fludrocortisone (53.8%), and droxidopa (53.8%), along with mechanical measures.

Despite at least two treatment strategies, orthostatic hypotension remained difficult to treat in 53.8% of patients, and none of the 4 patients on triple pharmacologic therapy survived to the end of the study.
The authors hypothesize that intraoperative vagus nerve injury during lung transplantation may contribute to post-transplant orthostatic hypotension and autonomic dysfunction.

Citing prior literature, the authors speculate that calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus, previously reported to cause peripheral polyneuropathy in renal transplant recipients, could plausibly contribute to autonomic dysfunction after lung transplant.
The vast majority of lung transplant recipients who developed OH were male, leading the authors to hypothesize a possible role of sex hormones in this syndrome.
OH was typically diagnosed early after transplant, with 92.3% of patients diagnosed within 3 months.
The median postural drop in blood pressure among affected patients was 56 mmHg systolic and 25 mmHg diastolic from supine to standing.

Deconditioning and failure to thrive were present in all patients with OH, and decubitus ulcers developed in 15.4%; clinical depression was treated in 30.8% and one patient developed anxiety related to fear of syncope.
The OC-FCa faecal calprotectin assay had a limit of blank of 3 µg/g, limit of detection of 8 µg/g, and limit of quantification of 20 µg/g of faeces.
Within- and between-run imprecision of the OC-FCa assay was less than 5%.
The OC-FCa assay showed good linearity with R>0.99, appropriate detection of prozone effect, recovery of 99.6%, and no observed carryover.
OC-FCa results showed a strong positive bias compared with the BÜHLMANN fCALturbo faecal calprotectin method.
When categorised using the local diagnostic pathway, OC-FCa and BÜHLMANN fCALturbo showed substantial agreement (Cohen's Kappa = 0.80) for calprotectin concentrations below 50 µg/g.
OC-FCa and BÜHLMANN fCALturbo showed substantial agreement (Cohen's Kappa = 0.63) for calprotectin concentrations above 150 µg/g.
The OC-FCa faecal calprotectin method showed a strong positive bias compared with the BÜHLMANN fCALturbo method in a patient sample comparison.
Categorical agreement between OC-FCa and the local pathway interpretation was substantial (Cohen's Kappa=0.80) for calprotectin concentrations below 50 μg/g.
Categorical agreement between OC-FCa and the local pathway interpretation was substantial (Cohen's Kappa=0.63) for calprotectin concentrations above 150 μg/g.

Agreement between OC-FCa and the local pathway interpretation was only fair (Cohen's Kappa=0.22) for the borderline 50-150 μg/g category, indicating poorer concordance in this diagnostically ambiguous range.
Across 29 RCTs of SSRIs/SNRIs in fibromyalgia, patients randomized to placebo showed a large and statistically significant reduction in pain from baseline to follow-up.
Placebo-treated fibromyalgia patients showed the largest placebo response among the three outcomes in functional disability, improving significantly from baseline to follow-up.
Placebo-treated fibromyalgia patients showed a large and statistically significant reduction in depression scores from baseline to follow-up.
Across the 29 included fibromyalgia RCTs, on average about 22% of patients also had comorbid Major Depressive Disorder.
The fibromyalgia patient population studied across the 29 RCTs was overwhelmingly female, consistent with known sex distribution of the condition.
A genetic study found KIT tyrosine kinase gene mutations in the majority of IBS patients tested, suggesting a possible genetic basis for mast cell dysregulation.
Meta-analyses show increased mast cell counts in the small intestine and colon of IBS patients compared with controls, with greater lamina propria area occupied by mast cells.
A meta-analysis of 22 studies found mast cell numbers increased to a similar degree in both IBS-C and IBS-D patients in the descending and rectosigmoid colon.
Small intestinal mast cells were higher in 10 of 11 studies from a meta-analysis and two systematic reviews, with regional differences showing higher counts in the ileum than duodenum and jejunum.
Mast cell numbers correlated with bloating and dysmotility-like dyspepsia symptoms in an IBS study.
Female IBS patients had higher mast cell numbers than male patients in one report.
Lamina propria mast cells are increased in patients with chronic gastrointestinal symptoms following Campylobacter-induced gastroenteritis (postinfectious IBS).
Mast cells are located closer to nerve endings (within 5-10 microns) in IBS patients than in healthy controls, and this proximity correlates with abdominal pain severity.
Electron microscopy showed 77% of IBS patients had higher mast cell density with a 150% increase in degranulating mast cells.
Tryptase expression is increased in IBS-D compared with IBS-C, and levels correlate with stool frequency and consistency in IBS-D.
Serum cytokines including IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-alpha are increased in some studies of IBS patients.
Elevated mast cell-derived NGF correlated with higher mast cell numbers in an IBS study.
Mucosal NGF, NTRK1, and TrkA expression were increased in IBS, potentially driving neuronal sprouting and neuroplastic changes in colon mucosa.
In IBS-D colon mucosa, mast cell numbers increase alongside upregulated tryptase, iNOS, and IL-1beta expression, implicating nitric oxide pathways in mast cell function.
Mast cell counts correlated with mucosal substance P and VIP content specifically in female IBS patients.
Mucosal serotonin release and abdominal pain intensity correlated with higher mast cell numbers in an IBS study.

In mouse models, mast cell-derived PGE2 (dependent on functional COX2) rather than histamine or tryptase directly is the final mediator producing visceral hypersensitivity, as hypersensitivity was restored by wild-type but not COX2-mutant (Ptgs2Y385F) bone marrow-derived mast cells.
Estrogen and a GPER agonist increased mast cell degranulation, tryptase and histamine release, and hypersensitivity in a rat stress model, while ovariectomy decreased these activities.
A placebo-controlled trial found that ketotifen (mast cell stabilizer with H1 antagonist properties) decreased IBS symptoms and improved quality of life, but did not reduce mast cell numbers.
In a controlled trial in IBS-D patients, ketotifen reduced hypersensitivity to noxious rectal distention compared with placebo.
In a placebo-controlled trial in 28 IBS patients, the H1 antagonist ebastine reduced abdominal pain and overall symptoms and improved quality of life.

A retrospective analysis of 307 children with functional gastrointestinal disorders reported symptom improvement with cyproheptadine, an antihistamine with anticholinergic and antiserotonergic properties.
Double-blind trials showed cromoglycate was superior to placebo in reducing symptoms in IBS patients with food intolerance.
Two more recent controlled trials found mesalamine did not show benefit over placebo in IBS, contrasting with earlier positive studies.
Corticosteroids were ineffective for IBS in one report, possibly due to an inability to affect mast cell appearance and degranulation.
Of 54 IBS-D patients, 39% had increased intestinal membrane permeability measured by the lactulose/mannitol ratio, and this subgroup also showed increased visceral and thermal sensitivity.
Reductions in the tight junction protein JAM-A in IBS are associated with worse abdominal pain and longer symptom durations.
Intestinal tissues from IBS-D patients had increased levels of MIR29A, a microRNA implicated in regulating tight junction protein expression.
Low FODMAP diets normalize fecal LPS levels and improve IBS symptoms in IBS-D patients, accompanied by improved colon barrier function and reduced mast cell activation.

A blood panel measuring mast cell-released interleukins showed 88% sensitivity and 86% specificity in distinguishing IBS patients from healthy controls, though not specifically attributed to mast cell abnormalities.
Increased gut permeability occurs in some IBS subgroups, particularly IBS-D and postinfectious IBS, and correlates with altered bowel habits and increased abdominal pain.
Claudin-3 expression and epithelial barrier function are regulated by mast cell protease-4 (Mcpt-4), and Mcpt-4-deficient mice show permeability alterations similar to mast cell-deficient (Wsh) mice.
Transcellular permeability across rectal mucosa of IBS-D patients, measured with horseradish peroxidase, correlates with mast cell numbers and increased tryptase activity.
Tryptase and chymase cleave tight junction proteins including claudin-1, claudin-3, claudin-5, and JAM-A, disrupting paracellular permeability.
Elevated colon paracellular permeability in IBS-D results from tryptase acting on PAR2 receptors, potentially via MLCK or cofilin-dependent pathways.
MicroRNA MIR29 may regulate expression of tight junction proteins (cingulin, claudin-1) to increase intestinal permeability in knockout mice.
Mast cell-dependent pathways involving substance P contribute to Clostridium difficile toxin-induced intestinal secretion in mice.

In IBS-D, tryptase levels correlate with epithelial tight junction ultrastructural changes including dilated junctions, redistribution and decreased ZO-1 and occludin, and increased claudin-2 expression.
Reductions in JAM-A in IBS patients are associated with worse abdominal pain and longer symptom durations.
TNF-alpha disrupts tight junctions via MLCK-mediated myosin light chain phosphorylation and reorganization of ZO-1 and occludin.
Intestinal tissues from IBS-D patients showed increased levels of MIR29A.
Of 54 IBS-D patients studied, 39% had increased intestinal membrane permeability by the lactulose/mannitol ratio, and the same patients also showed increased visceral and thermal sensitivity.
The mast cell stabilizer doxantrazole reversed increased secretion and permeability in stressed rodents and reduced substance P-elicited secretion.

In a rat model of postinfectious IBS, Trichinella spiralis infection increased mast cells, altered cytokine production, enhanced permeability, and elicited hypersensitivity, and these barrier and perceptual effects were normalized by a PAR2 antagonist.
In maternally separated rats, metformin inhibited loss of tight junction proteins and improved permeability and hypersensitivity.
Cromoglycate blocked stress- and CRH-induced increases in small intestinal permeability in healthy humans.
IBS patients exhibit gut microbiota alterations including increased Firmicutes and reduced Bacteroides species, though findings are inconsistent across studies and geographic regions.
Enterococcus faecalis reduces mast cell degranulation in vitro.
Hypersensitivity to colonic distention in IBS patients can be transferred to rats via fecal bacteria transplantation, demonstrating a microbiota contribution to sensorimotor dysfunction.
Mast cells recognize bacterial products via TLR4 (LPS), TLR5 (flagellin), and TLR2 (peptidoglycan) receptors.

Ketotifen reduces enteritis from Clostridium difficile toxin, blunts Vibrio cholerae toxin effects, decreases epithelial passage of E. coli and Salmonella typhimurium, and reverses Salmonella-induced occludin decreases in animal/in-vitro models.
Miltefosine reverses hypersensitivity in maternally separated rats in association with microbiome alterations and reduced mast cell degranulation.
Fungicides fluconazole and nystatin reversed gut sensitivity in the maternally separated rat model, and the human mast cell line HMC-1 released histamine in response to fungal antigens.

FODMAP foods increase visceral nociception by inducing gut dysbiosis and elevated fecal LPS, mediating intestinal inflammation and barrier dysfunction, providing a mechanism for symptom exacerbation with FODMAP intake.
In IBS-D patients, low FODMAP diets normalized fecal LPS levels and improved IBS symptoms, accompanied by improved colon barrier function and reduced mast cell activation.
Headache was one of the two most frequent subacute neurological complaints, occurring in 42% of patients after mild COVID-19.
Cognitive dysfunction was equally frequent as headache, reported in 42% of patients in the subacute stage after mild COVID-19.
Sleep disturbance was reported by 36% of patients as a subacute complaint following mild COVID-19.
Prolonged anosmia persisted into the subacute stage in 30% of patients after mild COVID-19.
Prolonged ageusia persisted into the subacute stage in 22% of patients after mild COVID-19.
Fatigue was reported by 22% of patients as a subacute neurological complaint after mild COVID-19.
Dizziness was reported as a subacute neurological symptom in 8% of patients following mild COVID-19.
Female sex is one of the most consistent and credible predictive risk factors for ME/CFS diagnosis, with a female-to-male prevalence ratio of approximately 3:1.
Endocrinological events across the female lifespan—including menstrual cycle fluctuations, pregnancy, post-partum, and perimenopause—are associated with ME/CFS onset or symptom moderation.
There is evidence for gonadal sex hormone involvement in ME/CFS, including changes in estrogen and progesterone compound levels, which show established sex differences.
Renal neuroendocrine systems, including aldosterone, are implicated in ME/CFS and show established sex differences.
Adrenal stress axis changes, including cortisol level alterations that show established sex differences, are implicated in ME/CFS.
A multi-block PLS-DA model combining 32 variables (blood analytes, PBMC miRNAs, and EV physical features) perfectly discriminated severe ME/CFS patients from healthy controls.
A validation PLS-DA model trained on a calibration subset and tested on held-out participants maintained perfect classification (AUC=1) of ME/CFS versus HC.
Raman spectroscopy of plasma-derived EVs revealed significantly higher carotenoid content (bands at 1,158 and 1,521 cm-1) in severe ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
A PLS-DA model based solely on whole EV Raman spectra showed limited but above-chance ability to discriminate ME/CFS from HC.

Adding discriminant Raman wavelength intervals to the original 32-variable model produced a refined PLS-DA model with perfect classification (AUC=1) while reducing the number of required PBMC miRNAs from 21 to 7.
Blood creatine phosphokinase (CK) levels were consistently selected as a discriminant PLS-DA feature and had previously been reported as reduced in an expanded ME/CFS cohort.

Higher counts of circulating EVs have been consistently found in ME/CFS patients across different cohorts and isolation procedures, though EV count itself was not selected among the 32 discriminant PLS-DA features.
Increased absolute zeta potential (more electronegative) values of EVs from severe ME/CFS patients were detected, and were among the discriminant physical features selected by the PLS-DA model.

GO pathway analysis of the differentially expressed PBMC miRNAs selected by the refined PLS-DA model showed that six of seven share gene targets enriched in immunity, neuroinflammation, and metabolism pathways.

Increased mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC), markers related to decreased red blood cell deformability, were identified as high-discriminant variables in the refined PLS-DA model, suggesting a possible red blood cell origin for the observed EV carotenoid differences.
Prior studies have shown reduced red blood cell deformability in ME/CFS, which the authors speculate may relate to the RBC-origin EVs detected here.
More than 50% of ME/CFS patients could not start or failed to complete graded exercise therapy programs, contributing to NICE removing GET from recommended treatment guidelines.
Multiple studies report intestinal microbiota alterations and dysbiosis in ME/CFS patients, though results are inconsistent and the exact mechanistic role remains unclear.
One study classified 83% of ME/CFS patients correctly using gut dysbiosis combined with elevated blood inflammatory markers attributed to microbial translocation.
Improvements in neurocognitive symptoms after antimicrobial and probiotic interventions support the existence of gut-brain communication in ME/CFS.
Symptom improvements were reported after rectal infusions of cultured bacteria in ME/CFS patients.
Symptom improvements were reported after antibiotic treatment in ME/CFS patients.
Significantly elevated IgA (66.7%) and IgM (40%) antibodies against the microbial translocation marker LPS were found in ME/CFS patients and correlated with illness severity.
Increased bacteria were found in the blood of ME/CFS patients following an exercise test.
Endotoxin damage from Gram-negative bacteria and bacterial translocation may activate immune responses and systemic inflammation in ME/CFS.
Multiple research teams reported a reduced abundance of SCFA (especially butyrate) producing bacteria in ME/CFS patients.
Increased fecal SCFA levels have been found in ME/CFS patients in one study.
Increased fecal colonization of D-lactic acid producing Gram-positive bacteria has been found in ME/CFS, alongside decreased absolute fecal lactate levels.
It has been hypothesized that D-lactic acid accumulation from excess bacterial fermentation increases levels in blood and brain, causing neurological symptoms in ME/CFS.
Targeting D-lactic acid producing bacteria with antibiotics and probiotics showed no improvement in fatigue in ME/CFS patients.

Increased IDO activity, resulting in tryptophan depletion and kynurenine generation, produces symptoms similar to ME/CFS, with an interventional study suggesting this mechanism may be more important in disease initiation than in established disease.

An alternative hypothesis proposes that mutations in IDO gene isoforms result in low kynurenine levels and tryptophan accumulation, producing the typical pathological steady state and clinical presentation of ME/CFS.
A study found that 78% of tested non-antibiotic drugs inhibited bacterial growth, relevant to microbiome alteration in ME/CFS.
Antibiotics provoke a risk of D-lactate toxicity, which clinically correlates with ME/CFS symptoms.
Antibiotics induce ROS and oxidative stress that damage not only bacterial cells but also mitochondrial components.
Despite risks of D-lactate toxicity and oxidative stress, benefits in some symptoms of ME/CFS patients were also seen after antibiotic treatment.
Nearly half (48.7%) of male patients with post COVID-19 condition met criteria for late-onset hypogonadism (LOH) based on a free testosterone cutoff of 8.5 pg/mL.
Median serum free testosterone was significantly lower in the LOH group compared to the non-LOH group of post-COVID patients.
Serum free testosterone showed a negative correlation trend with age among post-COVID patients, but this did not reach statistical significance.
LOH occurred at similar rates in patients under and over 50 years old, showing that many young post-COVID patients developed LOH despite it typically being an older-age condition.
General fatigue, anxiety, dysgeusia, hair loss, and cough were reported more frequently by patients with LOH than those without LOH among the 27 symptoms surveyed.
General fatigue, the most common symptom overall, was reported by nearly all LOH patients compared to three-quarters of non-LOH patients.

Fatigue assessment scale (FAS) and self-rating depression scale (SDS) scores did not differ between LOH and non-LOH groups, while FSSG (reflux symptom) scores tended to be higher in the LOH group without reaching significance.
Blood hemoglobin was significantly lower in the LOH group than the non-LOH group among post-COVID patients.

Serum free testosterone correlated positively with hemoglobin, total protein, and albumin across the whole post-COVID cohort, but these correlations became insignificant when analyzed only within the LOH group, suggesting hypogonadism may partly drive impaired erythropoiesis and protein anabolism.

The authors hypothesize that SARS-CoV-2 infects ACE2-expressing testicular Leydig cells, potentially causing primary hypogonadism, based on prior reports of viral detection in cadaveric testes and Leydig cell ACE2 expression.
The authors cite prior studies reporting that lower serum free testosterone is associated with severe inflammation and poorer prognosis in acute COVID-19.
Participants who did not improve at 6-month follow-up had lower heart rate variability, indicating greater autonomic dysfunction, compared with those who improved.
Individuals who did not improve reported lower mean intensity of behavioral uplifts (positive daily experiences) compared with those who improved.
No significant differences were found between improvement and nonimprovement groups in any self-reported activity pattern, including push-crash, activity limiting, or healthy pacing behaviors.

Glutathione peroxidase activity increased in the serum of CFS model rats following DBT treatment.
Malondialdehyde levels decreased in the serum of CFS model rats following DBT treatment, indicating reduced lipid peroxidation.
Interleukin-6 levels decreased in the serum of CFS model rats following DBT treatment.
Tumor necrosis factor alpha levels decreased in the serum of CFS model rats following DBT treatment.

Lower hemoglobin was part of the biomarker set explaining 43.0% of variance in the fatigue/GI/muscle tension/sadness/insomnia factor.
Lower albumin contributed to the biomarker factor explaining 43.0% of variance in fatigue and physio-somatic symptoms.
Lower zinc levels contributed to the biomarker factor explaining 43.0% of variance in fatigue and related physio-somatic symptoms.

Male sex was associated with greater severity of irritability, concentration, and memory impairment symptoms among ESRD patients.
The hEDS group showed reduced pressure pain thresholds compared to healthy controls.
hEDS patients demonstrated significantly greater temporal summation of pain after repeated painful pressure stimuli than healthy controls, suggesting enhanced central pain facilitation.
Compared to healthy controls, hEDS patients showed significantly less exercise-induced hypoalgesia at the quadriceps test location after a submaximal cycling protocol.
At the trapezius test location, exercise-induced hypoalgesia did not significantly differ between the hEDS group and healthy controls.

No significant differences were found between the hEDS and control groups in conditioned pain modulation response, using pressure as test stimulus and hot water hand immersion as conditioning stimulus.
One of 12 patients with hypermobile EDS developed corneal ectasia in both eyes after myopic LASIK surgery.
Dry eye symptoms were present in 83% of the hypermobile EDS patients after LASIK.
46% of eyes in hypermobile EDS patients post-LASIK had punctate epithelial erosions or decreased tear break-up time.
The uncorrected distance visual acuity was 20/20 or better in 68% of eyes, and the best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 or better in 92% of eyes following LASIK in hypermobile EDS patients.
Manifest refraction remained within 1 diopter of plano in 79% of hypermobile EDS patients an average of nearly 14 years after LASIK, indicating low rates of myopic regression.
Overall, 92% of hypermobile EDS patients reported being happy with having undergone LASIK surgery.
Among 96 patients with germline TPSAB1 duplications causing elevated basal serum tryptase, 28% had joint hypermobility, a twofold increase compared to the general population.
In the same TPSAB1 mutation cohort, 46% of patients exhibited orthostatic intolerance, suggesting a link among POTS, EDS, and MCAD.

A retrospective analysis of over 2 million patient charts found a significantly increased prevalence of idiopathic urticaria among EDS patients compared to expected random co-occurrence in the general population.
In a retrospective case series of 98 EDS patients at a physical medicine and rehabilitation clinic, 24% had a diagnosis of MCAS.
In a retrospective case series of 15 patients with POTS and EDS, 66% had symptoms suggestive of a mast cell disorder.
Patients with phenotypical signs of connective tissue disorder had a higher density of chymase-positive mast cells in undamaged skin than those without such signs.
Among 140 patients with hypermobility disorders, 66% reported headache or neck pain, with migraine being the most common headache type (83%).
Headache was reported by 32% of hEDS patients, compared to 76% of fibromyalgia patients and 1.6% of rheumatoid arthritis patients.
A questionnaire study of 250 EDS patients found that 48% reported headache.
HSD/hEDS patients with migraine had significantly more frequent headache symptoms and earlier age of onset compared to migraine controls without hEDS/HSD.
In 20 adults with HSD/hEDS, 19 reported neuropathic pain and all 20 showed decreased intraepidermal nerve fiber density.
Among 40 EDS patients, 85% had mild-to-moderate muscle weakness, 60% had reduced vibration sense, and 13% had axonal polyneuropathy.
Among 37 hEDS patients, 97% reported severe chronic pain, most commonly neuropathic pain.
Tissue biopsies from the middle meatus of HSD patients with sinusitis showed increased density and abundant collagen fibrils compared to control patients with sinusitis.
In a case series of 20 EDS patients, 25% had recurrent sinusitis.
HSD patients had significantly higher prevalence of asthma symptoms/atopy compared to healthy controls (OR 2.7).
EDS patients had significantly higher prevalence of asthma symptoms/atopy compared to healthy controls (OR 3.1).
Joint hypermobility was present in 70.1% of asthma patients compared to 29.9% of matched healthy controls.
Patients with connective tissue disorder had an eightfold increased risk of eosinophilic esophagitis compared to the general population.
Among 31 hEDS patients, 16% were diagnosed with celiac disease, representing over a tenfold increase in prevalence compared to the general population.
30.8% prevalence of hEDS was found among patients with a primary diagnosis of celiac disease.
In a hospital-based cohort, hEDS prevalence was 12.2% among Crohn's disease patients and 3.6% among ulcerative colitis patients.
32% prevalence of HSD/EDS was found in Crohn's disease patients and 21% in ulcerative colitis patients.
Among 21 hEDS patients, IBD-like symptoms included abdominal pain in 61.9% and constipation/diarrhea in 33.3%.
Among 82 post-pubertal women with joint hypermobility, dysmenorrhea (82.9%), menorrhagia (53.7%), irregular menses (46.3%), and vulvodynia (31.7%) were reported.
Among 775 reproductive-age women with EDS, 44.1% reported infertility, 32.8% intermenstrual bleeding, 32.9% heavy menstrual bleeding, 92.5% dysmenorrhea, and 77% dyspareunia.
Among 386 women with hEDS, 76% reported menorrhagia, 72% dysmenorrhea, and 43% dyspareunia.
Genetic testing confirmed a COL3A1 mutation causing a glycine substitution in the triple-helical domain, consistent with a diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

Emergent total aortic arch replacement was successfully performed in a patient with vEDS presenting with type A acute aortic dissection, with complete thrombosis of the false lumen and no new aortic aneurysm or dissection on postoperative CT, and the patient remained free of arterial events 24 months after surgery.

The patient's arterial wall was noted intraoperatively to be thickened due to inflammation rather than fragile, unlike the classic 'tofu-like' fragility described in her brother's prior vEDS aortic surgery.

Prior literature (Pepin et al.) found that natural history of vEDS varies by gender and type of COL3A1 mutation, with female sex and glycine substitutions associated with a relatively better prognosis, and survival also varying by the specific amino acid substituted for glycine.
Prior literature (Frank et al.) reported that glycine substitution mutations in COL3A1 were associated with a later age at first significant complication compared to splice-site variants.

Vascular EDS has a prevalence of less than 1 in 100,000 and accounts for about 4% of all EDS subtypes; over 80% of patients experience a significant complication by age 40, with a median survival age of 48 years.
Pregnancy in women with vEDS carries an estimated mortality risk of 5.3%-6.7% due to peripartum arterial or uterine rupture.
In a Mayo Clinic series of 31 vEDS patients over 30 years, 70% of vascular operations were performed urgently or emergently, and mortality for these operations was 47%.
Pepin et al. reported a high operative mortality of 41% in cases of arterial complications in vEDS patients.
Only 26% of patients with vEDS are diagnosed before the presentation of complications, making preoperative recognition of mutation type and prognosis difficult.

Subscale analysis showed the HCTD group had significantly lower parent-reported scores on Physical Functioning, Role/Social-Emotional/Behavioral, Role/Social-Physical, Bodily Pain, Mental Health, Self-Esteem, and General Health Perceptions versus the US sample.

Both male and female MFS subgroups had significantly lower parent-reported Physical HRQoL sum scores than US population samples, with no difference in Psychosocial sum scores.
Parent-reported psychosocial HRQoL did not differ significantly between MFS subgroups and the general population, unlike the hEDS group.
Parents of children with hEDS reported significantly lower Physical (large effect, d=2.2) and Psychosocial (small-moderate effect, d=0.4) HRQoL sum scores versus the US sample.

hEDS subgroup showed significantly lower parent-reported scores across seven CHQ-PF50 subscales (Physical Functioning, Role/Social-Emotional/Behavior, Role/Social-Physical, Bodily Pain, Mental Health, Self-Esteem, General Health Perceptions), with effect sizes ranging from moderate to large.
Parents of children with hEDS, but not MFS, reported significantly increased distress and limitations in personal time compared with the US sample.

Self-reported MFS children (both sexes) had significantly lower Physical Functioning, Mental Health, and General Health scores, and females with MFS also reported significantly lower Bodily Pain scores, versus US norms.
Children with hEDS self-reported significantly lower scores across eight HRQoL scales including Family Activities, with effect sizes ranging from small to very large (up to d=2.0 for Bodily Pain).

Parents reported that children with HCTD had significantly higher Total Difficulties and Internalizing scores (small effects) and higher Emotional Symptoms scores (medium effect) on the SDQ than the Dutch general population, with no difference in Externalizing scores.

A significantly higher percentage of children with HCTD scored above clinical cutoffs for Total Difficulties, Internalizing, Emotional Symptoms, and Hyperactivity-Inattention on the SDQ compared with the Dutch sample, while also showing higher clinical-level Prosocial behavior scores.

Male and female MFS subgroups showed no significant differences from the Dutch general population sample on any SDQ sum or subscale scores, indicating no evidence of compromised parent-reported mental health in MFS.
MFS subgroups showed significantly higher clinical-level Prosocial Behavior scores than the Dutch sample, suggesting well-developed prosocial behavior despite no other mental health differences.

Parents reported significantly higher Total Difficulties (small effect), Internalizing (large effect), Emotional Symptoms (large effect), and Hyperactivity-Inattention (small effect) SDQ scores for the hEDS subgroup versus the general population, with no Externalizing difference.

A significantly higher percentage of children with hEDS scored above clinical cutoffs for Total Difficulties, Internalizing, Emotional Symptoms, and Hyperactivity-Inattention compared with the Dutch general population sample.
The paper investigates serum type III procollagen propeptide (PIIINP) as a candidate biomarker for vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

A patient was found to carry a novel pathogenic variant in COL5A1 that produced a phenotype resembling vascular EDS rather than the classical EDS phenotype typically associated with COL5A1 pathogenic variants.
The patient exhibited prominent vascular and cardiac features, an atypical presentation for COL5A1-related classical EDS, which is more commonly associated with skin and joint findings.
In vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, skin biopsy findings on light and/or electron microscopy are described by some dermatopathologists but are considered nonspecific by most specialists.

The definitive diagnosis of vascular EDS now relies on molecular genetic testing for COL3A1 mutations from blood or skin samples, which outperforms skin biopsy light/electron microscopy in sensitivity and specificity.

In hypermobile EDS, light microscopy may show elastopathy and electron microscopy can reveal variability in fibril diameter, irregular interfibril spaces, and flower-shaped fibrils, but experts agree these findings are nonspecific.

Because the genetic basis of hypermobile EDS remains unknown, diagnosis is mainly clinical and relies on the Beighton score for joint hypermobility, which has controversial sensitivity/specificity and high inter-examiner variability.

Skin biopsy immunohistochemistry for intraepidermal nerve fiber density using anti-PGP9.5 antibodies has high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing peripheral autonomic/small-fiber neuropathy and distinguishes affected patients from controls.
Col5a1+/− mice showed increased mean linear intercept (MLI), indicating enlarged alveolar spaces and reduced alveolar septal density compared to wild-type littermates in both sexes.
Internal lung surface area (ISA), calculated from MLI, was markedly reduced in Col5a1+/− mice of both sexes, reflecting loss of alveolar density.
Respiratory system resistance (Rrs) was significantly reduced in male Col5a1+/− mice compared to WT, but not significantly different in females.
Respiratory system compliance (Crs) was significantly higher in both male and female Col5a1+/− mice compared to WT.
Respiratory system elastance (Ers) was significantly reduced in both male and female Col5a1+/− mice compared to WT.
Broadband forced oscillation measures (Newtonian resistance, tissue damping, tissue elasticity H, hysteresivity) showed no statistically significant differences between Col5a1+/− and WT mice.
At maximal inspiratory pressure (30 cmH2O) on partial pressure-volume curves, Col5a1+/− mice of both sexes reached significantly higher lung volumes than WT.
Quasi-static compliance (Cst) derived from partial pressure-volume curves was significantly higher in both male and female Col5a1+/− mice compared to WT.
The K curvature parameter of the deflation limb of the pressure-volume loop was significantly lower in Col5a1+/− mice of both sexes, reflecting reduced elastic recoil at higher pressures.
The derived inspiratory capacity estimate (A) from partial PV curves was markedly elevated in Col5a1+/− mice of both sexes compared to WT.
The area enclosed by the inflation/deflation limb of the pressure-volume loop, indicating decreased elastic recoil, was larger in Col5a1+/− mice of both sexes.
Full-range pressure-volume curves showed higher inspiratory volume at maximum pressure (35 cmH2O) in Col5a1+/− mice of both sexes compared to WT.
Derived inspiratory capacity at 30 and 35 cmH2O static pressures was significantly higher in Col5a1+/− mice of both sexes compared to WT.
Total lung capacity (TLC) was significantly larger in Col5a1+/− mice compared to WT in both males and females.
Vital capacity (VC) was significantly elevated in Col5a1+/− mice of both sexes compared to WT controls.
Functional residual capacity (FRC) trended higher in male Col5a1+/− mice but did not reach statistical significance, and was not different in females.
Compliance derived from the lung volume protocol was significantly higher in male Col5a1+/− mice compared to WT, but not in females.
Specific compliance (compliance normalized to FRC), residual volume, RV/TLC, and airway compliance did not differ between Col5a1+/− and WT mice.
V10_TLC (volume at 10 cmH2O as % of TLC), an index of PV curve shape, was significantly reduced in male Col5a1+/− mice with a similar borderline trend in females.
Forced expiratory volume at 0.1s (FEV0.1) from NPFE maneuvers was significantly higher in Col5a1+/− mice of both sexes compared to WT.
Forced vital capacity (FVC) was higher in Col5a1+/− mice of both sexes compared to WT, with no difference in FEV0.1/FVC ratio, indicating no airflow obstruction.
A prior human case series of 252 EDS patients (including 33 with classical EDS) found clinically significant pulmonary symptoms in nearly half of all patients.
In the classical EDS subgroup of that case series, clinically significant shortness of breath and chest pain were found in about a third of patients.
A prior human study of mostly classical EDS patients found high prevalence of dyspnea and FVC/VC/TLC >120% of predicted, consistent with the increased lung volumes seen in the Col5a1+/− mouse model.
In contrast to the mouse data showing no change in residual volume, a prior human EDS study found elevated residual volume (RV) in over half of mostly classical EDS patients.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is characterized by reduced production of type III collagen, leading to unpredictable vascular lesions throughout the body.

Rare thoracic complications of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome such as recurrent pneumothorax or spontaneous hemothorax can occur, and this report describes an extra-pleural hematoma treated successfully with conservative management.

Sex showed only a non-significant trend toward women having higher total Beighton scores.

Age group was significantly correlated with Beighton score ≥4 and ≥5 thresholds, but not with the ≥6 threshold.

Across the reviewed studies, language disorders had the highest reported prevalence among EDS patients at 63.2%.

Anxiety disorders were reported at a prevalence of 51.2% among EDS patients.
Learning disabilities were reported at a prevalence of 42.4% among EDS patients.
Depression was reported at a prevalence of 30.2% among EDS patients.

Mood disorders were the most frequently reported psychiatric category in the EDS literature, addressed in 11 of the 23 included studies, more often than any other disorder category despite not having the highest prevalence figure.
Neurodevelopmental disorders were reported in 7 of the 23 included studies as a psychiatric comorbidity category in EDS.

The authors cite Eccles et al. describing overlap between hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and fibromyalgia, as well as up to 90% overlap between fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome, suggesting a shared disease spectrum.
The authors note that patients with Marfanoid phenotype may have elevated TGF beta1-beta2 levels, which is proposed to worsen COVID-19 clinical course and prognosis.

The authors cite Dotan and Shoenfeld describing autonomic dysfunction, pain syndromes, and elevated autoantibodies to β2-adrenoceptor, α1-adrenoceptor, and angiotensin II receptor type 1 in COVID-19 convalescents.
The authors cite Ursini et al. finding that up to 30% of post-COVID syndrome patients may satisfy fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria, with obesity and male gender as the strongest risk factors.
In a cited study of more than 900 fibromyalgia patients, COVID-19 infection worsened core FM symptoms including fatigue, sleep disturbances, and muscle stiffness.
The authors note that while 1980s studies suggested a link between ANA and idiopathic fibromyalgia (implicating connective tissue disease), other studies failed to replicate this association.

The authors cite Hafiz et al. finding that chronic fatigue was common in ANA-positive individuals without sufficient criteria for rheumatic disease, and that fatigue correlated with fibromyalgia-related symptoms but was not associated with systemic inflammation.
The authors cite recent studies showing increased ANA titers in patients with COVID-19, noting this requires further research regarding autoimmune prognosis.
Pretreatment with capsaicin suppressed lipopolysaccharide-induced inflammation in cultured myoblast cells.

Capsaicin acts as an exogenous agonist of TRPV1, and when TRPV1 is co-expressed with its human splice variant TRPV1b, capsaicin dose-dependently inhibits TRPV1 channel function, likely via TRPV1/TRPV1b heterocomplex formation.

In a chronic restraint/intermittent cold stress mouse model of FM, the capsaicin analog RTX desensitized capsaicin-sensitive neurons, decreasing mechanical hyperalgesia and heat pain intolerance without affecting anxiety, depression, or peripheral inflammation.
Low doses of capsaicin produced antidepressant-like effects and acted synergistically with amitriptyline, a common FM medication, in an animal model.
In FM patients, topical capsaicin cream applied to tender points decreased tenderness and increased grip strength, with only transient burning as an adverse effect.

Patients severely affected by FM treated with topical capsaicin cream showed short-term improvements in pressure pain thresholds, fatigue severity, and myalgic symptoms compared to controls continuing usual treatment.
Repeated application of capsaicin cream over six weeks produced desensitization to pain and a decrease in depression symptoms in FM patients (Casanueva et al.).
Incubation with 6-shogaol, a bioactive component of ginger, significantly decreased iNOS expression and thus diminished nitric oxide release in vitro.
Ginger extract increased antioxidant gene expression in human chondrocytes and reduced IL-1β-induced ROS, lipid peroxidation, Bax/Bcl ratio, and caspase-3 activity, decreasing apoptosis.

In female mice with intermittent cold stress-induced FM-like symptoms, ginger rhizome supplementation significantly decreased mechanical and thermal allodynia and mechanical hyperalgesia, and suppressed pro-inflammatory mediators NO, PGE2, TXB2, and IL-1β, with improved cognitive/anxiety/depression-related behaviors.
In a complete Freud's adjuvant FM-like symptom model, red ginger oil decreased chronic hyperalgesia and increased the thermal response threshold.

In a chlorpyrifos-induced oxidative damage model in female rats, 6-GRF decreased hydrogen peroxide and MDA levels, increased catalase/SOD/GPX, and decreased NO, MPO, and TNF-α, suggesting a protective effect against oxidative damage and inflammation.

In a dextran sodium sulfate-induced chronic colitis model, ginger-derived nanoparticles accelerated healing of wounded intestinal epithelial monolayers, increased anti-inflammatory cytokines IL-10 and IL-22, and decreased pro-inflammatory MPO.

In a DSS-induced ulcerative colitis model, curcumin reduced visceral hyperalgesia in a dose-dependent manner (no effect at lower dose) and decreased TRPV1 expression in dorsal root ganglia and inflamed colon.

Curcumin decreased visceral hyperalgesia via reduced viscero-motor response to colorectal distension, and in ex vivo jejunum preparations reduced TRPV1 activation/hypersensitivity of afferent neurons and attenuated capsaicin-induced calcium/current rises in DRG neurons.

Using a superoxide anion (KO2) donor model with subcutaneous curcumin, mechanical and thermal hyperalgesia were diminished along with decreased leukocyte recruitment, myeloperoxidase activity, oxidative stress, and pro-inflammatory cytokines.
Curcumin was shown to work similarly to gabapentin by decreasing levels of the excitatory neurotransmitter substance P in animal models.

Grape seed extract from Koshu grapes decreased H2O2-induced neuronal cell death via upregulation of IL-6, COX-2, and IL-1α in astrocytes, a neuroprotective effect abolished by co-treatment with anti-IL-6 antibody.
In an acidic saline animal model mimicking FM, OPC administration produced anti-hyperalgesic effects and decreased ASIC3 expression in the M1 and M2 brain regions of hyperalgesic animals.

In an exhaustive exercise-induced fatigue mouse model, GSPE supplementation increased swim time and fatigue threshold, decreased lactic acid/LDH/creatine kinase, increased SOD/CAT/T-AOC and decreased MDA/TNF-α/IL-1β, and increased skeletal muscle SDH and Na+-K+-ATPase activity.

In a double-blind, randomized, crossover trial in FM patients, 80 mg/day anthocyanins over three months produced small but significant decreases in sleep disturbances and fatigue compared to baseline.

In a thermally-induced pain sensitivity mouse model, concentrated fish oil supplementation decreased central amplification and nociceptive sensitivity to heat pain, potentially via suppression of c-fos and ASIC1a/ASIC1β/TRPV1 mRNA expression.

In a double-blind placebo-controlled trial, 35-day EPA/DHA co-treatment in female FM/musculoskeletal pain patients decreased the AA/EPA blood ratio and tender point number/pain intensity versus placebo, but produced no change in mood or sleep disturbance.

In a forced swim-induced FM-like symptom mouse model, repeated naringin administration improved neurobehavioral activities (increased locomotion, decreased immobility/depression/anxiety-like behavior, increased social preference/cognition), decreased AChE activity, increased SOD/GPX/CAT, and decreased MDA/nitrite levels in the brain.

Naringenin significantly reduced inflammatory pain across multiple FM-like pain models (acetic acid, PBQ, formalin, CFA, capsaicin, carrageenan, PGE2) via NO/cGMP-PKG-ATP-sensitive K+ channel signaling, prevented GSH reduction, and inhibited hyperalgesic cytokines (IL-33, TNF-α, IL-1β) and NF-κB activation.
In a thermal hot-plate FM-like pain model, naringenin reduced production of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 in skin and decreased leukocyte infiltration of paw edema.

In an exercise-induced fatigue model, naringin significantly increased exhaustive swimming time and blood glucose while decreasing LDH and MMP-9 levels, suggesting anti-fatigue effects via improved energy metabolism and reduced muscle damage.
Ginger administration acted synergistically with paracetamol to reduce inflammation and FM-like symptoms in an experimental FM model.
Curcumin exerts anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects by suppressing NF-κB, STAT3, Nrf2, ROS, COX-2, leukocyte recruitment and oxidative stress signaling pathways.
In a DSS-induced ulcerative colitis model, curcumin reduced visceral hyperalgesia in a dose-dependent manner and decreased TRPV1 expression in the dorsal root ganglia and inflamed colon.
In a colorectal distension model, curcumin decreased visceral hyperalgesia via a decreased viscero-motor response to colorectal distension in rats.

Ex vivo mouse jejunum preparations showed curcumin decreased TRPV1 activation and hypersensitivity of jejunal afferent neurons, and attenuated capsaicin-induced calcium influx in dorsal root ganglia neurons.

Subcutaneous curcumin decreased mechanical and thermal hyperalgesia and reduced superoxide anion-induced leukocyte recruitment, myeloperoxidase activity, oxidative stress, and pro-inflammatory cytokines in a KO2 superoxide-donor animal model.
Curcumin was shown to act similarly to gabapentin by decreasing levels of the excitatory neurotransmitter substance P in animal models.

Grape seed extract from Koshu grapes decreased H2O2-induced neuronal cell death via upregulating IL-6, COX-2, and IL-1α in astrocytes, and this neuroprotective effect was abolished by co-treatment with anti-IL-6 antibody.
Koshu grape polyphenols/procyanidin oligomers protected MAPK phosphorylation and dendritic arborization while decreasing apoptotic activity in glutamate-treated hippocampal neurons.
OPC administration produced anti-hyperalgesic effects in an acidic saline FM animal model and decreased ASIC3 expression in the M1 and M2 brain regions of hyperalgesic animals.

GSPE-supplemented mice in an exhaustive-exercise fatigue model showed increased swim time and fatigue threshold, decreased lactic acid/LDH/creatine kinase, increased SOD/catalase/T-AOC and decreased MDA/TNF-α/IL-1β, and increased skeletal muscle SDH and Na+-K+-ATPase activity.

In a double-blind, randomized, crossover trial in patients with moderate to severe FM, an 80 mg/day anthocyanin dose produced small but significant decreases in sleep disturbances and fatigue from baseline to the end of treatment.

Dietary supplementation with concentrated fish oil decreased central amplification and nociceptive sensitivity to heat-induced pain in a mouse model, partly via suppression of c-fos protein and ASIC1a, ASIC13, and TRPV1 mRNA expression.

In a double-blind placebo-controlled trial, 35 days of EPA and DHA co-treatment in female patients with musculoskeletal pain and FM significantly decreased the AA/EPA blood ratio and the number/intensity of painful tender points compared to placebo, with no change in mood or sleep disturbance.

Repeated naringin administration in a forced-swim FM-like mouse model improved neurobehavioral activities, decreasing immobility, depression-like and anxiety-like behaviors while increasing locomotor activity, social preference and cognitive performance compared to controls.

Naringenin reduced inflammatory pain in animal models across multiple pain induction methods (acetic acid, PBQ, formalin, CFA, capsaicin, carrageenan, PGE2) via upregulating NO/cGMP-PKG-ATP-sensitive K+ channel signaling, preventing GSH reduction, and inhibiting hyperalgesic cytokines (IL-33, TNF-α, IL-1β) and NF-κB activation.
In a thermal (hot plate) FM-like pain model, naringenin reduced proinflammatory cytokine production (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6) in skin and leukocyte infiltration of paw edema in animals.

In an exercise-induced fatigue model, naringin-treated animals showed significantly increased exhaustive swimming time and blood glucose levels, and decreased LDH and MMP-9 levels versus controls, suggesting an anti-fatigue effect linked to improved energy metabolism and reduced muscle damage.

In an acid injection-induced FM-like model, genistein produced antinociception for acid pain in muscle nociceptors by suppressing substance P-mediated inhibition of ASIC3-selective current and phosphotyrosine kinase activity.

Genistein treatment significantly reduced glutamate-evoked mechanical hypernociception in masseter muscles of animals compared to vehicle control, via suppression of the NR2B subunit of the NMDA receptor (pNR2B) and phosphorylated ERK1/2 signaling in the hippocampus.

In FM patients, increases in stress levels preceded increases in pain levels, and cortisol levels were positively correlated with pain levels, suggesting cortisol may be involved in the diurnal fluctuation of pain in FM.
Siglec-6 was highly and stably expressed on primary human skin-derived mast cells at approximately 100,000 receptors per cell, remaining stable through at least 10 weeks in culture.

Multiple human mast cell lines (HMC-1.2, LUVA, ROSA KITWT, ROSA KITD816V) all consistently expressed high levels of Siglec-6 regardless of KIT gain-of-function mutation status, whereas ROSA KITWT and ROSA KITD816V lacked surface Siglec-8.
The acute myeloid leukemia cell lines THP-1 and U937 also expressed high cell-surface levels of Siglec-6.

Single-cell RNAseq of esophageal biopsies from two patient cohorts showed SIGLEC6 transcript was detected exclusively in the mast cell cluster, in both control and active/inactive eosinophilic esophagitis biopsies, establishing Siglec-6 as a highly specific human MC marker in tissue.

SIGLEC8 transcript was likewise restricted to the mast cell population in esophageal scRNAseq data across control and EoE biopsy samples, though this is attributable to loss of eosinophil mRNA during scRNAseq processing rather than eosinophil non-expression.

Antibody-engaged Siglec-6 is internalized slowly and incompletely from the MC surface without evidence of receptor shedding, remaining at the surface longer than similarly bound Siglec-8 on the same HSMCs.

Pre-incubation of HSMCs with anti-Siglec-6 antibody reduced FcεRI-triggered degranulation, as measured by decreased β-hexosaminidase release, particularly at lower concentrations of stimulating anti-FcεRIα antibody.

Anti-Siglec-6 antibody engagement also reduced MC degranulation triggered by C5a receptor stimulation and by compound 48/80 (an MRGPRX2 agonist), indicating inhibition extends beyond ITAM-dependent FcεRI signaling to GPCR pathways.

The inhibitory effect of anti-Siglec-6 pre-treatment on FcεRI-triggered degranulation was maintained regardless of pre-incubation time up to 4.5 hours prior to stimulation, indicating a prolonged inhibitory effect that does not depend on timing.

Co-crosslinking Siglec-6 with FcεRIα using a secondary antibody reduced the peak proportion of CD63+ and LAMP-1+ activated MCs and shifted the dose-response curve so that ~4-fold more stimulating antibody was needed to achieve similar activation.
Co-aggregation of Siglec-6 with FcεRIα at a single antibody concentration reduced CD63 upregulation, tryptase release, and secretion of MIP-1β, IL-8, and IL-1β relative to isotype control.

Co-engagement of Siglec-6 with FcεRIα reduced phospho-ERK1/2 levels and reduced phospho-p38 levels to baseline, consistent with inhibition of activating kinase signaling via recruited protein tyrosine phosphatases.

Co-aggregation of Siglec-6 with FcγRII on THP-1 cells significantly reduced intracellular phosphotyrosine levels compared to FcγRII aggregation alone, extending Siglec-6's inhibitory activity to another ITAM-bearing receptor on a non-mast cell type.

Streptavidin-tetramer co-aggregation experiments showed that Siglec-6-mediated inhibition of FcεRI-induced LAMP-1 upregulation was not due to reduced FcεRIα crosslinking, since unbound FcεRIα epitope levels were unchanged by anti-Siglec-6 versus isotype control, confirming a genuine ITIM-based inhibitory signaling mechanism rather than steric interference.

MCs co-stimulated with Siglec-6/FcεRIα streptavidin tetramers were unable to fully respond to secondary FcεRIα stimulation 24 hours later, indicating that co-engagement of Siglec-6 induces prolonged desensitization of mast cells to activation.
Long-term treatment with drugs that effectively inhibit KIT function leads to virtual eradication of tissue mast cells and a sustained decrease in serum tryptase levels.
In patients with KIT D816V-positive mastocytosis, effective mast cell eradication requires a potent inhibitor of this mutant, such as avapritinib.
Surface expression of CD45 on mast cells in omental adipose tissue (o-WAT) was significantly decreased in T2D patients compared to non-T2D patients.
In subcutaneous adipose tissue (s-WAT), CD45 surface expression on mast cells also decreased with T2D but the difference did not reach statistical significance in any group comparison.
Surface expression of CD117 (KIT) on mast cells in o-WAT was significantly decreased in T2D versus non-T2D and in pre-T2D versus non-T2D.
Surface expression of CD117 on mast cells in s-WAT was significantly decreased only between non-T2D and T2D.
Surface expression of FcϵRI on mast cells in o-WAT was significantly decreased in T2D compared to non-T2D patients.
In s-WAT, there were no significant differences in FcϵRI surface expression on mast cells among the three groups.
Under normal (non-T2D) conditions, mast cells express higher levels of FcϵRI in o-WAT than in s-WAT, and this depot difference is present across all three glycemic groups.
Surface expression of CD203c on mast cells in o-WAT was significantly decreased in T2D and pre-T2D compared to non-T2D.
In s-WAT, CD203c surface expression on mast cells showed no statistically significant difference between groups, though a decreasing trend was noted, possibly due to small sample size.
RT-qPCR gene expression of CD117, FcϵRI, and CD203c followed the same trend across T2D groups as their surface protein expression measured by flow cytometry, reinforcing the protein-level results.
Gene expression of β-hexosaminidase, mainly produced by mast cells, was significantly decreased in T2D versus non-T2D in both o-WAT and s-WAT.
Multiple regression analysis showed that HbA1c was significantly associated with age and with CD45 surface expression on mast cells in o-WAT, with CD117 in o-WAT nearly significant.
Linear discriminant analysis showed CD45 in o-WAT, age, and CD117 in o-WAT had the highest correlations with the first linear discriminant separating non-T2D, pre-T2D, and T2D groups.

Random forest analysis identified CD45 and CD117 surface expression on o-WAT mast cells as the first and third most important variables (by mean decrease in Gini index) for discriminating T2D status, ranking above lipid metabolism markers and BMI.
Prior work from this group found that mast cell numbers increased 10-fold in o-WAT and 4-fold in s-WAT after bariatric surgery.
Anti-SFL3 IgG antibody levels measured after 14 days post symptom onset discriminated patients with severe/moderate COVID-19 from those with mild disease with high accuracy.
Anti-nucleocapsid (NFL) IgE antibody levels measured after 14 days post symptom onset also discriminated severe/moderate from mild COVID-19 disease with good accuracy.

IgG levels against NFL, SRBD, SFL3, S1sub and SFL, anti-SFL IgA, and anti-S1sub, NFL and SFL IgE were all significantly higher in patients with severe/moderate versus mild COVID-19 disease (>14 days post symptom onset).

In samples taken early in the disease course (3-14 days post symptom onset), anti-SFL3 IgG and anti-SFL IgA levels were significantly higher in patients with moderate/severe disease than mild disease, but with only moderate discriminative accuracy, and combining antibody markers did not improve prognostic performance.
Among individually predicted epitopes, the S7 peptide located in the SD1 subdomain of the RBD showed the highest IgG seroprevalence, suggesting it is the immunodominant B cell epitope within the RBD.
The positivity rate for anti-ORF3b IgG antibodies was correlated with COVID-19 disease severity, consistent with a prior report.
Anti-NSP1 IgG response was not significantly correlated with COVID-19 disease severity, contrasting with a prior study, possibly due to lower assay sensitivity for this antigen.

IgG antibody responses against a cluster of SARS-CoV-2 antigens (S2sub, SRBD, S1sub, SFL, SFL3, S7 epitope, M and NFL) were highly and positively correlated with one another, with no evidence of mutually exclusive antibody targeting patterns between severity groups.

This is the first study to report that SARS-CoV-2 elicits serum IgE responses against N, S and M proteins in COVID-19 patients, with levels positively correlating with disease severity, suggesting a link between antibody responses and mast cell activation.

The authors hypothesize that elevated anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibody levels in severe COVID-19 patients may contribute to mast cell activation syndrome and hyperinflammation, supporting prior reports that mast cells are activated in severe COVID-19.
The authors propose that the observed IgE-mast cell activation link supports the potential use of IgE-blocking drugs such as omalizumab for treating COVID-19, though this was not tested in the study.
IgM antibody levels against SARS-CoV-2 antigens were lower than IgG and rapidly decreased starting around day 18 post symptom onset in nearly all patients, indicating no stable plateau phase.
An immunohistochemical study found that intra-epidermal nerve fiber density was significantly decreased in patients with sensitive skin, indicating alteration of the Aδ or C fiber population.
CGRP-immunoreactive nerve fiber density was reduced in patients with sensitive skin, supporting a neuronal basis for the condition.
In a study of 70 women with sensitive skin, 20% exhibited characteristics of neuropathic pain based on the DN-4 questionnaire.
A case-control study of 42 patients found significantly increased DN-4 and Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory (NPSI) scores in sensitive skin patients compared with controls.

Quantitative sensory testing showed a significant decrease in the heat-pain threshold in sensitive skin patients versus controls, but no difference in vibration or cold detection thresholds, consistent with selective C fiber alteration.

fMRI analysis of cerebral responses to cutaneous provocation showed significantly increased cerebral activity in the self-perceived sensitive skin group, extending into the ipsilateral primary sensorimotor cortex and bilateral peri-insular secondary somatosensory area.
A literature review meta-analysis of 13 studies (20,486 subjects) found cosmetics were the strongest triggering factor for sensitive skin, with an odds ratio of 7.12.
Global epidemiological surveys found sensitive skin prevalence of approximately 50%, with women more frequently affected than men (60% vs. 40%).

Transcriptomic studies suggested that adiponectin deficiency may play a role in the uncontrolled inflammation seen in sensitive skin, along with involvement of innervation, Merkel cells, keratinocytes, and innate immunity.

A study using the SF-12 scale showed that the mental component of quality of life, but not the physical component, was significantly altered in sensitive skin patients; depressive symptoms were not generally associated with sensitive skin except in those with facial flushing.

Sensitive skin syndrome is frequently associated (comorbid) with irritable bowel syndrome and sensitive eyes, conditions proposed to share a small-fiber neuropathy basis with possible central sensitization.
The frequency of sensitive skin is increased in people with clear (lighter) phototypes, though ethnicity-based variation has not been conclusively demonstrated.

A recent study demonstrated that skin cells (keratinocytes and fibroblasts) from patients with usual small-fiber neuropathies can induce nociceptor degeneration and sensitization, suggesting a mechanistic continuum between sensitive skin and classical small-fiber neuropathies.

A two-step cluster analysis of PHQ-15 subdimension scores in 550 subjects with somatic symptoms identified four distinct clusters, suggesting functional somatic syndromes are separate constructs rather than one unified syndrome.

The cluster characterized by high pain-fatigue and comorbid somatic symptoms showed the greatest degree of symptom-related life interference, and the highest depression and anxiety levels among the four clusters.
The cluster with high cardiovascular somatic symptoms was characterized by high excessive worry over health and illness (health anxiety) and by lower educational level.
The cluster dominated by high gastrointestinal symptoms showed relatively low levels of psychopathology compared with the other symptom clusters.

The authors conclude that population-based clustering supports functional somatic syndromes (e.g., chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, IBS) as distinct constructs with different psychological features rather than manifestations of a single overarching somatic syndrome.
Serum Gremlin-1 levels were significantly higher in early diffuse systemic sclerosis patients compared to healthy controls.
Among SSc patients, those with interstitial lung disease (ILD) had significantly higher serum Gremlin-1 levels than those without ILD.
A weak negative correlation was found between serum Gremlin-1 levels and skin thickness score (mRSS) in SSc patients.
In a prior related analysis, cultured SSc dermal fibroblasts did not show elevated Gremlin-1 levels compared to control fibroblasts, despite serum being elevated.
Increased intake of lactose or fructo-oligosaccharides (FOS) caused dysregulation of the colonic mucus barrier in mice.
Mucus discharge in the empty colon was increased following lactose or FOS treatment.
Average thickness of the mucus layer covering the fecal pellet was decreased, with increased variability, after lactose/FOS treatment.
Mucus barrier changes induced by fermentable carbohydrates were correlated with increased mast cell counts in the colon.
AGE levels in colonic epithelium were increased by treatment with lactose or FOS.
Co-treatment with the anti-glycation agent pyridoxamine prevented the mucus barrier dysregulation, AGE increases, and mast cell changes caused by fermentable carbohydrate intake.
Fermentation of non-absorbed FODMAP carbohydrates by gut microbiota can generate the toxic glycating metabolite methylglyoxal, which contributes to AGE formation and AGER activation.
BMP2 increased hyaluronan production in primary human granulosa-lutein cells in a dose-dependent manner, with significant increases at 10 and 100 ng/ml but not 1 ng/ml.
BMP2 significantly upregulated HAS2 mRNA expression but not HAS1 or HAS3 in primary human granulosa-lutein cells, identifying HAS2 as the main synthase mediating BMP2-induced hyaluronan production.
In SVOG cells, BMP2 upregulated HAS2 mRNA in a concentration-dependent manner, beginning at 3 hours and persisting to 24 hours after treatment.
BMP2 treatment significantly increased CTGF protein levels in a dose-dependent manner in primary hGL cells, and also increased CTGF accumulation in the conditioned culture medium.
In SVOG cells, BMP2 increased CTGF mRNA levels starting at 1 hour and protein levels starting at 3 hours after treatment, preceding the rise in HAS2 mRNA.
Stable overexpression of CTGF in SVOG cells increased HAS2 mRNA expression and hyaluronan production, demonstrating that CTGF is sufficient to drive HAS2/hyaluronan upregulation.
siRNA knockdown of CTGF completely reversed the BMP2-induced increase in HAS2 mRNA and hyaluronan production in SVOG cells, showing CTGF is required for BMP2's effect.
Pretreatment with the receptor inhibitor DMH-1 (ALK2/3 inhibitor) completely abolished the BMP2-induced upregulation of CTGF mRNA and protein in SVOG cells.
Pretreatment with dorsomorphin (ALK2/3/6 inhibitor) completely abolished the BMP2-induced upregulation of CTGF mRNA and protein in SVOG cells.
siRNA knockdown of ALK2 completely reversed the BMP2-induced increase in CTGF mRNA and protein levels in SVOG cells.
siRNA knockdown of ALK3 completely reversed the BMP2-induced increase in CTGF mRNA and protein levels in SVOG cells.
Unlike ALK2 and ALK3, siRNA knockdown of ALK6 did not reverse the BMP2-induced increase in CTGF expression, indicating ALK6 is not required for this effect.
siRNA knockdown of SMAD4 completely reversed the BMP2-induced upregulation of CTGF mRNA and protein in SVOG cells, showing SMAD4 signaling is required for this effect.

siRNA knockdown of SMAD4 also completely reversed the BMP2-induced increases in HAS2 mRNA and hyaluronan production in SVOG cells, indicating SMAD4 is required for BMP2's downstream effect on hyaluronan synthesis.
Fibromyalgia is characterized by chronic generalized pain, fatigue, disordered sleep, and cognitive difficulties persisting for at least 3 months.
Fibromyalgia commonly co-occurs with irritable bowel syndrome symptoms, headaches, intermittent paresthesias, and various mood disorders.
Fibromyalgia affects women more commonly than men.
Management of fibromyalgia should be individualized, addressing mood disorders, sleep, exercise, maladaptive pain responses, and stress coping.
Maternal separation (MS) stress did not alter colonic sensitivity (visceromotor response) in male BBDP-N rats.
