Serum MMP-13 was higher in patients with less severe skin involvement (mRSS≤20) at baseline and remained higher after AHSCT compared to the mRSS>20 group.
Cutaneous TGF-β expression was higher in patients with less severe skin involvement (mRSS≤20) than in the mRSS>20 group, both at baseline and after AHSCT.
Post-AHSCT change in cutaneous MMP-3 expression was significantly greater in patients with more severe baseline skin involvement (mRSS>20) than in those with mRSS≤20.
Post-AHSCT decrease in serum PDGF-BB was significantly greater in patients with more severe baseline skin involvement (mRSS>20) than in those with mRSS≤20.
Whole-exome sequencing identified a novel heterozygous missense mutation (c.220A>C, p.Thr74Pro) in exon 1 of TGFB2 in the proband, consistent with a diagnosis of Loeys-Dietz syndrome type 4.

Sanger sequencing confirmed the same TGFB2 mutation in the proband's sister and niece, who exhibited similar clinical features including lower extremity deformities and pes planus, supporting segregation of the variant with disease.
Echocardiography in the proband revealed dilatation of the aortic root at the level of the sinuses of Valsalva, a vascular manifestation of the TGFB2-related connective tissue disorder.
The identified TGFB2 variant was absent from ExAC and 1000 Genomes population databases and was predicted to be deleterious, supporting its pathogenicity.
Lower serotonin levels have been detected in fibromyalgia patients, with this imbalance linked to fatigue and cognitive deficits.
Disruption of serotonin balance has been associated with irritable bowel syndrome, celiac disease, neuroendocrine tumors, obesity and type 2 diabetes.

Increased quantities of serotonin-producing enterochromaffin cells have been observed in Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, linked to serotonin-dependent angiogenesis and increased gut vascularity.
Dysregulation of serotonergic signaling pathways has been implicated in migraine headache among other neurological and psychiatric conditions.
Dysregulation of serotonergic signaling pathways has also been implicated in autism spectrum disorder.
Melatonin level dysregulation is implicated in autism, along with epilepsy, anxiety, bipolar disorder, and depression, due to melatonin's role in circadian rhythm-dependent processes.
Impairment of the microbiome-gut-brain axis has been associated with IBS, as well as ASD, anxiety, depression, and Parkinson's disease.
Impairment of the microbiome-gut-brain axis has also been associated with autism spectrum disorder.
Germ-free mice have low blood and colon levels of serotonin compared to conventionally colonized mice, indicating gut microbiota regulate host serotonin production.

Turicibacter sanguinis regulates intestinal epithelial and luminal serotonin levels via a membrane transporter that imports serotonin to favor its own colonization, and alters host lipid/steroid metabolism, reducing systemic triglycerides and inguinal adipocyte size.
Short-chain fatty acids influence Tph1 mRNA levels in enterochromaffin cells, resulting in higher intestinal serotonin levels.
Fecal metabolites produced by Clostridial species increase serotonin levels in enterochromaffin cell cultures and in germ-free mice.
Elevated plasma tryptophan levels observed in germ-free mice normalize after gut microbial colonization, suggesting bacteria consume host tryptophan.
Oral administration of Campylobacter jejuni in mice caused anxiety-like behavior mediated through vagus nerve communication.

Ruminococcus gnavus tryptophan decarboxylase (TrpD) homologs were found in 9-17% of examined human gut metagenome samples, suggesting these bacteria may sequester dietary tryptophan and limit its availability to the host.
Tyrosine decarboxylase from gut Enterococcus and Lactobacillus strains converts the Parkinson's drug L-DOPA into dopamine, explaining why some patients require increased L-DOPA dosage.

IDO-1 is upregulated by cytokines and inflammatory molecules (LPS, amyloid peptides, IFN-γ), diverting tryptophan into the kynurenine pathway, linked to depressive states in chronic inflammatory diseases such as cancer and neurological disorders.
Serotonin levels decrease with age and neuroinflammation is associated with reduced serotonin precursors in the CNS, implicated in neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease.

The percentage of nNOS-immunoreactive neurons in myenteric ganglia of the large and small intestine was highest in newborn rats and decreased progressively until 60 days of age, after which it remained stable into senescence.

In the submucous plexus, nNOS-immunoreactive neurons were abundant in newborns, decreased sharply over the next 20 days and became very sparse by 30 days and 2 months, then reappeared in large numbers in aged rats.

In the myenteric plexus, the proportion of neurons co-expressing nNOS and choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) was highest in 1-day-old, 10-day-old, and 2-year-old rats, whereas in the submucous plexus co-localization with ChAT was high regardless of age.

In the myenteric plexus of all age groups, many nNOS-immunoreactive neurons colocalized VIP, with the maximal percentage of nNOS+/VIP+ neurons found in 2-year-old rats and the minimal percentage in newborns.

Self-reported chronic pain at baseline was associated with a higher risk of COVID-19 hospitalisation, with the association attenuated but remaining significant after adjustment for confounders and long-term conditions.
Number of chronic pain sites showed a dose-response relationship with COVID-19 hospitalisation risk, with those reporting pain at 4-7 sites having the highest risk even after full adjustment.
Chronic widespread pain (pain all over the body) was associated with COVID-19 hospitalisation, an association that persisted, though attenuated, after full adjustment.
The univariable association between chronic pain and COVID-19 mortality was fully attenuated to null after adjustment for confounders and long-term conditions.

A dose-response relationship between number of chronic pain sites and COVID-19 mortality was seen unadjusted and remained significant after adjusting for sociodemographic/lifestyle confounders, but was no longer significant after additionally adjusting for long-term conditions.
Chronic widespread pain was associated with increased COVID-19 mortality, an association that was attenuated but remained significant after full adjustment.
There was no clear association between chronic pain (binary or by number of sites) and COVID-19 case fatality among those hospitalised, with hazard ratios close to 1.

Chronic widespread pain showed a suggestion of increased COVID-19 case fatality among hospitalised patients, but the confidence interval was wide and not statistically significant, possibly reflecting the rarity of the outcome.

IL-6Ra mRNA expression was significantly reduced in the hippocampus and hypothalamus of IL-6Ra KD mice compared to Cre+/- controls, but not in cerebellum or frontal cortex, indicating region-specific (limbic) knockdown.
IL-6 stimulation increased p-STAT3 in hypothalamic slices from control mice but produced no change in IL-6Ra KD mice, demonstrating blunted central IL-6 signaling in the knockdown model.

Leptin injection produced an equivalent robust increase in hypothalamic p-STAT3 in both IL-6Ra KD and control mice, showing that leptin signaling fidelity is preserved despite reduced central IL-6Ra expression.

IL-6 injection stimulated increased p-STAT3 in liver, skeletal muscle, and white adipose tissue equally across genotypes, showing that peripheral IL-6 signaling is not impaired by the central/limbic IL-6Ra knockdown.
On standard chow, IL-6Ra KD mice had reduced percentage body fat mass compared with Cre+/- controls, whereas on high-fat diet they instead showed increased percentage body fat mass.
IL-6Ra KD mice demonstrated hyperphagia compared to Cre+/- controls on both standard chow and high-fat diets.

Fasted basal plasma insulin levels were lower in IL-6Ra KD mice compared to Cre+/- controls on standard chow diet, but this difference was absent under high-fat feeding where both genotypes were hyperinsulinemic.
Circulating NEFA levels were reduced in SC-fed IL-6Ra KD mice but elevated in HF-fed IL-6Ra KD mice, relative to genotype-matched Cre+/- controls.
Plasma IL-6 levels were elevated in IL-6Ra KD mice relative to controls on standard chow, and were increased by high-fat feeding in Cre+/- controls but not in IL-6Ra KD mice.
RER was significantly higher in IL-6Ra KD mice than Cre+/- controls during both light and dark phases on either diet, indicating a shift toward greater glucose oxidation and reduced fat oxidation.
IL-6Ra KD mice showed lower energy expenditure than Cre+/- mice, in both light and dark phases on standard chow and in the light phase on high-fat diet, independent of lean body mass.

During a 4°C cold challenge, IL-6Ra KD mice were less able to maintain core body temperature than Cre+/- controls, with a significantly greater temperature drop over 6 hours, necessitating early termination of the experiment.
High-fat fed IL-6Ra KD mice developed significantly greater hepatic triglyceride accumulation (steatosis) than HF-fed Cre+/- controls, while no difference was seen between genotypes on standard chow.
Hepatic Igfbp1 expression, a predictive marker of liver lipid accumulation, was increased in HF-fed IL-6Ra KD mice.

Glucose clearance during an oral glucose tolerance test was mildly impaired in IL-6Ra KD mice compared to controls on both standard chow and high-fat diets, with increased area-under-curve glucose excursion, while insulin sensitivity (ITT) was unaffected.

In vivo insulin secretion in response to an oral glucose challenge was substantially suppressed in IL-6Ra KD mice compared to controls on both standard chow and high-fat diets, accompanied by impaired glucose clearance.

Isolated pancreatic islets from IL-6Ra KD mice secreted insulin in response to high glucose or KCl challenge to a similar extent as islets from Cre+/- controls, indicating normal intrinsic beta-cell function despite the in vivo insulin secretion defect.

Blockade of autonomic ganglionic transmission with hexamethonium restored in vivo glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in IL-6Ra KD mice to a level indistinguishable from Cre+/- controls, implicating altered autonomic nervous system output as the mechanism underlying the impaired insulin secretion phenotype.
Pancreatic islet area and morphology (beta/alpha cell composition) were comparable between IL-6Ra KD and Cre+/- control mice.

Across all participants, negative background pictures caused a greater reduction in steady-state visual evoked potential (ssVEP) amplitude than neutral pictures, reflecting greater distraction by negative content.
Fibromyalgia patients showed overall reduced ssVEP responsivity to the task stimulus compared with healthy controls.

A significant triple interaction of time-window, group, and distractor-valence showed that FMS patients and healthy controls displayed distinct temporal dynamics in their ssVEP response to emotional versus neutral distractors.
During the early time window, healthy controls but not fibromyalgia patients were able to discriminate between neutral and negative background distractors in ssVEP amplitude.

In the late time window, fibromyalgia patients showed a strong attentional shift toward the negative stimulus, whereas healthy controls showed habituation/adaptation to it, indicating reduced normal habituation in FMS.

Fronto-occipital phase-locking values (an EEG connectivity index) showed different time-window dynamics between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls, with time-dependent changes present only in FMS.

Greater initial (early time-window) ssVEP amplitude bias toward the neutral rather than negative stimulus was correlated with more severe pain, as measured by the McGill pain questionnaire, in FMS patients.

The difference in fronto-occipital phase-locking values between early and late time-windows (transient disruption of synchrony upon viewing the distractor) was correlated with subjective sleep disturbance severity (PSQI) in FMS patients, and this correlation strengthened after controlling for anxiety, depression and pain.
Subjective anxiety (STAI-T) and depression severity (BDI) were not correlated with any of the altered ssVEP indices in FMS patients.
Within FMS patients, pain severity (McGill) was correlated with anxiety (STAI-T) and depression (BDI) scores, but not with sleep quality.
Depression and anxiety symptoms were highly correlated with each other in FMS patients, and sleep quality correlated with depression but not anxiety.
FMS patients as a group reported clinically significant pain, moderate-to-high anxiety, mild-to-moderate depression, and poor sleep quality (above clinical cutoff) at baseline.
Multisensory sensitivity to nonpainful stimuli was highest in fibromyalgia, followed by migraine, then low back pain, and lowest in pain-free individuals.
Patients with a single pain condition other than fibromyalgia did not show significantly elevated multisensory sensitivity compared to pain-free individuals.
Elevated multisensory sensitivity was associated with a 2-fold increase in the odds of having two or more pain comorbidities, excluding fibromyalgia.
Elevated multisensory sensitivity was associated with a 5.6-fold increase in the odds of having two or more pain comorbidities when fibromyalgia was included.
Low multisensory sensitivity levels were associated with 55% lower odds of having two or more pain comorbidities, excluding fibromyalgia, acting as a resilience marker.
Low multisensory sensitivity levels were associated with 87% lower odds of having two or more pain comorbidities when fibromyalgia was included, acting as a resilience marker.
Baseline serum tryptase levels were significantly higher in patients with indolent systemic mastocytosis than in patients with hereditary alpha-tryptasemia.
Patients with indolent systemic mastocytosis had significantly higher levels of urinary N-methylhistamine compared with patients with hereditary alpha-tryptasemia.
Patients with indolent systemic mastocytosis had significantly higher levels of urinary 2,3-dinor-11β-prostaglandin F2α compared with patients with hereditary alpha-tryptasemia.
Patients with symptomatic hereditary alpha-tryptasemia did not show elevated urinary mast cell mediator metabolites, suggesting granule- and membrane-derived mediators may not drive their symptoms.
Skin biopsy demonstrating loss of intraepidermal nerve fibers is a useful diagnostic tool for small-fiber neuropathy, with a reported diagnostic sensitivity of 80%.
The underlying cause of small-fiber neuropathy remains unidentified in 30-50% of cases despite many reported etiologies.
Patients with small-fiber neuropathy frequently show additional autonomic involvement affecting the gastrointestinal, urinary, or cardiovascular systems.
In small-fiber neuropathy, deep-tendon reflexes and standard nerve conduction studies typically yield normal results, distinguishing it from large-fiber neuropathies.
The patient with treatment-resistant small fiber neuropathy tested positive for anti-plexin D1 antibody by ELISA, supporting an autoimmune etiology.
Plasma exchange therapy was remarkably effective in treating the anti-plexin D1 antibody-positive autoimmune small fiber neuropathy case that had been unresponsive to symptomatic treatment.

The cause of small fiber neuropathy remains unknown in about 70% of cases, and among cases with known etiology roughly 50% are associated with diabetes, with others attributed to autoimmune, amyloidosis, or multifactorial causes.
A specific autoantibody-positive subgroup of SFN patients has been identified in recent years, in whom immunotherapy has been reported successful.
The paper notes an association between COVID-19 and small fiber neuropathy, which it intends to discuss alongside general SFN treatments.
After 4 weeks of streptozotocin-induced diabetes, mice showed significantly reduced corneal nerve occupancy limited to the middle of the sub-basal nerve plexus.
At 12-week study end, vehicle-treated diabetic mice had significantly reduced sub-basal nerve plexus density compared with vehicle-treated controls and diabetic mice treated with CNTF or exendin-4.

Nerve density in the superficial corneal stroma was not significantly different between diabetic and control groups at study end, indicating diabetes-related nerve loss was confined to the sub-basal plexus.
Topical ocular treatment with ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF) for the final 2 weeks of a 12-week diabetes protocol restored/prevented reduction of sub-basal corneal nerve density in diabetic mice.
Topical ocular treatment with the GLP-1 agonist exendin-4 for the final 2 weeks of the study restored corneal sub-basal nerve density in diabetic mice.
Topical ocular cyclopentolate (0.5-2.0%) for the final 4 weeks of an 8-week diabetes protocol prevented the diabetes-induced decline in sub-basal corneal nerve density.
Cyclopentolate caused dose-dependent alleviation of small fiber-mediated paw heat hypoalgesia in diabetic mice.
Cyclopentolate prevented large fiber motor nerve conduction velocity (MNCV) slowing in diabetic mice in a dose-dependent manner.
Cyclopentolate did not prevent large-fiber-mediated tactile allodynia (von Frey filament response) in diabetic mice, despite improving other neuropathy indices.
Systemic subcutaneous glycopyrrolate for 12 weeks starting at diabetes onset prevented reduced sub-basal corneal nerve density in diabetic mice, whereas gallamine did not.
Systemic gallamine (M2R-selective muscarinic antagonist) did not prevent the reduction in sub-basal corneal nerve density seen in diabetic mice.
Systemic glycopyrrolate prevented small fiber-mediated paw heat hypoalgesia and large fiber MNCV slowing in diabetic mice, whereas gallamine did not affect either measure.
Tactile allodynia (von Frey response) was not prevented by either glycopyrrolate or gallamine treatment in diabetic mice.
Twelve weeks of systemic gallamine treatment prevented weight gain in diabetic mice, resulting in significantly lower body weight than vehicle-treated diabetic mice at study end (adverse effect).
None of the tested treatments (CNTF, exendin-4, cyclopentolate, glycopyrrolate, gallamine) altered the severity of streptozotocin-induced hyperglycemia.
The corneal nerve deficit in diabetic mice was confined to the sub-basal nerve plexus with unaffected stromal nerve density, consistent with a 'dying back' pattern of small fiber neuropathy.

The M2R-selective antagonist gallamine had no effect on any measure of peripheral neuropathy, consistent with its lack of effect on sensory neurite outgrowth in vitro and the specificity of neuroprotection to M1 receptor antagonism.

M1 receptor-selective muscarinic antagonists (e.g., pirenzepine) have been previously reported to promote neurite growth in adult sensory neurons in vitro and correct multiple indices of neuropathy when given systemically to diabetic rodents.

Unlike other muscarinic antagonists tested, the selective M1R antagonist pirenzepine has been reported to prevent tactile allodynia when given systemically or applied topically to the paw of diabetic rodents.

In a prior study, low-dose systemic distribution of atropine applied to the paw of diabetic mice improved MNCV slowing and paw thermal hypoalgesia but did not prevent loss of corneal nerves, highlighting a discrepancy between systemic and corneal drug access.
Small fiber neuropathy is reported in over 40% of patients with systemic sarcoidosis, making it a common non-granulomatous peripheral nerve manifestation.
Granulomatous neuropathy in sarcoidosis is rare and typically presents as distal symmetric polyneuropathy or asymmetric polyradiculoneuropathy.
Granulomatous neuropathy in sarcoidosis typically responds to corticosteroid treatment.
Small fiber neuropathy associated with sarcoidosis may improve with intravenous immune globulin (IVIG) treatment.
Small fiber neuropathy associated with sarcoidosis may improve with infliximab treatment.
Small fiber neuropathy in sarcoidosis characteristically presents as non-length dependent pain and paresthesias, distinguishing it clinically from granulomatous neuropathy.

In male Fabry patients, withdrawal latency to painful heat stimuli (WLPHS) increased significantly with age and was markedly longer than in male controls, indicating progressive C-fiber (small-fiber) dysfunction.
SF-MPQ pain scores in male Fabry patients did not increase linearly with age but instead showed a bell-shaped distribution, peaking between the early 20s and late 40s and declining after age 48.
Female Fabry patients showed only mildly increased WLPHS compared with female controls, and this difference was not statistically significant.

Male Fabry patients had significantly greater increases in withdrawal latency to painful heat stimuli with age than female Fabry patients, indicating more severe small-fiber (C-fiber) dysfunction in males.
Neither male nor female Fabry patients showed a significant correlation between SF-MPQ pain scores and WLPHS values.
The authors' previous study found significantly lower AGA enzyme activity levels in male Fabry patients compared to female Fabry patients, consistent with more severe nerve fiber loss in males.
Enzyme replacement therapy has been reported in other studies to improve pain scores, quality of life, and C-fiber function in Fabry disease patients.
The IOM report estimates 83,000 to 2.5 million individuals suffer from ME/CFS in the United States, with an annual economic burden of 17-24 billion USD.
A four-year Wichita, Kansas study found a CFS prevalence of 235 per 100,000 persons, occurring four times more commonly in women than men.
Pro-inflammatory cytokines induce IDO-1 activity, the primary rate-limiting enzyme diverting tryptophan into the kynurenine pathway in ME/CFS.
ME/CFS severity may correlate with poor NK cell function, and low-functioning NK cells increase susceptibility to viral infections such as EBV, CMV, and human herpesviruses.
Up to 60% of ME/CFS patients have high titre autoantibodies, including IgM-associated responses against degraded membrane lipids and S-farnesyl-l-cysteine.

Nakatomi et al. (2014) reported increased binding potential of the microglial activation ligand 11C-(R)-PK11195 in the brains of ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls, indicating microglial activation.

IL-1β, released by activated microglia, is detected at significantly high concentrations in ME/CFS patients and can induce upregulation of astrocytic serotonin transporter (5-HTT), lowering extracellular serotonin.
ME/CFS patients have significantly higher iNOS activity compared to healthy people, consistent with increased nitric oxide production.

A SWATH-MS proteomic analysis of ME/CFS peripheral blood mononuclear cells found a decline in ATP and energy production alongside upregulation of Complex V in the mitochondrial respiratory chain, suggestive of increased ROS production.
Deficiencies in natural coenzyme Q10 and NADH, required for mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and ATP production, have been reported in ME/CFS patients.

Giloteaux et al. reported lower gastrointestinal microbial diversity in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls, along with higher blood levels of bacterial LPS, CD14, and LPS-binding protein, and increased IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, and TNFα.
Up to 92% of ME/CFS patients suffer from Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS).

Frémont et al. reported significant differences in gut microbial composition between ME/CFS patients and healthy individuals, including an increased number of the genus Alistipes within the Bacteroidetes phylum.
Lupo et al. reported increased abundance of genus Bacteroides and a reduction in Firmicutes (except Lactonifactor) in ME/CFS patients.
Increased levels of IL-6 have been reported in several studies of ME/CFS patients, linked to gut microbiota alterations and increased IDO-1 activity.

Maes et al. (2011) reported that depressive symptoms, particularly somatization, were directly associated with increased serum KYN:KYNA and KYN:TRYP ratios and negatively related to serum TRYP levels.

Supplementation with CoQ10 (200 mg/day) and NADH (20 mg/day) enhanced cellular bioenergetics, reduced fatigue and lipoperoxides, and improved biochemical parameters including CoQ10, ATP, citrate synthase, and NAD+:NADH redox ratio.
A study in a Spanish CFS cohort showed a significant reduction in anxiety and maximum heart rate following CoQ10/NADH supplementation.
Treatment with NADH (10 mg/day) demonstrated a significant reduction in symptoms compared to placebo.
Oral NADH supplementation was more effective for symptom reduction than conventional nutritional supplements and psychotherapy over a 24-month period.
CoQ10 (50 mg/day) and NADH (5 mg/day) supplementation significantly reduced maximal heart rate during cycle ergometer tests and fatigue perception, but no improvements were seen for pain and sleep.
Nicotinic acid (NA) therapy for raising NAD+ induces unwanted adverse effects including significant skin flushing in most individuals below therapeutic doses, limiting its clinical use.

NR has been shown in animal models to prevent cognitive decline, ameliorate brain degeneration, and correct social deficits and anxiety disorders, suggesting potential benefit in ME/CFS, though no clinical trials in ME/CFS exist yet.
ME/CFS has an estimated pre-pandemic prevalence of 0.2-0.4%, affects females about three times more often than males, with two incidence peaks in the late teens and between 30-40 years.
Endothelial dysfunction has been consistently identified across multiple studies of ME/CFS patients.

A PET study found increased TSPO binding (indicating microglial/astrocyte activation) in the cingulate cortex, hippocampus, amygdala, thalamus, midbrain, and pons of ME/CFS patients, correlating with symptom severity.
MRS studies found decreased myo-inositol, a putative marker of glial dysfunction, in the anterior cingulate cortex of ME/CFS patients.
MRS studies found increased choline, indicating increased glial cell membrane turnover, in the left anterior cingulate and basal ganglia of ME/CFS patients.
Reduced regional FDG uptake was found in the right mediofrontal cortex, brain stem, and orbitofrontal cortex, indicating regional brain hypometabolism in ME/CFS.

A BOLD fMRI study of 34 ME/CFS patients versus 24 controls found exercise uniquely reduced global cerebral blood flow and paradoxically increased activity in the anterior default mode network node, an effect not seen in other conditions.
An increase in pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and IL-1β at 8 hours after exercise was predictive of higher post-exercise fatigue scores in ME/CFS patients.
After exercise, exosome-associated mtDNA increased in ME/CFS patients but not controls, and exposure of these exosomes to human microglial cells caused significantly increased IL-1β secretion.
GPCR autoantibody levels in ME/CFS patients generally correlate with disease severity.
Single nucleotide polymorphisms in genes encoding the muscarinic acetylcholine receptor M3 (M3R) have been found in ME/CFS patients.

CBF reduction on tilt table testing in ME/CFS patients occurs independent of heart rate and blood pressure changes, independent of capnia status, and is also seen in the subset of ME/CFS patients with joint hypermobility.

An MRI study of 31 ME/CFS patients using pseudo-continuous arterial spin labeling found significant regional cerebral blood flow abnormalities in limbic system regions at rest, without orthostatic or exercise challenge.
ME/CFS patients show decreased blood pressure variability, indicating impaired baroreflex-mediated adjustment to adrenergic and vagal stimuli.
Administration of the alpha-1 agonist phenylephrine increased cerebral blood flow and decreased cognitive dysfunction in ME/CFS patients.
Small fiber neuropathy is assumed to be present in at least one third of ME/CFS patients, possibly reflecting secondary autoimmune processes.
An ELISA analysis failed to identify GPCR autoantibodies in the CSF of ME/CFS patients, leaving unclear whether blood-borne GPCR aAB access the CNS.
Serum autoantibodies against muscarinic acetylcholine receptor M1 correlated with impeded receptor binding on brain PET imaging, suggesting these autoantibodies may cross the blood-brain barrier.
The quantity of blood autoantibodies against β1 and β2 adrenergic receptors correlated with brain network alterations in ME/CFS patients.

Transfer of IgG from fibromyalgia patients into a rodent model induced symptoms, with the IgG fraction binding to satellite glial cells in the dorsal root ganglia, supporting a glial-autoimmune mechanism relevant to related disorders.
Blood cytokines including IL-7, TNF-α, TGF-β1, nerve growth factor, CCL11 and CXCL10 correlated with ME/CFS symptom severity.

An immune network analysis of CSF in a larger ME/CFS sample found an altered immune signature indicative of CNS immune activation with a shift toward a Th2 pattern, and increased CCL11 and CXCL10 levels.

A network analysis of over 2500 CSF proteins in ME/CFS patients identified several enriched pathways including β-adrenergic signaling, protein kinase A signaling, alpha-adrenergic signaling, GPCR signaling, and, most significantly, CDK5 signaling.
Even mild SARS-CoV-2 infection induced large CCL11 increases associated with 'brain fog' symptoms in patients who developed post-acute sequelae of COVID-19.
Monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1/CCL2) was identified among the biomarkers most strongly associated with post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC).
Small fiber neuropathy is estimated to be present in at least one third of ME/CFS patients and may reflect autoimmune processes similar to those affecting the CNS.
Overexpression of CD70 on blood CD4+ T lymphocytes may identify lymphocytes with increased potential to migrate into the CNS and thus may indicate CNS inflammation.
Decreased blood pressure variability in ME/CFS patients indicates reduced ability to adjust blood pressure in response to adrenergic and vagal stimuli, supporting abnormal baroreflex function.
Administration of the alpha-1 agonist phenylephrine increased cerebral blood flow and decreased cognitive dysfunction in ME/CFS patients.

An MRI study using pseudo-continuous arterial spin labeling in 31 ME/CFS patients found significant regional cerebral blood flow abnormalities in limbic system regions even at rest, without orthostatic or exercise challenge.

Cerebral blood flow decreases on tilt table testing in ME/CFS patients independent of heart rate/blood pressure response and independent of hypocapnia versus normocapnia, and were also observed in the subset with joint hypermobility.
ME/CFS is reported to be approximately 10 times more common in patients with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome than in the general population, and most hEDS patients meet ME/CFS criteria.
Single nucleotide polymorphisms in the gene encoding the muscarinic acetylcholine receptor M3 (CHRM3) have been found in ME/CFS patients.
The largest ME/CFS genome-wide association study to date found the most significant risk locus in the tubulin polymerization promoting protein (TPPP) gene region, a gene involved in myelination.

The largest human proteomics dataset of proteins unique to ME/CFS patients robustly highlighted the Eph/ephrin signaling pathway, involved in bidirectional astrocyte-neuron signaling, synaptic plasticity, and axon guidance.
Peroxisomal dysfunction with associated depletion of plasmalogens has been found in ME/CFS, relevant given peroxisomes' enrichment in neuroglia and role in axonal/myelin integrity.

Transfer of IgG from fibromyalgia patients into a rodent model induced symptoms, with the causative IgG component binding to satellite glial cells in the dorsal root ganglia, suggesting autoimmunity against glial cells as a pathomechanism.

In ME/CFS patients, serum autoantibodies against the muscarinic acetylcholine receptor M1 correlated with impeded receptor binding in a brain PET study, suggesting these autoantibodies can cross the blood-brain barrier.
The quantity of autoantibodies against β1 and β2 adrenergic receptors in blood correlated with brain network alterations in ME/CFS patients.
An ELISA analysis failed to identify GPCR autoantibodies in the CSF of ME/CFS patients, raising uncertainty about whether blood GPCR autoantibodies enter the CNS.

In an MRI study of 272 severely affected ME/CFS patients, signs of possible increased intracranial pressure were found in 83%, with 32% classified as definitely abnormal, and signs of craniocervical obstruction in 37%.
Mildly increased intracranial pressure was detected by lumbar puncture in most of 20 ME/CFS patients examined, and CSF drainage temporarily improved symptoms in 17 of them.
Increased quinolinic acid, an excitotoxic byproduct of the tryptophan-kynurenine pathway produced by reactive microglia, has been reported in ME/CFS and has been implicated in central fatigue.
Increased quinolinic acid has also been reported in post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC).

An immune network analysis of CSF in a large ME/CFS sample found an altered immune signature indicative of CNS immune activation with a shift toward a TH2 pattern, along with increased levels of CCL11 and CXCL10.

A network analysis of over 2500 CSF proteins in ME/CFS patients identified several relevant pathways, most significantly enriched for CDK5 signaling, along with β-adrenergic, protein kinase A, alpha-adrenergic and GPCR signaling pathways.

Monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1/CCL2) was identified among the biomarkers most strongly associated with post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC), and is involved in microglial recruitment and leukocyte trafficking across the BBB.
Even mild SARS-CoV-2 infection induced large CCL11 increases that were associated with 'brain fog' symptoms in patients who went on to develop PASC.

Relating inflammatory blood markers to clinical symptoms in ME/CFS patients found cytokines correlating with symptom severity, including general inflammation markers (IL-7, TNF-alpha) and markers suggestive of CNS inflammation (TGF-beta1, NGF, CCL11, CXCL10).
Pre-illness blood samples showed significant metabolite differences between students who later developed severe ME/CFS after infectious mononucleosis and those who recovered.
Glutathione metabolism was identified as a potentially dysregulated pathway in pre-illness samples distinguishing those who developed severe ME/CFS from those who recovered.
Nucleotide metabolism was identified as a potentially dysregulated pathway distinguishing pre-illness samples of those who later developed severe ME/CFS from recovered controls.
The TCA cycle was identified as a potentially dysregulated pathway distinguishing pre-illness samples of those who later developed severe ME/CFS from recovered controls.

A leave-one-out cross-validated logistic regression model using pre-illness metabolite data classified severe ME/CFS cases versus recovered controls with 97.2% accuracy, 94.4% sensitivity, and 100.0% specificity.
The metabolite pathway changes observed are consistent with previously reported elevations in pro-inflammatory cytokines in patients who later developed severe ME/CFS after infectious mononucleosis.
Among 178 ASFC members with a declared ME/CFS diagnosis, 150 (84%) met the SEID criteria derived from IOM/NAM recommendations.
Diagnostic delay was significantly longer in patients who met SEID criteria compared to those who did not (7.2 vs 5.3 years).
Unrefreshing sleep, cognitive impairment, and orthostatic intolerance were reported significantly more frequently in SEID patients than in non-SEID patients.
Three of four IOM/NAM post-exertional malaise (PEM) symptom questions strongly discriminated SEID from non-SEID patients.
All three IOM/NAM unrefreshing sleep symptom questions distinguished SEID from non-SEID patients.
Only two of nine cognitive impairment questions ('hard to concentrate/focus' and 'cannot do several tasks at once') significantly separated SEID from non-SEID patients.
None of the IOM/NAM orthostatic intolerance symptom questions distinguished SEID from non-SEID patients, despite orthostatic intolerance overall being more frequent in the SEID group.
Among patients able to identify a trigger for their fatigue onset, infection was the most commonly reported trigger, followed by psychological causes, surgery, and hormonal disorders.
Generalized pain was reported by 83% of ME/CFS subjects, alongside sore throat (48%), swollen cervical (36%) and axillary (11%) lymph nodes, cold sensation (73%), and unusual sweats (61%).
The average delay between fatigue onset and ME/CFS diagnosis was 7 years, longer than diagnostic delays reported in US cohorts.

A cited study using active standing test and blood pressure measurement found that the proportion of POTS among CFS patients (5.7%) and among those meeting SEID criteria (5.2%) was very low, suggesting POTS is not a good marker of ME/CFS.
Among SEID patients, activity limitation, unrefreshing sleep, and pain were most frequently rated as the single most disabling symptom.
Less than half of respondents (46%) considered the term 'SEID' more appropriate than 'CFS', while 39% disagreed and 15% had no opinion.
A majority of subjects believed the SEID label would give a negative image of their disease to family, medical staff/social workers, and colleagues at work.
Actometer (objective activity) reanalysis of three Dutch CBT trials by Wiborg et al. found that CBT did not produce objective improvement despite prior claims of efficacy.

PACE trial endpoint changes created an overlap between entry and recovery criteria such that 13.3% of enrolled patients already met recovery thresholds on one or two primary outcomes before receiving any treatment.
The PACE trial's post-hoc endpoint changes resulted in a four-fold increase in reported recovery rates for CBT and GET compared with the original protocol definitions.
At 52 weeks, the PACE trial found no statistically significant difference in improvement of the CFS symptom count between GET and SMC, GET and APT, or CBT and APT.
Net improvement in quality-of-life scores (EQ-5D) at end of treatment in the PACE trial was minimal: 2.3% for GET over APT and 0.5% for CBT over APT.
In its cost-effectiveness analysis, the PACE trial ignored that more patients were unable to work and were reliant on illness benefits after CBT/GET treatment than before it.
At long-term follow-up, PACE trial results showed no difference in efficacy between CBT, GET, APT and no additional treatment, indicating none of the treatments were effective long-term.
Individual participant data from PACE showed 20% of participants who subjectively reported improved physical functioning had actually deteriorated on the objective six-minute walk test.

The FITNET internet-based CBT trial for adolescents found no significant difference in recovery rates at long-term follow-up, its primary study goal, despite multiple design biases favoring the intervention.

In Gotaas et al., the difference in physical functioning scores between interpersonal CBT and control was only 6.8 points, below the study's own pre-specified 10-point minimal important difference threshold for efficacy.

Núñez et al. found that multidisciplinary treatment combining CBT, GET and pharmacological treatment did not improve health-related quality of life and led to worse physical function and bodily pain scores at 12 months versus usual treatment.
In Moss-Morris et al., after GET, physical functioning subjectively improved by 30% while objectively (via cardiopulmonary exercise testing) it deteriorated by 15%.

In Jason et al., a substantial subjective baseline difference in physical functioning existed between exercise and control groups, but no such difference was found objectively via the six-minute walk test.
In Jason et al., quality-of-life scores after CBT improved 5% less than after relaxation therapy.

An Oxford Brookes University patient survey (n=2274) commissioned by NICE found symptom worsening after treatment reported by 58.3% of CBT patients and 81.1% of GET patients, with severe bedridden/dependent status increasing substantially after both treatments.

An evaluation of a 12-month GET program in a Dutch hospital sports medical department found dropout rates of 55%, 73%, and 80% at 6, 9, and 12 months respectively when excluded early dropouts were properly included.

In the GETSET trial, only 8% of patients subjectively benefited from graded exercise self-help (GES) over specialist medical care alone, once the control group's own improvement (6%) was subtracted from the treatment group's (14%).
In the GETSET trial, only 42% of participants adhered completely or very well to the graded exercise self-help programme, with up to 59% adhering only moderately, slightly or not at all.
A pilot trial by Gordon et al. in adolescents found no intervention (graded aerobic exercise vs progressive resistance training) was significantly better than the other for any outcome.
Chalder et al. found no difference between family-focused CBT and psychoeducation for CFS in adolescents aged 11-18, in a study where only 69% of participants met Fukuda criteria.

Lloyd et al. found that neither immunological therapy (dialyzable leukocyte extract) nor CBT, alone or combined, provided greater benefit than nonspecific treatment regimens, and the CBT-associated graded exercise did not significantly increase non-sedentary physical activity.
In Windthorst et al., 27% of GET participants dropped out compared with 0% of the heart-rate-variability biofeedback control group.

The Windthorst et al. study comparing GET to heart-rate-variability biofeedback in 28 patients had a 27% dropout rate from the GET group versus 0% from the control group, and the authors concluded superiority remained unclear.

A 2019 Oxford Brookes University survey of 2274 patients commissioned by NICE found that worsening of symptoms after treatment was reported by 58.3% after CBT and 81.1% after GET, with severe bedridden dependency increasing substantially post-treatment.

Van Berkel et al.'s evaluation of a 12-month GET program in a Dutch hospital sports medicine department found dropout rates of 55%, 73%, and 80% at 6, 9, and 12 months respectively when previously excluded early dropouts were included.

In the PACE trial, quality-of-life (EQ-5D) improvement after treatment was minimal (2.3% for GET over APT and 0.5% for CBT over APT), and post-treatment quality-of-life scores remained worse than those reported for several other chronic diseases.

At the PACE trial's 52-week follow-up, there was no statistically significant difference in the chronic fatigue syndrome symptom count between GET and standard medical care, GET and adaptive pacing therapy, or CBT and adaptive pacing therapy.

In Jason et al. (2007), subjective physical functioning scores differed substantially between exercise and control groups at baseline, yet objective six-minute walk test results showed no such baseline difference, illustrating unreliability of subjective outcomes.

In Moss-Morris et al. (2005), after GET, subjective physical functioning improved by 30% while objective cardiopulmonary exercise testing showed a 15% deterioration, demonstrating divergence between subjective and objective measures.
In the PACE trial's released individual participant data, 20% of participants whose physical functioning improved subjectively had actually deteriorated on the objective six-minute walk test.

A systematic review by Haywood et al. (2011) of patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) used in ME/CFS, including the Chalder Fatigue Scale, found poor quality and a mismatch between measured research outcomes and outcomes relevant to patients.

An influential systematic review by Whiting et al. (2001) concluded that subjective 'improvement' ratings can reflect reduced expectations rather than true recovery, and recommended objective measures such as return to work/school or increased activity.

Núñez et al. found that a multidisciplinary treatment combining CBT, GET and pharmacological treatment did not improve health-related quality of life at 12 months and led to worse physical function and bodily pain scores than usual treatment, concluding the combination may be harmful.

A review of PACE trial long-term follow-up data found that patients who did not receive additional CBT/GET after trial completion had lower fatigue and higher physical functioning scores than those who received additional treatment, suggesting continued post-trial CBT/GET may have been detrimental.

In the GETSET study, only 8% of patients subjectively benefited from guided graded exercise self-help beyond the control group, meaning approximately 12 patients would need to be treated for one to benefit, and up to 59% did not adhere well to the treatment.
The Cochrane exercise review reanalysis found the impact of GET on serious adverse reactions to be uncertain because most included studies did not adequately report on safety.

A large study by Baraniuk (n=6175) concluded that the Oxford criteria were untenable because they inappropriately selected healthy subjects with mild fatigue and chronic idiopathic fatigue and mislabeled them as CFS.

Belgian researchers (2010) noted that severe symptom exacerbation following exercise, characteristic of ME/CFS, is not present in other fatiguing conditions such as depression, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, or multiple sclerosis, supporting post-exertional malaise as a distinguishing feature.

Colleagues from the Dutch knowledge centre of fatigue concluded that self-report questionnaires should be used cautiously as measures of actual activity level because none of the self-report questionnaires had strong correlations with actometer (objective activity) measurements.

The BRANDO project (including Professor Ioannidis) concluded that lack of blinding in trials is associated with an average 13% exaggeration of intervention effects, recommending that unblindable trials with subjective outcomes should not form the basis of clinical/policy decisions.

Five different methods for operationalizing 'substantial reduction in functioning' (four based on the SF-36 and one single-item DSQ measure) produced broadly comparable results in an international dataset of ME/CFS patients and controls.
Among the five methods tested, the single self-report DSQ item was found to be the most valid in differentiating ME/CFS patients from controls.
All 58 patients presenting to a long COVID clinic showed endoscopically confirmed chronic epipharyngitis, regardless of whether they had throat symptoms.
One month of weekly epipharyngeal abrasive therapy (EAT) with ZnCl2 significantly reduced the endoscopic inflammatory grade of chronic epipharyngitis in long COVID patients.
EAT significantly reduced fatigue severity (VAS) in long COVID patients after one month of treatment.
EAT significantly reduced headache severity (VAS) in long COVID patients after one month of treatment.
EAT significantly reduced attention disorder severity (VAS) in long COVID patients after one month of treatment.

Patients whose epipharyngeal inflammation improved by ≥1 grade after EAT showed a significantly greater improvement in fatigue than patients without inflammation improvement, indicating fatigue relief is linked to reduction of epipharyngitis.

Improvements in headache and attention disorder VAS scores were not significantly associated with the degree of epipharyngeal inflammation reduction, suggesting these symptoms improve via a mechanism independent of visible inflammation reduction (e.g., vagus nerve stimulation).
The paper notes that fatigue was the most severe of the three assessed symptoms (fatigue, headache, attention disorder) before EAT treatment, paralleling the ME/CFS symptom profile.

The authors propose that chronic epipharyngitis produces neuroexcitatory inflammatory molecules (TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-1) that activate brain immune cells, causing low-grade brain inflammation associated with ME/CFS-like symptoms in long COVID.
A cited study found that 14.3% of long COVID patients with fatigue lasting more than 6 months met formal ME/CFS diagnostic criteria.
Depending on study design, Long COVID prevalence in controlled studies of children and adolescents ranges from 0.8% to 13%.

The English CLoCK study found a 13% Long COVID prevalence three months after infection, but the authors note this study relied only on PCR testing without serostatus and had low questionnaire response, likely leading to overascertainment of symptomatic patients.
Other English studies estimate Long COVID frequency at 4-5% after 4 weeks and 1-2% after 8 weeks, while a Danish cohort found 0.8% in schoolchildren, considerably lower than the CLoCK study estimate.
SARS-CoV-2-positive adolescents showed more long-term complaints and school absence days compared to a control group.
Myocarditis, which should be excluded when evaluating Long COVID, occurred in 0.045% of infected boys up to 82 days after infection, with girls less frequently affected.
In MIS-C/PIMS, the cardiovascular system is involved in more than 50% of cases, with most residual findings affecting the circulation (e.g., coronary aneurysms).
Myocarditis after mRNA vaccination most commonly affects male adolescents after the second dose (rate 1:17,000), with no statistically relevant increased risk in girls.

Up to 30% of children/adolescents with Long COVID show orthostatic dysregulation, such as postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), which can significantly impair the ability to attend school in an upright position.
POTS in pediatric Long COVID is diagnosed via an adapted 10-minute stand test or a tilt-table examination, showing a heart rate increase with stable blood pressure upon standing.
In pronounced POTS cases, pharmacologic treatment (fludrocortisone, midodrine, ivabradine, beta-blockers) can be attempted in consultation with a specialized center.

POTS management aims to increase intravascular volume (salt-rich diet, increased fluid intake), redistribute blood volume (compression stockings, positioning), avoid triggering/worsening factors (e.g., large meals), and achieve physical reactivation where possible.
Up to 40% of children/adolescents report persistent cough at 8-12 weeks post-infection, and about 15% report persistent dyspnea.

Cardiac complaints such as palpitations or chest pain are reported by 2-31% of children/adolescents 8-12 weeks after SARS-CoV-2 infection, though most cases have no organic correlate on imaging or lab testing.
Myalgia and arthralgia are reported in 1-61% of children/adolescents with Long COVID depending on the study.
10% of patients with chilblain-like lesions ('COVID toes') reported a familial occurrence.
Smell disorder prevalence in pediatric study populations ranges from 5-40%, with higher rates found using standardized smell testing compared to self-reported assessment.
COVID-associated taste disorders are considerably rarer than COVID-associated smell disorders.
Fatigue prevalence in children/adolescents post-infection ranges widely from 3% to 87% depending on the study, and can result in markedly impaired daily function and reduced quality of life.
Post-exertional malaise (PEM), worsening of symptoms for hours to weeks after minor or moderate daily exertion, is described as the cardinal symptom of ME/CFS.
ME/CFS must be worked up when, in addition to fatigue and PEM, pain, sleep disturbances, and autonomic, neurocognitive, neuroendocrine and/or immunological disturbances are present.
Rigid, stepwise graded activation is contraindicated in ME/CFS because it can lead to severe post-exertional malaise (PEM); consequent pacing is instead recommended.
Sleep disturbances occur postvirally with a general frequency of 25-40% in children/adolescents and may require differential diagnostic work-up and therapy if distressing or persistent.

WHO estimates postviral long-term complaint prevalence at 10-20% among SARS-CoV-2-infected adults, with possible risk factors including initially severe infection, certain underlying diseases, and female sex.

Retinal studies show disturbed microcirculation in Long COVID, likely attributable to endotheliitis with endothelial dysfunction, which may also contribute to dysfunction of other organs such as the brain, possibly mediated in part by reduced deformability of blood cells.
After the first dose of COVID-19 vaccination, 57.9% of long COVID patients reported an overall improvement in symptoms while 17.9% reported deterioration.
Average symptom score improvement after first vaccine dose differed by vaccine type, being greatest with Moderna compared to AstraZeneca/Oxford and Pfizer/BioNTech.

After adjustment for baseline symptom score, sex, age group and symptom duration, the Moderna vaccine was associated with significantly greater improvement in fatigue than the AstraZeneca/Oxford vaccine.
Moderna vaccine was associated with significantly greater improvement in brain fog than the AstraZeneca/Oxford vaccine after adjustment.
Moderna vaccine was associated with significantly greater improvement in myalgia than the AstraZeneca/Oxford vaccine after adjustment.
Moderna vaccine was associated with significantly greater improvement in gastrointestinal symptoms than the AstraZeneca/Oxford vaccine after adjustment.
Moderna vaccine was associated with significantly greater improvement in autonomic dysfunction (including POTS-type symptoms) than the AstraZeneca/Oxford vaccine after adjustment.
For approximately half of participants who improved after vaccination, this improvement had abated by the time of survey completion, with a median duration of improvement of 14-21 days.

Among participants who experienced a decline in symptoms after vaccination, exactly half had recovered by survey completion, with a median time to improvement of 3-7 days, suggesting a transient vaccine reaction rather than true long COVID exacerbation.

In a sensitivity analysis restricted to 328 participants with PCR- or antigen-confirmed COVID-19, vaccine-associated improvements in fatigue, brain fog and myalgia were numerically similar to the full cohort but no longer statistically significant between vaccines due to reduced power.
No respondent demographic characteristics (age, sex, ethnicity, duration of symptoms) were identified as predictors of vaccine effect on long COVID symptomatology.

The paper cites evidence (from a prior Norwegian cohort study) that long COVID sufferers show a distinct immunological profile characterised by low levels of IgM and IgG3, which together with prior asthma history and primary symptoms accurately predicts risk.

The paper cites a Hong Kong study of 106 people with long COVID showing gut microbiome abnormalities that differ between those who develop long COVID and those who recover fully, worsening over time in long COVID.
CFS mice subjected to sustained forced swimming stress showed increased iNOS expression in heart tissue and increased serum NO levels compared to controls.
Electroacupuncture (EA) at acupoint BL15 inhibited the CFS-induced increase in cardiac iNOS expression and serum NO levels.
EA treatment ameliorated impaired motor function in CFS mice induced by sustained forced swimming stress.
EA treatment improved cardiac function, as measured by echocardiography, in CFS mice.
Administration of l-arginine raised serum NO levels and abolished the beneficial effects of EA in CFS mice, supporting a causal role for NO signaling in EA's mechanism.
The patient presented with leukocytosis, lymphomonocytosis, and elevated CRP consistent with acute viral infection, later confirmed as EBV mononucleosis.
Transaminases were initially elevated but normalized at 4-week follow-up, and lymphomonocytosis fully resolved.
Acute EBV infection can trigger chronic fatigue and can induce chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) in 11-13.5% of infected individuals.
Chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) affects approximately 0.1-1.9% of adolescents and shows two age peaks, one in adolescence (12-19 years) and one between 30-39 years.
Initial serum CRP level and clinical-neurological symptomatology were positively associated with subsequent development of CFS, while vitamin B12 level was negatively associated.
Lower vitamin B12 levels were negatively associated with (i.e., predictive of) development of CFS following infection.

During the further course of CFS illness, serum CRP is even found to be lower compared to healthy adolescents, possibly due to T-cell suppression and negative effects of depression, sleep disturbance and emotional impairment.

Neither initial viral load nor inflammatory-immunological-hormonal changes have proven useful as predictive tools for CFS development, per the CEBA project (chronic fatigue following acute Epstein-Barr virus infection).

Experienced physicians using initial symptom severity of adolescent mononucleosis patients could correctly classify 75% of those who would not develop CFS at 6 months, but only 18% of those who would develop CFS.

In a hospitalized pediatric COVID-19 cohort with average patient age, fever occurred in 58%, cough in 52%, and fatigue in 19% of cases, whereas in ambulatory patients rates were much lower (fever 7%, cough 5.5%, fatigue 2.3%).
The authors note that similar to EBV, SARS-CoV-2 is increasingly implicated in the development of chronic fatigue syndrome-like problems (Long-COVID), warranting causal work-up of fatigue symptoms.
Patients showed a significant improvement of 240 points on the WOSI (shoulder-specific quality of life) after 12 weeks of home-based exercise therapy.
After 24 weeks of home-based exercise, patients improved 325 points on the WOSI, indicating sustained improvement in shoulder function.
Patients improved 8.6 points on the DASH disability score after 24 weeks of home-based exercise therapy.
Patients improved 4.3 points on the Patient-Specific Functional Scale (PSFS) after 24 weeks of home-based exercise therapy.
Patients improved 1.02 points on the Global Rating of Change (GROC) scale after 24 weeks, indicating perceived overall improvement.
Kinesiophobia, measured by the Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia (TSK), did not significantly improve with home-based exercise therapy.
There was no significant difference in outcomes between the two randomized home-based exercise program groups (A and B).

Whole-genome sequencing identified a heterozygous 27-base in-frame deletion in COL5A2 predicted to remove 9 amino acids (three Gly-Xaa-Yaa triplets) in an EDS-affected Chihuahua, confirmed by Sanger sequencing.
Genotyping of both unaffected parents showed the mutant allele was absent from their buccal cell DNA, indicating the COL5A2 deletion arose de novo in the affected dog.

Histopathological examination of a skin biopsy from the affected dog showed markedly reduced dermal thickness and reduced density of collagen fibers, producing a loose dermal appearance with moderate variation in fiber size.

The affected Chihuahua presented clinical signs matching human classical EDS diagnostic criteria: hyperextensible skin with atrophic scarring (major criterion) plus easy bruising, skin fragility/traumatic splitting, and hernia (minor criteria), supporting classification as classical EDS.

The authors propose that, unlike COL5A1 haploinsufficiency which reduces total type V collagen, this triple-helix-domain COL5A2 deletion likely produces a structurally defective proα2(V) chain causing a dominant-negative gain-of-function effect on type V collagen heterotrimer assembly.

The paper notes that prior reports identified two independent COL5A1 variants causing EDS in a Labrador Retriever and a mixed-breed dog, contrasting with the COL5A2 mechanism found in the present Chihuahua case.

This study represents, to the authors' knowledge, the first reported case of COL5A2-related Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in dogs, whereas only one prior COL5A2 variant (p.Gly789Val) had been described in Holstein cattle.
Low back pain measured by VAS significantly improved after sectioning of the filum terminale in hEDS patients with tethered cord syndrome.
Walking distance improved significantly after filum sectioning in the subset of patients with pre- and postoperative data.
Leg weakness improved postoperatively in the majority of patients following filum sectioning.
Lower extremity sensory loss improved in a substantial minority of patients after surgery.
Urinary incontinence improved in 40% of patients postoperatively and was not worsened in any patient.
Urinary frequency improved in a third of patients postoperatively with no worsening reported.
Nocturia improved in a third of patients but worsened in 17%, indicating a mixed response.
Difficulty emptying the bladder improved in most affected patients but worsened in some.
Preoperative MRI classification of tethered cord syndrome as occult (normal conus position) versus radiographic (low-lying conus) had no significant effect on surgical outcomes.
The large majority of patients reported satisfaction with surgical sectioning of the filum terminale.
Greater reduction in low back pain VAS score was the sole significant predictor of patient satisfaction in multivariate analysis.
Improvement in leg weakness after surgery was significantly associated with patient satisfaction in bivariate analysis.
One patient developed a postoperative dural leak requiring surgical repair after hyperflexion of the lumbosacral junction.
Preoperative urodynamic testing confirmed neurogenic bladder in the large majority of hEDS/TCS patients.

Prior biomechanical studies (Klinge et al.) found the filum terminale of hEDS/TCS patients loses elasticity at a much lower strain than in non-EDS patients, supporting a stretch-induced pathophysiology.
A subset of adults with hypermobile EDS show reduced serum tenascin-X levels, implicating this ECM glycoprotein as a candidate factor in generalized joint hypermobility.
Reported prevalence of generalized joint hypermobility varies widely by assessment method and population, ranging from 5%-40% in children and 10%-20% in adults.
Joint hypermobility is more prevalent in females than males, and the post-pubertal decline in joint mobility is more pronounced in males.

Several studies suggest a higher prevalence of joint hypermobility in people of African, Asian, and Middle Eastern descent compared with White populations, though race is underreported in most studies.
Based on a population study of Welsh health care records, the combined prevalence of hEDS and generalized hypermobility spectrum disorder (previously JHS) is estimated at 1 in 500-600.
hEDS is by far the most common EDS subtype, accounting for over 95% of all EDS presentations seen in specialist clinics.

About two-thirds of patients with symptomatic joint hypermobility report multisystemic functional symptoms extending beyond the musculoskeletal system, including GI dysfunction, orthostatic intolerance, POTS, urogynecological problems, mast cell activation symptoms, fatigue, and anxiety/depression.
People with symptomatic joint hypermobility show decreased functional capacity, lower isometric strength, and suboptimal muscle activation and force control strategies.
Orthostatic intolerance in hypermobile individuals has been proposed to arise from increased vascular distensibility due to altered connective tissue or from peripheral small fiber neuropathy.
Gastrointestinal disorders in hypermobile patients are linked to autonomic dysfunction/dysmotility, interoceptive sensitivity, and altered stretch/mechanoreceptor function of the intestines.
The pathogenesis linking mast cell activation to joint hypermobility remains undetermined.
Despite high interlimb mobility correlation, several reports indicate the nondominant limb can be more hypermobile than the dominant, with side-to-side differences attributable to training effects.

The Beighton score, though quick and widely used for GJH screening, is heavily upper-limb biased, covers a limited number of joints, assesses only sagittal-plane motion, and omits joints (shoulder, foot/ankle, patellofemoral) most commonly reported as unstable by patients.
In case no. 1, a heterozygous 22 bp deletion removing the exon1/intron1 boundary of COL5A1 was identified as the candidate causal variant for classical EDS.
Cases no. 2 and 3 (presumed related) shared an identical heterozygous nonsense variant in COL5A1 predicted to truncate 36% of the coding sequence.
In case no. 4, a heterozygous one base-pair deletion in COL5A1 causing a frameshift predicted to truncate 44% of the open reading frame was identified as a de novo pathogenic variant.
Two heterozygous TNXB missense variants identified in case no. 4 were excluded as causal after targeted genotyping of the family showed they did not segregate uniquely with the affected phenotype.

Skin biopsies from EDS-affected cats showed haphazardly arranged, shortened, curled, wispy dermal collagen fibers with widened interfibrillar spaces and a slightly thinner epidermis compared with normal skin.

Transmission electron microscopy of case no. 4 skin showed loosely packed, disorganized collagen fibers with curled fibrils and irregularly outlined fibrils of variable diameter (up to twice normal), in contrast to densely packed, uniform round fibrils in an age-matched control cat.
Affected cats showed elevated skin extensibility indices (19% in case 2, 22% in case 4) compared with unaffected family members of case 4 (father 15.6%, mother 6.6%, brother 17.6%, sister 10.7%).

Case no. 2 experienced partial and grand mal seizures requiring phenobarbital and presumptive hyperesthesia/self-mutilation, which the authors suggest may represent neurological manifestations of feline EDS, paralleling epilepsy and small fiber neuropathy reported in human EDS and a previously described EDS-affected Burmese cat.
Case no. 4 was diagnosed with concurrent feline atopic skin syndrome (FASS), and pruritus-driven scratching led to traumatic skin splitting that exacerbated the EDS phenotype.

In case no. 4, short courses of systemic prednisolone (2 mg/kg injectable or 0.6 mg/kg oral once daily) fully resolved scratching and healed lesions, whereas oral antihistamines alone only partially controlled pruritus and new lesions continued to develop.
Family genotyping confirmed that COL5A1:c.3066del arose as a de novo mutation, being absent from leukocyte DNA of both parents of case no. 4.

The authors propose that all three feline COL5A1 variants lead to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, producing COL5A1 haploinsufficiency and about half the normal amount of type V collagen, thereby disrupting collagen fibril formation and connective tissue integrity.

The patient, previously diagnosed with EDS, presented with complete agenesis of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL), a rare condition frequently associated with EDS among other systemic or intra-articular conditions.
MRI classified the deformity as a Type III combined ACL and PCL agenesis per the Manner classification, with minimal posterior instability despite PCL absence.

An extra-epiphyseal, over-the-top, bony-tunnel-free ACL reconstruction using an Achilles tendon allograft successfully restored knee stability without impairing skeletal growth in this pediatric EDS patient over a 2-year follow-up.
An Achilles tendon allograft was chosen over an autograft because the patient's EDS-related connective tissue compromise would likely predispose an autologous tendon graft to instability and failure.

In a previously reported pediatric EDS case (Erdman and Warnick), an initial non-anatomic physeal-sparing iliotibial band autograft failed and required all-epiphyseal revision reconstruction with a posterior tibialis allograft.

Two crossed Kirschner wires were placed transarticularly as an additional stabilization measure due to the patient's joint instability and altered connective tissue composition, to prevent early graft failure.

EDS is described as a hereditary connective tissue disorder caused by autosomal-transmitted mutations affecting collagen-coding genes, producing dermatological, musculoskeletal, and cardiovascular manifestations including joint hypermobility and skin hyperextensibility.
Gain-of-function variants in C1R have recently been described and are associated with periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a structural rather than immune/infectious phenotype.
Gain-of-function variants in C1S have recently been described and are associated with periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a structural rather than immune/infectious phenotype.
Loss-of-function variants in the classical pathway components C1, C4, and C2 are most commonly associated with lupus and systemic infections with encapsulated bacteria.
C3 deficiency differs from other classical pathway deficiencies, presenting predominantly with membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and infection.
Gain-of-function variants in C3 are associated with endothelial manifestations, including hemolytic uremic syndrome and vasculitis.
Gain-of-function variants in C2 have thus far been reported specifically in patients with C3 glomerulopathy.
Pooled analysis of 11 skin biopsy studies (591 patients) found that 50% of fibromyalgia patients had reduced intraepidermal nerve fibre density.

Across all somatic small fibre testing modalities (skin biopsy, corneal confocal microscopy, laser-evoked potentials, microneurography; 14 studies, 769 patients), the overall pooled prevalence of somatic small fibre impairment in fibromyalgia was 43%.
Two corneal confocal microscopy studies (56 patients) found reduced corneal nerve fibre length, density, and branching in fibromyalgia, with a pooled prevalence of small fibre abnormality of 60%.
Two microneurography studies (57 patients) found abnormal somatic small fibre function, including spontaneous activity and mechanical sensitization, with a pooled prevalence of 35%.

Pooled analysis of seven studies using heterogeneous autonomic testing methods (tilt testing, HRV, skin conductance, sympathetic skin response; 141 patients) found an overall autonomic small fibre impairment prevalence of 43% in fibromyalgia.

Of 29 HRV studies, 26 found abnormal HRV parameters in fibromyalgia patients, with eight studies homogeneously showing an increased low-to-high frequency (LF/HF) ratio consistent with high sympathetic and low parasympathetic tone.
Four of seven studies found reduced baseline skin conductance in fibromyalgia patients compared with healthy controls, while two found no difference and one found higher conductance.
Of seven sympathetic skin response studies, three found prolonged latencies and two found reduced amplitude in fibromyalgia patients versus controls, while three found no significant difference.
Two of three head-up tilt testing studies demonstrated a higher frequency of tilt-test positivity in fibromyalgia patients compared with healthy controls (43.7% and 64.7%).
Laser Doppler flowmetry studies showed that fibromyalgia patients had longer time to peak (reduced blood flux) over tender points and weaker vasodilatory response to local heat than healthy controls.
One skin biopsy study found that GAP43-immunostained (regenerating) intraepidermal nerve fibre density was lower in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.

One skin biopsy study of glabrous hypothenar and trapezius skin found increased peptidergic sensory innervation of cutaneous arteriole-venule shunts in fibromyalgia patients, suggesting abnormal small blood vessel function and upregulated adrenergic receptor signalling.

One skin biopsy study found reduced mean axon diameter in fibromyalgia patients compared with small fibre neuropathy patients and healthy controls, consistent with prior electron microscopy findings of Schwann cell ballooning and smaller axons.

Skin biopsy studies investigating cytokine gene expression in fibromyalgia gave contradictory findings, with some showing increased inflammatory cytokine expression and others finding no difference from controls.

One corneal confocal microscopy study showed altered corneal innervation and Langerhans cell distribution in fibromyalgia and small fibre neuropathy patients, potentially reflecting altered Langerhans cell signalling.

Five studies found increased amplitude of laser-evoked potentials and reduced habituation in fibromyalgia patients, supporting abnormal central pain processing and pain matrix hyperexcitability rather than peripheral small fibre dysfunction.

Most quantitative sensory testing and recent laser-evoked potential studies found that warm and cold detection thresholds (small fibre-mediated) in fibromyalgia patients fell within normative ranges, contrasting with morphometric evidence of small fibre pathology.

MCAS diagnosis requires three criteria: multisystem symptoms of mast cell degranulation in >2 organs occurring in more than one episode, elevation of at least two mast cell-specific mediators, and symptomatic response to anti-mediator drugs.
Neuromuscular blocking agents account for an estimated 60% to 70% of perioperative anaphylaxis events, more than any other drug class.
Among neuromuscular blockers, succinylcholine and cisatracurium show the lowest mast cell activation potency, while mivacurium and atracurium show the highest.
Penicillin and cephalosporins are the leading causes of antibiotic-related anaphylaxis, followed by betalactams, vancomycin, and quinolones.
Thiopental, unlike most intravenous anesthetics, has historically been associated with increased anaphylaxis risk and is a caution in MCAS anesthetic planning.
Synthetic opioids such as fentanyl, remifentanil, and buprenorphine cause less mast cell mediator release than morphine, meperidine, and codeine.
There is no conclusive evidence that regional anesthesia or local anesthetics increase adverse event risk in MCAS patients compared to the general population.

A retrospective study of 459 adult patients found increased risk of MCAS symptoms in those undergoing more invasive surgeries and receiving general anesthesia rather than regional anesthesia or sedation.
Combined H1 and H2 receptor antagonists demonstrate a synergistic effect with a relatively low side effect profile in MCAS management.
An estimated 20% to 50% of patients with systemic mastocytosis will experience systemic anaphylaxis; the prevalence among all MCAS patients is unknown.

In Case 1, a 34-year-old woman with MCAS undergoing emergent cesarean under general anesthesia with premedication (diphenhydramine 50 mg, famotidine 20 mg, methylprednisolone 125 mg IV) had no signs or symptoms of mast cell degranulation intra- or postoperatively.

In Case 2, despite an extensive multi-drug preoperative premedication regimen (cromolyn, ketotifen, levocetirizine, montelukast, famotidine, cetirizine), the patient developed acute postoperative respiratory distress with stridor about 2 hours after surgery, and recurrent pruritus/cough/chest tightness about 22 hours postoperatively.
Epinephrine boluses (0.2 mg then later 0.5 mg) rapidly resolved two separate episodes of postoperative anaphylactic respiratory distress in Case 2.

For acute anaphylaxis in MCAS, epinephrine is recommended intramuscularly (0.5 mg for patients >60 kg) into the lateral thigh or intravascularly (1-10 μg/kg), repeatable every 2 to 5 minutes, with infusion in some cases.

A diagnostic rise in serum tryptase or other mast cell mediators, together with severe systemic recurrent symptoms responsive to mast cell-targeted drugs, supports a diagnosis of mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS).

The authors propose a new ICD-10-CM-adjusted classification of mast cell activation disorders (MCADs), distinguishing confirmed MCAS, MCAD not fulfilling MCAS criteria, and suspected but unconfirmed MCAD.
Basophil activation testing is discussed as a surrogate marker for IgE-dependent hypersensitivity when attempting to confirm suspected mast cell activation.
The authors discuss discrimination between overt mast cell activation disorder and predisposing conditions such as atopic states, mastocytosis, and hereditary alpha tryptasemia.
Hereditary alpha tryptasemia (HαT), caused by extra copies of the TPSAB1 gene, is associated with elevated basal serum tryptase and an increased risk of anaphylaxis and MCAS.
The HαT carrier status is found in nearly 20% of systemic mastocytosis (SM) cases, compared to around 5% in the general population, and is even more prevalent among symptomatic SM patients.
In patients with systemic mastocytosis, HαT carrier status is associated with a high prevalence of severe mediator-related symptoms and with concomitant IgE-dependent allergies.
A somatic KIT mutation (D816V) causing ligand-independent receptor activation and autonomous mast cell expansion underlies systemic mastocytosis in the vast majority of patients.

IgE-dependent activation of KIT D816V-transduced ROSA cells and KIT D816V+ bone marrow mast cells from SM patients did not result in augmented mediator release, supporting a hypothesis that D816V+ mast cells exist in a desensitized state.
During anaphylaxis, serum tryptase rises substantially above baseline, peaks around 2 hours after the event, and returns to baseline 4-12 hours after symptom resolution.
The consensus MCAS diagnostic criterion for a biomarker rise requires serum tryptase to increase over the individual's baseline following the 120% + 2 ng/mL formula.
Carriers of HαT or the ADGRE2 p.C492Y variant may develop vibration-induced urticaria as a manifestation of altered mast cell reactivity.
IgE-depleting therapy with omalizumab may help avoid MCAS events and keep anaphylaxis under control in high-risk patients with documented IgE involvement.

MC-reducing drugs including cladribine and KIT D816V-targeting tyrosine kinase inhibitors (midostaurin, avapritinib) reduce mast cell burden, decrease mediator-related symptom severity, and improve quality of life in advanced systemic mastocytosis.
Midostaurin blocks IgE-mediated histamine release from mast cells and basophils, a mechanism thought to contribute to its clinical efficacy.

A case of complete MCAS control was reported after sequential therapy with cladribine to reduce mast cell numbers followed by omalizumab to control IgE-dependent reactions in a patient with HαT+ smoldering SM and drug-resistant allergy.
Life-long venom immunotherapy is standard in SM patients with documented bee/wasp venom allergy (mixed MCAS), because discontinuation has been followed by new fatal anaphylactic episodes.
Patients with HαT appear to have slightly elevated numbers of bone marrow mast cells even in the absence of systemic mastocytosis, suggesting HαT may predispose to mast cell expansion.
Anaphylaxis has also been reported in systemic mastocytosis cases lacking the KIT D816V mutation or with other KIT mutations, indicating D816V is not obligatory for MCA/anaphylaxis in SM.

Exosomes derived from the plasma of CSU patients (both antihistamine-sensitive and antihistamine-resistant) increased tryptase-1 expression in HMC-1 human mast cells compared to healthy-derived exosomes.
CSU-derived plasma exosomes increased histamine production in HMC-1 mast cells relative to healthy-derived exosomes.
CSU-derived plasma exosomes increased TLR2 levels in HMC-1 mast cells.
CSU-derived plasma exosomes increased TLR4 levels in HMC-1 mast cells.
CSU-derived plasma exosomes increased phosphorylated MAPK levels in HMC-1 mast cells.
