Antihistamine-resistant CSU-derived exosomes produced significantly greater mast cell-activating and histamine-release effects than antihistamine-sensitive CSU-derived exosomes.
Pharmacologic inhibition of TLR2, TLR4, and MAPK (using CC-401, TAK-715, and SCH772984 respectively) reduced CSU-derived exosome-stimulated production of inflammatory mediators in HMC-1 cells.
Topical 7-Methoxyisoflavone significantly reduced FITC- and OXZ-induced ear thickness in mice, comparable to the dexamethasone positive control.
Unlike dexamethasone, which caused a marked reduction in spleen index indicating severe immunosuppression, 7-Met treated mice did not show this same degree of spleen index reduction.
Mast cell infiltration in the ear and dorsal skin was increased in FITC/OXZ-induced AD model mice compared to controls, and was reduced by 7-Met treatment.
Serum total IgE was elevated in FITC- and OXZ-induced AD model mice and was reduced following 7-Met treatment.
Skin IL-13 levels did not change significantly between AD model and control mice.
Neutrophil infiltration (CD11b+ staining) was increased in AD model mice ear and dorsal skin compared to control, and reduced by 7-Met administration.
Keratinocyte proliferation (CK14 staining) was increased in AD model mice ears versus control, and 7-Met treatment decreased epidermal thickness.
RNA-seq of FITC-induced AD ear tissue showed upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-4 and chemokines Ccl17, Ccl22, and Cxcl2, implicating Th1/Th2 balance in FITC-induced AD.
RNA-seq of OXZ-induced AD tissue revealed upregulation of chemokines Cxcl2, Cxcl3, and Cxcl5, with key pathways including MAPK, JAK-STAT, Ras signaling and neutrophil chemotaxis.
7-Met treatment decreased mRNA transcription of Th1 cell-associated chemokines (Cxcl9, Cxcl10) and Th2 cell-associated chemokines (Ccl17, Ccl22) in the FITC-induced AD mouse model.
Serum IFN-γ and IL-4 levels were elevated in FITC-induced AD model mice and decreased in the 7-Met-treated group; the IL-4/IFN-γ ratio was also reduced by 7-Met.
TSLP protein expression was significantly increased after FITC treatment and this increase was significantly lowered by 7-Met.
7-Met significantly inhibited NF-κB signaling in FITC-treated mice, as shown by downregulation of phospho-IκBα and p65.
7-Met reversed FITC-induced activation of the Ras/c-Raf/MAPK (ERK, JNK, p38) pathway and reduced nuclear AP-1 components (c-Fos, c-Jun) in mouse ear and dorsal skin.

PPI network analysis of OXZ-induced differentially expressed chemokine mRNAs was enriched in the IL-17 signaling pathway; RT-qPCR and Western blotting confirmed upregulation of Cxcl1, Cxcl2, and Cxcl3.
IL-17A mRNA levels decreased remarkably in the 7-Met treated group of the OXZ-induced AD model.
7-Met treatment decreased IL-17+ Th17 cells and downregulated STAT3/phospho-STAT3 expression in the OXZ-induced AD model.
7-Met reversed activation of the Ras/c-Raf/MAPK (ERK, JNK, p38) pathway and reduced AP-1 nuclear translocation (c-Fos, c-Jun) in the OXZ-induced AD model.
Mast cells, unlike resting basophils, express MRGPRX2, allowing mast cell activation tests to study IgE-independent drug hypersensitivity mechanisms not accessible via the basophil activation test.

The basophil activation test has practical limitations including reliance on fresh blood, loss of utility in non-responder patients, and difficulty with standardization and batch analysis, which passive mast cell activation tests using frozen/stored serum may overcome.
Topical PBMCsec pre-treatment reduced compound 48/80-induced ear swelling in mice compared to medium control.

scRNAseq of murine dermal mast cells showed 292 genes downregulated and 208 genes upregulated by PBMCsec compared to medium, with downregulated genes enriched for histamine secretion, Fc receptor signalling, and type I hypersensitivity pathways.
Interleukin-4 (Il4) and Il13 expression in dermal mast cells were significantly downregulated by PBMCsec compared to medium.
Expression of Il4ra, Stxbp2 (vesicle trafficking) and Gab2 (FcεR signalling adaptor) was diminished in PBMCsec-treated mast cells.
Fcer1a was downregulated by PBMCsec in mast cells while the other FcεR subunits Fcer1b and Ms4a2 were induced.
Expression of the tyrosine kinases Lyn and Syk, both involved in FcεR signalling, was significantly inhibited by PBMCsec in dermal mast cells.
PBMCsec pre-treatment reduced compound 48/80-induced β-hexosaminidase release from primary human dermal mast cells compared to medium.
PBMCsec pre-treatment reduced IgE/α-IgE-induced β-hexosaminidase release from primary human dermal mast cells compared to medium.
PBMCsec strongly inhibited Bet v 1 allergen-induced CD63+ basophil activation in cells from birch pollen-allergic donors.
PBMCsec largely abrogated α-IgE-induced CD63+ basophil activation compared to medium.
PBMCsec showed only diminished, non-significant inhibitory activity against fMLP-induced (IgE/FcεRI-independent) basophil activation, unlike its strong effect on IgE-dependent activation.

Transcriptomic profiling of basophils from allergic donors identified 909 differentially expressed genes (231 down, 678 up) following PBMCsec treatment, with downregulated genes linked to neutrophil degranulation, Fc-receptor signalling, IL-1 signalling and antigen processing.

Specific genes involved in neutrophil degranulation (GPR84, NFAM1, CYBA, LILRA6) and proteasomal subunits involved in Fc-receptor/IL-1/antigen presentation pathways (PSMB3, PSMB10) were downregulated by PBMCsec in basophils.
FcεRI surface protein expression on basophils was unaffected by PBMCsec after 1 hour or 24 hour treatment with either Bet v 1 or α-IgE challenge.
Phosphorylation of LYN at Tyr397 in basophils was not altered by PBMCsec in response to Bet v 1 stimulation.
CD300A mRNA and surface protein expression were upregulated in non-activated PBMCsec-treated basophils compared to medium, the only inhibitory receptor induced.
Histamine receptor H2 (HRH2), SIGLEC7 and SIGLEC8, known inhibitory receptors on basophils/mast cells, were decreased by PBMCsec compared to medium.
Lipids isolated from PBMCsec reduced compound 48/80-induced mast cell degranulation to a similar extent as whole PBMCsec.
Lipids isolated from PBMCsec abolished IgE/α-IgE-induced mast cell mediator release comparably to whole PBMCsec.
PBMCsec-derived lipids inhibited basophil activation upon α-IgE stimulation as effectively as PBMCsec, and inhibited Bet v 1-induced basophil activation even more strongly than PBMCsec.
Lipidomic analysis showed PS 41:6 and PS 41:7 were more abundant in PBMCsec than medium, while PS 34:0 and PS 36:3 were more abundant in medium.

Neutralizing the PS-CD300A signalling axis with Annexin V and antibodies against PS and CD300A did not abrogate lipid-mediated inhibition of basophil activation, suggesting PS is not solely responsible for the lipid effect.
PBMCsec induced upregulation of PTPN11 (SHP-2) and PTP4A1 (PRL-1), non-receptor protein tyrosine phosphatases, in basophils from allergic donors.
Baseline mean flow velocity (Vm) in both middle cerebral arteries was significantly lower in good responders to anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies compared with non-responders.
There were no significant differences in pulsatility index (PI) between good responders and non-responders in any of the assessed cerebral arteries.
Unilateral pain localization was positively and independently associated with ≥50% response to anti-CGRP mAbs in multivariate logistic regression.
Higher HIT-6 (headache impact) score was positively and independently associated with ≥50% response to anti-CGRP mAbs.
Higher baseline Vm in the right middle cerebral artery was negatively and independently associated with ≥50% response to anti-CGRP mAbs.
Lack of relatives with migraine (i.e., no family history) was negatively associated with ≥50% response to anti-CGRP mAbs.
Good responders to mAbs were predominantly younger and had longer disease duration and unilateral pain localization compared with non-responders.
72 of 123 patients (58.5%) achieved ≥50% reduction in monthly migraine days and 43 (35%) achieved ≥75% reduction after anti-CGRP mAb treatment.
Monthly migraine days, monthly headache days, acute medication days, NRS pain scores, and HIT-6 scores all significantly decreased after mAb treatment compared with baseline in both responder groups.
One patient had an allergic reaction leading to treatment discontinuation after 3 months, and three patients developed mild constipation.
Vm in both MCAs correlated positively with post-treatment monthly migraine days, monthly headache days, and acute medication days.
Vm in the right MCA and basilar artery correlated positively with baseline NRS pain intensity scores.

Sensory Guillain-Barre syndrome (SGBS) represents a clinical spectrum including acute sensory demyelinating neuropathy, acute sensory large-fiber axonopathy-ganglionopathy, acute sensory small-fiber neuropathy-ganglionopathy, and acute autonomic and sensory ganglionopathy with profound autonomic failure.

In the case reported by Min et al. (2021) classified as acute small fiber neuropathy-ganglionopathy following ChAdOx1 vaccination, skin biopsy showed decreased intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD).

Nerve conduction studies performed within 4 weeks of symptom onset in classic SGBS cases (Oh et al., 2001) showed demyelinating abnormalities in motor nerve conduction in seven patients and sensory nerve conduction in two patients, explaining absence of weakness in some cases with only slowed conduction.

In a large cohort of 455 GBS patients (Fokke et al., 2014), the cyto-albuminologic dissociation in CSF, a classic hallmark of GBS, was found in less than half of patients when tested within the first days after symptom onset, meaning normal CSF protein levels do not rule out GBS diagnosis.
A previously proposed mechanism for post-vaccination sensory GBS (Waheed et al., 2021) is immune-mediated hypersensitivity to the vaccine solvent/adjuvant polyethylene glycol (PEG).

In the biopsy-proven post-COVID-19 small fiber neuropathy case described by Waheed et al. (2021), involvement of autonomic functions was not mentioned, despite SFN frequently involving autonomic fibers.
VEGF was actively expressed in fibroblast-like cells, periosteal osteoblasts, and osteonal osteoblasts within hypertrophic nonunion callus.
Osteoblasts expressing BMP-2 were localized in the periosteum and loose connective tissue of Haversian canals, with dysfunction of morphogenetic protein expression implicated in nonunion.
The number of immunopositive cells expressing TGF-β1 in nonunion callus exceeded that in control samples of consolidated fracture callus.
TNFα-expressing immunopositive cells were increased in nonunion callus relative to consolidated fracture controls, correlating with caspase-3 expression.

Caspase-3 expression in fibroblast-like cells, osteoblasts, chondroblasts, and microvascular endotheliocytes correlated with TGF-β1 and TNFα expression, implicating apoptosis in nonunion pathogenesis.

The authors conclude that fracture nonunion results from overproduction of cytotoxic and proapoptotic factors during chronic inflammation combined with dysfunctional expression of morphogenetic proteins.
Pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PCPG) tumors showed the highest expression of all three autonomic nervous system (ANS) gene signatures (TNG, SNS, PNS) among the 32 TCGA cancer types studied.

Squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck (HNSC), uterine carcinosarcoma (USC), and testicular germ cell tumor (TGCT) were consistently ranked in the top 10 for expression of all three ANS signatures.
Brain tumors (low grade glioma and glioblastoma multiforme) expressed strong overall neuron growth (TNG) and parasympathetic (PNS) signatures but relatively weak sympathetic (SNS) signatures.
Sarcoma (SARC) showed high expression of TNG and SNS gene markers but not the PNS signature.
Breast cancer (BRCA) ranked low on all three ANS gene expression signatures, while prostate cancer (PRAD) showed strong expression of both SNS and PNS signatures.
Uveal melanoma (UVM), skin cutaneous melanoma (SKCM), and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBC) were at the lower end of the spectrum for ANS signature expression.

The overall neuron growth (TNG) signature was significantly positively correlated with angiogenesis markers in 18 of 25 (72%) tested cancer types, with the strongest correlation in pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
The TNG signature was also positively associated with TGF-β pathway activation in 17 of 25 (68%) tested cancer types, with the strongest correlation in liver hepatocellular carcinoma.
The sympathetic nervous system (SNS) signature showed its strongest positive correlation with TGF-β activation in thyroid carcinoma.
Higher TNG signature levels were associated with significantly lower lymphocyte fraction in bladder, cervical, colon, esophageal, and head and neck cancers.
Decreased cytolytic activity was observed with higher ANS signature levels in lung squamous cell carcinoma and head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.
Increased regulatory T-cell (T-reg) levels were found in renal clear cell carcinoma with higher ANS signature levels.
The SNS signature was positively correlated with PD-1 or PD-L1 expression in nine cancer types: BRCA, ESCA, LGG, LIHC, LUAD, PAAD, PRAD, THCA, and THYM.
TNG signature levels were higher in larger tumors of kidney renal papillary cell carcinoma and rectal adenocarcinoma, but lower in larger lung adenocarcinoma tumors.

SNS signature levels were increased with higher stage and lymph node involvement in colon adenocarcinoma and lymph node involvement in thyroid carcinoma, but were lower in more advanced stages of renal clear cell carcinoma.
Increased PNS signature levels were found in more advanced stages of colon adenocarcinoma and in larger tumors of rectal adenocarcinoma.
In esophageal carcinoma, higher levels of TNG and PNS signatures were associated with increased all-cause mortality.
In bladder urothelial carcinoma, higher SNS signature levels were associated with increased all-cause mortality.
In head and neck squamous cell carcinoma and rectal adenocarcinoma, higher TNG signature levels were associated with lower all-cause mortality.
In testicular germ cell tumor, higher TNG and SNS signature levels were both associated with lower all-cause mortality.
Serum NGF levels were significantly reduced in acute symptomatic and future long-COVID-19 boys and girls compared to healthy controls, with a significant COVID-19 x gender interaction.
Reduced NGF levels were also observed specifically in post-infected asymptomatic girls (but not asymptomatic boys) compared to healthy controls.
Serum BDNF levels were significantly elevated in acute symptomatic and future long-COVID-19 girls compared to healthy girls, while remaining unchanged in asymptomatic individuals and in boys.

Oxidative stress markers FORT (reactive oxygen species) and FORD (antioxidant defense) showed no significant COVID-19, gender, or interaction effects between post-infected COVID-19 adolescents and healthy controls.

TGF-β serum levels were higher in acute symptomatic and future long-COVID-19 girls compared to healthy girls, identified via Tukey's post hoc comparisons despite non-significant overall ANOVA effects.
No significant COVID-19, gender, or interaction effects were found for the cytokines/chemokines IL-1α, IL-2, IL-6, IL-10, IL-12, MCP-1, and TNF-α across groups one month after negativization.
Spearman correlation tests showed no significant associations between BMI or age and any of the measured serum biomarkers across all groups.
In carefully selected patients with chronic pelvic pain, the majority experience complete or significant pain improvement after hysterectomy.
The paper recommends that all patients with chronic pelvic pain be evaluated for chronic overlapping pain conditions, including irritable bowel syndrome and fibromyalgia, prior to hysterectomy.

Depression, pain catastrophizing, and central sensitization are identified as risk factors for persistent pain or chronic postsurgical pain in patients undergoing hysterectomy for chronic pelvic pain.

In an LPS-induced chronic inflammation hypertension model, microglial activation and increased IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, and superoxide production in the RVLM were observed and were blunted by inhibiting microglial activation.

Targeted depletion of microglia in the PVN attenuated neuroinflammation, plasma vasopressin, kidney norepinephrine concentration, and blood pressure in angiotensin II- and L-NAME-induced hypertension models.

Minocycline (oral, 50 mg/kg/day) inhibited microglial activation and sympathetic activity and attenuated hypertension in spontaneously hypertensive rats and chronic angiotensin II-infused rats, but other studies using different doses/routes (systemic 25 mg/kg/day or central 0.5 µg/50 nL) failed to decrease BP despite observed microglial activation.
Brain (pro)renin receptor (PRR) immunoreactivity was significantly correlated with systolic blood pressure, and targeted knockdown of PRR attenuated angiotensin II-induced hypertension in mice.
Intracerebroventricular administration of AZD8797, a CX3CR1 inhibitor, attenuated fructose-induced hypertension and pro-inflammatory cytokine expression.

B1R is markedly upregulated with inflammation or tissue injury, and its antagonist R715 reduced blood pressure, decreased sympatho-excitation, and inhibited neuroinflammation in a DOCA-salt hypertension mouse model.

The B1R antagonist Leu8-des-Arg9-BK had conflicting effects on blood pressure across studies, showing no change when acutely injected into the fourth ventricle in WKY rats or female SHRs, but reducing BP and heart rate when infused into the lateral ventricle in male SHRs, a discrepancy attributed to sex, dose, and administration route differences.

TREM2 was significantly upregulated in microglia in an angiotensin II infusion hypertension model, and its overexpression mitigated the microglial inflammatory response, suggesting a beneficial effect on BP regulation.
Ablation of HMGB1 and its receptor RAGE attenuated persistent chronic noise-induced M1-type microglial activation and hypertension.

TGF-β supplementation in Ang II-induced hypertensive mice inhibited neuroinflammation and renal norepinephrine levels and shifted microglia toward the immunosuppressive resting M0 phenotype, affecting the onset of hypertension.

Chronic calcitriol (vitamin D) treatment shifted microglial polarization from pro-inflammatory M1 to immunoregulatory M2 phenotype in SHRs, though no significant difference in the trend of blood pressure reduction was observed.

TAK-242, a TLR4 inhibitor, abolished microglial activation, preserved blood-brain barrier integrity in PVN/RVLM/NTS, attenuated mean arterial pressure increases, and protected against autonomic dysfunction in spontaneously hypertensive rats.

ICV administration of chemically modified tetracycline-3 (CMT-3) inhibited microglial activation and neuroinflammation in the PVN, decreased sympathetic activity, and attenuated mean arterial pressure in Ang II rats, possibly via effects on gut microbial communities.

Kefir treatment decreased blood pressure and improved endothelial dysfunction in SHRs, mediated in part through improved intestinal wall integrity and abolition of microglial activation and neuroinflammation within the PVN and RVLM.

Aerobic training restored PVN autonomic nerve function, normalized HMGB1 content and microglial activation, reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine expression, and improved autonomic control while reducing BP and HR in SHRs.

After myocardial infarction, activated microglia were detected in the PVN, RVLM, NTS, and PAG, and ICV minocycline beginning one week prior to infarction reduced microglial and neuronal activation by at least 50% in these regions.

P2X7R, expressed on microglia, mediates increased pro-inflammatory cytokines in the PVN and augmented sympathetic activity after myocardial infarction; P2X7R antagonists or siRNA attenuated these effects and improved cardiac function.

Mincle expression in PVN microglia markedly increased 24 hours post-MI alongside sympathetic hyperactivity; targeted Mincle knockdown attenuated microglial activation and sympathetic nerve activity and reduced ventricular arrhythmia susceptibility post-MI, mediated via the NLRP3/IL-1β axis.

TLR4 expression in PVN microglia increased markedly 3 days post-MI; TLR4 knockdown via shRNA decreased microglial activation, Fos+ neuron activation, sympathoexcitation, and the incidence of malignant ventricular arrhythmias post-MI.

Acute LPS treatment increased TLR4 and TNF-α protein expression in PVN neurons colocalized with the ER stress marker GRP78, contributing to increased heart rate and plasma norepinephrine and decreased heart rate variability and HF components, effects attenuated by inhibiting TLR4 or ER stress.

Acute hypertension for 6 hours increased microglial synaptic contacts by 30% in the CVLM and RVLM, while acute hypotension for 6 hours reduced synaptic contacts by more than 20% in both regions, without accompanying changes in microglial morphology or M1/M2 phenotype numbers.

LED (light-emitting diode) therapy targeted at the PVN through the scalp/skull attenuated infarct size, reduced inducibility of ventricular arrhythmias, and decreased microglial activation and peripheral sympathetic activity following cardiac ischemia/reperfusion injury.
Syndromic mitral valve prolapse is commonly associated with genetic connective tissue disorders including Marfan syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome, and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

In patients with inherited connective tissue disorders such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, myxomatous mitral valve degeneration typically manifests only with advanced age, and most detailed molecular data come from Marfan syndrome rather than EDS itself.
Loeys-Dietz syndrome arises from mutations that alter transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β) signalling, underlying its connective tissue phenotype.

Across 3896 reported LDS cases, the most commonly reported clinical features and complications were aortic aneurysms and dissections, arterial tortuosity, high arched palate, abnormal uvula and hypertelorism.
LDS Type 2 (associated with TGFBR2 mutations) shares many clinical features with LDS Type 1 but demonstrates more aggressive aortic disease.
LDS Type 3 (linked to SMAD3 mutations) demonstrated an increased prevalence of mitral valve prolapse and arthritis compared with other LDS types.
LDS Types 4 and 5 (associated with TGFB2 and TGFB3 mutations respectively) demonstrated a lower prevalence of musculoskeletal and cardiovascular involvement compared with other LDS types.
Among 222 women with LDS who underwent 522 pregnancies, 4% experienced an aortic dissection and the peripartum mortality rate was 1%.
DHA at concentrations of 40 μM or higher significantly inhibited proliferation of both GO-derived and non-GO orbital fibroblasts across 24, 48, and 72 hours.
Baseline (untreated) proliferation rate measured by EdU incorporation was slightly higher in Graves' ophthalmopathy orbital fibroblasts compared to non-GO orbital fibroblasts.
DHA suppressed proliferation and DNA synthesis dose-dependently in both GO and non-GO orbital fibroblasts, with a significantly stronger inhibitory effect in GO-derived cells.
TGF-β1 stimulation markedly increased α-SMA, CTGF, COL1A1, and FN1 mRNA in both GO and non-GO orbital fibroblasts, with α-SMA and FN1 significantly higher in GO than non-GO TGF-β1-treated cells.
Pretreatment with DHA (10 or 20 μM) for 3 hours dose-dependently downregulated TGF-β1-induced fibrotic marker mRNA expression.
Western blot analysis showed DHA exposure suppressed α-SMA and CTGF protein expression in TGF-β1-stimulated orbital fibroblasts.
Immunofluorescence staining confirmed that TGF-β1-mediated upregulation of α-SMA and COL1A1 protein was remarkably repressed by DHA exposure in GO orbital fibroblasts.
Wound healing assays showed DHA significantly delayed wound closure (migration) of TGF-β1-treated GO-derived orbital fibroblasts at 24 and 48 hours.

RNA-seq identified 2589 differentially expressed genes between TGF-β1-alone and TGF-β1+DHA treated GO orbital fibroblasts, with DHA pretreatment downregulating genes in MAPK/ERK signaling and fibrosis-associated processes.
Western blotting confirmed that DHA treatment inhibited TGF-β1-induced phosphorylation of ERK1/2 in GO-derived orbital fibroblasts.
DHA reduced TGF-β1-induced STAT3 phosphorylation but had no significant effect on Smad2 or Smad3 phosphorylation, indicating a non-Smad-dependent mechanism.

Pharmacologic inhibition of ERK1/2 (U0126) or STAT3 (Stattic) suppressed TGF-β1-induced α-SMA and CTGF protein expression, reproducing the antifibrotic effect of DHA, which similarly blocked ERK and STAT3 signaling.

DHA significantly suppressed IL-1β-induced mRNA expression of inflammatory markers (IL-6, IL-8, CXCL1, MCP-1, ICAM-1) in orbital fibroblasts from both GO and non-GO patients, with GO OFs showing a more pronounced inflammatory response to IL-1β than non-GO OFs.
IL-1β stimulation upregulated HAS1 and HAS3 mRNA expression specifically in GO-derived orbital fibroblasts (not in non-GO OFs), an effect inhibited by DHA pretreatment.
IL-1β increased hyaluronic acid production in GO-derived orbital fibroblast culture supernatants, and DHA pretreatment decreased this effect in a dose-dependent manner.

Loeys-Dietz syndrome is molecularly diagnosed by pathogenic variants in one of six genes (TGFBR1, TGFBR2, SMAD2, SMAD3, TGFB2, TGFB3) encoding components of the TGF-beta receptor signaling cascade that regulate differentiation of bone, cartilage, blood vessel and heart tissue.
Heterozygous loss-of-function variants in TGFBR1 and TGFBR2 are the most commonly identified mutations in LDS, accounting for up to 80% of cases.
The mean age of death in Loeys-Dietz syndrome (26 years old) is significantly lower than in Marfan syndrome, reflecting more aggressive vascular disease.

Trio-based whole exome sequencing in the first neonatal case identified a novel, de novo, heterozygous missense TGFBR2 variant (c.1378C>G, p.(Arg460Gly)) confirming the diagnosis of LDS within the first month of life.
In Patient 1, the aortic root dilation progressed rapidly from 13 mm (Z score +3) at birth to 18 mm (Z score +4.7) by 5 months and 24.5 mm (Z score +6.7) by 13 months of age.
Low-dose losartan (angiotensin receptor blocker) at 0.6 mg/kg/day was started in Patient 1 to slow aortic dilation, producing only transient stabilization before the aneurysm continued to enlarge.

A connective tissue disorder gene panel in the second case identified an already-known heterozygous pathogenic TGFB3 variant (c.899G>A, p.Arg300Gln), which segregated with a mildly affected mother and brother, confirming familial LDS.
Across the pooled literature review of 16 early-diagnosed LDS patients, TGFBR2 mutations were the most common (75%), while TGFBR1 and TGFB3 were each found in only one subject.
Among the 16 pooled neonatal/infant LDS cases, the aorta was involved in all but one patient (93.7%), predominantly as ascending aortic dilation or aneurysm (75%).
Pulmonary artery dilation was found in 9 of 16 (56.2%) pooled LDS patients, indicating frequent pulmonary vascular involvement alongside aortic disease.
Arterial tortuosity, a hallmark distinguishing LDS from Marfan syndrome, was reported in 10 of 16 (62.5%) pooled neonatal/infant LDS patients.

Joint laxity/dislocation and articular contractures (e.g., camptodactyly, clenched hands) were each reported in 10 of 16 (62.5%) pooled LDS patients, reflecting the connective-tissue/hypermobility component of the syndrome.
Hypertelorism was present in 81.2% and bifid/broad uvula or cleft palate in 87.5% of the 16 pooled LDS patients, consistent with the classic LDS craniofacial triad.

Of the 16 pooled neonatal/infant-diagnosed LDS patients, 14 (87.5%) were alive at the time of report; one died at 21 days of life from pulmonary artery rupture and another at 9 years from aortic dissection.

Among the pooled cohort, ARBs (mainly losartan) were the most frequently used medical therapy (31.2%), followed by ACE-inhibitors and beta-blockers (25% each), with 3 patients receiving more than one drug.
Of the 10 pooled patients on medical therapy, 3 remained clinically stable and one improved while on losartan.
Half of the pooled LDS cohort (8/16, 50%) underwent surgical vascular procedures, generally without complications.

Drawing on Marfan syndrome trial data, combined beta-blocker plus losartan therapy has shown greater efficacy in reducing aortic root dilation than beta-blocker monotherapy, supporting extrapolated use in LDS.
Dexamethasone improved extracellular matrix deposition in fibroblasts carrying TGFBR1 and TGFBR2 mutations in vitro, but no in vivo clinical studies have confirmed a benefit.

Multiple distinct amino-acid substitutions at TGFBR2 residue 460 (R460G, R460C, R460H, R460L) have been reported across a spectrum of phenotypes from classic LDS to isolated thoracic aortic aneurysm, indicating this conserved residue is critical for receptor signal transduction.

The authors note that about one-third of LDS cases are familial and tend to have milder clinical signs than sporadic cases, as illustrated by the second reported case where LDS features were subtle at birth and diagnosis relied on family history.
Chronic musculoskeletal pain lasting more than three months was reported by 85% of participants with LDS and 67% of those with vEDS.

The overall prevalence of chronic musculoskeletal pain in LDS/vEDS patients (79%) was much higher than in the Norwegian general population (24%) and higher than in a US Marfan syndrome population (67%).
LDS patients reported significantly higher mean pain intensity during activity than vEDS patients, though not at rest.
The number of pain locations did not differ significantly between LDS and vEDS patients.
Participants with LDS reported significantly higher cardiovascular disease burden than those with vEDS.
Participants with vEDS scored significantly higher on the HADS depression subscale than those with LDS.
Perceived sleep problems were significantly associated with reporting chronic musculoskeletal pain.
Higher fatigue symptom levels were significantly associated with reporting chronic musculoskeletal pain.
Higher multi-organ symptom burden was significantly associated with reporting chronic musculoskeletal pain.
58% of the LDS/vEDS study population reported clinically relevant (high) levels of fatigue symptoms.
The prevalence of high fatigue levels was higher in LDS (64%) than vEDS (44%) and both were higher than Norwegian Marfan syndrome patients (42%).
Fatigue severity scores did not differ significantly by sex, diagnosis (LDS vs vEDS), or age.
Low physical activity level was significantly associated with higher fatigue scores.
Sleep problems were significantly associated with higher fatigue scores.
Presence of chronic musculoskeletal pain was significantly associated with higher fatigue scores.
Higher cardiovascular disease burden was significantly associated with higher fatigue scores.
Higher multi-organ symptom burden was significantly associated with higher fatigue scores.
Higher anxiety symptom scores (HADS-A) were significantly associated with higher fatigue scores.
Sleep problems were common, reported by 67% of participants, with difficulty falling asleep the most frequent complaint.
More than half of participants with chronic pain reported that their pain first developed during childhood or adolescence.
Chronic pain interfered with participation in leisure activities, housekeeping, and work life among those affected.
Loeys-Dietz syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in genes encoding components of the TGF-beta signaling pathway: TGFBR1, TGFBR2, SMAD3, and TGFB2.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome results from pathogenic variants in COL3A1, which encodes type III collagen, the major collagen in blood vessels and hollow organs.
In LDS patients, pain may be connected to joint contractures and osteoarthritis linked to SMAD3 variants.
Pain intensity during activity and at rest did not differ significantly by gender or age in the study population.
The patient's heart rate rose from 79 bpm supine to 126 bpm standing during active-standing TCD testing, consistent with postural tachycardia syndrome.
Middle cerebral artery blood flow velocity decreased from supine to standing position during the TCD test.
Blood pressure remained normal throughout the supine-to-standing TCD test despite the heart rate increase.
Physical examination revealed hypermobility of the metacarpophalangeal joints and increased skin elasticity, consistent with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome/joint hypermobility.
Genetic testing identified a variant in the LDB3 gene in this patient with POTS and EDS.
The patient's symptoms were relieved following fluid infusion and rehabilitation therapy.
Mothers with EDS reported significantly more pregnancy losses (miscarriage, stillbirth, termination) than mothers without EDS, regardless of infant EDS status.
Live birth rate was lower for EDS mothers (68.9%) than non-EDS mothers (82.1%), with a correspondingly higher rate of non-live outcomes among EDS mothers.

Among the three maternal/fetal EDS groups, the EDS mother/EDS infant group had the highest percentages of birth complications and treatment for preterm birth, and the lowest mean gestational age at preterm birth, while the non-EDS mother/EDS infant group had the highest rate of preterm birth.

When comparing mothers with EDS versus mothers without EDS (regardless of infant status), there was no difference in birth complications, cesarean delivery, treatment for preterm birth, occurrence of preterm birth, or mean gestational age.
When comparing infants with EDS versus without EDS (regardless of maternal status), an increased rate was observed in EDS infants for all outcome categories except cesarean delivery.
The occurrence of preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) as a subcategory of preterm birth complications was significantly different among the three maternal/fetal EDS groups.
Mothers without EDS had a significantly higher percentage of PPROM than mothers with EDS, with a relative risk of 0.36 favoring EDS mothers (i.e., non-EDS mothers had ~2.8x the risk).
No significant difference in PPROM occurrence was found between EDS and non-EDS infant groups.
Mean gestational age at preterm birth was associated with the EDS status of the infant but not with the EDS status of the mother, suggesting fetal genotype drives timing of preterm delivery.
Two family members (III:1 and III:2) with severe EDS-consistent phenotypes carried compound heterozygous B3GALT6 variants (c.883C>T:p.R295C and c.510_517del:p.L170fs*268).

Heterozygous carriage of the c.510_517del:p.L170fs*268 variant co-segregated with a moderate, non-EDS phenotype (radioulnar joint limitation, S-shaped scoliosis, thick vermilion of lips) in three family members (I:1, II:1, II:2), consistent with an autosomal-dominant mode of inheritance.

In HeLa cells, the mutant R295C β3Galt6 protein mislocalized to the cytoplasm instead of the Golgi apparatus, indicating loss of function, despite showing significantly increased protein expression relative to wild-type.

The L170fs*268 frameshift-elongation variant produced a larger-molecular-weight mutant protein with significantly reduced expression compared to wild-type, but the mutant protein was still correctly localized to the Golgi apparatus.

The R295C variant has a low allele frequency (0.0005) in the East Asian gnomAD population and is not located in the catalytic galactosyltransferase domain, with the affected residue not highly conserved across species and predicted benign/tolerant by 13 of 23 in silico tools.
Both novel variants (R295C and L170fs*268) were classified as pathogenic according to ACMG/AMP criteria, with L170fs*268 meeting PVS1/PM1/PM2/PP1/PP4 and R295C meeting PS3/PM2/PM3/PP1/PP4.

Prior literature reports approximately 60 patients from 40 unrelated families with autosomal-recessive B3GALT6 pathogenic variants causing spondylodysplastic EDS, comprising 41 distinct pathogenic variants (28 missense, 2 start-codon loss, 2 in-frame deletions, 2 in-frame duplications, 5 truncating frameshifts, and 2 elongating frameshifts), none previously reported to cause a dominant phenotype.
FM patients showed an increased IFN-score in peripheral B-cells compared to healthy controls.
A 'high inflammatory subset' of seven FM patients showed a markedly higher IFN score than controls.
The 'high inflammatory subset' of seven FM patients showed a higher IFN signature than the remaining 18 FM patients.
RNA-sequencing of B-cells identified 60 differentially expressed genes between FM patients and controls, 33 upregulated and 27 downregulated.
The cluster of genes with increased expression in FM patients was largely composed of interferon-responsive genes (25 of 33, 76%).
Within the upregulated gene cluster, the highest expression was seen for the interferon-regulated and proinflammatory genes S100A8, VCAM, CD163 and ANXA1 in a subset of seven FM patients.

Pathway enrichment analysis of differentially expressed B-cell genes showed upregulation of Endogenous TLR signaling, KRAS activation, Inflammatory response, Complement system, and Interferon alpha and gamma response pathways in FM patients.

Comparing the high inflammatory subset (7 patients) to the remaining 18 FM patients identified 54 differentially expressed genes with enrichment for TNF-alpha signaling via NF-kB, inflammatory response and endogenous TLR signaling.
The FM-score in the high inflammatory subset trended slightly higher than the remaining 18 FM patients but was not statistically significant.
Of 92 serum inflammatory proteins tested, 19 were significantly increased in FM patients compared to controls, and none were reduced.
Among the elevated serum inflammatory proteins, AXIN1, STAMBP and SIRT2 showed the highest relative increase in FM patients, consistent with a prior independent FM cohort study.
A subset of 13 FM patients with more pronounced increases in serum inflammatory protein levels had a significantly higher FM-score than the remaining 17 patients.
No difference in fatigue severity score (FSS) was found between the subset of 13 patients with elevated inflammatory proteins and the remaining patients.
Serum levels of TNF-α, IL-8, CD40, TNFSF14 (LIGHT) and TNFRSF9 (CD137) were confirmed elevated in FM patients, consistent with prior studies.
Increased serum levels of the chemokines CCL3 and IL-8 were found in FM patients, consistent with prior reports of chemokine elevation implicated in central sensitization and pain.
Serum IL-18 receptor 1 (IL-18R1) was increased in FM patients while IL-1β and IL-18 themselves showed no significant increase, arguing against classical inflammasome activation as the driver.
The study found no correlation between fatigue severity (FSS) and either the B-cell inflammation/interferon score or serum inflammatory protein levels.
Most FM patients reported that regular, low-intensity exercise improved their fatigue, consistent with prior reports that aerobic exercise improves fatigue and pain in FM.
NBIF treatment reduced leukotriene C4 (LTC4) production in IgE/Ag-stimulated mouse bone marrow-derived mast cells.
NBIF treatment reduced prostaglandin D2 (PGD2) production in IgE/Ag-stimulated mast cells.
NBIF treatment reduced production of inflammatory cytokines in IgE/Ag-stimulated mast cells.
NBIF decreased degranulation of bone marrow-derived mast cells stimulated by IgE/Ag.
NBIF suppressed phosphorylation of mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs) in activated mast cells.
NBIF repressed the nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB)-related signaling pathway in activated mast cells.
Oral administration of NBIF inhibited the IgE-induced passive systemic anaphylaxis (PSA) reaction in mice in a dose-dependent manner.
A fluorogenic assay detected specific thrombin activity in skin biopsies of both mice and rats, and this activity was essentially abolished by the specific thrombin inhibitor SIXAC.
Rat skin biopsies weighed significantly more than mouse skin biopsies.
Thrombin activity normalized to tissue weight was significantly higher in rat skin than in mouse skin.
Rats had a significantly thicker epidermal layer than mice on H&E staining.
Rats showed significantly higher intra-epidermal small-fiber density (IENFD) than mice.
One week after subcutaneous adjuvant injection, mice showed significantly increased heat sensitivity (shorter response latency) compared with controls, though not at 24 hours.
Twenty-four hours after focal adjuvant injection, thrombin activity was markedly higher in the injected paw skin than in the contralateral paw or control skin.

One week after adjuvant injection, thrombin activity in the injected paw declined from its peak but remained elevated, and the contralateral paw also showed significantly increased thrombin activity relative to controls, suggesting spread of inflammation.
One week after systemic LPS injection, mice did not show increased heat sensitivity compared with controls.

Despite no behavioral change, LPS-injected mice showed significantly higher skin thrombin activity than controls one week post-injection, though the increase was smaller than seen with focal adjuvant inflammation.
In human skin biopsies from patients evaluated for small-fiber neuropathy, thrombin activity did not correlate with patient age.
Across all studied patients, skin thrombin activity significantly correlated with the percentile of intra-epidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD).
Among patients with severe skin denervation meeting SFN criteria, thrombin activity no longer correlated with IENFD percentile.
Patients with known autoimmune/inflammatory disease or elevated inflammatory markers showed significantly lower skin thrombin activity than idiopathic patients.
Basal skin thrombin activity did not differ significantly between ICR and C57BL/6J mouse strains, ruling out strain as a confound for the inflammation model differences.
A low but statistically significant correlation between thrombin activity and IENFD percentile was observed in the inflammatory patient subgroup but not in the idiopathic subgroup.
Molecular docking showed gallic acid binds the P2X7 receptor at a pocket formed by its B and C chains via hydrogen bonds with a binding affinity of 6.4 kcal/mol, indicating a stable interaction.

Model rats (comorbid visceral pain and depression) showed significantly higher AWR pain scores than sham rats under all pressures before treatment, confirming successful establishment of visceral hyperalgesia.

Four weeks of gallic acid intragastric administration or one week of P2X7shRNA intrathecal injection significantly lowered AWR pain scores at 20, 40, and 60 mmHg compared with the untreated model group.
At the highest pressure tested (80 mmHg), the pain-relieving effect of gallic acid or P2X7shRNA on AWR score was weaker and less evident than at lower pressures.
Comorbidity model rats moved a shorter distance and spent less time in the center of the open field than sham rats, indicating anxiety/depression-like behavior.

Gallic acid and P2X7shRNA treatment significantly increased moving distance and time spent in the center of the open field compared with the model group, indicating alleviated depression/anxiety-like behavior.
Comorbidity model rats showed no preference between sucrose water and pure water (SCPT rate near 50%), indicating anhedonia relative to sham rats.
Comorbidity model rats showed shorter immobility time in the forced swim test than sham rats, which the authors interpreted as indicating greater despair-like behavior.
Gallic acid and P2X7shRNA treatment significantly increased SCPT rate and reduced immobility time in the FST compared with the model group, indicating relief of depression-like symptoms.

H&E staining showed the colonic wall structure was complete, uniform, and free of edema or inflammatory infiltration across all groups, indicating the CRD modeling method did not cause structural intestinal damage, consistent with a functional (IBS-like) rather than organic disorder.
P2X7 receptor mRNA and protein expression were significantly higher in the hippocampus, spinal cord, and dorsal root ganglion of comorbid visceral pain/depression model rats compared with sham rats.
Gallic acid and P2X7shRNA significantly reduced P2X7 receptor mRNA and protein levels in hippocampus, spinal cord, and DRG compared with the model group, while non-code shRNA (ncRNA) had no effect.

Gallic acid and P2X7shRNA administration decreased GFAP levels and cell number in the hippocampus compared with the model and ncRNA groups, and reduced co-expression of GFAP with P2X7 receptor in hippocampus and DRG.

Phosphorylated ERK1/2 (p-ERK1/2) levels were significantly higher in hippocampus, spinal cord, and DRG of model and ncRNA groups compared with sham, while total ERK1/2 levels were unchanged across groups.
Gallic acid and P2X7shRNA treatments largely reduced p-ERK1/2 expression in hippocampus, spinal cord, and DRG compared with the model group.
Serum IL-1β and TNF-α concentrations were significantly higher in the model group than in the sham group, while serum IL-10 was significantly lower.
Gallic acid and P2X7shRNA significantly increased serum IL-10 levels in comorbid visceral pain and depression rats compared with the model group, reversing the disease-associated decrease.
In the hippocampus, IL-1β and TNF-α mRNA were upregulated while IL-10 and BDNF mRNA were downregulated in model and ncRNA groups compared with sham rats.
Gallic acid and P2X7shRNA treatment reversed the hippocampal downregulation of IL-10 and BDNF and the upregulation of IL-1β and TNF-α seen in the model group.

The authors concluded that P2X7 receptor expression was negatively associated with hippocampal BDNF concentration, proposing that gallic acid alleviates depression via P2X7 receptor downregulation and consequent BDNF elevation.
Following neonatal colorectal distension, approximately 84.1% of male rats developed visceral pain, and of those, 43.6% also developed comorbid depression-like behavior.

Of 139 male neonatal rats subjected to CRD, 51 rats fully met criteria for comorbid visceral pain and depression on behavioral testing after reaching adulthood, giving a modeling (comorbidity) rate of about 36%.

The recurrent MAP3K7 variant c.1454C>T (p.(Pro485Leu)) is the most common cause of frontometaphyseal dysplasia type 2 (FMD2) and produces a severe skeletal phenotype with keloid scarring and intellectual disability in a subset of patients.
CSCF is caused by nonrecurrent heterozygous missense MAP3K7 mutations, most often considered loss-of-function, in contrast to the recurrent gain-of-function mutations causing FMD2.
In a cohort expansion, congenital heart defects (mostly left-sided) were found in 7 of 13 CSCF patients, ranging from mitral valve prolapse to hypoplastic left heart syndrome spectrum.

Cardiomyopathy (one hypertrophic, three dilated) was observed in 4 of 12 CSCF patients, with the most severe case in a neonate carrying the c.143G>A (p.(Gly48Glu)) variant who is on the heart transplant waiting list.
Joint laxity was a consistent feature in pediatric CSCF patients, present in 8 of 10 patients assessed.
No intellectual disability was described in any of the CSCF patients, in contrast to FMD2 where ID has been reported.
Autism spectrum disorder was present in 3 of 7 CSCF patients for whom neurological information was available.

Overexpression of all tested CSCF-causing MAP3K7 missense mutations in HEK293T cells resulted in significantly lower protein expression levels compared to wild-type MAP3K7, whereas FMD2-causing mutations showed similar or higher expression.
Cotransfection with TAB1 normalized the reduced expression levels of most CSCF-causing MAP3K7 mutations to wild-type levels, except for MAP3K7Trp241Gly, suggesting TAB1 stabilizes the mutant protein.

Autophosphorylation of MAP3K7 at Thr187 was reduced for most CSCF-causing mutations compared to wild-type upon TAB1 coexpression, while FMD2-causing mutations showed normal or increased autophosphorylation, except for MAP3K7Arg83His which behaved like wild-type.

Phosphorylated NF-kB was reduced in cells overexpressing most CSCF-causing MAP3K7 mutations (except Arg83His) compared to wild-type, and also reduced for several FMD2-causing mutations, indicating this downstream target does not clearly distinguish the two disorders.

Contrary to the RAS/MAPK pathway hyperactivation typical of Noonan syndrome, most CSCF-causing MAP3K7 mutations resulted in reduced phospho-ERK levels compared to wild-type, except MAP3K7Arg83His, suggesting a distinct mechanism underlies the clinical overlap with Noonan syndrome.

The MAP3K7Arg83His variant, found in a patient with a clear CSCF clinical phenotype, showed lower baseline expression but behaved similarly to wild-type in autophosphorylation, NF-kB, and ERK assays, suggesting a milder molecular effect than other CSCF mutations despite a full clinical phenotype.

A pediatric FMD2 patient with the recurrent p.(Pro485Leu) variant presented with a complex congenital cardiac defect (VSD, pulmonary atresia, bicuspid aortic valve, progressive aortic root dilatation, PLSVC, ectopic atrial tachycardia) that was a major cause of failure to thrive.
Genes belonging to the TGF-beta cascade, including MAP3K7, appear predisposed to left-sided heart lesions and progressive aortic dilatation, suggesting need for serial echocardiographic screening.

Five independent Dutch pediatric patients suspected clinically of having Noonan syndrome were found by whole-exome sequencing to carry MAP3K7 variants of unknown significance, and further assessment confirmed CSCF diagnosis instead.

CSCF patients show substantial clinical overlap with Noonan syndrome (short stature, cardiac abnormalities, hypertelorism, ptosis, widely spaced nipples, epicanthal folds), which the authors argue should place MAP3K7 mutations in the differential diagnosis of Noonan syndrome despite molecular findings showing pathway downregulation rather than the upregulation typical of RASopathies.
A majority of hospitalized COVID-19 survivors developed new impairment in activities of daily living, fatigue, or worsened general physical function within one month of hospitalization.
Among those with impairment at 1 month, most participants showed partial or full recovery in ADL, fatigue, or HAQ severity by 6 months, though a substantial minority did not recover.
A subset of COVID-19 hospitalization survivors developed new functional impairment between 1 and 6 months after discharge, despite not having it at 1 month.
Lower socioeconomic status was significantly associated with failure to improve in ADL impairment at 6 months after COVID-19 hospitalization.
Age of 65 years or older showed a trend toward association with failure to improve in ADL impairment at 6 months, though it did not reach statistical significance.
Stress urinary incontinence was reported by 60% of cisgender women with EDS in this survey.
Urgency urinary incontinence was reported by 54% of participants with EDS.
Fecal incontinence was reported by 24% of women with EDS.
Pelvic organ prolapse was reported by 21% of participants with EDS.
Among the pelvic floor symptoms assessed, bladder symptoms were rated as the most bothersome by participants with EDS.
Prolapse symptoms had a greater impact on quality of life in women with EDS under age 40 compared with older participants.
Pelvic pain was reported by 71% of women with EDS.
Among pelvic pain types, dysmenorrhea, muscle and joint pain, and backache had the highest pain ratings, each with a median score of 7 out of 10.
IL-33 expression induced in response to SARS-CoV-2 correlates with seropositivity in COVID-19 convalescent individuals.

Elevated CRH levels in COVID-19 may activate CRH receptors on mast cells, influencing vascular permeability, and COVID-19-related psychological stress can induce MC-related disease including mastocytosis via CRH-driven degranulation.
Circulating S1P has emerged as a negative biomarker of severity and mortality in COVID-19 patients, and S1P generation induces calcium mobilization leading to mast cell degranulation.

Development of clinical COVID-19 involves dysfunctional MC activation and histamine release, and histamine signaling has been suggested as a potential therapeutic target to prevent progression to ARDS.
MRGPRX2, a low-affinity IgE-independent mast cell activation receptor, has been proposed as a therapeutic target for COVID-19.
PAF activates mast cells and induces chemotaxis, and COVID-19 manifestations including pulmonary microthrombosis and inflammation are mediated via the PAF receptor.

Tryptase released from mast cells can activate PAR-2 in an autocrine/paracrine manner, and protease-activated receptor signaling has been suggested to play a role in COVID-19-induced hyperinflammation.
Women with high levels of estradiol exhibited a lower risk of developing severe COVID-19 symptoms and a lower incidence of death, based on preliminary research.

Serum estradiol levels in COVID-19 patients may reflect infection severity because acute critical illness can suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, biochemically manifesting as low FSH, LH, and E2.

Hyperthyroidism is common in female COVID-19 patients and coexists with TSH suppression related to elevated IL-6, with degranulated mast cells and histamine-induced CD86 overexpression in thyroid tissue implicated in the mechanism.

Approximately one-fifth of COVID-19 patients exhibited menstrual volume decrease or cycle prolongation, approximately one-fifth exhibited menorrhagia, and approximately 30% experienced new dysmenorrhea.
Endometriosis does not appear to increase susceptibility to COVID-19 infection but may alter the manifestation of the disease, though thoracic endometriosis may confer increased risk.

Single-cell RNA-sequencing studies indicate low coexpression of ACE2 and TMPRSS2 in myometrium, uterus, ovaries, and fallopian tube, and in preconceptional endometrium, suggesting these tissues are likely not highly susceptible to SARS-CoV-2 infection.

In contrast to other studies, coexpression of ACE2 and TMPRSS2 was confirmed within the human ovarian cortex and medulla, including oocytes of different stages and granulosa cells, with no marked difference between young/old or low/high-reserve ovaries.

Placental tissues showed significantly lower expression of both ACE2 and TMPRSS2 compared with adult lung tissues, with term placenta expressing low to no ACE2, limiting the ability of SARS-CoV-2 to pass from maternal blood to fetus.

Single-cell transcriptomic studies of early placenta (6-14 weeks gestation) revealed stable coexpression of ACE2 and TMPRSS2 in decidual stromal/perivascular cells and villous trophoblasts, suggesting early pregnancy infection may allow transplacental transmission.

Severe COVID-19 has been associated with impaired fetal growth, an approximately 2-fold increased risk of stillbirth, and a 3-fold increased risk of preterm birth (likely influenced by iatrogenic deliveries), with prematurity-related worse perinatal outcomes.
MCAS is estimated to affect up to 17% of some populations and has a strong female predilection, with a broad and heterogeneous pathophysiological spectrum.

Long COVID resembles MCAS in high residual cardiovascular risk and persistent inflammatory/procoagulative blood chemistry, with NLRP3 inflammasome hyperactivation potentially crucial to coagulation disorders in female reproductive organs in both conditions.

There is no evidence that a history of asymptomatic or mild SARS-CoV-2 infection in females negatively affects normal female fertility, embryo laboratory outcomes, or clinical outcomes in ART treatments, and cohort studies of SARS-CoV-2-positive mothers with asymptomatic/mild disease showed no adverse maternal or neonatal effects.

Available data do not demonstrate an increased teratogenic potential of SARS-CoV-2, and limited evidence has not shown any association between COVID-19 and increased risk of miscarriage; pregnant women do not appear more likely to contract SARS-CoV-2 than nonpregnant women of the same age, though ICU admission and invasive ventilation are more common among pregnant women with COVID-19.

Neutralization of histamine inhibits nuclear translocation of NF-κB and proinflammatory cytokine release, and this MC-targeted approach has been used successfully in treating chronic dyspareunia, vaginitis, and dysfunctional uterine bleeding.
The SSL12 allelic variant from S. aureus strain NCTC8325 induces degranulation of murine mast cells.
The SSL12 allelic variant from S. aureus strain MRSA252, despite 82% sequence similarity to the active NCTC8325 variant, did not induce mast cell degranulation.

Domain-swap mutants harboring the oligonucleotide/oligosaccharide binding (OB)-fold domain of the active SSL12 variant retained the ability to activate mast cells, localizing the responsible region to the OB-fold.
The single amino acid substitution L56F in the OB-fold domain diminished the mast cell stimulatory activity of SSL12.
The combinatorial substitution L56F/K92E abolished the mast cell stimulatory activity of both the OB-fold-harboring mutant and the intact active SSL12 variant.
The combinatorial substitution L56F/D95S abolished the mast cell stimulatory activity of both the OB-fold-harboring mutant and the intact active SSL12 variant.
The combinatorial substitution L56F/S100V abolished the mast cell stimulatory activity of both the OB-fold-harboring mutant and the intact active SSL12 variant.
Antisense oligonucleotides targeting the 3' UTR of LCP2 mRNA knocked down LCP2 expression in a human T-cell line and in primary human T cells.
LCP2-targeting ASOs suppressed T-cell receptor mediated T-cell activation following LCP2 knockdown.
LCP2-targeting ASOs also suppressed FcεR1-mediated mast cell activation, consistent with LCP2's known role in mast cells.
LCP2 is considered an 'undruggable' target lacking structural features amenable to standard small-molecule inhibitor development, motivating the use of an ASO drug modality.
Exposure of mouse bone marrow-derived mast cells to Aedes albopictus saliva significantly increased beta-hexosaminidase release, indicating mast cell degranulation.
Recombinant alADA at 10 μg/ml significantly increased release of beta-hexosaminidase, tryptase activity, and IL-6 from mast cells, indicating mast cell activation and degranulation.
Challenge of mast cells with al34k2 did not significantly change beta-hexosaminidase, tryptase activity, or IL-6 levels, indicating al34k2 does not directly activate mast cells.
Recombinant human tryptase degraded alADA, with complete degradation observed overnight at high concentration and significant cleavage at 3 and 6 hours.
Recombinant human tryptase progressively cleaved al34k2 into smaller peptides over time.
alADA was clearly cleaved by recombinant human chymase at a concentration of 0.2 μg.
al34k2 was sufficiently degraded by recombinant human chymase at a low concentration of 0.02 μg, appearing more sensitive to chymase cleavage than alADA.
The chymase inhibitor HY-109059 (Fulacimstat) significantly reduced chymase-mediated degradation of both alADA and al34k2, confirming that the degradation observed was chymase-specific.
al34k2 dose-dependently enhanced the enzymatic activities of both recombinant human tryptase and chymase toward their respective chromogenic substrates.
alADA had a dose-dependent enhancement effect on recombinant human tryptase activity, significant even at the lowest concentrations tested.
A high concentration (10 μg) of alADA inhibited chymase activity up to 30 minutes, whereas lower concentrations had no effect on the substrate conversion rate.
Neither alADA nor al34k2 alone had detectable enzymatic activity on the tryptase (S-2288) or chymase (L-1595) chromogenic substrates, confirming they are not intrinsic proteases.
Sequence analysis showed that alADA and al34k2 each contain four predicted chymase target sites, and eight and three predicted tryptase target sites respectively.
Prior studies cited by the authors report that Aedes aegypti ADA is upregulated after blood feeding, enhances dengue virus replication, and inhibits chikungunya virus.
IgG antibody response against al34k2 has been proposed in prior literature as a candidate biomarker for detecting human exposure to Ae. albopictus.
Small fiber neuropathy, characterized by pain and dysautonomia, occurs in up to 60% of patients with sarcoidosis.
Small fiber neuropathy in sarcoidosis is often under-recognized and its diagnosis requires exclusion of large fiber disease, aided by skin biopsy and sudomotor testing.

No established treatment exists for sarcoidosis-associated small fiber neuropathy; palliative options used case-by-case include tramadol, anticonvulsants, topiramate, GABA analogues, and intravenous immunoglobulin.
Fatigue affects at least 60% of sarcoidosis patients and compromises quality of life, but it is not directly related to granulomatous disease activity.
Gain-of-function mutations in SCN9A (encoding Nav1.7) have been identified in about 5% of patients with painful idiopathic small fiber neuropathy.
Faber et al. (2012) identified a heterozygous c.554G>A, p.R185H mutation in SCN9A in two unrelated patients with painful small fiber neuropathy.
The R185H mutation caused hyperexcitability of rat DRG neurons when transfected in vitro.
The same R185H mutation was also found to be associated with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy.
Biallelic SCN9A loss-of-function mutations cause congenital insensitivity to pain, whereas monoallelic carriers have normal pain sensitivity.
Scn9a mRNA expression in DRG and spinal cord was comparable between R185H mutant and wild-type mice, with no significant effect of genotype.
Nav1.7 protein was expressed in 78.4±3.4% of DRG neurons in both wild-type and mutant mice with a comparable profile across cell sizes.
In sciatic nerve, Nav1.7 immunofluorescence density showed a sex effect (higher in females) but no genotype effect.
Body weight measured weekly from week 1 to week 31 did not differ between mutant and wild-type mice.
No genotype or sex effect was found for muscle strength (string test) or motor coordination (crenelated bar test).
First-response latencies on the hot plate at 48, 52, and 56°C showed no genotype or sex effect.
Homozygous R185H females showed shorter (more sensitive) jump latency on the 56°C hot plate compared to wild-type females.
Homozygous R185H females showed increased coping reactions (flicks, licks, jumps) on the 52°C hot plate compared to wild-type.
Mutant females showed shorter tail-flick reaction latencies (greater heat sensitivity) than wild-type controls, while mutant males showed no phenotype.
No genotype or sex effect was found in the Hargreaves plantar test of heat sensitivity.
Thermal gradient ring preference at non-noxious temperatures (15-40°C) did not statistically differ between mutant and wild-type mice.
Homozygous mutant males showed increased duration of paw reactions to acetone application, indicating hypersensitivity to cool stimuli.
On the cold plate test (5°C), there was a trend for a genotype effect on number of paw lifts that did not reach significance.
Both homozygous females and males showed enhanced mechanical sensitivity (lower withdrawal thresholds) in the von Frey test, following a gene-dosage effect.
Wild-type and Scn9aR185H mice had similar mechanical pain thresholds in the tail pressure test, indicating no hyperalgesia to noxious pressure.

In a conditioned place preference test, homozygous Scn9aR185H mice of both sexes preferred the clonidine-paired chamber, indicating presence of ongoing spontaneous pain, while wild-type mice showed no chamber preference.
Homozygous mutant mice showed no anxiety-like behavior differences in the light-dark box or despair-like behavior differences in the forced-swim test compared to wild-type.

Multivariate (Gdaphen) analysis identified sex, von Frey threshold, cold plate paw lifts, acetone paw-reaction number and duration, and tail-flick latency as the six variables most discriminating between the three Scn9aR185H genotypes.

The SCN9A I228M mutation, found in chronic pain patients with reduced IENFD, produced DRG neuron hyperexcitability in vitro but caused no neuropathy and no pain behavior phenotype in mice, contrasting with the R185H model.
The SCN10A G1662S mutation, found in pain patients with normal IENFD, caused DRG neuron hyperexcitability in vitro and, in Scn10aG1663S mice, normal IENFD with increased pain sensitivity.

DRG neuron size distribution and sciatic nerve PGP9.5/Nav1.7 fluorescence density were comparable across genotypes, indicating the R185H mutation did not cause loss of small DRG neurons or sciatic nerve fiber loss, despite human patients with this mutation showing reduced IENFD.
Three human patients with the SCN9A R185H mutation and chronic pain had decreased intraepidermal nerve fiber density.

Sex-specific pain phenotypes were observed: Scn9aR185H females showed more heat-related pain behaviors (hot plate jump latency, coping reactions, tail flick) while mutant males showed more cool-related reactions (acetone test), though touch sensitivity and spontaneous pain were not sexually dimorphic.
IL-8 was detectable only in the serum of benign atrophic papulosis patients, not in healthy controls.
VEGF levels were reduced in patients with benign atrophic papulosis compared with healthy controls.
Cardiolipin IgG/A/M antibodies were increased in patients with benign atrophic papulosis compared with healthy controls.
β2-glycoprotein IgG/A/M antibodies were increased in patients with benign atrophic papulosis compared with healthy controls, supporting a non-ANCA immune-complex small vessel vasculitis picture.
Antinuclear antibodies were detected in only three of the six benign atrophic papulosis patients, while extractable nuclear antigen antibodies were negative in all.
No significant differences were found between patients and controls for the remaining cytokines, ANCA markers, and other phospholipid antibodies tested.

The overall pattern of increased antiphospholipid antibodies and immune-complex-related markers without ANCA positivity supports classifying benign atrophic papulosis as a non-ANCA immune-complex small vessel vasculitis under the Chapel-Hill classification, indicating a systemic disease character despite lack of overt systemic organ involvement.
Among participants with a prior psychiatric disorder, having two or more prior psychiatric disorders was the strongest independent predictor of subsequent new-onset IBS.
In the prior-psychiatric-disorder subgroup, top-quartile impaired sleep was independently associated with more than double the odds of new-onset IBS.
In the prior-psychiatric-disorder subgroup, top-quartile low BMI was independently associated with increased odds of new-onset IBS.
In the prior-psychiatric-disorder subgroup, top-quartile somatization score was independently associated with increased odds of new-onset IBS.
In the prior-psychiatric-disorder subgroup, negative general health perception was independently associated with increased odds of new-onset IBS.
In participants without prior psychiatric disorder, female sex was the strongest predictor of new-onset IBS, with a much larger effect than in the psychiatric subgroup.
In participants without prior psychiatric disorder, top-quartile impaired sleep was independently associated with increased odds of new-onset IBS.
In participants without prior psychiatric disorder, top-quartile somatization was independently associated with increased odds of new-onset IBS.
In participants without prior psychiatric disorder, impairment through bodily pain was independently associated with increased odds of new-onset IBS.

In participants without prior psychiatric disorder, negative general health perception was independently associated with increased odds of new-onset IBS, and each of the three constituent items independently predicted onset.
Among participants without prior psychiatric disorder, having had no contact with a doctor in the past 5 years was associated with a 50% reduction in the odds of developing IBS.

The authors suggest that part of the strong female predominance in IBS onset is explained by psychiatric disorders, since the female-sex effect was much weaker in the psychiatric subgroup than in the non-psychiatric subgroup.
Migraine was significantly associated with IBS onset in univariable analysis but was not retained as an independent predictor in the multivariable regression.

Of 132,922 participants free of IBS at baseline, 1507 (1.1%) reported a new onset of IBS over the subsequent 2.4 years, an incidence rate consistent with physician-diagnosed IBS incidence in prior literature.
27.6% of new IBS onset cases reported one or more prior psychiatric disorders, and IBS incidence increased with the number of prior psychiatric disorders reported.

Participants with and without a prior psychiatric disorder showed different risk factor profiles for IBS onset: fibromyalgia, gallstones, asthma, reported allergies, impairment through bodily pain, and healthcare use pattern were risk factors only in the group without prior psychiatric disorder, while female sex, PPI use, impaired sleep, somatization, and negative health perception were risk factors in both groups.
The paper notes that psychiatric disorder, GERD, asthma, fibromyalgia, and sleep disorder have an established bidirectional relationship with IBS, suggesting shared etiological mechanisms.
PPI use was a risk factor for IBS onset in both subgroups; the authors propose PPIs may mark underlying GERD or may directly affect the gut via small intestinal bacterial overgrowth.
Depression was the most commonly reported prior psychiatric disorder in the overall cohort at baseline.
The proportion of new IBS onsets preceded by a psychiatric disorder in this study (27.6%) closely matched the median (24.0%) reported across eight previous prospective studies.
The authors cite twin studies indicating that the genetic variance for IBS may be mediated by anxiety and depression, suggesting a shared genetic pathway.
A cited twin study concluded that IBS and depression share the same underlying biological pathway, though causal direction could not be determined.

The paper cites UK Biobank studies showing that self-reported IBS is associated with altered gut microbiota composition, two genome-wide-significant SNP loci, and high comorbidity with depression specifically when depression precedes IBS onset with marked somatic symptoms.

The patient's Mayo Clinic Paraneoplastic Autoantibody Panel showed an elevated ganglionic acetylcholine receptor antibody titer, establishing the diagnosis of autoimmune gastrointestinal dysmotility (AGID).
The same autoantibody panel also detected an elevated neuronal voltage-gated calcium channel antibody titer in this patient, supporting the paraneoplastic/autoimmune dysautonomia diagnosis.

Treatment with the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor pyridostigmine led to dramatic clinical improvement, including increased oral intake, weight gain, weaning off TPN, resolution of neuropathy and vitamin deficiencies, and return of ambulation without assistance.

High-resolution esophageal impedance manometry showed complete failed peristalsis (distal contractile integral <100 mm Hg/s−1/cm−1 per Chicago Classification 4.0) and a hypotensive lower esophageal sphincter.

Scleroderma-specific autoantibodies (anti-Scl70/topoisomerase 1, anti-centromere, anti-RNA polymerase II) were negative despite manometry findings resembling scleroderma esophagus, helping rule out systemic sclerosis and prompting the AGID workup.
Prior treatment with alternating metoclopramide and erythromycin produced only minimal symptomatic improvement before the AGID diagnosis and pyridostigmine trial.

Unlike most previously reported AGID cases with esophageal dysmotility, which showed achalasia-like findings with increased lower esophageal sphincter tone, this patient exhibited a hypotensive lower esophageal sphincter with scleroderma-like aperistalsis.
Females have a higher relative risk of ME/CFS than males, reported between 1.238 and 3.2 across different studies.
Two trials of essential fatty acid supplementation produced contradictory results, with one showing significant improvement and the other showing none versus placebo.
In a randomized trial of 30 CFS patients, valganciclovir significantly improved fatigue and cognitive function scores versus placebo.
Azithromycin treatment produced favourable clinical and serological responses in ME/CFS patients with confirmed Chlamydia pneumoniae infection.
Rintatolimod improved fatigue (via exercise tolerance test) and quality of life, and delayed disease progression, in a subset of ME/CFS patients in clinical trials.
Fluge et al. reported overall symptom improvement in 67% of patients in their largest study of rituximab (anti-CD20 B-cell depletion) in ME/CFS.
A multicentre Norwegian trial of 151 patients found no significant improvement with rituximab versus placebo, with more serious side effects in the rituximab group.
A 2008 study found ALC treatment significantly improved muscle pain, post-exercise fatigue, sleep, physical and mental fatigue, functional status, and cognitive scores compared to placebo.
Intramuscular magnesium injections relieved muscular symptoms only in ME/CFS patients with pre-existing magnesium deficiency, not in those without.
Frequent high-dose methylcobalamin injections combined with high-dose oral folic acid reduced fatigue as measured by the Fibro Fatigue scale in ME/CFS patients.
An 8-week randomized double-blind trial of 80 CFS patients found NADH plus CoQ10 supplementation reduced perceived fatigue across follow-up visits versus placebo.
A 2011 review found insufficient evidence to recommend NADH monotherapy as an effective treatment for CFS due to methodological shortcomings of prior RCTs.
In 135 ME/CFS patients, 12 weeks of KPAX002 treatment reduced fatigue and concentration disturbance symptoms compared to before treatment.
60 ME/CFS patients receiving FMT reported 50% and 70% significant symptom improvement across two studies, with improvements persisting over 15-20 years.
Two RCTs of staphylococcal toxoid vaccination reported significant improvement in pain and psychometric measures, with 50% of patients able to return to half- or full-time work at 6-month follow-up.
Low-dose naltrexone (3.0-4.5 mg/day) produced positive treatment response in 73.9% of 218 ME/CFS patients regarding vigilance, physical and cognitive performance.
Surgical correction of cervical spinal stenosis led to marked improvement in myelopathic symptoms, light-headedness, hemodynamic dysfunction, and global ME/CFS symptoms in severe cases.
A study of 114 ME/CFS patients found a skew in T helper polarization toward Th2-type immune response, with more severe symptoms such as poor sleep.
ME/CFS patients have higher B-cell numbers compared to healthy controls, confirmed across various studies.
A subset of B-cells in ME/CFS patients showed lower TRPM3 cation channel expression on CD19+ B-cells compared to healthy controls.

Findings on NK cell subset differences in ME/CFS are inconclusive: one study reported lower CD56DimCD16Bright NK cells, while a 2019 study of 251 patients versus 107 controls found no significant difference.

53% of 60 ME/CFS patients tested positive for autoantibodies against muscarinic cholinergic receptor 1, with positive patients showing higher scores for muscle weakness, painful nodes and forgetfulness than healthy controls.
High-resolution HLA typing in a 2020 cohort of 426 ME/CFS patients identified HLA-C*07:04 and HLA-DQB1*03:03 as strongly associated alleles.
Exercise induced higher oxidative stress markers in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls, linked to post-exertional malaise and muscle pain.

Anderson et al. proposed that imbalanced tryptophan metabolism and a drop in tryptophan levels contribute to physico-somatic symptoms including fatigue, autonomic symptoms, somatic presentation and hyperalgesia in ME/CFS.
Acute tryptophan depletion in a female cohort of ME/CFS patients produced no significant improvement in fatigue, depression, or lack of concentration.
ME/CFS patients show reduced gut microbial diversity compared to healthy controls, with increases in pro-inflammatory bacterial species and reductions in anti-inflammatory species.
Increased microbial fermentation-derived short-chain fatty acid production in urine/serum correlated with deteriorated energy metabolism in ME/CFS patients.
Serum indole-3-lactic acid, a kynurenine pathway-related metabolite, was found lower in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls, and half of the ME/CFS patients also reported IBS.
High plasma kynurenic acid/tryptophan ratio was reported in severe cases of irritable bowel syndrome.
A 2003 study found significantly higher free tryptophan concentrations in ME/CFS patients compared to age- and sex-matched controls.
A follow-up study replicated higher serum free tryptophan levels in ME/CFS patients versus healthy controls.

A 2019 mathematical model, the 'IDO metabolic trap', proposed that absent or dysfunctional IDO2 combined with IDO1 substrate inhibition and disrupted LAT-1 transport drives kynurenine pathway dysregulation in ME/CFS.
A 2019 study reported a lower ratio of kynurenine to tryptophan and lower 3-hydroxykynurenine in CFS patients compared to healthy controls.

A 2021 study found lower kynurenic acid/quinolinic acid ratio and lower anthranilic acid levels in CFS patients compared to healthy controls, indicating reduced KP neuroprotective activity, with similar findings noted in fibromyalgia patients.

A recent study found higher 3-hydroxykynurenine and lower kynurenine levels in ME/CFS patients versus matched healthy controls, with a further reduction of kynurenine in patients whose illness onset followed an infection.

Among ME/CFS patients, those whose illness began following an infection had lower kynurenine levels than those without a preceding infection, and no correlations were found between KP metabolites, cytokines, and fatty acids.
Quinolinic acid, but not kynurenic acid, was significantly elevated in the CSF of medication-free suicide attempters compared to controls.
Lower mean kynurenic acid concentration was reported in patients with major depression compared to normal controls.
Alzheimer's disease patients show reduced tryptophan and elevated kynurenine/tryptophan ratio, indicating enhanced tryptophan degradation via the kynurenine pathway.
A large 2021 study found lower tryptophan pathway metabolite concentrations in both urine and serum samples of Alzheimer's disease patients.

Fisher et al. reported degradation of amino acids and dysregulated mitochondrial function in ME/CFS patients, highlighting a relationship between the kynurenine pathway, mitochondrial dysfunction, and energy production.
The kynurenine pathway is proposed to induce immunosuppression in ME/CFS-relevant inflammatory states via T-cell apoptosis, NK cell inhibition, and increased regulatory T cell differentiation.

Under sustained inflammation, initial rises in quinolinic acid increase NAD+ production, but after saturation of converting enzymes and oxidative activity, NAD+ production subsequently drops, affecting numerous NAD+-dependent cellular functions.
