Oxidative stress from elevated quinolinic acid can overactivate PARP, depleting NAD+ and ATP and disturbing energy production and mitochondrial function, changes also reported in ME/CFS.
Using flexible telephone and text-based support with no fixed deadline, all five patients with very severe ME/CFS who initially expressed interest went on to fully complete the study questionnaire.

Prior surveys of severely affected ME/CFS patients using online-only or lengthy/complex questionnaires had very high dropout and low completion rates compared with this study's simplified, supported approach.
Direct outreach to charity members too unwell to read the newsletter increased study uptake by two fifths compared with newsletter advertisement alone.

Not imposing a completion deadline allowed participants with very severe ME/CFS to complete the questionnaire at their own pace, with completion time ranging from three days (completed by a family member) to one year (due to illness severity and need for rest between appointments).
Participants in this very severe ME/CFS case series experienced comorbid migraine and seizures that caused scheduled research appointments to be cancelled or terminated mid-conversation.

Only one of the five participants with very severe ME/CFS was well enough to complete the questionnaire independently; the others required completion via family members, homecare workers, or the investigator using telephone/text over multiple appointments.
Plasma acetaminophen levels were increased in ME/CFS cases compared to controls in the biogenic amines panel.

In the complex lipid panel, ME/CFS cases had decreased levels of plasmalogens, unsaturated phospholipid ethers, most unsaturated phosphatidylcholines, an unsaturated sphingomyelin, and an unsaturated lysophosphatidylcholine compared to controls.
In the oxylipin panel, Resolvin D1 levels were decreased in ME/CFS cases compared to controls.
Levels of choline (food exposome cluster) were reduced in ME/CFS cases compared to controls.
Succinic acid, a dicarboxylic acid and TCA cycle intermediate, was elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to controls.
Alpha-ketoglutarate, a TCA cycle intermediate, was elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to controls.
In female subjects, levels of the drug metabolites alprazolam and acyclovir were up-regulated in ME/CFS patients compared to female controls.
Elevated acetaminophen levels seen in the overall ME/CFS population were not replicated when restricting analysis to female subjects only.
No metabolites were significantly associated with ME/CFS in male subjects when analyzed separately.
In the subgroup without self-reported IBS, levels of unsaturated PC, plasmalogens and PLE were decreased in ME/CFS patients compared to controls without sr-IBS.
A Lasso classifier using metabolites with Bayes Factor > 1 distinguished female ME/CFS patients from female controls with an AUC of 0.794.
A Lasso classifier using metabolites with Bayes Factor > 3 distinguished ME/CFS without sr-IBS from controls without sr-IBS with an AUC of 0.873.
Machine learning classifiers were unable to differentiate the overall ME/CFS group from all controls using the metabolomics panel.
In male ME/CFS patients, plasma levels of unsaturated long-chain triglyceride TG(56:6) were positively correlated with MFI general fatigue scores.
In male ME/CFS patients, plasma levels of TG(54:7) B were positively correlated with MFI physical fatigue scores.
Within male controls (not cases), alpha-ketoglutarate levels were positively correlated with MFI physical fatigue, reduced activity, and reduced motivation scales.
Higher levels of two specific plasmalogens were associated with more severe MFI reduced activity symptoms.
Lower levels of SM(d40:3) were negatively correlated with MFI reduced activity scores.

In an independent validation cohort, machine learning classifiers using overlapping metabolites achieved AUC values of 0.514-0.738 (all subjects), 0.616-0.784 (female subgroup), and 0.614-0.828 (no sr-IBS subgroup), similar to the discovery cohort's performance.

Enrichment analysis showed reduced plasmalogens, sphingomyelins, unsaturated phospholipid ethers, unsaturated ceramides, carnitines, saturated lysophospholipids, unsaturated lysophosphoethanolamines, unsaturated lysophosphatidylcholines, saturated triglycerides and prostaglandins, alongside increased hydroxy-eicosapentaenoic acid, dicarboxylic acids, and unsaturated long-chain triglycerides in ME/CFS.
ME/CFS subjects showed a significant reduction in levels of carnitines, which are implicated in fatty acid transport into mitochondria and compensatory peroxisomal β-oxidation.
SNP rs11157573 in the TRA locus, previously reported associated with ME/CFS, showed no significant allele frequency difference between ME/CFS patients and controls in the Norwegian cohort.
SNP rs17255510, previously reported associated with ME/CFS, was not associated with disease status in either the Norwegian or UK Biobank cohorts.
Two-locus haplotype analysis across the TRA locus did not reveal significant associations with ME/CFS, with the strongest signal (rs2001022 and rs11626312) reaching only P=0.07.
TRA allele frequencies did not differ significantly between ME/CFS patients carrying HLA-risk alleles (HLA-C*07:04 and/or HLA-DQB1*03:03) versus non-carriers.
In the UK Biobank cohort, three TRA SNPs (rs17183131, rs8021297, rs8005677) showed nominal association with self-reported CFS (P<0.05), but these did not survive correction for multiple testing.
In a meta-analysis combining Norwegian and UK Biobank cohorts, rs8021297 and rs17183131 showed weak signs of association with ME/CFS that did not withstand multiple-testing correction.
Stratifying combined Norwegian and UK datasets by HLA-risk carrier status revealed one SNP, rs8572, with a reduced odds ratio associated with HLA-risk carriage.

In an extended analysis of 6769 SNPs in the TRA region using UK Biobank data, rs8016431 showed the most significant association with self-reported CFS, but this did not survive multiple-testing correction.

Allele frequencies for rs17255510 and rs11157573 in the Norwegian and UK Biobank cohorts closely matched control frequencies from the 1000 Genomes CEU dataset and were comparable to control frequencies reported by Schlauch et al., but the case frequencies reported by Schlauch et al. were markedly higher, driving their originally reported association.
ME/CFS affects an estimated 250,000 people in the UK and approximately 1.5 million people in the USA.
Approximately one in four people with ME/CFS are house-bound, reflecting the severity and functional impairment associated with the disease.

Having a first-, second-, or third-degree relative diagnosed with CFS significantly increases an individual's own risk of receiving the same diagnosis, supporting a genetic contribution to ME/CFS risk.
Candidate genes previously proposed to explain ME/CFS risk have not been independently replicated in larger, better-powered studies.
ME/CFS is often diagnosed following infection such as Epstein-Barr virus, and a substantial minority of people infected with SARS-CoV-2 may eventually be diagnosed with ME/CFS.
An estimated 506,000 people in the UK self-reported Long COVID symptoms persisting at least one year, of whom approximately half (~200,000) could meet the ME/CFS criteria used in this study.
In an informal Twitter poll of the ME/CFS community, over 75% of respondents (or the person they care for) reported having had ME/CFS symptoms for more than 6 years.

PET imaging with the PK11195 tracer showed widespread neuroinflammation in ME/CFS patients, with regional severity correlating with specific symptom scores (amygdala with cognitive impairment, hippocampus with depression, thalamus with pain).
An MRI study reported prefrontal cortical atrophy in patients with ME/CFS.
PET imaging studies suggested reduced neurotransmitter biosynthesis in ME/CFS brains, estimated via acetyl-L-carnitine and serotonin transporter densities.
In rodents, a peripheral LPS challenge elevated proinflammatory cytokine expression (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) in the brain within 2 hours and increased plasma IL-6.
A central poly I:C challenge upregulated proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) in the brain, with maximal gene expression at 4 hours.
Intracerebroventricular infusion of recombinant IL-1ra completely blocked the poly I:C-induced decrease in locomotor activity in the animal model.

Neutralizing endogenous IL-1ra with an antibody significantly delayed recovery of spontaneous activity during poly I:C-induced neuroinflammation, indicating a protective role for endogenous IL-1ra against prolonged inflammation.
Intraperitoneal pretreatment with minocycline attenuated poly I:C-induced IL-1β mRNA expression in rat brain, transient fever, and decrease in locomotor activity.

Intrathecal pretreatment with minocycline attenuated chronic stress-induced muscular hyperalgesia and mechanical allodynia via suppression of spinal cord microglial activation in a rat model of ME/CFS.
Minocycline did not suppress neuroinflammation when administered after poly I:C injection without prior pretreatment, suggesting limited efficacy once neuroinflammation is established.
In vitro, 6-MSITC treatment inhibited activation of murine macrophage cells following LPS application.
6-MSITC attenuated TNF-induced upregulation of IL-6 in human umbilical vein endothelial cells.
6-MSITC alleviated several inflammatory responses in a murine model of inflammatory bowel disease.

Long-term 6-MSITC administration relieved neuroinflammatory responses following peripheral poly I:C injection, but showed no anti-inflammatory effect on neuroinflammation following a central LPS challenge.
Minocycline may suppress neuroinflammation by affecting the gut microbiome and intestinal permeability, as shown in a rat model of Gulf War illness.
Peripheral IL-1ra plays a role in regulation of the gut microbiota, a mechanism the authors note is distinct from their own i.c.v. IL-1ra administration studies.
ME/CFS affects an estimated 0.5–1.5% of the global population, and diagnosis is difficult using conventional medical examination.

In a phase III trial of rintatolimod, only a subset of ME/CFS patients with relatively short disease duration (symptom onset within 2-8 years) showed improved exercise tolerance in response to treatment.
The male-to-female sex ratio in the Registry cohort is 23:100, consistent with prior reports of female predominance in ME/CFS.

Nearly one-third of the ME/CFS cohort (30.5%) and 15.7% of the post-COVID-19 cohort who completed the Karnofsky Performance Status survey were classified as severely-to-very-severely ill, including house- or bed-bound individuals.
Up to 90% of people with ME/CFS are estimated to have not received an official clinician diagnosis, reflecting widespread misdiagnosis and underdiagnosis of the disease.
A meaningful proportion of Registry participants live in nonurban areas: 12.3% of ME/CFS and 10.9% of long-COVID registrants who provided zip code data.

Mobile symptom-tracking app engagement was highly variable: 56.1% of eligible participants downloaded the app, 93.1% of downloaders initiated tracking, but only 8% were 'superusers' with high engagement (3-7 days/week) while 75% had low engagement (less than 1 day/week).

Among participants who completed a community feedback survey, 70.9% rated their overall satisfaction with the Registry as 7 or higher on a 1-10 scale, and the Registry qualified as 'great' by net promoter score.
Long COVID symptoms have been reported to be strikingly similar to those of ME/CFS, motivating the Registry's expansion to include long-COVID participants for cross-disease comparison.
Orthostatic intolerance is commonly a predominant symptom in adolescents with ME/CFS, distinguishing their symptom cluster from adults.

The Registry cohort is predominantly non-Hispanic White, and the control cohort (10.9% of participants) remains below the 30% target, reflecting known recruitment and selection biases in ME/CFS research.
POTS, defined as a heart-rate increase >30 bpm during the 10-min NASA Lean Test, was significantly more common in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls.
POTS prevalence in Long COVID patients (28%) was not significantly different from ME/CFS (46%) or healthy controls (19%).
Orthostatic hypotension was rare, occurring in only one Long COVID patient and none of the ME/CFS or healthy control subjects.
Both ME/CFS and Long COVID patients showed a higher, though not statistically significant, incidence of presyncope or syncope during the NLT compared with healthy controls.
Systolic blood pressure during the NASA Lean Test did not differ significantly among Long COVID, ME/CFS, and healthy control groups at any time point.
Heart rate at completion of the NASA Lean Test was somewhat higher in both Long COVID and ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
Diastolic blood pressure was significantly higher at 5.5 and 10 minutes of the NASA Lean Test in Long COVID patients compared to healthy controls, narrowing pulse pressure.

The pulse pressure to systolic blood pressure ratio (PP/SBP×100) was significantly reduced below the abnormal threshold of 25% at 5.5 and 10 minutes of the NLT in Long COVID patients compared to healthy controls.
PP/SBP×100 continued to fall throughout the NLT in Long COVID patients, dropping to approximately 20% at 10 minutes, significantly lower than healthy controls.
The difference in PP/SBP×100 between Long COVID and ME/CFS patients was not statistically significant, though the study was noted to be underpowered to detect this difference.

ME/CFS patients ill for less than 4 years had lower (narrower) PP/SBP×100 values than those ill longer, replicating a prior study finding that pulse pressure ratio narrows early in illness and widens with increasing duration.

Severity of all six symptoms (fatigue, brain fog, lightheadedness/dizziness, nausea, chest discomfort, pain) was significantly greater in both Long COVID and ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls at every time point.
There was no significant difference in symptom severity between people with Long COVID and people with ME/CFS at any time point during or after the orthostatic challenge.

In Long COVID and ME/CFS patients, symptom severity rose considerably during and following the orthostatic challenge compared to baseline, whereas in healthy controls symptom severity typically dropped immediately after the test.

Several symptoms in Long COVID (brain fog, dizziness, nausea, chest pain, pain anywhere) had returned to baseline by Day 7, whereas in ME/CFS only nausea had returned to baseline by Day 7, indicating more persistent symptom exacerbation in ME/CFS.

Cognitive efficiency on all three reaction-time tests (PRT, SRT, GNG) dropped immediately after the NASA Lean Test in both Long COVID and ME/CFS patients, while it rose in healthy controls, with significant differences for PRT and SRT.

Cognitive efficiency in ME/CFS patients did not improve above baseline for any of the three reaction-time tests even 7 days after the orthostatic challenge, whereas Long COVID patients' SRT and GNG performance recovered to a level similar to healthy controls.
When comparing all 92 ME/CFS patients to healthy controls without subgroup stratification, no EBV-derived antibody response reached genome-wide (FDR 5%) significance.

In ME/CFS patients who reported an infectious trigger at disease onset, IgG antibody responses against three EBV peptide antigens (EBNA6_0066, EBNA6_0070, EBNA4_0529) were significantly elevated compared to healthy controls.
ME/CFS patients without a clear infectious trigger (or unknown trigger) showed no significant EBV antibody differences compared to healthy controls.
Direct comparison of the two ME/CFS subgroups (infectious trigger vs. non-infectious/unknown trigger) showed no significant EBV antibody differences after FDR correction.

A final classification model combining antibody levels against EBNA4_0529 and EBNA6_0070 (with age and gender interactions) discriminated ME/CFS patients with an infectious trigger from healthy controls with an AUC of 0.835.

Higher log10 antibody levels against EBNA4_0529 were associated with a roughly 9.5-fold increase in the estimated odds of being an ME/CFS patient (infectious-trigger subgroup) per fold-change in antibody level.

The relationship between EBNA6_0070 antibody levels and probability of being an ME/CFS patient with infectious trigger showed a significant interaction with age and gender: in women, higher antibody levels with increasing age raised patient probability, whereas in men both younger low-antibody and older high-antibody profiles were associated with higher patient probability.

When the infectious-trigger classification model was applied to the whole ME/CFS cohort, discrimination performance fell (AUC 0.731) and was close to random when restricted to the non-infectious/unknown-trigger subgroup (AUC 0.583), indicating the biomarker signature is specific to the infectious-trigger subgroup.

The median pairwise correlation among EBV antibody levels was lower in ME/CFS patients with an infectious trigger (0.40) than in healthy controls (0.56), all ME/CFS patients (0.56), or ME/CFS patients with a non-infectious/unknown trigger (0.48), suggesting reduced coordinated antibody production against EBV antigens in the infectious-trigger subgroup.

Linear discriminant analysis using the full EBV antibody panel achieved classification AUCs ranging from 0.86 (healthy controls vs. ME/CFS with non-infectious/unknown trigger) to 0.91 (ME/CFS infectious-trigger vs. remaining ME/CFS patients), indicating the multivariate antibody data can discriminate groups even though no single antibody was individually significant in some comparisons.

The authors note (citing a prior study) that serum citrulline levels were reported elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls, potentially relevant to arginine-related post-translational modification of the candidate EBV antigens.
The authors cite a prior study reporting increased IgM antibodies against oxidative/nitrosative stress-derived neoepitopes, including NO-Arginine, in ME/CFS patients.

EBNA6_0066 and EBNA6_0070 both contain an arginine-repeat sequence homologous to putative epitopes from several human proteins, and T cell clones recognizing such arginine-repeat sequences have been isolated from a multiple sclerosis patient, supporting a molecular mimicry hypothesis for ME/CFS pathogenesis.
Among untreated PCS support group members, 72% reported severe fatigue, a rate much higher than in the general female population.
63% of untreated PCS respondents reported dizziness, higher than expected in the general population.
61% of untreated PCS respondents reported IBS symptoms.
33% of untreated PCS respondents reported brain fog.
49% of untreated PCS respondents reported migraines.
41% of untreated PCS support group respondents reported polyuria or dysuria.
31% of untreated PCS support group respondents reported excessive sweating.
31% of untreated PCS support group respondents reported TMJ pain.
18% of untreated PCS support group respondents reported loose skin or lax joints, a hypermobility-related feature.
29% of the overall 398 respondents self-reported a formal diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome.
13% of the overall 398 respondents self-reported a formal diagnosis of fibromyalgia, higher than general population prevalence.
18% of the overall 398 respondents self-reported a formal diagnosis of spinal nerve problems.
10% of the overall 398 respondents self-reported a formal diagnosis of interstitial cystitis.
9% of the overall 398 respondents self-reported a formal diagnosis of postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS).
Self-reported hypertension was noted in 11% of PCS support group members, but unlike other comorbidities this rate was not described as elevated relative to the general population.
Ten percent of PCS support group respondents self-reported a formal diagnosis of chronic fatigue syndrome, a rate reported as higher than in the general population.

Six percent of PCS support group respondents self-reported a diagnosis of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, which the authors highlight as notably common among self-identifying PCS women relative to the general population.
After 12 weeks, the PLWNT qigong group had a significantly higher total effective rate (62.22%) than the CBT group (50%) for CFS symptom improvement.
Fatigue severity (MFI-20 total score) significantly decreased from baseline to 12 weeks in both the PLWNT and CBT groups.
PSQI-measured sleep quality, subjective sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep duration, sleep disturbance, and daytime dysfunction significantly improved after intervention.
Habitual sleep efficiency and sleep medication usage did not significantly improve after either PLWNT or CBT intervention.
HADS anxiety and depression scores significantly improved within both the PLWNT and CBT groups after intervention.
Plasma NPY levels decreased after PLWNT intervention but increased after CBT, with a significant between-group difference favoring PLWNT.
In the PLWNT group, fatigue level was positively correlated with sleep quality after treatment.
In the PLWNT group, fatigue level was positively correlated with anxiety level after treatment.
In the CBT group, fatigue level was correlated with anxiety but showed no correlation with sleep quality.

Six adverse events were reported across the trial; two were judged definitely or probably related to abdominal massage manipulations, with no significant difference in adverse event rates between PLWNT and CBT groups.
Although the PLWNT group showed greater average improvement than the CBT group across MFI-20, PSQI, and HADS scores, the between-group difference was not statistically significant.
All five WES patients shared the same nonsynonymous missense mutation in MUC3A, resulting in amino acid change p.S2495L.
All five WES patients shared the same frameshift insertion in RHBG, producing p.D425Rfs*18.
ZNF717 was mutated in all five HSD patients with multiple distinct nonsynonymous variants, more than the other two shared genes.
Functional enrichment of the 1162 HSD-mutated genes showed the extracellular matrix structural constituent as the top overrepresented molecular function.
KEGG pathway analysis found ECM-receptor interaction as the only significantly enriched canonical pathway among HSD-mutated genes.
Reactome pathway analysis identified ECM organization and degradation as the most significant canonical pathways among HSD-mutated genes.
IPA core analysis identified hereditary connective tissue disorders, ECM organization, and DNA damage pathways as relevant bio-functions enriched among HSD-mutated genes.
NOTCH1, a transcription regulator in the IPA-generated hEDS gene network, has been previously linked to hEDS.
ZNF469 and PRDM5, present in the HSD-associated network, have previously been linked to joint hypermobility mainly through brittle cornea syndrome.
GZF1 emerged as a new gene in the sparser HSD-specific IPA network; prior reports link GZF1 mutations to joint laxity, short stature, and severe myopia in a Saudi family.
FLNA, encoding filamin A involved in cytoskeleton development and integrin binding, appeared in the hEDS IPA network and has been previously associated with an EDS-like collagenopathy.
FLNB, encoding filamin B expressed in chondrocytes and involved in prenatal skeleton development, appeared in the HSD-associated IPA network.
Among the 55 genes shared between HSD-mutated genes and the matrisome list, MUC16 had the highest mutation count (six mutations) followed by FREM2 (four).
COL22A1 and LAMA5 each carried three mutations and mapped to ECM structural constituent function and ECM organization pathway.
Transcriptomic reanalysis of hEDS/JHS skin fibroblasts vs healthy controls found 133 differentially expressed genes, with 83 (62%) downregulated and 50 (38%) upregulated.
Only seven genes (0.5%) overlapped between the HSD WES mutated-gene list and the hEDS/JHS transcriptomic DEG list: LIMCH1, ACSL5, FLG, DSP, EDIL3, PRUNE2, and ZFPM2.
Comparison of HSD-mutated genes with a published hEDS dermal myofibroblast proteome identified five shared genes: MYO1C, TXNDC5, PEPD, CKAP4, and a fourth (labelled KFT10 in the source text).

MUC3A variants have been linked to inflammatory bowel disease and colorectal cancer progression, and in this HSD cohort three of five patients presented gastrointestinal symptoms, consistent with reports that up to 62% of hEDS patients have IBS.
RHBG encodes a renal ammonia transporter; the authors propose it as a candidate for a non-invasive urinary diagnostic biomarker in HSD.

The authors note ZNF717 has also been implicated in autism spectrum disorder, and that ASD and HSD share clinical features including proprioceptive impairment (3/5 patients) and autonomic dysfunction (4/5 patients) in this cohort.
DSP (desmoplakin), identified with one mutation in the HSD cohort, is proposed as a weak candidate 'susceptibility locus' biomarker for HSD given its role in desmosome-based cell adhesion.
FREM2, an ECM adhesion protein gene mutated in the HSD cohort, is linked in prior literature to Fraser syndrome and to prognosis in colorectal cancer.

A prior proteomic study cited by the authors identified S100A4, a calcium-binding protein driving fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition and MMP-mediated ECM degradation, as a key factor in hEDS fibroblasts and a potential therapeutic target.
The patient carried a novel homozygous nonsense variant in DSE (NM_013352.4:c.2601C>A:p.(Tyr867*)) causing musculocontractural Ehlers-Danlos syndrome due to dermatan sulfate epimerase deficiency.
Dermatan sulfate moieties on chondroitin sulfate/dermatan sulfate proteoglycans were significantly decreased, though still present, in the patient's skin fibroblasts.

Electron microscopy with cupromeronic blue staining revealed a mosaic pattern of collagen fibril assembly, with coexisting normally assembled fibrils bearing curved GAG chains and dispersed fibrils bearing linear GAG chains bridging interfibrillar spaces.

The authors propose that residual DS-epi1 activity and/or compensatory activity of its minor homolog DS-epi2 may explain the milder skin phenotype through a mosaic pattern of collagen fibril assembly.

The patient exhibited mild skin hyperextensibility without fragility and small joint hypermobility, but developed recurrent large subcutaneous hematomas, expanding the clinical phenotype of mcEDS-DSE.
All surveyed providers (100%) reported some familiarity with EDS, most commonly from medical texts (94%) and medical training (79%).
Only 9% of respondents were completely or very comfortable with the 2017 EDS diagnostic criteria, and only 4% were completely or very comfortable diagnosing EDS.
39% of providers were completely or very comfortable executing care plans developed by a specialist, whereas only 9% were comfortable developing their own EDS care plans.
29% of providers reported educating families about EDS, but only 7% were completely or very comfortable doing so.
The most common barriers preventing provider comfort caring for, managing, and educating patients with EDS were lack of educational materials, knowledge, and confidence.
Residents reported significantly more comfort executing specialist-developed plans than nonresidents.
Residents reported significantly less comfort developing their own EDS care plans compared to nonresidents.
Residents were significantly less comfortable educating families with EDS compared to nonresidents.
Residents reported less interest in attending EDS educational workshops or webinars than nonresidents.
38% of respondents reported no current EDS patients under their care, while 25% were unsure whether they currently had a patient with EDS.
All 35 individuals in this pEDS cohort carried (likely) pathogenic heterozygous missense or insertion/deletion variants in C1R.
Twenty-one of 23 dentate individuals were diagnosed with periodontitis stage 3 or 4, indicating severe periodontal destruction even in young participants.
Despite severe clinical attachment loss, probing pocket depths remained shallow (median 2 mm, 94% ≤3 mm), a distinctive feature of pEDS.
Marked gingival recession was universal, with 93% of teeth per individual affected by GR ≥1 mm, and recession ≥5 mm in 16 probands.
All 23 dentate individuals presented with a complete lack of attached gingiva on all buccal surfaces of maxilla and mandible, a pathognomonic feature of pEDS.
Increased visibility of palatal vessels due to thin, translucent palatal gingiva was observed in 18 of assessable dentate individuals.
A notably high pain perception during periodontal probing was reported in 16 of 23 dentate individuals.
Fused-appearing roots of the upper second molars were the most frequent dental finding, present in 9 of 12 assessable individuals.
Taurodontic molars were identified radiographically in six of 23 individuals (26%), a higher rate than in the general Caucasian population.
Hypoplasia of tooth roots, mostly affecting premolars, was present in 13 of 23 (57%) dentate individuals, with a crown-to-root ratio of 1:1.08.
Tooth rotation greater than 45 degrees, mostly affecting first upper premolars, was diagnosed in 10 of 16 individuals with teeth in that region.
An anatomical kink between the first and second lower premolars, caused by diverging tooth roots or mandibular abnormality, was found in 12 of 20 individuals with teeth in that region.
Pulp stones were present in seven individuals and abnormalities in pulp chamber shape were noted in six individuals.
The probability of being edentate between ages 35-44 was 28-47% in this pEDS cohort, vastly higher than the general UK population rate of under 0.5% in 2009.
The retrospectively reported median age of complete tooth loss among edentate individuals was 25.5 years (range 14-48).
The median reported age of first tooth loss due to periodontal reasons among dentate individuals was 21.5 years, higher than the mean age of 15 years previously reported.

The authors propose that intracellular activation of C1r and/or C1s and extracellular secretion of activated C1s may activate the classical complement cascade independent of microbial triggers, driving hyperinflammatory periodontal destruction in pEDS.
Periodontal risk assessment showed a high risk of disease progression in 45% of dentate individuals, middle risk in 45%, and low risk in only 10%.

Two individuals with excellent oral hygiene and regular professional cleaning had only mild or no clinical attachment loss despite genetically confirmed pEDS, while other family members with the same variant had stage 3/4 periodontitis or were already edentulous, indicating no consistent genotype-oral phenotype correlation.
Genetic testing revealed a novel frame-shift mutation in the COL3A1 gene, confirming a diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (vEDS) in a patient presenting with acute aortic dissection.

vEDS is characterized by tissue vulnerability with an estimated 80% of patients experiencing vascular complications by age 40 and a reported median lifespan of 48 years, with most deaths due to aortic dissection or rupture.

Extended surgical repair combining valve-sparing root replacement (VSRR) and total arch replacement (TAR) with frozen elephant trunk (FET) was successfully performed for massive acute type A aortic dissection with root rupture and multiple malperfusion in a patient with vEDS, resulting in good recovery without spinal cord injury or permanent neurological dysfunction.

To reduce risk of spinal cord injury (SCI) during FET placement at zone 4, the shortest available device (6 cm length) was used, and the patient did not develop SCI, with the distal FET end located above the T8 level.
A 10-year-old boy with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome developed a massive subgaleal hematoma after minor occipital head trauma from a fall.
Compressive bandaging failed to control hematoma expansion, requiring needle aspiration of approximately 400 cc of blood from the subgaleal space.
The patient was treated with Vitamin K, intravenous immunoglobulin, and fresh frozen plasma as supportive therapy for the bleeding diathesis associated with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

Prolonged compressive bandage use (10 days) resulted in compression necrosis of a large area of scalp tissue extending from the occipital area to bilateral parietal bones, requiring surgical debridement and reconstruction.
A new hematoma formed after reconstructive surgery extending from the front of the ear to the ipsilateral neck, causing facial palsy that fully resolved after evacuation and drain placement.

The patient's clinical features were considered compatible with EDS Kosho type, a connective tissue disorder associated with massive subcutaneous hematomas, though genetic testing to confirm this was declined by the family.

Due to compromised connective tissue in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, even minor trauma can lead to catastrophic vascular complications such as ruptured viscera, aneurysms, arterial dissections, and arteriovenous fistulas.

Seven of 23 patients with pathogenic COL1A1 or COL1A2 variants (41% of those aged over 20 years) developed life-threatening vascular complications, including arterial dissections, aneurysms, arteriovenous/arterial fistulas, and subarachnoid hemorrhage.
A specific COL1A1 variant, p.Arg312Cys, causes classical EDS with additional vascular fragility including rupture and dissection of medium-sized arteries.
Heterozygous COL1A1 variants p.Arg312Cys, p.Arg574Cys, and p.Arg1093Cys are also associated with vascular EDS, in addition to the primary cause COL3A1.

Arthrochalasia EDS is caused by heterozygous variants causing partial or complete loss of exon 6 in COL1A1 or COL1A2, inhibiting procollagen N-terminal cleavage and disrupting collagen fibril assembly.
Homozygous or compound heterozygous COL1A2 variants cause cardiac-valvular EDS via complete absence of pro-alpha-2 chains and formation of pro-alpha-1 homotrimers.

Patients with mixed OI/EDS phenotypes (later termed C1ROD) harbor heterozygous COL1A1/COL1A2 variants near the N-terminal helical region that interfere with procollagen N-propeptide cleavage, distinct from variants causing other COL1-related EDS subtypes.

Among 23 patients with COL1A1/COL1A2 pathogenic variants recruited on OI- or EDS-like suspicion, final diagnoses were classical OI in 17 (74%), C1ROD in 5 (22%), and COL1-related classical EDS in 1 (4%).
Patients in the EDS group (C1ROD/cEDS) showed markedly higher frequencies of skin hyperextensibility, soft/doughy skin, and piezogenic papules compared to patients in the OI group.
Transmission electron microscopy of skin specimens from two C1ROD patients (#22, #23) showed abnormal cauliflower-like collagen fibrils with irregular margins, consistent with prior C1ROD reports.
The COL1A2 rs42524 SNP, previously linked to cerebral aneurysm occurrence in a Japanese cohort, was not found in any patient in the current cohort.
Coexisting autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease may have contributed to accelerated cerebral aneurysm formation in one patient (#1) with a COL1A1 variant.
The prevalence of intracranial aneurysms among adult patients in this cohort (31%, 4 of 13) was markedly higher than the reported general population prevalence (0.5-3%).

Beta-blockers, effective in managing vascular lesions in other hereditary connective tissue disorders (Marfan syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome, vEDS), might be a reasonable therapeutic or prophylactic option for vascular complications in COL1-related OI or C1ROD, though no consensus currently exists.

Genotype-phenotype correlation underlying C1ROD appeared weaker than that observed in COL1-related classical/vascular EDS, suggesting additional genetic or nongenetic modifiers contribute to the prominent EDS phenotype.
Five novel pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were identified in this cohort: COL1A1 p.Gly191Cys, p.Gly191Val, p.Arg187Valfs*78, and p.Gly560Valfs*20, and COL1A2 p.Gly655Arg.

The nonsense variant COL1A1 p.Arg220*, causing C1ROD in patient #22 of this cohort, was previously reported to cause OI type I in a different patient, illustrating phenotypic variability for the same variant.

Intrafamilial phenotypic variability was observed, including presumably age-dependent severity in an OI family (family #4) and age-independent variability in an EDS family (family #12), with one member (patient #19) showing bilateral hip dislocation suggestive of phenotypic overlap between C1ROD and aEDS.
Clinical suspicion of EDS in this cohort was based on generalized joint hypermobility (Beighton score >4 points) and skin hyperextensibility with or without bone fragility.

Arterial tortuosity syndrome is frequently misdiagnosed as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or other connective tissue disorders due to nonspecific symptoms and phenotypic overlap, though ATS is associated with more extensive vascular changes.
CT angiography revealed approximately 50% short-segment narrowing of the distal aortic arch and severe narrowing (0.9 cm diameter over ~10 cm length) with tortuosity of the descending thoracic aorta.

Cinematic rendering demonstrated extensive collateralization and dilation of abdominal wall vasculature (superior/inferior epigastric arteries) and severe dilation of internal mammary arteries, consistent with chronic aortic obstruction.

Cinematic rendering, a photorealistic 3D reconstruction technique, provided greater diagnostic accuracy for coarctation of the aorta with arterial tortuosity syndrome than standard volume rendering, aiding diagnosis and surgical planning.

The patient was treated preoperatively with a combination of antihypertensives (Nifedipine 30mg BID, bendrofluazide 2.5mg daily, methyldopa 250mg BID) prior to referral for cardiothoracic surgical evaluation, consistent with guidance to control hypertension before corrective procedures.

Coarctation of the aorta accounts for 5-8% of congenital heart diseases, occurs in approximately 3 per 10,000 live births, and has a male predilection (male-to-female ratio 1.27:1 to 1.74:1), with 89-92% of affected children showing upper extremity hypertension.
EDS-related joint laxity from collagen malformation predisposes patients to spinal instability, scoliotic deformities, and high-grade spondylolisthesis.

Intraoperative positioning caused the patient's spondylolisthesis to dynamically worsen from radiographic grade IV to grade V, consistent with EDS-associated joint laxity causing dynamic exacerbation of spondylolisthesis grade.

Use of the minimally invasive sagittal adjusting screw (SAS) system with distractor/compressor and fracture reducer devices allowed reduction of the patient's spondylolisthesis from grade V to grade I in a single-stage, single-level MI TLIF procedure.

Following surgical reduction and fusion, the patient's functional disability scores markedly improved: Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) fell from 54 preoperatively to 2 at 6 months and 0 at 1 year, and SF-12 physical component score (PCS) improved from 32.1 preoperatively to 30.6 at 6 months and 46.9 at 1 year.
At 2- and 3-year postoperative imaging, the patient maintained grade I spondylolisthesis with solid bony interbody fusion, indicating durable long-term correction and stabilization.
A high-quality case-control study (Czaprowski) found a significantly higher prevalence of generalised musculoskeletal hypermobility in AIS patients compared with controls.
A larger female-only case-control study (Czaprowski 2014) using a higher hypermobility cut-off again found higher prevalence of hypermobility in AIS patients versus controls.
Weber found roughly equal hypermobility scores between scoliosis patients and controls, with prevalence actually higher in the control group.
Mattson found females with idiopathic scoliosis were not more flexible than controls, and were actually less flexible on some measures.

Veldhuizen found poor correlation among flexibility measures with AIS patients tending towards less flexibility, and no significant difference in trunk bending stiffness between AIS and control groups.
Fuller found no significant association between four flexibility measures and AIS, though a non-significant trend toward reduced trunk flexibility to the dominant side was seen in the AIS group.
Fernandez-Bermejo reported hypermobility prevalence of 23% among AIS patients recruited from a scoliosis clinic, within the expected regional range.
Kobesova found the AIS group was more mobile than controls on all ten hypermobility tests, with 2 of 10 tests reaching statistical significance and total scores approaching significance.
Erkula found that a hypermobile subgroup of schoolchildren had significantly higher angle of trunk rotation and higher Beighton scores were associated with AIS.
Farro-Uceda found no significant difference in scoliosis prevalence between hypermobile and non-hypermobile schoolchildren.
The highest-quality cross-sectional study (Dolphens) found no association between hypermobility and trunk asymmetry after adjustment for confounders in a pre-pubertal population.
Bozkurt found no association between generalised hypermobility and AIS in Turkish schoolchildren.
Pratelli found a higher mean Beighton score in schoolchildren with clinical evidence of spinal curvature compared to those without, though scores were too low to indicate generalised hypermobility.
Longworth found both musculoskeletal hypermobility and AIS were markedly more prevalent in adolescent dancers than in matched non-dancer controls.
Within the dancer subgroup itself, Longworth found no significant association between hypermobility (Beighton score) and AIS.
Steinberg reported high co-prevalence of musculoskeletal hypermobility and scoliosis in adolescent female dancers, with most scoliosis cases also being hypermobile.
Tanchev found rhythmic gymnasts, a highly hypermobile population, had a markedly increased prevalence of AIS compared with the general adolescent female population.

In surgically treated AIS patients, Hasankhani found hypermobile individuals had smaller pre-operative curves, greater pre-operative spinal flexibility, smaller post-operative curves, and greater post-operative curve correction than non-hypermobile individuals.

Haller found a weak negative correlation between Beighton score and Cobb angle in females with AIS, indicating milder curves associated with higher hypermobility scores, which persisted after age adjustment.

Haller found reduced spinal (rather than peripheral joint) hypermobility, specifically inability to touch palms to the floor, conferred a 2.5-fold increased risk of requiring surgery for AIS after adjusting for age.

Adib described a highly selected cohort referred to a specialist hypermobility clinic in which scoliosis was reported in 9% of individuals; this low-quality descriptive study was excluded from further synthesis.

Overall, the systematic review found no convincing population-based evidence for an association between isolated musculoskeletal hypermobility and AIS, with substantial heterogeneity and risk of bias precluding meta-analysis; only two high-quality case-control studies from mild AIS clinic populations supported an association.
Preterm infants with joint laxity at pre-school age scored significantly lower on total and subscores of the M-ABC-2 than those without laxity.
Children with benign joint hypermobility syndrome (BJHS) and children with DCD showed a similar range of functional daily difficulties in fine and gross motor function.
Children with DCD had a significantly higher prevalence of joint hypermobility syndrome symptoms (pain in joints, pes planus) compared with typically developing children.
Children with DCD had a higher prevalence of joint hypermobility than healthy controls, with a significant negative correlation between M-ABC total score and degree of knee hyperextension.
Nearly half of Italian children with DCD had joint hypermobility, and these children showed significantly more frequent falls and easy bruising than DCD children without hypermobility.
Among children with BJHS, a substantial proportion scored in the impaired range on the M-ABC-2, indicating impaired motor control.
No significant association was found between generalized joint hypermobility and total motor performance in a Dutch pediatric cohort.
No differences in Beighton hypermobility scores were found across children with different levels of motor competence measured by M-ABC-2.
No significant association was found between delay in motor development and Bulbena hypermobility score; hypermobility was seen in children both with and without severe motor delay.

Both gross and fine motor performances were significantly delayed at 4.5-5 years in children who had both joint hypermobility and motor delay at 18 months, but not in those with joint hypermobility alone.
Children with BJHS had significantly more hypermobile joints, more pain, lower balance test scores, and more affected daily activity compared with typically developing children.
In a large cohort of children with BJHS recruited from a paediatric rheumatology clinic, arthralgia, clumsiness, poor coordination, handwriting difficulties, and PE limitations were common.
Children with DCD showed pes planus foot posture and lower limb hypermobility at the top end of the hypermobility scale, offering preliminary support for podiatric intervention such as foot orthoses.
No correlation was found between Beighton score and motor competence tests; children with a high level of positive Beighton tests (≥6) performed better on motor competence tests than others.

Danish children with generalized joint hypermobility had better static balance and speed/reaction test scores, and did not perform worse than non-hypermobile children on motor competence tests or physical activity level.

Probable DCD was significantly more prevalent in children attending physiotherapy than in a typically developing school group, though generalized joint hypermobility prevalence itself did not differ significantly between children with and without probable DCD within the physiotherapy group.

Across the reviewed literature, children referred for hypermobility showed a 33-48% incidence of motor delay, and children with DCD showed a 28-46% prevalence of enhanced joint hypermobility, with an overlapping range of functional difficulties, suggesting a multisystem disorder involving proprioceptive/CNS dysfunction.

The paper notes as background that multiple brain aneurysms are known to occur in certain connective tissue disorders, including Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome, and fibromuscular dysplasia, though the reported case patient did not have EDS.

A 38-year-old man developed bilateral internal carotid artery dissection with recurrent transient ischemic attack symptoms seven days after a COVID-19 infection accompanied by severe persistent nonproductive cough.

The patient had no personal or family history of connective tissue disease such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or Marfan syndrome, indicating his carotid dissection occurred without an identifiable underlying connective tissue disorder.
Congenital connective tissue diseases are reported in an estimated 1-5% of carotid artery dissection patients, with about 5% having a family member with a connective tissue disease.
Two prospective studies found a higher prevalence of recent infection among patients whose stroke was due to carotid dissection compared with patients whose stroke had other causes.
Several studies suggest an association between pertussis infection with severe coughing and carotid artery dissection.
Infection is proposed to increase inflammatory factors and oxidative radicals, causing diffuse endothelial inflammation and extracellular matrix injury that may predispose arteries to dissection.
Autopsy specimens of spontaneous coronary artery dissection have shown eosinophilic infiltration, suggesting an inflammatory component in spontaneous arterial dissection.

Simultaneous bilateral carotid artery stenting was performed for the patient's symptomatic bilateral ICA dissection refractory to medical therapy, with no neurological complications and, at 3-month follow-up, complete occlusion of the right pseudo-aneurysm and recanalization of the left ICA without residual stenosis.
Carotid artery dissection is reported in the literature to carry up to a 20% risk of causing ischemic stroke.

Fibromyalgia patients who reported subjective sleep quality improvement after CBT showed a significant increase in nocturnal HF power (parasympathetic index) during NREM sleep stages N2 and N3, regardless of CBT modality.
No significant change was observed in RR intervals, LF power, or the LF/HF ratio following CBT treatment.
Increases in HF power during stage N2 sleep were significantly correlated with greater improvement (decrease) in PSQI sleep quality scores after CBT.
Unlike stage N2, changes in HF power during stage N3 were not significantly correlated with improvement in PSQI sleep quality scores.
No significant relationship was found between changes in HF power in any sleep stage and changes in daily pain, depression, or anxiety scores.
A higher proportion of patients receiving the combined pain-and-insomnia CBT (CBT-C) reported sleep quality improvement compared to those receiving pain-focused CBT alone (CBT-P).

Prior literature cited in the introduction indicates that fibromyalgia patients show autonomic imbalance at rest, including higher muscle sympathetic nerve activity, lower HF power, and higher LF/HF ratio compared with healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia subjects showed reduced intracortical inhibition compared to healthy controls in pooled observational studies.
Fibromyalgia subjects showed higher resting motor thresholds compared to healthy controls.
Interventions including exercise, pregabalin, and non-invasive brain stimulation increased intracortical inhibition compared to placebo or sham stimulation in RCTs of fibromyalgia patients.
Interventions including exercise, pregabalin, and non-invasive brain stimulation increased cortical silent period duration compared to placebo or sham stimulation.
Increases in intracortical inhibition following treatment moderately correlated with reductions in pain, depression, and pain catastrophizing in fibromyalgia patients.
Reductions in intracortical facilitation following treatment moderately correlated with reduced fatigue in fibromyalgia patients.
The core clock gene Clock regulates expression of the high-affinity IgE receptor FcεRI on mast cells in a time-of-day-dependent manner.
The core clock gene Clock also controls expression of the IL-33 receptor ST2 on mast cells in a time-of-day-dependent manner.
IgE-dependent and IL-33-dependent mast cell activation thresholds differ between daytime and nighttime, potentially explaining diurnal variation in allergic symptom severity.

Environmental and lifestyle factors such as irregular eating habits can disrupt circadian rhythmicity, causing loss of circadian control of mast cell activation so that activation becomes equally strong at all times of day, potentially worsening allergic symptoms.
Naïve human mast cells (hMCs) exposed to BCG did not show significant degranulation compared to untreated cells.
BCG infection of naïve hMCs did not significantly induce secretion of IL-8, MCP-1, GM-CSF or MIP-1α compared to unstimulated controls.
Unlike THP-1 macrophages, hMCs did not support intracellular BCG growth as measured by luminescence of BCG-Lux.
Confocal microscopy showed hMCs did not internalize BCG mCherry nor retain bacteria at the cell membrane, despite bacterial proximity.
hMCs incubated with the 19-kDa Mtb lipoprotein secreted significantly increased IL-8, MCP-1, GM-CSF, and IL-13 compared to untreated controls.
HSP70 stimulation of hMCs showed no significant effect on mediator (IL-8, MCP-1, GM-CSF, IL-13) release, in contrast to the 19-kDa lipoprotein.
The 19-kDa lipoprotein significantly increased CD48 and TLR2 expression on hMCs, with CD48 expression considerably higher than TLR2, and showed a non-significant trend toward increased TLR4.
IL-33 priming of hMCs significantly increased secretion of IL-8, MCP-1, and IL-13 upon subsequent BCG stimulation, whereas IFN-γ priming showed no such effect.
Although IL-33 pre-treatment enhanced IgE/anti-IgE-mediated degranulation, it was not sufficient to induce BCG-mediated degranulation in hMCs.
Neither IL-33 nor IFN-γ pre-treatment promoted BCG intracellular growth in hMCs, as measured by BCG-Lux luminescence.
IL-33 treatment significantly induced CD48 expression in hMCs compared to both untreated control and IFN-γ treatment.
IFN-γ upregulated both TLR2 and TLR4 in hMCs, while IL-33 increased TLR4 expression but not TLR2, compared to control.
RNA-seq analysis showed IL-33 treatment enhanced expression of NOD2 and CD48, genes involved in Mtb recognition, and MHC class II molecules indicating hMC activation.
IL-33 priming significantly increased expression of the adhesion molecule ICAM-1 in hMCs.
IL-33-primed hMCs established significantly higher numbers of rapid (<1 min) membrane interactions with BCG compared to untreated hMCs, based on live confocal imaging.
α-Asarone inhibited degranulation of LAD2 mast cells in vitro.
α-Asarone treatment decreased release of IL-8, MCP-1, histamine, and TNF-α from mast cells in vitro.
α-Asarone reduced paw swelling and Evans blue leakage in a mast cell-dependent in vivo model.
α-Asarone reduced serum histamine, CCL2, and TNF-α levels in vivo.
In an asthma model, α-asarone inhibited airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR), lung inflammation, mast cell activation, inflammatory cell infiltration, and IL-5/IL-13 release in lung tissue.
α-Asarone decreased C48/80-induced phosphorylation of JAK2, ERK, and STAT3, indicating inhibition of the ERK/JAK2-STAT3 pathway underlying mast cell stabilization.
The number of mast cells in atopic dermatitis skin lesions correlated with disease severity as measured by the EASI score, but did not decrease after short-term topical tacrolimus treatment.
Filaggrin gene mutations are associated with increased prevalence of ichthyosis vulgaris and atopic dermatitis.
Flaky-tail (Flgft) mice with filaggrin mutations spontaneously develop dermatitis with increased serum IgE and dermal mast cell numbers, resembling human AD.
Dupilumab, which blocks IL-4/IL-13 signaling via IL-4Rα, improved AD signs and symptoms including pruritus, anxiety, depression, and quality of life compared with placebo.
Meta-analyses, systematic reviews, and RCTs have not established concrete evidence of overall omalizumab effectiveness for atopic dermatitis.
An H4 receptor antagonist (ZPL-3893787) lowered EASI scores in AD patients compared with placebo.
Omalizumab was reported to provide clinical benefit for chronic spontaneous urticaria.
The number and proportion of MRGPRX2-positive skin mast cells were increased in inflamed lesions of chronic urticaria patients compared with healthy control skin.

Intradermal substance P induced greater wheal reactions in chronic spontaneous urticaria patients than in healthy subjects, suggesting substance P/MRGPRX2-mediated mast cell degranulation as an alternative disease pathway.
Increased expression of IL-25 and IL-33 on mast cells was observed in lesional skin of chronic spontaneous urticaria patients, potentially driving mast cell proliferation and Th2 cytokine production.
More than 200 distinct IgE autoantibodies, including those recognizing IL-24, were detected in sera of chronic spontaneous urticaria patients.
Mast cell numbers were greater in pruritic than in non-pruritic psoriasis lesions.
Activated mast cells were more abundant in psoriatic lesions than in non-lesional psoriatic skin and healthy subjects, while resting mast cells were nearly absent in psoriatic lesions.
During etanercept therapy for psoriasis, the proportion of resting mast cells in lesional skin gradually normalized.
Mast cell density in the papillary and reticular dermis was significantly greater in patients with early progressive systemic sclerosis than in control subjects.
Histamine and tryptase each enhanced proliferation and collagen synthesis in cultured human skin fibroblasts, implicating mast cell mediators in fibrosis.
In aged tight-skin mice, mast cells and chymase were responsible for augmentation of fibrosis in a model resembling scleroderma.
IL-17A-positive mast cell numbers were increased in lichen planopilaris lesions compared with normal scalp, suggesting a role via IL-17R on follicular epithelial cells.
Mast cell numbers in skin were increased in patients with more severe acute graft-versus-host disease.
Mast-cell-deficient WBB6F1-KitW/W-v mice had significantly higher survival than Kit+/+ mice after induction of acute GVHD, indicating mast cells act as effector cells promoting GVHD.

Mast-cell-derived IL-10 was shown to inhibit acute GVHD caused by MHC antigen mismatch, since GVHD reactions resolved in mast-cell-deficient mice engrafted with wild-type but not IL-10-deficient mast cells.
Serum IgE specific to the Malassezia-derived allergen MGL_1304 was higher in patients with atopic dermatitis and cholinergic urticaria than in normal controls.

Degranulation of the LAD2 human mast cell line sensitized with AD patient sera and stimulated with MGL_1304 was greater than with healthy control sera, suggesting MGL_1304 is a major allergen exacerbating AD and cholinergic urticaria.
Mast-cell-deficient KitW/KitW-v mice were more susceptible to HSV-2 infection than wild-type Kit+/+ mice, indicating mast cells are important for antiviral host defense.

A 9-year-old girl developed Kounis syndrome (acute coronary syndrome/coronary vasospasm) following a weekly subcutaneous allergen immunotherapy injection, believed to be mediated by mast cell activation and inflammatory cytokine release during an allergic reaction.

The review states that excessive mast cell activation is linked to a growing number of inflammatory, stress-associated, and neuroimmune disorders, including allergy/anaphylaxis, autoimmune disease, migraine, and chronic pain.
The review reports a strong sex bias in mast cell-associated diseases, with females frequently at increased risk compared to males.

The review highlights that both adult gonadal sex hormones and perinatal (organizational) gonadal hormone exposure influence mast cell activity and development, contributing to sex differences in mast cell-associated disease.
The KIT D816V mutation is detected in over 90% of systemic mastocytosis patients regardless of subtype and is considered the oncogenic driver mutation.
KIT D816V mutation is linked to aberrant expression of CD25 and/or CD2 on mast cells.
Multilineage KIT D816V involvement (in non-mast cell hematopoietic lineages) was the most important prognostic factor for progression of indolent SM to more aggressive SM subtypes.
Serum tryptase is notably higher (≥200 ng/mL) in aggressive SM and SM with associated hematologic neoplasm compared to indolent SM.
About 20% of ISM patients lack mast cell clusters in the bone marrow and about 30% have serum tryptase below the 20 ng/mL diagnostic threshold, illustrating diagnostic limitations.
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia, which is linked to elevated basal tryptase and mast cell activation predisposition, is significantly more prevalent in SM patients than in healthy controls.
In ISM patients, mast cell mediator levels correlated substantially with bone marrow neoplastic mast cell burden but not with mast cell mediator-release symptoms.
Mastocytosis patients with hereditary alpha-tryptasemia show considerably higher serum tryptase levels and more mast cell mediator-release symptoms independent of bone marrow mast cell burden.

Well-differentiated systemic mastocytosis (WDSM) is a rare morphologic variant (~5% of neoplastic mast cell proliferations) with low frequency of KIT D816V, low serum tryptase, CD25/CD2 negativity, but recurrent aberrant CD30 expression.
One study reported CD30 expression is preferentially higher in aggressive SM and mast cell leukemia compared to indolent SM.

A subsequent flow cytometry study found aberrant CD30 expression across all SM subtypes with no clear association between CD30 levels and clinicopathological characteristics, contradicting the earlier report of preferential expression in aggressive disease.
Bone marrow mastocytosis patients with low disease burden (absence of B-findings, tryptase <125 ng/mL) have superior prognosis compared to patients with typical ISM or SSM.
Bone marrow mastocytosis is strongly associated with osteoporosis and potentially life-threatening severe anaphylactic reactions despite its indolent clinical course.
More than half (50-70%) of mast cell leukemia cases harbor the KIT D816V mutation, with the remainder harboring other KIT mutations or wild-type KIT.
In a retrospective study of 40 AML patients with t(8;21)(q22;q22.1);RUNX1-RUNX1T1, 12.5% were diagnosed with SM or myelomastocytic leukemia after bone marrow testing for KIT D816V.

The WHO class-independent Mayo Alliance Prognostic System (MAPS) stratifies SM patients into five risk groups with markedly different median overall survival, from not-reached (low-risk) to 8 months (very high-risk).

Avapritinib produced a 75% overall response rate with median response onset of 2 months and reduced mast cell burden by ≥50% along with KIT D816V variant allele frequency in the EXPLORER and PATHFINDER trials for advanced SM.
A systematic review adjusting for differences between trial populations found avapritinib superior to midostaurin for overall response rates, disease burden reduction, and survival in advanced SM.
Avapritinib is roughly ten-fold more potent than midostaurin against KIT D816V in vitro (IC50 0.27 nM vs 2.9 nM).
The Mutation-Adjusted Risk Score (MARS) model stratifies advanced SM patients into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups with median OS of not reached, 3.9 years, and 1.9 years respectively.
Midostaurin demonstrated sustained responses and more favorable outcomes in advanced SM patients who did not harbor high-risk SRSF2/ASXL1/RUNX1 mutations.
A registry-based analysis using MARS parameters and KIT D816V VAF demonstrated midostaurin's superiority over cladribine for overall survival and leukemia-free survival in advanced SM.
A single institution study of 42 advanced SM patients found that lack of the KIT D816V mutation was an indicator of cladribine treatment resistance.
Imatinib is effective only in SM patients with wild-type KIT or imatinib-sensitive mutations (F522C, V560G) as seen in WDSM, while KIT D816V and V559I confer intrinsic resistance.

Mast cell activation syndrome diagnosis requires fulfillment of three criteria: recurrent systemic mast cell activation symptoms, elevated serum mast cell-derived markers, and symptomatic response to treatment.

MCAS is classified into primary/monoclonal MCAS (defined by clonal KIT mutation or aberrant CD25 mast cell expression), secondary MCAS (associated with IgE-dependent allergy without neoplastic mast cells), and idiopathic MCAS (criteria met without clonal or reactive cause identified).
Treatment with KIT-targeting agents may partially or fully eradicate the mast cell lineage in patients with mast cell activation syndrome.

Alpha-Gal, an oligosaccharide found in non-catarrhine mammalian tissues, is the causal antigen of AGS, an IgE-mediated delayed anaphylaxis occurring 3–6 hours after consumption of mammalian meat or dairy.

IgE sensitization in AGS is initiated by bites from hard-bodied ticks (Ixodes ricinus, Amblyomma americanum, Haemaphysalis longicornis, Ixodes holocyclus) via alpha-Gal-containing salivary glycoproteins and other non-alpha-Gal salivary biomolecules such as PGE2.
Anaphylaxis has been reported to occur in up to 60% of AGS cases and can be fatal without prompt treatment.
Individuals lacking blood group B or AB antigens may be at higher risk of developing alpha-Gal sIgE, since the B antigen (structurally similar to alpha-Gal) confers immune tolerance to the epitope.
A positive correlation between anti-alpha-Gal IgM antibodies and Plasmodium falciparum infection has been reported, associated with decreased transmission of the parasite.
Anti-alpha-Gal antibody levels negatively correlate with SARS-CoV-2 infection and with COVID-19 symptom severity.
Conventional skin prick testing with commercially available mammalian meat extracts lacks sensitivity for AGS, producing low-reactive wheals (2-4 mm) that can lead to misdiagnosis.
Cetuximab can be used as a sensitivity agent in skin testing because it induces strong skin reactivity in AGS patients due to its high alpha-Gal epitope content.

Serum anti-alpha-Gal IgE measured by bovine thyroglobulin-conjugated ImmunoCAP is the standard confirmatory test for AGS, though the clinical relevance of the widely used 0.35 kU/L cut-off remains unclear.

In a German cohort of 300 hunters, 19.3% (58 individuals) tested positive for anti-alpha-Gal IgE at a 0.35 IU/mL cut-off, but only 1.67% (5 individuals) reported allergic reactions to mammalian meat, illustrating that IgE positivity does not equate to clinical AGS.

Specific IgE levels are not a reliable biomarker for predicting severity of allergic reactions, as some AGS patients experience anaphylaxis while maintaining stable or even negative anti-alpha-Gal IgE results.

The basophil activation test, which measures CD63 and CD203c expression by flow cytometry, is used as a diagnostic clarifier to distinguish asymptomatic alpha-Gal sensitized individuals from patients with clinical AGS.

The mast cell activation test measures CD63 upregulation on MRGPRX2-expressing LAD-2 mast cell lines and shows high sensitivity with dose-dependent responses to allergens, presenting logistical advantages over BAT since serum can be frozen prior to use.
Basophil reactivity measured via the histamine release assay was found to be higher in AGS patients compared to alpha-Gal sensitized individuals, with sensitivity/specificity similar to BAT.

Proteomic analysis of tick sialome and alphagalactome identified the 14-3-3 family chaperone as a protein recognized by IgE in the sera of AGS patients, proposing it as a potential future diagnostic biomarker.

A machine-learning based diagnostic algorithm combining clinical symptoms, risk factors, and anti-alpha-Gal sIgE levels has been proposed to improve AGS diagnosis, with potential implementation via mobile applications.
Long-term (1-2 years) avoidance of tick bites is associated with a higher chance of recovering tolerance to meat products, allowing reintroduction of red meat into the diet.

Only three successful case reports (two adults, one pediatric) describe oral desensitization to beef meat in AGS patients, requiring daily consumption of 120 grams of cooked mammalian meat to maintain desensitization.

Omalizumab has been sporadically used as monotherapy in AGS patients in specialized centers, successfully controlling continued reactivity and allowing reintroduction of small amounts of mammalian meat into the diet.

A case report described abnormal neuro-psychiatric behavior (abulia, aphasia, abnormal gait, reduced limb movement) associated with AGS, suggesting possible alpha-Gal-driven immune-mediated hypothalamic dysfunction requiring further investigation.

A zebrafish model of AGS exhibited allergic hemorrhagic anaphylactic-type reactions, behavior changes and mortality in response to tick salivary compounds and mammalian meat, associated with tissue-specific toll-like-receptor-mediated Th1/Th2 responses.

Knockout of the alpha1,3-galactosyltransferase gene in C57BL/6 mice (and pigs) eliminates alpha-Gal epitope synthesis, creating a humanized model used to study tick-induced IgE responses to alpha-Gal and other immunological approaches such as tick-borne allergies and Chagas disease.
Adding antigen-specific IgA to IgE-sensitized bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs) markedly reduced surface LAMP-1 expression upon antigen challenge, indicating suppressed degranulation.
IgA directed against an irrelevant antigen (OVA) did not suppress IgE-mediated BMMC degranulation, demonstrating that the inhibitory effect of IgA is antigen-specific.
Anti-TNP IgA physically binds to bone marrow-derived mast cells in a dose-dependent manner but does not bind purified splenic T cells.
IgA binds to primary peritoneal mast cells (CD11b- c-Kit+ FcεRI+), confirming binding is not limited to cultured cells.
Chelation of calcium with EGTA dramatically impaired IgA binding to BMMCs, showing that IgA-mast cell interaction is calcium-dependent, whereas IgE binding was unaffected.
Removal of N-linked glycans (PNGase F) or terminal sialic acid (neuraminidase) from IgA completely abolished its ability to bind BMMCs, without affecting antigen (TNP-OVA) binding.
Pre-incubating BMMCs with free sialic acid competitively suppressed IgA binding to undetectable levels, supporting a lectin-like, sialic acid-dependent receptor interaction.

Desialylated anti-TNP IgA lost its ability to suppress IgE-mediated BMMC degranulation, whereas untreated IgA retained inhibitory function, demonstrating sialic acid is required for functional suppression.
Antigen-specific IgA attenuated IgE-induced phosphorylation of Syk in BMMCs at the earliest signaling time point, indicating IgA acts proximally in the FcεRI signaling cascade.
IgA addition to IgE-sensitized, antigen-stimulated BMMCs resulted in complete suppression of IL-13, TNF-α, and IL-6 production.

Purified peanut-specific IgA from peanut-allergic patients' post-oral immunotherapy sera dose-dependently suppressed CD63-based basophil activation induced by crude peanut extract in whole blood from a peanut-allergic donor.
Fluorescently labeled human IgA bound to basophils and neutrophils in whole blood from peanut-allergic donors but not to T cells.

Screening of mast cells from mice with targeted deletions of candidate C-type lectin receptors (SIGN-R1, CD33, Siglec F) or FcγR2b showed IgA-mediated suppression of IgE activation remained intact, indicating none of these are the responsible receptor.

Intraepidermal nerve fiber density was reduced in type 2 diabetic patients compared with age-matched controls and correlated with increased heat perception thresholds and reduced sural sensory nerve amplitudes.
Diabetes causes early degeneration of skin nerve fibers whose severity correlates with the duration of disease, as shown in prospective studies.
An inverse association exists between intraepidermal nerve fiber density and severity of diabetic neuropathy.
There is strong evidence of reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density in patients with glucose intolerance, even with normal nerve conduction recordings.
There is preliminary indication that lifestyle interventions can improve nerve fiber density in glucose intolerance, though this requires confirmation in a larger sample.
In idiopathic small-fiber neuropathy, skin biopsy usually shows decreased distal intraepidermal nerve fiber density with normal proximal densities, indicating a length-dependent process.

Repeated skin biopsies over 12 to 28 months in patients with idiopathic small-fiber sensory neuropathy showed a progressive decrease in intraepidermal nerve fiber density in the legs, demonstrating disease progression.

Skin biopsy determination of intraepidermal nerve fiber density was considered more sensitive than the quantitative sudomotor axonal reflex test or quantitative sensitivity test in diagnosing small-fiber neuropathy.
In patients with sensory ganglionopathy, skin biopsies show nerve fiber loss at all sites without the proximal-distal gradient typical of distal sensory polyneuropathy.
Intraepidermal nerve fiber density was reduced in a length-dependent manner in HIV-infected patients with neuropathic signs on physical examination, independently of neuropathic symptoms.

Skin biopsy has demonstrated depletion of intraepidermal nerve fibers, of varying extent, in hereditary neuropathies including Fabry disease, familial dysautonomia, and congenital insensitivity to pain.
In Friedreich's ataxia, which primarily causes degeneration of dorsal root ganglia and large-caliber myelinated fibers, skin biopsy revealed involvement of small-diameter nerve fibers as well.
In Charcot-Marie-Tooth 1A patients, dermal myelinated fibers examined on skin biopsy showed shortening of internodal length.

Recent studies show small-diameter nerve fiber involvement with decreased intraepidermal nerve fiber densities in systemic lupus erythematosus, mediated in part by immunoglobulin deposition on the nerve surface and activation of the dermal vascular endothelium.

In SLE patients with pain and decreased warmth sensation in the feet, more than a third required skin biopsy to diagnose small-fiber neuropathy because conventional neurological examinations were not sufficiently effective.

Quantifying intraepidermal nerve fibers in skin lesions has been suggested as an additional diagnostic tool, along with skin smear examination and nerve conduction studies, to improve detection of neuropathy in leprosy control programs.
A case report described clinical and neuropathological recovery of small-fiber neuropathy after thyroid hormone replacement therapy in a patient with hypothyroidism.
Intraepidermal nerve fiber loss has been reported in Ross syndrome, erythromelalgia, type 1 complex regional pain syndrome, and late-onset restless legs syndrome.
It has been suggested that in restless legs syndrome, hyperactivity of spinal structures may be triggered by nociceptive deafferentation in a subgroup of patients with painful polyneuropathy.
Skin biopsies in Parkinson's disease have demonstrated degeneration of autonomic nerves in blood vessels, sweat glands, and erector pili muscles.
A small-fiber-predominant neuropathy may be a complication of celiac disease, and patients improved with a gluten-free diet.
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis reduces intraepidermal nerve fiber densities, indicating the presence of a distal sensory axonopathy in ALS.
Corneal sensitivity measured by Cochet-Bonnet aesthesiometer was significantly reduced in Sjögren's Syndrome patients compared to both healthy controls and MGD patients.
The density of inflammatory cells detected by IVCM was significantly increased in Sjögren's Syndrome patients compared to healthy controls.
Subbasal corneal nerve plexus density was significantly reduced in Sjögren's Syndrome patients compared to both healthy controls and MGD patients.
Corneal subbasal nerve tortuosity was significantly increased in Sjögren's Syndrome patients compared to both healthy controls and MGD patients.
The average number of subbasal nerve plexus neuromas was significantly increased in Sjögren's Syndrome patients compared to healthy controls.
Among Sjögren's Syndrome patients, those with associated small fiber neuropathy had significantly more corneal neuromas than those without SFN, suggesting neuroma count may help detect SFN in SS.
AIM2 receptor stimulation with Poly dA:dT significantly increased IL-1α release from PBMCs of post-COVID-19 patients with lung fibrosis-like changes, but not from patients without fibrosis.
AIM2 stimulation did not increase IL-1α release from PBMCs of post-COVID-19 patients without lung fibrosis.
Pharmacological inhibition of caspase-1 (YVAD) or caspase-4 (ICH2) did not reduce AIM2-induced IL-1α release, indicating an inflammasome-independent mechanism.
Inhibition of cGAS (G140) or STING (H151) did not alter AIM2-induced IL-1α release, indicating cGAS-STING is not involved in this pathway.
AIM2 stimulation significantly increased IFN-α release from PBMCs of post-COVID-19 patients with fibrosis-like changes, but not from patients without fibrosis.
Inhibition of caspase-1 or caspase-4 significantly reduced AIM2-induced IFN-α release, showing this cytokine release is inflammasome-dependent.
AIM2 stimulation did not induce IFN-β release from PBMCs regardless of fibrosis status.
AIM2 stimulation did not induce IL-33 release from PBMCs of PC patients regardless of fibrosis status.
AIM2 stimulation did not induce IL-18 release from PBMCs of PC patients with or without lung fibrosis.
AIM2 stimulation did not induce IL-1β release from PBMCs of PC patients regardless of fibrosis status, despite IL-1β being generally elevated in acute COVID-19.
AIM2 stimulation substantially increased pro-fibrotic TGF-β release from PBMCs of PC patients with lung fibrosis, but not from those without fibrosis.
Inhibition of caspase-1 or caspase-4 did not reduce AIM2-induced TGF-β release, indicating an inflammasome-independent mechanism for TGF-β release.
Inhibition of cGAS or STING did not significantly reduce AIM2-induced TGF-β release, though non-significant decreasing trends were observed.
AIM2 mRNA levels in total PBMCs were similar between HV subjects and PC patients regardless of fibrosis status, though a non-significant trend to increase was seen in fibrotic patients.
AIM2 protein expression on classical (CD14+) monocytes was significantly higher in fibrotic post-COVID-19 patients compared to non-fibrotic patients and healthy vaccinated controls.

The percentage of inflammatory monocytes (CD14+HLA-DR+) expressing AIM2 was significantly higher in PC patients than HV subjects, regardless of fibrosis status, with the highest levels in responsive fibrotic patients.
NLRP3 inflammasome triggering with LPS and ATP did not induce IL-1α release from PC-derived PBMCs, suggesting impaired NLRP3 responses in post-COVID patients (data not shown).

In a prior study by the same group, post-COVID-19 patients with ground-glass opacities on CT had higher plasma IL-1α and TGF-β levels than healthy subjects, increasing the relative risk of fibrotic-like changes.
Low-dose naltrexone (3 mg) reduced the patient's burning mouth syndrome pain intensity by 50% after one month, with no pain upon awakening.
After 2 months of LDN, the widespread pain associated with her chronic comorbidities (including fibromyalgia) reduced by 50%.
The patient's headache resolved completely after 2 months of LDN treatment.
At 6 months, after adjusting the LDN dose to 4.5 mg, the patient remained stable with a sustained 50% reduction in widespread pain and burning mouth pain of 2/10, with no reported side effects.
The patient with burning mouth syndrome had multiple comorbid chronic conditions including fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome, headache, and interstitial cystitis.
The patient's ankylosing spondylitis was associated with a positive HLA-B27 assay, consistent with the known strong genetic association between AS and this allele.
Serum and CSF anti-AQP4 antibodies were positive by cell-based assay, confirming a diagnosis of AQP4-positive NMOSD presenting as longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis.

The concurrent occurrence of AQP4-positive NMOSD and ankylosing spondylitis in the same patient is reported as a rare comorbid association, suggesting a possible shared but distinct immune-mediated pathogenic basis.

Treatment with pulse intravenous methylprednisolone followed by cyclical rituximab (anti-CD20) led to remarkable improvement in lower limb power and no residual neurological deficit except paresthesias at 3-month follow-up, with clinical improvement in AS disease activity by 6 months.

The authors note that Th17 and Th2-related cytokines have been reported elevated in the CSF of NMO patients, indicating T-cell-mediated inflammatory involvement in NMOSD pathogenesis beyond the classical B-cell/antibody model.
