A heterozygous SMAD3 missense variant c.200T>G (p.I67S) in exon 1 segregated with disease across three generations of a family with Loeys-Dietz syndrome type 3, confirming pathogenicity.
Upon TGF-β1 stimulation, HEK293 cells expressing SMAD3 (p.I67S) showed less SMAD3 phosphorylation than cells expressing normal SMAD3.
Cells expressing SMAD3 (p.I67S) displayed significantly lower luciferase reporter (ARE-Luc) activity than cells expressing normal SMAD3, in both presence and absence of TGF-β1.
Expression of TGF-β/SMAD3 target genes SERPINE1, COL1A1, CCN2 (CTGF), and MMP2 was reduced in SMAD3 (p.I67S) mutant-expressing HEK293 cells compared with normal SMAD3.

SMAD3 (p.I67S) protein displayed reduced stability compared with normal SMAD3 in cycloheximide-chase experiments in both patient dermal fibroblasts (non-significant) and transfected HEK293 cells (significant).

CD14+ PBMC-derived osteoclasts from the patient with SMAD3 (p.I67S) showed increased number and area of TRAP-positive multinucleated osteoclasts compared to an age- and gender-matched healthy control.
Osteoclast marker genes ACP5, ATP6V0D2, and DCSTAMP were upregulated in osteoclasts differentiated from the SMAD3 (p.I67S) patient's cells compared with a non-LDS individual.
TGF-β signaling target gene expression was decreased in CD14+ PBMCs/osteoclasts from the index patient with SMAD3 (p.I67S), consistent with reduced TGF-β signaling in vivo.

Transiliac bone biopsy histomorphometry in the index case (age 15.6y) showed markedly reduced cortical width (-67.5%), trabecular thickness (-31.8%), osteoblast surface/bone surface (-32.9%), mineralizing surface/bone surface (-43.2%), and bone formation rate/bone surface (-50.3%), with increased mineralization lag time (+65.3%) and normal osteoid volume.

Quantitative backscattered electron imaging (qBEI) of the index patient's bone biopsy revealed substantial undermineralization of both trabecular and cortical bone, with decreased CaMean, CaPeak and CaHigh, and increased CaLow and CaWidth compared to healthy children reference values.

Three doses of zoledronic acid between ages 16-18 in the index patient were associated with improved lumbar spine bone mineral apparent density, increasing the Z-score from -2.3 at age 15.7 to 0.1 at age 21.
The index case (IV.2) had a trial of Atenolol and Losartan which was discontinued due to poor tolerability.
Two of the SMAD3 (p.I67S)-affected siblings (IV.1 and IV.2) in this family were diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder and selective mutism.

Findings in the human LDS3 patient bone biopsy (reduced bone mass, cortical/trabecular thickness, mineralization, osteoblast differentiation) were concordant with prior data from Smad3 knockout mice, which similarly show reduced bone mass, formation, mineralization, and osteoblast survival.

Non-hospitalized adults with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection had a 26% higher hazard of reporting at least one WHO-defined long COVID symptom beyond 12 weeks compared to a propensity-matched uninfected cohort.
Anosmia showed the strongest association with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection among all 62 significant symptoms at ≥12 weeks.
Hair loss was a novel symptom strongly associated with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection at ≥12 weeks, not widely reported previously.
Sneezing was significantly associated with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection at ≥12 weeks, though with a wide confidence interval.
Difficulty ejaculating was a novel male sexual dysfunction symptom significantly associated with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection at ≥12 weeks.
Reduced libido was a novel symptom significantly associated with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection at ≥12 weeks.
Shortness of breath at rest was significantly associated with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection at ≥12 weeks.
Fatigue was significantly associated with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection at ≥12 weeks, consistent with prior systematic reviews.
Pleuritic chest pain was significantly associated with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection at ≥12 weeks.
Fever was significantly associated with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection at ≥12 weeks.
Women had a significantly higher risk of developing long COVID than men.
After adjustment for comorbidities, older non-hospitalized adults had a lower risk of long COVID than younger adults, contrary to the unadjusted trend.
Black Afro-Caribbean ethnic group was associated with increased long COVID risk compared to white ethnicity.
Mixed ethnicity was associated with increased long COVID risk compared to white ethnicity.
Greater socioeconomic deprivation was associated with increased risk of long COVID.
Current and former smokers had increased risk of long COVID compared to never smokers.
Obesity (BMI >30) was associated with increased risk of long COVID compared to healthy weight.
Pre-existing COPD had the largest comorbidity association with long COVID risk.
Pre-existing fibromyalgia was associated with increased risk of developing long COVID.
Pre-existing erectile dysfunction was associated with increased risk of long COVID.
Pre-existing migraine was associated with increased risk of developing long COVID.
Pre-existing multiple sclerosis was associated with increased risk of long COVID, though with a wide confidence interval.

Latent class analysis of 50 consolidated symptoms among long COVID patients identified three distinct phenotype clusters: a broad multisystem symptom cluster (80.0%), a respiratory cluster (5.8%), and a mental health/cognitive cluster (14.2%).
The association between SARS-CoV-2 infection and long-term cough was substantially stronger for infections during the pandemic's second surge than the first.
Baseline fibromyalgia was associated with a 37% increased risk of developing long COVID symptoms after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Baseline migraine comorbidity was associated with a 26% increased risk of developing long COVID.
COPD as a baseline comorbidity showed the largest association with development of long COVID among comorbidities studied.
Baseline anxiety was associated with a 35% increased risk of long COVID.
Baseline depression was associated with a 31% increased risk of long COVID.
Baseline multiple sclerosis was associated with a 26% increased risk of long COVID.

Older age above 30 was associated with higher risk of long COVID in univariate analysis, but after adjustment for baseline covariates, increasing age was associated with progressively lower risk, with those ≥70 years having 25% lower risk than those aged 18-30.
Black Afro-Caribbean, mixed ethnicity, and other ethnic minority groups had significantly increased risk of long COVID compared to white ethnic groups.
Increasing socioeconomic deprivation was associated with an 11% increased risk of long COVID among the most deprived compared to least deprived groups.
Current and former smokers had increased risk of reporting long COVID symptoms compared to never smokers.
Obesity (BMI >30) was associated with a 10% increased risk of reporting long COVID symptoms compared to healthy weight.

A latent class analysis of 50 consolidated long COVID symptoms identified an optimal three-class model; class 1, comprising 80% of symptomatic patients, was dominated by a broad spectrum of symptoms including pain, fatigue and rash.
Latent class 2, comprising 5.8% of symptomatic long COVID patients, was dominated by respiratory symptoms including cough, shortness of breath and phlegm.

Latent class 3, comprising 14.2% of symptomatic long COVID patients, was dominated by mental health and cognitive symptoms including depression, anxiety, insomnia and brain fog, and this class was more likely to include younger patients.
The association between SARS-CoV-2 infection and reported cough symptoms beyond 12 weeks was substantially stronger for patients infected during the second pandemic wave than the first.

At baseline (3-12 months before index date), the two propensity-matched cohorts showed no significant differences in symptom reporting except for bowel incontinence and sore throat, confirming good matching quality.
Patients infected with SARS-CoV-2 were more likely than uninfected comparators to report multiple concurrent symptoms after 12 weeks, with the gap widening as symptom count increased.

History of SARS-CoV-2 infection was independently associated with 62 distinct symptoms spanning 14 of 15 symptom domains at 12 or more weeks after infection, after adjustment for confounders and baseline symptoms.
A substantial proportion of Long-COVID cases, possibly around 20%, clinically manifests as ME/CFS.
Pre-pandemic epidemiological data from the US estimated that 0.4% of the population is affected by ME/CFS.
Extrapolating post-COVID rates meeting ME/CFS diagnostic criteria to the general population, the number of ME/CFS cases in Germany is expected to at least double in coming years.
ME/CFS can occur at any age, with incidence peaks in adolescence and in adults aged 30-40 years, and women are affected 2-3 times more often than men.
After orthostatic provocation (e.g., tilt-table testing), cerebral blood flow drops on average 7% in healthy individuals but 26% in ME/CFS patients.
Cardiopulmonary exercise testing consistently demonstrates abnormal cardiorespiratory and metabolic responses to physical exertion in ME/CFS patients.
Endothelial vascular function is impaired in many ME/CFS patients, and these vascular, cerebral blood flow, and exercise abnormalities are also found in SARS-CoV-2-triggered ME/CFS.

Autoantibodies against adrenergic, muscarinic, and other G-protein coupled receptors (GPCR) of the vascular, immune, and nervous systems are detectable in a subset of ME/CFS patients, including SARS-CoV-2-induced cases, though these are not disease-specific.

Post-exertional malaise (PEM) is a worsening of symptoms after even mild everyday exertion that typically begins hours later or the next day, persists at least 14 hours after exertion, and often lasts days to weeks; it is considered the near-pathognomonic hallmark of ME/CFS.
A genetic predisposition to ME/CFS is suggested based on twin studies, and in over two-thirds of patients a temporal association between symptom onset and an infectious illness can be identified.
About 25% of ME/CFS patients are so severely affected that they are housebound.

About 40% of ME/CFS patients improve clinically over the long-term course, but around 60% remain unable to work due to disease-related disability, and complete remission in adults is rare (single-digit percentage).
Concomitant Hashimoto thyroiditis is found in 10-20% of ME/CFS patients, and antinuclear antibodies (ANA) are elevated in approximately 20%.

In one study, about 25% of ME/CFS patients showed a deficiency of total immunoglobulin or immunoglobulin subclasses, 15% had mannose-binding lectin deficiency, while 25% showed polyclonal immunoglobulin elevation.
Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS) is frequently associated with ME/CFS, for reasons that remain unknown.

POTS, diagnosed when heart rate rises persistently by >30/min in adults (>40/min in children/adolescents) within 10 minutes of standing, or sustained heart rate >120/min, frequently co-occurs with ME/CFS as orthostatic intolerance.
Ivabradine, which specifically affects heart rate unlike beta-blockers, is used off-label for POTS when non-pharmacological measures are exhausted.
Amitriptyline should not be used in ME/CFS patients with tachycardia and POTS.
In uncontrolled studies and case reports, prolonged antibiotic therapy with azithromycin or minocycline sometimes led to improvement in ME/CFS, possibly due to their immunomodulatory effects.
Melatonin at 2-5 mg (e.g., extended-release) can be effective for sleep disturbances in ME/CFS, along with first-generation antihistamines, tryptophan, and low-dose antidepressants.
Anti-CD3/CD28-stimulated T cells from ME/CFS patients showed significantly more apoptotic cells than healthy controls at both 200x and higher magnification.
Anti-CD3/CD28-stimulated T cells from ME/CFS patients showed significantly more necrotic cells than healthy controls at both magnifications.

The extremely severe ME/CFS patient showed markedly greater apoptosis and necrosis in stimulated T cells than the unrelated healthy control, with a larger fold-increase than the moderately affected twin, suggesting severity correlates with cell death extent.
The average number of mitochondria per stimulated T cell did not differ significantly between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.

Stimulated T cells from ME/CFS patients showed substantially higher proportions of swollen and morphologically abnormal (vesicular/compartmentalized and/or swollen) mitochondria compared to healthy controls.
Within both the discordant twin pair and the unrelated pair, the ME/CFS-affected individual showed higher numbers of swollen mitochondria than their matched control.
A significantly higher percentage of stimulated T cells contained more than 3 swollen mitochondria in ME/CFS patients versus healthy controls.

A significantly higher percentage of stimulated T cells carried 6 or more morphologically abnormal mitochondria in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls, and this was more pronounced in the extremely severe patient than the moderately affected twin.
No significant difference in apoptotic cell death was found between the discordant twins in unstimulated PBMC subpopulations lacking T cells.
PMA-stimulated non-T PBMCs from the extremely severe ME/CFS patient showed a borderline, non-significant increase in necrotic cell death compared to the unrelated healthy control.
Stimulated PBMCs lacking T cells from the extremely severe ME/CFS patient contained significantly more giant intracellular lipid droplet-like vesicles than the unrelated healthy control.

Whole exome sequencing revealed a rare homozygous SMPD1 missense variant of uncertain significance in the metallophosphatase domain in the extremely severely ill ME/CFS patient, which was absent in the twins and unrelated healthy control, and may contribute to the observed lipid droplet accumulation.

Stimulated T cells from the extremely severe ME/CFS patient showed significantly more large platelets and a nonsignificant increase in platelet clumps compared to the unrelated healthy control, suggesting platelet hyperactivation.

Across the whole small cohort, platelet clumps and giant rosette-like platelet aggregates were increased in ME/CFS patients' stimulated T cells relative to controls, but this did not reach statistical significance, likely due to small sample size.

Giant rosette-like platelet aggregates (8-12 microns) were observed exclusively in stimulated T cell samples and not in unstimulated or stimulated PBMC-lacking-T-cell populations, suggesting they are associated specifically with T cell activation, a novel structural observation.
ME/CFS participants scored significantly worse (higher impairment) than healthy controls on all four PROMIS sleep and pain short forms, with large effect sizes.

PROMIS sleep and pain T-scores increased monotonically across ME/CFS subgroups with low, medium, and high functional impairment (defined by vertical/horizontal activity hours and SF-36 PCS), supporting known-groups validity, with small-to-medium effect sizes.
All four PROMIS sleep and pain short forms demonstrated high internal consistency in ME/CFS participants, with categorical omega coefficients ranging from 0.92 to 0.97.

IRT-based standard errors of measurement for the PROMIS T-scores ranged from 2.1 to 2.7, below the 3.2 threshold needed for reliable individual-level assessment, indicating the measures are precise enough for individual patient monitoring in ME/CFS.
After correcting for multiple comparisons, no items on the four PROMIS sleep and pain short forms showed significant differential item functioning by sex or age group among ME/CFS participants.

Mean PROMIS T-scores for ME/CFS participants ranged from 57.68 to 62.40 across the four measures, roughly one standard deviation above the general US population norm of 50, indicating substantially greater sleep and pain problems.
No substantial floor or ceiling effects (>15% at extreme scores) were found for any of the four PROMIS sleep/pain short forms among ME/CFS participants.

About 10% of ME/CFS participants reported no pain at all on both pain interference and pain behavior items, indicating a subgroup of ME/CFS patients without current pain symptoms, consistent with pain not being a required diagnostic symptom.

Among the four PROMIS measures, only the pain interference short form showed strong responsiveness to change over a 10-14 month follow-up in ME/CFS, with medium-to-large Guyatt's responsiveness statistics when groups were defined by SF-36 PCS change.

The two sleep-related PROMIS short forms (sleep disturbance and sleep-related impairment) and the pain behavior short form did not show sufficient evidence of responsiveness to change in functional status over a 10-14 month follow-up in ME/CFS.

Confirmatory factor analysis showed excellent unidimensional model fit for the pain short forms (CFI/TLI >0.95) but only marginal fit for the sleep short forms (>0.90), which improved to acceptable ranges with bi-factor modeling.
The estimated crude prevalence of ME/CFS in Australian primary care in 2015 was 101.5 per 100,000 population.
Crude ME/CFS prevalence estimates for 2016-2019 remained similar to 2015, ranging between 94.9 and 103.9 per 100,000 population.
Across all study years, crude ME/CFS prevalence was substantially higher in females than in males.
ME/CFS prevalence was generally highest in the 50-59 year age group (60-69 years in 2017; 40-49 years for females in 2019).
ME/CFS prevalence was higher among patients residing in inner regional areas than those in major cities, remote or very remote regions.

No clear socioeconomic gradient was observed for ME/CFS prevalence across IRSAD (socioeconomic advantage/disadvantage) quintiles, though the lowest quintile had the lowest and the highest quintile the highest prevalence.

Qualitative interviews and focus groups revealed that people with ME/CFS commonly experienced a prolonged, multi-year path to diagnosis, often involving multiple GPs and incorrect differential diagnoses such as depression before ME/CFS was recognized.

Qualitative data indicated that stigma, disbelief from healthcare providers, lack of specialist services (especially rural/regional), and absence of definitive treatments led many patients to stop seeking GP care specifically for ME/CFS, which likely contributes to underestimation of prevalence in primary care records.

A prior UK primary-care study (Nacul et al.) reported comparable but variable ME/CFS prevalence depending on diagnostic criteria: 0.19% (CDC/Fukuda), 0.11% (Canadian Consensus Criteria), and 0.003% (Epidemiological Case Definition).

Community-based studies have reported substantially higher ME/CFS prevalence than clinic/primary-care based estimates, ranging from 75-267 per 100,000 up to 0.42% and 1.0% depending on case definition and ascertainment method.
A systematic review with meta-analyses reported ME/CFS prevalence estimates that varied substantially by case definition: 0.89% (CDC-1994), 0.17% (Holmes), and 1.41% (Oxford criteria).
A recent meta-analysis reported higher ME/CFS prevalence in females (1.36%) than males (0.86%), consistent with the present study's sex disparity.

A UK survey of hospital-based medical doctors found low ME/CFS training and confidence: only 27% had received formal ME/CFS training, 89% did not know how to diagnose it, 93% did not feel confident managing these patients, and 82% considered ME/CFS to be partly or entirely a psychological condition.
A US-based study reported a much higher female-to-male prevalence ratio for ME/CFS of 11.2:1.0.

The only previous Australian ME/CFS prevalence study (1990/1993) reported a higher rate for the 40-49 year age group (110 per 100,000) using the Australian case definition, which the current authors note no longer reflects current understanding of the condition.

Among 279 long COVID patients evaluated at a COVID-19 aftercare clinic, 16.8% (47 patients) met all three standardized ME/CFS diagnostic criteria (Fukuda, CCC, IOM) after face-to-face physician examination and exclusion of other diseases.
Acute-phase hospitalization was significantly more frequent among patients who later met ME/CFS criteria than in those who did not (44.7% vs. 27.6%).
A significantly larger proportion of ME/CFS patients had moderate-to-severe acute COVID-19 compared with non-ME/CFS patients.
Patients meeting ME/CFS criteria had a significantly longer duration from COVID-19 onset to first clinic visit than non-ME/CFS patients.
Fatigue Assessment Scale (FAS) scores were significantly higher in ME/CFS patients compared to non-ME/CFS long COVID patients.
Quality of life, measured by EQ-5D and EQ-VAS, was significantly lower in ME/CFS patients than in non-ME/CFS long COVID patients.
Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS) scores were significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than in non-ME/CFS patients, suggesting a depressive mood already present at the first visit.

The sex ratio in the ME/CFS group derived from long COVID (48.9% male, 51.1% female) was approximately 1:1, notably different from previously reported ME/CFS epidemiology where 70-80% of patients are female.

General fatigue and post-exertional malaise were the most frequent symptoms in ME/CFS patients (89.4%) versus non-ME/CFS patients (44.8%), while dysosmia, dysgeusia and hair loss were less frequent in ME/CFS patients.
Dizziness was the symptom most predictive of ME/CFS status; 44% of long COVID patients complaining of dizziness met ME/CFS criteria, higher than for other symptoms.

Vital signs and heart rate/orthostatic parameters at first visit showed no statistically significant differences between ME/CFS and non-ME/CFS patients, despite ME/CFS criteria including orthostatic dysregulation.
COVID-19 vaccination status (incomplete vs. at least two doses) did not significantly differ between ME/CFS and non-ME/CFS groups.
A genotyping study of 426 ME/CFS patients versus 4511 healthy controls identified HLA-C*07:04 as a risk allele for ME/CFS.
The same 426 vs 4511 HLA study identified HLA-DQB1*03:03 as a Class II risk allele for ME/CFS.
HLA-B*08:01, part of the C*07:01-B*08:01-DRB1*03:01-DQB1*02:01 haplotype, was found less prevalent among ME/CFS patients than controls and is proposed as a protective allele.

Six HLA Class II alleles were less prevalent in veterans with Gulf War Illness compared to healthy Gulf War veterans, suggesting these alleles confer protection, and lower allele frequency correlated with greater GWI symptom severity.
In vitro N2A neuroblastoma apoptosis induced by GWI patient serum correlated strongly and significantly with the severity of patients' neurocognitive-mood symptoms.

Adding antibody against the anthrax vaccine antigen PA63 to GWI patient serum substantially reduced (but did not fully eliminate) serum-induced apoptosis in N2A neuroblastoma cultures from 15 GWI patients.
GWI patient serum reduced cell spreading and induced apoptosis in N2A cultures, and these harmful effects were prevented by concomitant addition of serum from healthy Gulf War veterans.

Addition of pooled human IgG to N2A cultures reduced but did not fully eliminate the apoptosis induced by GWI serum, likely because pooled IgG lacks antibodies against rare vaccine antigens (anthrax, botulinum toxin, plague).

Intratracheal instillation of the SARS-CoV-2 spike S1 subunit alone caused COVID-19-like lung injury (weight loss, elevated BALF white cells and protein, cytokine upregulation, histological lung damage) in K18-hACE2 transgenic mice, whereas saline or the S2 subunit did not.
Elevated C-reactive protein, a marker of inflammation, is associated with cortical thinning, hippocampal atrophy, and decreased white matter integrity in veterans with Gulf War Illness.

One-quarter of veterans with Gulf War Illness are positive for lupus anticoagulant, an autoantibody linked to blood clot formation, and LAC-positivity is associated with significant brain atrophy in these veterans.
Presence of the GWI-protective HLA allele DRB1*13:02 was shown to protect against subcortical brain atrophy in Gulf War Illness.
An early clinical attempt to treat ME/CFS with pooled human IgG did not produce a beneficial effect.
Women are more frequently or more severely affected than men across all three conditions reviewed: long-COVID-19, ME/CFS, and Gulf War Illness.
SARS-CoV-2 RNA or protein has been found to persist in the olfactory mucosa for at least 6 months after infection.
SARS-CoV-2 RNA was found to persist in various organs for up to 230 days post-infection.
The SARS-CoV-2 antigen has been detected in cerebrospinal fluid, shown to persist, and is associated with adverse clinical outcomes in long-COVID.

A multisystem syndrome resembling Gulf War Illness has been reported in spouses of GWI veterans, at a prevalence independent of the veteran's deployment status, raising the possibility of persistent-antigen transmissibility.
Brainstem structural/functional abnormalities are among the most consistently documented brain anomalies in ME/CFS.
Intestinal flora dysbiosis is proposed to contribute to the occurrence and development of chronic fatigue syndrome via inflammatory response and metabolic disturbance.

Acupuncture and moxibustion are proposed to exert anti-fatigue effects in CFS by modulating intestinal flora diversity/quantity, improving intestinal barrier function, and regulating brain-gut peptides.

A regression model combining the paracellular/transcellular molecule ratio, pro-inflammatory cytokines, IgM to zonulin, and IgA to tryptophan catabolites (all positively) plus IgM to oxidative specific epitopes (inversely) explained 42.3% of the variance in total fibromyalgia/chronic fatigue symptom score.
IgM responses to zonulin were positively associated with fibromyalgia/chronic-fatigue symptom severity, indicating increased zonulin-related paracellular pathway disruption.
IgA levels directed against tryptophan catabolites were positively associated with fibromyalgia/chronic fatigue symptom severity, implicating TRYCAT pathway induction.
Serum pro-inflammatory cytokines were positively associated with fibromyalgia/chronic fatigue symptom severity, consistent with immune activation driving physiosomatic symptoms.
Lower natural IgM responses to oxidative specific epitopes were inversely associated with (i.e., predicted higher) fibromyalgia/chronic fatigue symptom severity.
The total fibromyalgia/chronic fatigue (FF) symptom score correlated highly significantly with the general cognitive decline index (G-CoDe) in schizophrenia patients.
The total FF symptom score correlated highly significantly with the schizophrenia symptomatome (overall symptom burden).
The total FF symptom score correlated highly significantly (inversely) with the quality-of-life phenomenome in schizophrenia patients.
The total FF symptom score correlated highly significantly with the behavioral-cognitive-physical-psychosocial (BCPS)-worsening index.

The authors conclude that fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue-like symptoms form a common core with cognitive decline, symptomatome, and quality-of-life phenomenome, indicating they are part of the overall phenome of schizophrenia and its BCPS-worsening.
Combined acupuncture plus moxibustion markedly improved overall treatment response rate compared with no-treatment control.
Moxibustion alone improved overall treatment response rate compared with no-treatment control, the most effective single therapy of those assessed for this outcome.
Acupuncture alone improved overall treatment response rate compared with no-treatment control.
Western medicine (e.g., vitamin C, oryzanol) showed a smaller but still significant improvement in overall response rate versus no-treatment control compared with TCM therapies.
Acupuncture plus moxibustion produced the greatest improvement in FS-14 total fatigue score versus no-treatment control among network meta-analysis comparisons.
Western medicine did not show a statistically significant improvement in FS-14 total score compared with no-treatment control.
Traditional Chinese herbal medicine alone did not show a statistically significant improvement in FS-14 total score compared with no-treatment control.
Acupuncture plus moxibustion improved FS-14 physical subscore compared with no-treatment control.
Western medicine did not significantly improve FS-14 physical subscore versus no-treatment control.
Acupuncture plus moxibustion improved FS-14 mental subscore compared with no-treatment control, but no clear distinction was found among TCM methods for mental symptom improvement.
Rank probability analysis identified moxibustion combined with traditional Chinese herbal medicine as the top-ranked therapy for overall response rate, followed by acupuncture plus moxibustion.
Adverse reactions related to acupuncture (hematoma, fainting) and moxibustion (minor scalds) were rare, self-resolving within a week, with low overall incidence.

Moxibustion is proposed to exert therapeutic effects in CFS via upregulation of hippocampal progranulin (PGRN), which has neurotrophic, neurogenic, and anti-inflammatory effects and may modulate the HPA axis.

Neuroinflammation involving microglial activation and cytokine production, leading to HPA axis and mitochondrial dysfunction, is proposed as a key mechanism in CFS pathogenesis, and acupuncture stimulation may inhibit microglial activation and reduce neuroinflammation.
The efficacy of moxibustion on CFS may also relate to regulation of intestinal (gut) flora balance, per cited prior work.

Subgroup analysis found that age, gender, disease course, treatment duration, and acupoint selection principle had no significant impact on treatment efficacy or FS-14 score change, except that syndrome-differentiation-based acupoint selection appeared more effective than fixed points, and patients ≤40 years old appeared to respond better.
Patients supplemented with 1-MNA showed a significantly greater mean increase in 6-minute walk test distance after one month compared with patients not receiving supplementation.
Within the 1-MNA group, 6MWT distance significantly increased from baseline to 1 month of supplementation.
In the non-supplemented group, 6MWT distance increased slightly from baseline to 1 month but the change did not reach statistical significance.
A significantly greater proportion of 1-MNA-supplemented patients improved their 6MWT distance compared with unsupplemented patients.
Both groups reported an increase (worsening) in FSS fatigue scores after one month, with no significant between-group difference in FSS score itself.
After one month, significantly fewer 1-MNA-supplemented patients had severe fatigue (FSS≥4) compared with unsupplemented patients.
At baseline (Phase 0), the two randomized groups did not differ significantly in age, BMI, oxygen saturation, 6MWT distance, dyspnea, or FSS fatigue score.
Post-COVID-19 patients in this cohort had FSS fatigue scores much higher than the healthy population and comparable to patients with multiple sclerosis or after stroke.

1-MNA is proposed to act through anti-inflammatory, anti-thrombotic, endothelial nitric oxide/prostacyclin-enhancing, and SIRT1-dependent mitohormetic mechanisms that could underlie its benefit for post-COVID-19 fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance.

After 12 weeks of PLWNT Qigong intervention, patients showed significantly enhanced amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF) in the right superior frontal gyrus compared with the control (CBT) group.
After PLWNT intervention, patients showed significantly enhanced ALFF in the left median cingulate gyrus compared with the control group.
The PLWNT group showed decreased ALFF value in the left middle occipital gyrus compared with the control group.
The PLWNT group showed decreased ALFF value in the left middle temporal gyrus compared with the control group.
Whole-brain functional connectivity analysis showed enhanced connectivity between the median cingulate gyrus and middle temporal gyrus in the PLWNT group compared with controls.
Functional connectivity between the left and right middle occipital gyrus was enhanced in the PLWNT group compared with controls.
MFI-20 fatigue severity scores improved after PLWNT intervention compared with pre-intervention/control values.
SF-36 quality-of-life scores improved after PLWNT intervention compared with pre-intervention/control values.
SF-36 quality-of-life scores correlated positively with neuronal activity (ALFF) in the left middle occipital gyrus, superior frontal gyrus, and median cingulate gyrus.
MFI-20 fatigue scores correlated negatively with neuronal activity (ALFF) in the superior frontal gyrus and median cingulate gyrus.
Two adverse events were reported during the study (hypoglycemia from fasting and mild discomfort from improper abdominal massage), both judged unrelated or unlikely related to the Qigong exercise.
All participants with hEDS/HSD reported gastrointestinal symptoms.
Participants with hEDS/HSD had significantly lower femoral bone mineral density Z-scores compared to healthy controls.
Participants with hEDS/HSD had significantly lower lumbar spine bone mineral density Z-scores compared to healthy controls.
There was no significant difference in body composition (body fat percentage and lean body mass) between hEDS/HSD participants and healthy controls.
There was no significant difference in caloric intake between hEDS/HSD participants and healthy controls, though both groups showed caloric deficits.
Participants with hEDS/HSD consumed significantly less protein than healthy controls.
Participants with hEDS/HSD consumed significantly more carbohydrates than healthy controls.
There was no significant difference in grip strength between hEDS/HSD participants and healthy controls.
In patients with hypermobile EDS, inspiratory capacity decreased between the 30% and 80% peak power output workloads during a constant load exercise test, consistent with dynamic hyperinflation.
End-expiratory lung volume increased from 30% to 80% peak power output, further supporting dynamic hyperinflation during exercise in hEDS patients.
Half of the hEDS patients exhibited expiratory flow limitation during exercise, indicating mechanical ventilatory constraint.
The authors conclude that mechanical ventilatory constraints occur during exercise in hEDS patients and may contribute to respiratory symptoms such as exertional dyspnea and breathing difficulties.
Next-generation sequencing identified 117 gene variants in 76 of 100 consecutive patients referred for a suspected heritable connective tissue disorder.
Ten gene variants were classified as pathogenic or likely pathogenic and were identified in nine of the 100 patients.

The remaining variants were classified as of unknown clinical significance, with 36 variants meeting three of four pathogenicity criteria (defined as 'potentially pathogenic' by the study) identified in 33 patients.
Gene variants affecting collagen-related proteins were the most frequently identified variant category in this connective tissue disorder cohort.
ZNF469 was among the most frequently identified variant-containing genes in the cohort of patients referred for connective tissue disorder testing.
ADAMTSL2 was among the most frequently identified variant-containing genes in the cohort of patients referred for connective tissue disorder testing.
Joint hypermobility was the most frequently observed clinical finding among patients referred for a connective tissue disorder in this cohort.
Among patients referred for a heritable connective tissue disorder who displayed distinct clinical features, 76% had an identified gene variant on NGS testing.
Genetic testing identified a novel, likely pathogenic COL3A1 variant (c.2555G>T, p.(Gly852Val)) confirming a diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (vEDS) in the patient.
The patient developed spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) of the obtuse marginal branch of the left circumflex artery, causing acute coronary syndrome, in the setting of underlying vEDS.

Posteromedial papillary muscle rupture with severe mitral regurgitation occurred, most likely caused by the dissected obtuse marginal coronary branch, representing an ischemic complication of SCAD in a patient with vEDS.

During cardiac surgery, marked tissue fragility attributable to vEDS caused spontaneous rupture of the right atrium upon cannulation and rupture of the brachiocephalic vein at the end of the procedure, complicating surgical management.

The literature and the authors note that celiprolol, a cardioselective β1 blocker with vasodilatory effect, may reduce the frequency of arterial events in vEDS, and the patient was started on it postoperatively with uneventful follow-up.
In addition to the coronary dissection, the patient had a spontaneous dissection of the right renal artery, illustrating multi-site arterial dissection consistent with underlying vEDS.

The patient's past medical history included fibromyalgia along with longstanding joint and muscle pain and easy bruising, symptoms later recognized in retrospect as part of her connective tissue disorder (vEDS) presentation.

SCAD is an underrecognized but important cause of acute coronary syndrome, estimated to account for 1% to 4% of all ACS cases and up to 35% of ACS in women aged 50 or younger, with connective tissue disorders such as vEDS, Marfan syndrome, and Loeys-Dietz syndrome implicated as rare risk factors underlying no more than 5% of cases.

Compared with having one or fewer shoulder diagnoses, participants with two clinical shoulder diagnoses (anterior instability, multidirectional instability, and/or localised shoulder hypermobility) did not have significantly worse shoulder function.
Compared with having one or fewer shoulder diagnoses, participants with two clinical shoulder diagnoses did not have significantly worse pain intensity.
Compared with having one or fewer shoulder diagnoses, participants with three clinical shoulder diagnoses did not have significantly worse shoulder function or pain.
The number of positive clinical shoulder tests (out of 0-10) was not significantly associated with shoulder function as measured by WOSI.
The number of positive clinical shoulder tests was not significantly associated with pain intensity as measured by NPRS.
Plantar arch index (PAI) was not correlated with the Beighton hypermobility score in preschool children.
PAI showed no significant correlation with the newly developed thumb-to-forearm laxity grading test.
PAI showed no significant correlation with the newly developed thumb-thrust laxity grading test.
Logistic regression showed no significant association between the Beighton score and the incidence of flexible flatfoot.
Logistic regression showed no significant association between thumb-to-forearm grade and the incidence of flexible flatfoot.
Logistic regression showed no significant association between thumb-thrust grade and the incidence of flexible flatfoot.
PAI (plantar arch index, a measure of flatfoot severity) was negatively correlated with age, indicating flatter feet in younger preschool children.
PAI was negatively correlated with body weight in preschool children.
Male sex was significantly associated with higher incidence of flexible flatfoot, with boys roughly twice as likely as girls to have flatfoot.
Older age was associated with lower odds of flexible flatfoot.
Greater height was associated with lower odds of flexible flatfoot.
Higher weight was associated with lower odds of flexible flatfoot.
A cited prior study by Lin et al found that a joint laxity score was significantly related to flatfoot in preschool children.
A cited prior study by El et al in 579 primary school children found the Beighton hypermobility score was significantly related to flatfoot.
A cited prior study by Corten et al found that the 'hands on floor' (HOF) maneuver did not add additional diagnostic value to the Beighton score in children of Black African and mixed ancestry.

A cited prior study found that children with delayed motor development had a 1.5-fold higher risk of flatfoot compared with normal children, suggesting a role for muscular/motor development in arch formation.
This case report describes what the authors state is the first documented association of camptodactyly with benign joint hypermobility syndrome.
The patient scored 6 on the Beighton hypermobility score, reflecting significant hyperextensibility at both elbows, knees, and metacarpophalangeal joints.

The patient fulfilled the revised Brighton's criteria for benign joint hypermobility syndrome, meeting one major criterion (polyarthralgia in ≥4 joints lasting >3 months) and two minor criteria (Beighton score of 6 and striae).
The patient scored 3 out of 5 on a five-point hypermobility screening questionnaire, a result reported to be over 90% specific for benign joint hypermobility syndrome.
Camptodactyly occurs unilaterally in about 66% of cases and bilaterally in 33%, is very rarely seen in children (1%), and may be inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.
Benign joint hypermobility syndrome has an estimated global prevalence of approximately 3%.
Benign joint hypermobility syndrome shows a strong genetic association consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.

Patients with benign joint hypermobility syndrome are prone to developing fatigue, headache, orthostatic hypotension, anxiety, hernias, functional gastrointestinal disturbances, vasovagal syncope, dysautonomia, and genitourinary symptoms.
Topical corticosteroids were prescribed for the patient's psoriasiform eczema and resulted in a good clinical response.
A multidisciplinary management approach (rheumatology, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, podiatry, counseling) improved the patient's functional capacity and mental wellbeing.

Prolotherapy, involving injection of irritants such as dextrose into joints, is described as inducing a reparative inflammatory cascade that increases extracellular matrix/collagen strength and may slow degenerative changes and delay osteoarthritis in joint hypermobility syndrome.

A prior case report from Southern Turkey described camptodactyly-arthropathy-coxa vara-pericarditis syndrome, caused by mutation in the proteoglycan 4 (PRG4) gene, that mimicked juvenile idiopathic arthritis and was inappropriately treated.
A reported case of Blau syndrome, caused by mutation in the NOD2 gene, presented with camptodactyly and bilateral intermediate uveitis and responded well to subcutaneous adalimumab.

Graded stretching exercises were reported in prior literature to restore proximal interphalangeal joint mobility and produce radiographic remodeling of the proximal phalangeal head in infantile-type camptodactyly.
Surgical correction of camptodactyly is generally reserved for patients with preoperative proximal interphalangeal joint contracture greater than 60 degrees.
The patient's arm span to height ratio was 0.8 and thumb and wrist signs were negative, findings used to help clinically exclude Marfan syndrome.
FM patients showed significantly higher Dizziness Handicap Inventory (DHI) and Situational Vertigo Questionnaire (SVQ) scores than healthy controls, indicating greater vestibular symptom burden.

Only 5.6% of FM patients had been diagnosed for vestibular problems by a specialist despite the high self-reported handicap, and most were diagnosed by rheumatologists (67.5%) rather than neurologists (3.2%).
PainDETECT questionnaire scores in FM patients indicated a sharp prevalence of neuropathic or central pain component.
DHI overall scores correlated positively with PD-Q scores and with pain intensity in the last week among FM patients.
SVQ scores (visual vertigo/VID) correlated positively with PD-Q scores and pain intensity in the last week among FM patients.
DHI and SVQ scores correlated with various pain type subscales (e.g., pressure pain, numbness, tingling, burning) in FM patients.
The distribution of FM patients across DHI handicap severity levels was significantly non-random, with the majority classified as having severe dizziness handicap.
DHI handicap levels correlated with diagnosis delay and with PD-Q neuropathic pain scores.

DHI and SVQ scores were significantly associated with abnormal CBA-H cognitive/behavioral scale results (anxiety, depression, psychological distress, fear, well-being, neuroticism) and with presence of non-pain symptoms in FM patients.
The number of non-pain symptoms reported by FM patients correlated positively with both DHI and SVQ scores.

Nearly half of FM participants reported childhood/adolescence trauma (physical, emotional, sexual abuse, neglect, parental loss, economic hardship), and DHI/SVQ scores negatively correlated with self-rated quality of childhood and adolescence.

Cluster analysis of DHI data identified three distinct FM patient subgroups (G1, G2, G3) differing significantly in overall DHI scores and in dizziness, migraine, and depression severity, with G1 showing the highest handicap.

Factor analysis of DHI items in FM patients revealed a three-factor structure that did not correspond to the conventional Emotional/Functional/Physical components of the DHI, distinguishing FM dizziness from typical vestibular patient patterns.
Unlike the DHI, SVQ data did not yield a distinct multi-cluster or multi-factor structure in FM patients, with most variability explained by a single factor.

A study comparing D2T-RA to non-D2T-RA patients found coexistent fibromyalgia, along with limited drug options, comorbidities, and poor coping mechanisms, to be among the factors associated with the difficult-to-treat state.

The same cohort study identified a distinct subgroup of D2T-RA patients characterised by 'pain syndromes and obesity', separate from non-adherent/dissatisfied patients and those with 'true refractory RA'.
Secondary fibromyalgia and osteoarthritis can overestimate patient global health scores and tender joint count assessments in RA, complicating accurate evaluation of disease activity.
EULAR points to consider highlight obesity and fibromyalgia as prevalent comorbid conditions in RA that must be accounted for when assessing disease activity and progression to difficult-to-treat RA.

For D2T-RA patients where residual pain and secondary fibromyalgia (rather than active inflammation) are the key drivers, EULAR points to consider recommend education, self-management and psychological interventions to improve shared decision-making, symptom profile, and coping.

A Netherlands survey found that patients with difficult-to-treat RA incurred almost twice the annual direct healthcare utilisation costs of non-D2T RA patients, plus higher indirect costs from informal care and lost work productivity.
In a British Society for Rheumatology Biologics Register cohort of 13,502 RA patients, 6% received more than three different bDMARDs, with a median time to the third bDMARD of 8 years.

Within the same registry, RA patients diagnosed from 2011 onward were 15 times more likely to be identified as refractory, which the authors suggest may reflect stronger treat-to-target practice and drug availability rather than truly increased disease refractoriness.

The ORAL Surveillance post-authorisation safety trial found that in a CV-disease-enriched RA population, tofacitinib was not non-inferior to TNF inhibitor therapy for the co-primary endpoints of major adverse cardiovascular events and malignancy.

For third/fourth line targeted therapy, tocilizumab and JAK inhibitors have shown greater efficacy than placebo, whereas other bDMARDs (TNF inhibitors, abatacept, rituximab) lack such evidence in this setting.
Duloxetine is approved not only for major depressive disorder but also for diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia, and generalized anxiety disorder.
Patients with hepatic cirrhosis show a three-fold increase in duloxetine AUC and half-life compared with healthy individuals, raising hepatotoxicity risk in a drug also used for fibromyalgia.

Duloxetine caused dose- and time-dependent cytotoxicity in both enhanced hepatic spheroids (EHS) and 2D HepaRG cultures, with EHS showing greater sensitivity at lower concentrations and with repeated dosing.
CYP2D6 and CYP1A2 enzyme activities were substantially higher in EHS than in 2D culture, correlating with greater sensitivity of EHS cells to duloxetine.

Co-treatment with CYP2D6-specific inhibitor quinidine, CYP1A2-specific inhibitor alpha-naphthoflavone, or broad-spectrum CYP inhibitors ABT/ATI increased cell viability and reduced duloxetine-induced GSH depletion, supporting CYP-dependent bioactivation of duloxetine toxicity.
Duloxetine rapidly depleted glutathione even at the lowest tested dose (0.01 mM) and later generated reactive oxygen species, similar to the positive control GSH-depleting agent diethyl maleate.
The antioxidant NAC effectively reduced duloxetine-induced cytotoxicity and increased IC50, restoring GSH and ROS levels close to control.
Duloxetine treatment upregulated antioxidant/stress-response genes SOD, MnSOD, HSP70 and FOXO3, indicating redox disorder, and this upregulation was reduced by NAC co-treatment.

High-content imaging showed dose-dependent decreases in mitochondrial membrane potential and bile canalicular CMFDA intensity, increased caspase-3/7 apoptosis signal, and increased steatosis (Nile Red) with duloxetine, with oxidative stress showing the largest magnitude change of all parameters measured.
Duloxetine caused a 66% reduction in mitochondrial DNA content (cytb) and significant downregulation of mtDNA-encoded transcripts COX1 and ND5.

Duloxetine reduced basal OCR to near zero after 200 minutes and significantly decreased ATP production and maximal respiratory capacity, indicating inhibition of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation; NAC co-treatment prevented the basal OCR collapse.

Duloxetine increased mitochondrial membrane depolarization, with the red/green fluorescence ratio decreasing in 79.23±5.06% of cells by flow cytometry, indicating increased susceptibility to apoptosis.
Duloxetine induced early apoptosis in 46.52±2.22% of cells (vs 1.81±0.40% control) and increased sub-G1 fraction to 38.7±5.7%, which was reduced to 9.3±1.5% by NAC co-treatment.

S-071031B, a benzodioxole-substituted analog of duloxetine, showed no significant change in GSH/ROS content or live/dead ratio compared to control, and no cytotoxicity under single or repeated dosing, unlike duloxetine.

Pre-injuring EHS cells with LPS, H2O2, CCl4, or ethanol exacerbated duloxetine-induced cell damage but did not exacerbate S-071031B-induced damage, mirroring the clinical risk in patients with pre-existing liver disease.

In CCl4 pre-injured rats, duloxetine co-treatment increased plasma LDH, ALT, AST and ALP and worsened liver histopathology, whereas S-071031B did not cause these alterations or serious hepatotoxicity.
Duloxetine dramatically increased lipid droplet area/intensity (Nile Red) and fatty acid uptake (BODIPY) in EHS cells, whereas S-071031B did not disturb normal fatty acid transport.

Duloxetine increased mRNA of lipid synthesis genes (PDK4, ACSL4, AGPAT1, SLC2A4, ACLY, FADS2, ELOVL1) while decreasing ApoB expression, impairing VLDL-mediated lipid removal and driving steatosis, changes not seen with S-071031B.
Duloxetine abnormally elevated CYP2E1 expression and increased malondialdehyde (MDA)-associated lipid peroxidation, feeding back into a vicious cycle of ROS generation.

Duloxetine damaged bile canalicular structure and, in combination with a physiological bile acid mixture, showed cholestatic risk (CIx=0.653 single dose, 0.383 repeated dose), whereas S-071031B plus bile acids showed no meaningful synergistic toxicity (CIx=0.975/0.987).
Duloxetine decreased cellular ATP content and downregulated the bile transporters BSEP, MDR1, NTCP and OATP2B1, contributing to cholestasis, with reduced changes when switched to S-071031B.

The naphthyl ring of duloxetine is proposed as the key toxicophore, bioactivated by CYP2D6/CYP1A2 and attacked by GSH to form adducts, which is avoided by replacement with a benzodioxole group in S-071031B.
Global health status (QLQ-C30) was markedly lower in both MCAS and SM patients compared to healthy controls, with very large effect sizes.
All five EORTC QLQ-C30 functional scales (physical, role, emotional, cognitive, social) were significantly reduced in both MCAS and SM patients compared to healthy controls.
There was no significant difference in global health status between MCAS and SM patients, contradicting the hypothesis that SM would show lower HRQOL.
Role function impairment was significantly greater in MCAS patients than in SM patients, indicating a higher disease impact on daily life and work.

All EORTC QLQ-C30 symptom scales (fatigue, nausea/vomiting, pain, dyspnea, insomnia, appetite loss, constipation, diarrhea, financial difficulties) were significantly higher (worse) in both MCAS and SM compared to controls.
Fatigue was significantly more pronounced in MCAS patients than in SM patients, contrary to the study's hypothesis that SM would show greater fatigue.
MCAS patients reported significantly lower disease-related health literacy (INFO-25 Global Score) compared to SM patients.
Several INFO-25 subscales (INFODIS, INFOMEDT, INFOTREAT, INFOHELP, SATINFO, OVERHELP) were significantly lower in MCAS versus SM, with strong effect sizes for INFODIS and INFOTREAT.
Linear regression showed that the INFO-25 Global Score (disease-related health literacy) significantly predicted global health status/QoL (QLQ-C30) in both MCAS and SM patients.
Almost all patients (99%) with MCAS or SM wanted to receive more information about their disease from physicians, while only one SM patient wanted less information.
The paper notes that the KIT D816V point mutation is the most frequently described cause of systemic mastocytosis, while this activating mutation is characteristically absent in MCAS.
Mast cells release excessive inflammatory mediators such as histamine, heparin, cytokines, prostaglandins and leukotrienes in response to triggers in mast cell activation syndrome.
Diagnostic biomarkers for MCAS, including urinary N-methyl histamine and prostaglandins, are difficult to assess owing to rapid degradation, whereas serum tryptase is stable and used in the UK.

Self-management techniques, medications and trigger avoidance may improve quality of life in MCAS, with treatments including mast cell mediator blockers, mast cell stabilisers and anti-inflammatory agents.

It is theorised that COVID-19 infection could exaggerate pre-existing undiagnosed mast cell activation syndrome or activate normal mast cells owing to persistence of viral particles, contributing to long COVID symptoms.

MCAS and long COVID share clinical features including multiple overlapping symptoms, a relapse-remission cycle, and improvement with similar treatments, though long COVID may also be attributable to other conditions besides mast cell disorders.
Substance P produced a concentration-dependent calcium mobilization response in HEK cells expressing the neurokinin-1 receptor with an EC50 of 0.4 nM.

The C-terminally truncated SP metabolites SP(1-9)-COOH and SP(1-7)-COOH failed to significantly activate NK1R even at high concentrations, confirming that the SP C-terminus is essential for NK1R activation.

Substance P stimulated concentration-dependent Ca2+ mobilization in HEK293 cells transiently transfected with MRGPRX2, though at much higher concentrations than required for NK1R activation, with no response in mock-transfected cells.
SP(1-9)-COOH, but not SP(1-7)-COOH, retained agonist activity at MRGPRX2 in transfected HEK cells, though with reduced potency compared to intact SP.
SP triggered both Ca2+ mobilization and degranulation in the human LAD2 mast cell line, with EC50 values of 1.8 μM and 5.9 μM respectively.
SP(1-9)-COOH stimulated both Ca2+ mobilization and degranulation in LAD2 mast cells, with approximately 10-fold lower potency than full-length SP, while SP(1-7)-COOH failed to activate the cells.

In CRISPR-generated MRGPRX2 knockdown LAD2 cells, both Ca2+ mobilization and degranulation responses to SP, SP(1-9)-COOH, and compound 48/80 were significantly diminished compared to wild-type cells, while IgE-dependent pathway responses were unaffected.

The selective NK1R antagonist GR205171 blocked SP-induced Ca2+ mobilization in NK1R-transfected HEK cells but had no effect on SP- or SP(1-9)-COOH-induced Ca2+ mobilization in LAD2 mast cells, confirming these responses are NK1R-independent and mediated by MRGPRX2.
Both SP and SP(1-9)-COOH produced concentration-dependent CCL2 cytokine release from LAD2 mast cells, whereas SP(1-7)-COOH-mediated CCL2 release was minimal and comparable to spontaneous release.

C-terminal amidation of SP(1-9) enhanced its potency at MRGPRX2 (measured by both Ca2+ mobilization and degranulation) compared to the carboxylated form, though it remained less potent than full-length SP.

Unlike SP(1-7)-COOH, the C-terminally amidated SP(1-7)-NH2 variant was able to stimulate moderate Ca2+ mobilization and a weak degranulation response in LAD2 cells, showing a biased agonism profile similar to that described for the small molecule MRGPRX2 activator rocuronium.
6-OAP at concentrations up to 10 µM did not significantly affect the viability of LAD2 or HCMC mast cells.
6-OAP dose-dependently suppressed anti-IgE-induced histamine release (degranulation) in both LAD2 and HCMC mast cells.
6-OAP dose-dependently inhibited anti-IgE-induced IL-8 release in both LAD2 and HCMC.
6-OAP dose-dependently down-regulated anti-IgE-induced TNF-α release in both LAD2 and HCMC.
6-OAP significantly reduced anti-IgE-induced GM-CSF release from HCMC.
6-OAP significantly reduced anti-IgE-induced VEGF release from HCMC.
6-OAP significantly reduced anti-IgE-induced CCL2 release from HCMC.
