A high proportion (72.4%) of CFS patients presented with generalized worry at baseline assessment.
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy produced a significant, sustained reduction in generalized worry from baseline to discharge and follow-up.
Patients classified as severe baseline worriers had greater overall fatigue scores than mild worriers across time-points.
Severe baseline worriers showed worse overall work and social adjustment than mild worriers across time-points.
Avoidance behavior was found to mediate the relationship between generalized worry and work and social adjustment.

Nineteen percent of the DIOS cohort (90/484) met diagnostic criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome, i.e. post-infective fatigue syndrome (PIFS), at 6 months following acute EBV, RRV, or Q fever infection.
Each one-unit increase in baseline illness severity principal component score was associated with 2.4-fold higher odds of developing PIFS at 6 months.

Higher baseline overall illness severity was associated with delayed recovery from illness (Cox hazard ratio 0.39, indicating lower likelihood of recovery at any timepoint per unit increase in severity).
Higher baseline mood disturbance severity was associated with delayed recovery from mood disturbance (Cox hazard ratio 0.36).
Ross River virus infection was associated with greater likelihood of prolonged illness at 6 months compared to EBV infection, even after adjusting for age, sex, serology and NPY haplotype.
Female sex, along with greater baseline mood disturbance, was independently associated with prolonged (delayed recovery) mood disturbance after acute infection.
Females reported significantly greater overall illness severity than males during the acute phase of infection.
Older age was independently associated with lower mood disturbance severity during the acute infection, an unexpected finding contrary to typical age-related depression/anxiety risk.

NPY gene haplotypes/diplotypes, including the previously reported low-NPY-producing high-risk HB1/HB1 diplotype, were not associated with overall illness severity or mood disturbance during acute infection.
NPY haplotypes/diplotypes were not associated with prolonged overall illness, prolonged mood disturbance, or PIFS caseness at follow-up.

The Brief Disability Questionnaire (BDQ) total disability score was moderately correlated with the baseline overall illness severity principal component score, functionally validating the severity measure.
The mood disturbance principal component score was strongly correlated with the POMS depression and anxiety subscales, validating the mood disturbance measure.
Baseline illness severity and mood disturbance PC scores were strongly correlated, reflecting mood disturbance as an intrinsic component of the acute sickness response.

Individuals with serologically unconfirmed acute infection had comparable illness severity indices and prolonged illness course, including PIFS rates, to those with confirmed EBV, RRV or Q fever infection.
The Ross River virus infection group showed greater severity of musculoskeletal pain, consistent with the typical arthralgia/arthritis presentation of RRV disease.

Recovery trajectories diverged sharply by baseline severity quartile: by day 100, 86% of 'mild' illness-severity subjects had recovered versus only 23% of 'severe' subjects, and 99% of 'mild' mood-disturbance subjects had recovered versus 31% of 'severe' subjects.
Functional impairment (activity cutback and social functioning impact) increased progressively across illness-severity and mood-disturbance severity quartiles from mild to severe.
Women with BJHS had significantly lower femoral neck, total femoral, and trochanteric bone mineral density than controls and were 1.8 times more likely to have low bone mass.
Mishra et al. found no statistically significant difference in lumbar or femoral neck BMD between BJHS patients and normal population, though BMD trended poorer in those under 45 years old.
Cohorts of EDS patients (multiple types combined) consistently showed poorer femoral neck BMD than healthy controls across several studies.
Mazziotti et al. found that EDS-HT patients had poorer femoral neck BMD compared to both classical EDS and control subjects, with no lumbar spine differences.
Peripheral fracture incidence in EDS populations (Types I, II, III) has been reported to be up to 10 times greater than in healthy controls, with vertebral fractures also elevated.

Banica et al. found hEDS/HSD patients had smaller cortical bone area, lower cortical bone mineral content, smaller cortical thickness, decreased strength strain index in the lower leg, and higher major fracture incidence, though no differences in trabecular/cortical volumetric BMD or lumbar/whole-body BMD were found.
Multiple studies consistently document hEDS/EDS Type III/EDS-HT patients to have lower muscular strength, endurance, and functional performance compared to healthy controls.
Rombaut et al. (2012) reported no differences in lower leg muscle cross-sectional area between EDS-HT cases and healthy age-matched controls.

Banica et al. (2020) reported hEDS/HSD patients had smaller lower leg muscle cross-sectional area than controls even after adjusting for height, weight, and physical activity, contradicting the earlier Rombaut 2012 null finding.
hEDS/HSD individuals show lower passive muscle tension and lower Achilles tendon stiffness compared to healthy controls.

Scheper et al. found muscle weakness significantly impacts activity limitations (sit-to-stand performance and 6-minute walk test) in EDS-HT, with proprioceptive ability confounding only the sit-to-stand relationship.

To and Alexander found individuals with EDS-HT gained muscular strength at a similar rate as controls during a resistance training program, with approximately 40% strength improvement over 12 weeks (lower than the >150% gains reported in healthy untrained young adults).
Females with EDS Type III had significantly poorer knee joint position sense than healthy controls, with higher passive and active absolute angle errors at 30° and 60° flexion.

Women with EDS-HT showed greater postural sway on flat and cushioned surfaces (eyes open/closed) and walked slower with shorter step/stride length than controls; dual-task walking further slowed EDS Type III patients while controls maintained speed.
The vertical component of ground reaction force decreased as self-reported fatigue increased in EDS-HT, suggesting fatigue-related gait pathology.
EDS-HT patients had significantly higher BMI than healthy controls in two separate cohorts.

Banica et al. found hEDS participants had higher BMI, less lean mass, and greater fat mass than controls at baseline; at 8-year follow-up they retained higher BMI and fat mass but no longer had significantly less lean mass.
A questionnaire-based study found 26.6% of hEDS/HSD patients exercised 60-150 minutes per week and 26.2% exercised more than 150 minutes per week, though intensity was not recorded.

In a 1986 case report, a 10-year-old girl with EDS Type III/VI achieved full pain-free shoulder ROM and no further subluxations after 5 weeks of an intensive exercise program, with symptom recurrence when adherence lapsed.

In children/adolescents with BJHS, both a generalized whole-body and a targeted joint-specific exercise program significantly decreased pain, with effects sustained 3 months post-therapy; no significant difference in six-minute shuttle test performance between programs.
In children/adolescents with BJHS undergoing 8 weeks of knee-focused resistance training, thigh strength increased significantly across both extension and hyperextension exercise groups combined.
Resistance training combined with exposure therapy increased knee extension/flexion strength and endurance and produced a 63% decrease in pain scores in adolescents with hEDS/HSD and kinesiophobia.

An 8-week closed kinetic chain exercise program in BJHS participants significantly improved knee proprioception (threshold detection angle) and balance, along with increased hamstring and quadriceps torque.

Sahin et al. found an 8-week supervised proprioceptive exercise program significantly improved knee joint position sense (AAAEV) in BJHS patients compared to both a non-exercising hypermobile control group and baseline.

Daman et al. found a 4-week accelerated proprioceptive training program significantly reduced knee joint position error in BJHS women compared to controls and to baseline, in both weight-bearing and non-weight-bearing positions.
An 8-week lumbar stabilization training program significantly increased trunk flexion, extension, and side bridge muscular endurance in women with BJHS, with no changes in the control group.

A 1986 case report described a 10-year-old girl with EDS Type III/VI who, after 5 weeks of an intensive exercise program, achieved pain-free full shoulder range of motion and no further subluxations, with symptoms returning when adherence lapsed.
A case report of a 14-year-old with EDS-HT and recurrent shoulder dislocations found a two-phase, 6-month exercise program significantly increased shoulder stability and pain-free range of motion.

A 2000 case study of an active JHS patient (a physical therapist) counseled her to decrease activity and terminate calisthenic strengthening exercises without prescribing an alternative strengthening program.

A case study of a 35-year-old EDS-HT triathlete found that 16 weeks of supervised spinal, abdominal, cervical and scapular stabilization exercise resulted in pain-free cervical and lumbar range of motion and increased periscapular and hip strength.

A brief report of two adult women with EDS Type III found both reported less pain following a 6-8 week exercise intervention, though the specific contribution of exercise among multiple treatments was unclear.

In 57 children/adolescents with BJHS, both a generalized whole-body exercise program and a targeted joint-specific program significantly reduced pain (sustained at 3-month follow-up), with no significant difference between programs in six-minute shuttle test performance.

In 25 children/adolescents with BJHS undergoing an 8-week knee resistance program, pain decreased significantly in both extension-based and hyperextension-based training groups, and pooled analysis showed a significant increase in thigh strength.
In adolescents with hEDS/HSD and kinesiophobia, combined resistance training and exposure therapy increased knee extension/flexion strength and endurance and decreased pain scores by 63%.
In 18 BJHS participants, 8 weeks of closed kinetic chain exercise significantly improved knee proprioceptive threshold detection angle, balance (time out of balance), and hamstring/quadriceps torque.

In 40 BJHS participants, an 8-week supervised balance-focused exercise program significantly improved knee joint proprioception (average absolute angle error) compared to a non-exercising hypermobile control group.

In women with BJHS (excluding regular exercisers), a 4-week accelerated combined proprioception program significantly reduced knee joint angle error in both non-weight-bearing and weight-bearing positions compared to controls and baseline.

In 38 women with BJHS randomized to lumbar stabilization training or control, the exercise group showed significant increases in trunk flexion, extension, and side bridge muscular endurance, while the control group showed no change.

In 12 women with EDS-HT/BJHS, a combined physical and cognitive-behavioral inpatient/home training program improved ADL performance and satisfaction in most participants, improved tandem walking, stair climbing, and calf raises, and significantly reduced kinesiophobia.

In female hEDS patients with reduced inspiratory muscle strength, 6 weeks of inspiratory muscle training significantly increased maximal sniff nasal inspiratory pressure and 6-minute walk test distance versus a non-training control group.

In a 16-week personalized resistance training program comparing JHS, GJH, and healthy controls, JHS participants had significantly lower baseline strength and required nearly the full study duration to reach the baseline strength level of the other groups, gaining approximately 40% strength over 12 weeks.

A 12-week self-guided resistance training program in women with GJH (43% hEDS/HSD eligible) produced no significant changes in isometric knee extensor/flexor strength, muscle cross-sectional area, or muscle mass, despite participants doubling their leg press resistance.

A feasibility study of a 16-week heavy shoulder strengthening program in hEDS/HSD patients with shoulder symptoms found high adherence, only minor adverse events, isometric shoulder strength gains of 28-31%, and improvements in joint laxity/instability and proprioception.

The review notes that heavy or maximal training loads (≥60% 1RM for untrained, 80% 1RM for recreationally active individuals) are typically required to maximize strength gains, but such intensities are often deemed inappropriate for the hEDS/HSD population due to pain and instability, and 1RM testing itself is often avoided due to injury risk.

A relatively high proportion of hEDS/HSD patients participate in regularly scheduled physical therapy compared to healthy controls, though many report being treated dismissively or that therapy had a negative or neutral effect.

A questionnaire-based study found that 26.6% of hEDS/HSD patients participated in 60-150 minutes of exercise per week and another 26.2% participated in more than 150 minutes per week, though exercise intensity was not recorded.

A 24-year-old woman with classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and prior developmental dysplasia of the hip treated with Salter osteotomy developed severe hip osteoarthritis with a deformed, flattened femoral head and subchondral cyst.
A UK study in 2019 identified 553 patients diagnosed with EDS in a sample size of 1,298.
Classical EDS is characterized by mutations in COL5A1 or COL5A2.
The vascular subtype of EDS is caused by a COL3A1 mutation affecting type III collagen, making it the most severe form with spontaneous organ rupture and shorter lifespan.
Hip joint hypermobility leads to instability and dysfunction associated with early onset osteoarthritis prompting surgical intervention.
EDS patients have a higher rate of periprosthetic dislocation and shorter implant survival after total hip arthroplasty compared to non-EDS patients.

Orthopedic surgical interventions in EDS patients are associated with operative and postoperative complications, including difficulty making incisions, wound dehiscence, and extensive bleeding from friable vessels.
For acute and chronic pain control in EDS, patients perceive opioids, massage, splints/braces, heat therapy, and avoidance of dangerous activities as the most effective interventions.
Fluoroquinolone antibiotics are associated with an increased risk of aortic rupture and should be avoided in EDS patients per FDA guidance.
Dual-mobility components for total hip arthroplasty are suggested as an alternative approach to reduce the rate of dislocations in EDS patients requiring surgery.
EDS cases were significantly enriched in a combined phase II/III gastroparesis clinical trial cohort compared to the expected population incidence of EDS.
When considering all screened gastroparesis patients (not just enrolled), EDS enrichment remained significant relative to expected population incidence.
The COL5A1 p.G530S variant, a known pathogenic classic EDS variant, was found duplicated among EDS cases and was significantly more frequent in idiopathic than diabetic gastroparesis patients.
The COL5A1 p.G530S variant is classified pathogenic in ClinVar and associated with classic type EDS, with heterozygosity linked to milder/subtle phenotypes and homozygosity linked to classic EDS.
A second recurrent variant, TNXB p.K3015R, was identified twice among the EDS cases with a high predicted deleteriousness score.

Among 13 EDS patients with whole-genome sequencing, 12 carried at least one nonsynonymous or splicing variant in the core EDS gene set (COL1A1, COL1A2, COL3A1, COL5A1, COL5A2, ADAMTS2, FKBP14, PLOD1, TNXB), and 9 of 19 unique variants were confirmed in ClinVar as EDS-associated.

Gene set enrichment analysis showed significantly higher frequency of core EDS gene variants (MAF<5%), particularly COL5A1 and TNXB, and nominally COL1A2, in idiopathic gastroparesis patients compared with sex-, ancestry-, and age-matched non-gastroparesis controls.
TNXB gene variant enrichment in idiopathic gastroparesis patients remained statistically significant after Bonferroni correction for multiple testing.

The discussion notes that tenascin-X (TNX) regulates peripheral sensory and motor neurons, and TNX-deficient patients report increased sensory and motor GI symptoms and upper gastric dysfunction consistent with mouse models.
The discussion cites prior literature reporting a strong correlation between joint hypermobility disorders and gastrointestinal disorders, consistent with the paper's findings.
Discussion notes that haploinsufficiency of COL5A1, which regulates heterotypic collagen fibril formation and diameter, is a common cause of classic EDS.

The authors propose a hypothesized mechanism in which collagen fibril density and turnover of collagen tripeptides modulate macrophage polarization (M2-like), potentially linking EDS and gastroparesis pathophysiology.
The 2017 EDS classification recognizes 13 subtypes linked to 19 causal genes, most of which are involved in collagen synthesis.
Five of the thirteen EDS subtypes have documented spinal manifestations.
Chiari malformation is described as a spinal/craniocervical pathology associated with EDS.
Craniocervical instability is described as a spinal manifestation associated with EDS.
Kyphoscoliosis is described as a spinal manifestation associated with EDS.
Segmental instability and kyphosis are described as spinal manifestations associated with EDS.
Spontaneous CSF leaks are described as a spinal manifestation associated with EDS.
Tarlov cyst syndrome is described as a spinal manifestation associated with EDS.
Tethered cord is described as a spinal manifestation associated with EDS.
The case series suggests that fetal (rather than maternal) vEDS disease status is the main risk factor for developing amniotic band sequence.
Clinical presentation of ABS in the vEDS patients was highly variable, ranging from a single constriction ring to complex craniofacial clefts to limb reduction deformities.
The authors recommend exploring family history and clinical features suggestive of vEDS in patients presenting with amniotic band sequence.
Spondylodysplastic EDS can be caused by deficiency of the enzyme β4GalT7, which impairs formation of the GAG tetrasaccharide linker region.
Spondylodysplastic EDS can alternatively be caused by deficiency of the enzyme β3GalT6, which also impairs formation of the GAG tetrasaccharide linker region.
Musculocontractural EDS can result from deficiency of D4ST1, impairing dermatan sulfate formation.
Musculocontractural EDS can alternatively result from deficiency of DS-epi1, impairing dermatan sulfate formation.
Most EDS types are caused by defects in fibrillar type I, III, or V collagen or their modifying enzymes, distinguishing them from the rarer GAG-biosynthesis-linked EDS subtypes.
Preterm birth (<37 weeks) was significantly more common among children with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome than in the general US population.
Although raw low birthweight rates were higher in VEDS patients than the general population, gestational-age-adjusted birthweight z-scores did not differ significantly from the population reference.
No differences in gestational age or birthweight were observed by fetal sex or maternal affected status.

Children with high-risk (missense or splice site) COL3A1 variants tended to be born preterm more often than those with haploinsufficient variants, but this difference did not reach statistical significance.
Among affected mothers, perinatal complications were common, occurring in 5 of 6 affected mothers.
Maternal affected status was not associated with preterm birth, suggesting that preterm birth risk in VEDS is conferred by the fetal genotype rather than the maternal condition.
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and hypermobile syndromes were among the comorbidities with the highest female-to-male sex ratios in patients with Sjögren's disease.
Women with Sjögren's disease had a markedly increased risk of developing hypermobile syndromes compared to men.
Women with Sjögren's disease had a significantly increased risk of developing Ehlers-Danlos syndrome compared to men.
Patients with Sjögren's disease diagnosed after age 50 were more likely to have fibromyalgia, pain and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome at diagnosis than younger patients.
Fibromyalgia occurred in about a quarter of Sjögren's disease patients overall, with a 12:1 female-to-male ratio.
Women with Sjögren's disease had over twice the risk of developing fibromyalgia compared to men.
At the time of Sjögren's disease diagnosis, women were significantly more likely than men to already have fibromyalgia, with a 7:1 female-to-male ratio.
Women with Sjögren's disease had a nearly 4-fold increased risk of developing migraine compared to men.
Women with Sjögren's disease had a modestly increased risk of developing chronic pain compared to men.
Women with Sjögren's disease had increased risk of several rheumatic autoimmune diseases/syndromes (systemic sclerosis, CREST, Raynaud's syndrome, SLE, rheumatoid arthritis) compared to men.
Men with Sjögren's disease had a higher risk of developing cardiovascular diseases (myocardial infarction, atherosclerosis/CAD, cardiomyopathy, congestive heart failure, stroke) than women.
Women with Sjögren's disease tested positive for ANA and SSA/Ro autoantibodies more often than men.
Low DHEA levels were found more often in men than women with Sjögren's disease.

In women with Sjögren's disease specifically, SSA positivity, rheumatoid factor positivity and low DHEA were more common after age 50, whereas no such age differences were seen in men (though male DHEA data were too sparse to draw conclusions).
Men with Sjögren's disease were more likely to be current or past smokers than women.
Sjögren's disease was diagnosed at an older mean age in men than women, and diagnosis occurred primarily post-menopause in women and after age 50 in men.
In this large cohort, Sjögren's disease occurred in women at a ratio of 6.4 to 1 compared to men, lower than some prior estimates.

The authors note EDS/hypermobile syndromes were likely underrepresented in the medical record despite being common in the same demographic (predominantly white women) and having high overlap with fibromyalgia, suggesting historical under-diagnosis.
Using the National Inpatient Sample (2010-2017), the estimated national incidence was 18 per 100,000 for Marfan syndrome and 22.4 per 100,000 for Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
In-hospital mortality did not significantly differ between MFS and EDS patients presenting with aortic dissection or aneurysm.
EDS patients with aortic dissection/aneurysm were significantly more likely to undergo TEVAR (thoracic endovascular aortic repair) than MFS patients.
MFS patients were more likely than EDS patients to develop acute kidney injury as a complication.
EDS patients presenting with aortic disease were significantly older than MFS patients.
EDS patients presenting with aortic disease were significantly more likely to be female than MFS patients.
EDS patients presenting with thoracic aortic disease were significantly older and more likely to be female compared to MFS patients.
MFS patients were more likely than EDS patients to present with a type A aortic dissection.
The majority of MFS and EDS patients with aortic dissection/aneurysm were treated at urban teaching hospitals.
Aortic dissection was identified as a significant predictor of in-hospital mortality in patients with MFS or EDS.
The specific type of connective tissue disease (MFS vs EDS) was not a significant predictor of mortality.
On average it takes patients 6 to 8 years to obtain an accurate diagnosis of a rare genetic disorder such as EDS.
Roughly a quarter of participants had been misdiagnosed with other conditions (e.g., fibromyalgia, lupus, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson disease) before eventually being diagnosed with EDS.
All 30 participants reported experiencing constant, daily pain that had a major impact on their daily life.
Most participants felt their medical team was unsupportive, did not trust their reports of pain, and sometimes attributed symptoms to psychological causes.
Nearly all participants actively searched the internet, including PubMed and Google, to learn about EDS and find management solutions, often bringing findings back to their doctors.

Most participants used online peer support groups (Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, Reddit, Inspire) to obtain pain management solutions, physician/product referrals, natural remedies, and practical tips.
Nearly all participants reported that their healthcare management changed as a result of participating in online peer support groups, and most said this change was positive.
Participants reported using a variety of nonmedical pain mitigation techniques including hot/cold packs, mindfulness/meditation, topical creams, dietary changes, braces, distraction, and salt baths.
Participants had mixed positive and negative experiences with physical therapy, dry needling, and acupuncture, with outcomes depending heavily on the provider's familiarity with EDS.
About half of participants had used opioids or cannabis for pain, and about a third of these expressed concern about addiction or developing drug tolerance with reduced long-term relief.
Most participants found that pain killers and anti-inflammatory medications alone were not sufficient to manage their pain, requiring multiple concurrent techniques.

Despite overall positive views, most participants had significant reservations about online support groups, including information overload, doubts about accuracy/trustworthiness, negative tone, and privacy/anonymity concerns.

Provider-led pain management classes were reported as unsatisfactory by some participants because the providers lacked EDS-specific knowledge and prescribed generic protocols that could be harmful for EDS patients.
The study's sex distribution (93% women) closely mirrored the reported general EDS population distribution of 73.9% women and 26.1% men.
Women with high hypermobility scores had significantly higher rates of MRI-detected trapezium cartilage abnormalities than those with low hypermobility scores.
Women with high hypermobility scores had significantly higher rates of MRI-detected metacarpal cartilage abnormalities than those with low hypermobility scores.
Women with high hypermobility scores had significantly higher rates of MRI-detected trapezium bone abnormalities than those with low hypermobility scores.
No significant differences in age, body mass index, parity, functional index, or hand pain scores were found between women with high versus low hypermobility scores.
Radiographic changes at the first carpometacarpal joint did not significantly differ between high and low hypermobility score groups, unlike MRI findings.

A highly-cited systematic review (Berman 1999) found acupuncture more effective than sham acupuncture for pain relief in fibromyalgia, raising pain threshold and reducing morning stiffness, though the duration of benefit was unclear.
An RCT by Vas (2016) found that acupuncture, but not sham acupuncture, effectively relieved fibromyalgia symptoms, with pain relief persisting for 1 year on follow-up.
Karatay (2018) proposed that changes in serum pain neuromediator levels may be one mechanism by which acupuncture affects fibromyalgia symptoms.

Animal studies in the 'mechanism of acupuncture analgesia' cluster found electroacupuncture at specific frequencies promotes release of neuropeptides in the CNS and may interfere with adenosine metabolism and inhibit CNS signaling pathways to relieve pain.
Acupuncture down-regulates phosphorylation of NMDAR subunits NR1 and NR2 in the spinal cord to alleviate pain in mouse models of fibromyalgia.
Acupuncture down-regulates expression of TRPV1 and TRPV4 in the spinal cord to alleviate pain in mouse models of fibromyalgia.

In a rat model of fibromyalgia, spinal cord neurons were hyperactivated with higher background firing, increased mechanical responses, increased excitatory synaptic input and decreased inhibitory input, producing nociceptive hypersensitivity.

Both subcutaneous and deep muscle acupuncture increase blood flow to the trapezius, tibialis anterior muscle, and overlying skin in fibromyalgia patients, with similar efficacy between the two acupuncture types.
Blood flow to the deep muscles was found to be positively correlated with muscle pressure pain thresholds in fibromyalgia patients.

Baseline pain pressure threshold predicts differential response to acupuncture vs sham acupuncture: patients with higher thresholds respond better to real acupuncture, while those with lower thresholds respond better to sham acupuncture.
Both acupuncture and sham acupuncture relieved fibromyalgia symptoms, but the benefit persisted for 3 months only in the true acupuncture group and not the sham group.

Acupuncture was reported to effectively improve fatigue and sleep quality in patients with high-severity fibromyalgia refractory to conventional pharmacological therapy, though the study lacked a control group and most patients were also on concurrent drug treatment.
Acupuncture improved dynamic equilibrium and postural control in women with fibromyalgia, with effects sustained for 5 weeks.
Retrospective studies found that acupuncture reduces the risk of coronary heart disease and stroke in Taiwanese patients with fibromyalgia.

A neuroimaging study found electroacupuncture increased connectivity between the trunk sensory cortex and the anterior/posterior insula in fibromyalgia patients, raising GABA levels in the anterior insula and relieving pain symptoms.
Fibromyalgia patients show altered cytokine profiles including IFN-γ, IL-5, IL-6, IL-8, and anti-inflammatory IL-10 following activation of peripheral blood mononuclear cells.
Fibromyalgia patients show a disconnect between pain inhibitory centres and the insular cortex along with higher glutamate levels compared to healthy persons.
Central neuroinflammation with elevated substance P, brain-derived neurotrophic factor, and NGF has been identified in the spinal fluid of fibromyalgia patients.

Fibromyalgia patients show increased mast cells in the skin and blood vessels that release bradykinin, histamine, TNF, and tryptase, contributing to neurogenic inflammation and mast cell-microglia crosstalk.
Fibromyalgia patients have increased levels of inflammatory chemokines (CCL17, CXCL9, CCL22, CXCL11, CCL11) that attract innate and adaptive immune cells.
Fibromyalgia patients show increased sympathetic nervous system activity that moderates peripheral nociceptor neurons, indicating peripheral neuroinflammation.
Approximately 50% of fibromyalgia patients show abnormalities of small nerve fibres, including thinly myelinated or unmyelinated fibres and reduced average axon diameter (small fibre polyneuropathy).
Fibromyalgia patients demonstrate dopamine dysregulation alongside alterations in endogenous opioids, neuroendocrine factors, and oxidative stress.
Fibromyalgia patients have increased levels of free radicals and decreased antioxidant capacity, with oxidative stress disproportionately affecting the lipid-rich CNS.
Fibromyalgia has an estimated prevalence of 5% and predominantly affects females, with reduced pain tolerance and abnormal temperature sensitivity.
Fibromyalgia has an economic burden roughly twice that of ankylosing spondylitis treatment and similar to chronic lumbalgia.
Fibromyalgia patients have a higher prevalence of autoimmune diseases including rheumatoid arthritis, lupus erythematosus, Sjögren's syndrome, IBD, and type 1 diabetes.
Fibromyalgia is associated with migraine, TMJ dysfunction, pelvic pain, complex regional pain syndrome, restless legs syndrome, IBS, interstitial cystitis, hypotension, and hypersensitivities.
Autoantibodies including anti-polymer antibody (APA), anti-68/48 kDa, and anti-45 kDa have been detected in fibromyalgia, CFS, and psychiatric disorder patients, potentially serving as biomarkers.
In the five years preceding diagnosis, 25% of IBS patients and 51% of FM patients were diagnosed with depression or anxiety.
In IBS patients, TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-17 serum levels are associated with abdominal pain and symptom severity, with IL-6 and IL-8 elevated in some cohorts and anti-inflammatory IL-10 decreased.
Elevated levels of CRF in intestinal eosinophils correlate with the severity of symptoms in IBS-diarrhoea (IBS-D) patients.
70% of mast cells in the gastrointestinal tract are in direct contact with nerve cells, regulating intestinal permeability, peristalsis, nociception, and immunity.
IBS patients show altered neuron activity in the submucosal plexus that is stimulated by immune mediators.
Certain CFS/ME patients present with antibodies against muscarinic, acetylcholine, and beta-adrenergic receptors, along with cerebral cytokine dysregulation.
CFS/ME patients show reduced cerebral blood flow and altered sympathetic and parasympathetic signalling in the brain stem.
Immune system dysfunction in CFS/ME patients includes autoantibodies, impaired natural killer cell function, excess cytotoxic T cells, and higher levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
Approximately 75% of CFS/ME patients are unable to work and 25% become housebound or bedbound due to symptom severity.
Long-COVID patients following COVID-19 infection have been shown to meet the diagnostic criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome.
Pregabalin, duloxetine, and milnacipran are pharmacologically approved treatments for fibromyalgia targeting neuronal activity and serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake.
Cognitive behavioural therapy appears to be the most beneficial treatment for functional somatic syndromes among available options.

Vagus nerve electrical stimulation reduced inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-2, IL-6, TNF) in rat models of rheumatoid arthritis and reduced inflammatory symptoms and cytokine production in human RA patients.
Patients with CFS, IBS, musculoskeletal pain, and other functional somatic syndromes show increased levels of CRP compared to healthy persons, indicating a sensitized immune-inflammatory system.
NGF increases nociception and hyperalgesia and stimulates mast cell activity, causing secretion of IL-17, IL-6, and TGFβ.
Among 20 MCAS patients who took hydroxyurea for at least 2 months, all evaluated symptom domains (bone pain, abdominal pain, diarrhea, bloating, nausea) showed statistically significant improvement.
70% (14/20) of patients treated with hydroxyurea for at least 2 months experienced significant clinical benefit and continued therapy long-term, averaging 32.6 months.
61.5% of the HU-treated MCAS cohort had comorbid postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, a higher rate than reported in other MCAS case series.
34.6% of the HU-treated MCAS cohort had comorbid hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

Adverse laboratory changes with hydroxyurea were mild and reversible, including leukopenia, neutropenia, liver enzyme elevation, and creatinine elevation, all resolving with dose reduction or cessation.
Symptom improvement on hydroxyurea did not differ significantly between patients with bone pain (N=15) versus those without bone pain (N=5).
Omalizumab used concomitantly in eight patients often improved urticaria but did not affect other MCAS symptoms.
Patients had failed an average of 10.6 prior medications (range 8-13) before hydroxyurea was added, with 6.0 concomitant medications on average, reflecting a highly treatment-refractory cohort.
The mean baseline mast cell mediator release syndrome (MCMRS) symptom score across the 26 patients was 24, well above the ≥14 threshold suggestive of MCAS with 95% probability.
The authors propose that hydroxyurea's benefit in MCAS may derive from reducing mast cell activity independent of its anti-proliferative, ribonucleotide reductase-inhibiting mechanism.

In essential thrombocythemia patients, long-term hydroxyurea use was not associated with an increased rate of secondary malignancy compared with untreated patients, cited to support HU's long-term safety profile.

The study reports outcomes of COVID-19 vaccination in a cohort of 323 patients with clonal and non-clonal mast cell activation disorders, but no specific quantitative outcome is provided beyond the title.
The patient's serum tryptase level was markedly elevated compared to the normal reference range, consistent with systemic mastocytosis.
Soluble IL-2R was markedly elevated above the reference range in this patient with systemic mastocytosis.
Bone marrow biopsy showed abundant mast cell infiltration exceeding 80% of cellularity, strongly positive for CD117 and CD25 and slightly positive for CD2.
Skin biopsy of the maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis rash showed marked dermal mast cell infiltration positive for CD117, CD25, and CD2.
The classic KIT D816V point mutation was not detected in this patient's peripheral blood despite confirmed systemic mastocytosis.

Abdominal CT revealed a characteristically swollen and edematous small intestine and splenomegaly without evidence of mechanical obstruction, consistent with anaphylactic intestinal edema from mast cell activation.
The patient showed skeletal involvement with osteopenia/osteoporotic lesions of the pelvic bones and spine, a recognized manifestation of systemic mastocytosis.

Treatment with oxygen, intravenous antihistamine (d-chlorpheniramine maleate), H2 antagonist (famotidine), and corticosteroid (methylprednisolone) resolved the patient's abdominal cramps within 6 hours and respiratory compromise within about 3 hours.
The discussion states that gastrointestinal symptoms are reported in more than 50% of systemic mastocytosis patients, based on prior literature.
The paper notes that skeletal involvement in systemic mastocytosis may serve as a prognostic factor, per cited literature.
Serum CCNB1 protein levels measured by ELISA were significantly higher in psoriasis patients than in healthy controls.
Serum CCNB2 protein levels measured by ELISA were significantly higher in psoriasis patients than in healthy controls.
CCNB1 mRNA expression was significantly higher in psoriasis patients than healthy controls across four public GEO datasets.
CCNB2 mRNA expression was significantly higher in psoriasis patients than healthy controls across four public GEO datasets.
CCNB1 and CCNB2 expression levels were significantly negatively correlated with resting mast cell abundance in psoriasis samples.
CCNB1 and CCNB2 levels were negatively correlated with M2 macrophage abundance but positively correlated with M1 macrophage abundance, suggesting a role in macrophage polarization in psoriasis.
CCNB1 and CCNB2 expression were positively correlated with IL17A expression in psoriasis datasets.
CCNB1 and CCNB2 expression showed strong positive correlations with IL22 expression in psoriasis datasets.
CCNB1 and CCNB2 expression were strongly positively correlated with IL23R expression in psoriasis datasets.
CCNB1 and CCNB2 expression were strongly positively correlated with TNF expression in psoriasis datasets.

Twelve immune-related genes were identified as common differentially expressed genes associated with both CCNB1 and CCNB2 across four psoriasis GEO datasets, enriched in cell cycle, p53 signaling, cellular senescence, and FoxO signaling pathways.
Miniature C-arm fluoroscopy units in main operating rooms had significantly more contamination prior to draping than those in ambulatory surgery center operating rooms.
A high rate of intraoperative MCA contamination occurred in both settings, with 46.2% of MOR cases and 37.5% of AOR cases showing contamination.
Use of a below hand-table MCA technique was associated with higher contamination rates compared to an above hand-table technique in both MOR and AOR settings.
Surgical case length in the main operating room trended toward being longer than in the ambulatory surgery center but did not reach statistical significance.

Patient 1 developed acute small fiber neuropathy with abnormal thermal detection thresholds and reduced intra-epidermal nerve fiber density 7 days after her first ChAdOx1-S vaccine dose, with symptoms resolving within 3 months then recurring after the second dose.

Patient 2 developed bilateral burning pain and dysaesthesias with abnormal intra-epidermal nerve fiber density 10 days after first ChAdOx1-S vaccine dose, confirming small fiber neuropathy, with normal nerve conduction studies and worsening after the second vaccine dose.

Patient 3 developed dysaesthesias and altered temperature sensation with abnormal thermal thresholds and reduced intra-epidermal nerve fiber density 15 days after first ChAdOx1-S vaccine dose, confirming small fiber neuropathy that had not resolved at follow-up.
Two of the three patients continued to experience chronic neuropathic pain at follow-up after developing acute small fiber neuropathy post-vaccination.

The authors explicitly decline to assign a causal relationship between Oxford-AstraZeneca ChAdOx1-S vaccination and acute small fiber neuropathy because only a minority of Bradford Hill criteria are met.
The authors cite a prior study reporting that small fiber neuropathy was detected in 62.5% (10/16) of patients diagnosed with post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (long COVID).

The authors note a small increased risk of hospital admission for Guillain-Barré syndrome, myasthenic disorder, and Bell's palsy after Oxford-AstraZeneca ChAdOx1-S vaccination, though this risk is lower than after primary SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Patient 2 was started on gabapentin and amitriptyline for severe neuropathic pain, but gabapentin was later switched to pregabalin due to cognitive side effects, alongside referral for psychological support.

The authors note that several previously reported cases of small fiber neuropathy after a preceding illness showed albumin-cytological dissociation on CSF analysis, suggesting a proximal demyelinating process similar to inflammatory polyradiculoneuropathies.
The authors cite a separate case series in which corticosteroid therapy produced dramatic improvement in acute small fiber neuropathy.

Low-positive ANA and ANCA (with low PR3/MPO titers) were detected in patients 1 and 2 but were considered clinically insignificant and not indicative of a concomitant autoimmune process such as lupus, Sjogren's syndrome, or vasculitis.
Nearly half of cryptogenic small fiber neuropathy patients tested positive for one or more of three novel autoantibodies (TS-HDS, FGFR-3, or Plexin D1).
Among seropositive patients, TS-HDS antibodies were the most prevalent, found in 62.5% of those with a positive antibody result.
FGFR-3 antibodies were present in 29.2% of seropositive patients and were more likely to be found in male patients.
Plexin D1 antibodies were present in 20.8% of seropositive patients, though their clinical role is less established.
Male patients were significantly more likely than female patients to test positive for FGFR-3 antibodies.
Facial involvement was significantly more common among patients seropositive for the antibodies compared to seronegative patients.
Patients with higher Utah Early Neuropathy Scale scores (indicating greater disease severity) had higher TS-HDS antibody titers.
Seropositive patients trended toward higher SFN screening list scores, more abnormal QSART results, and more prior erroneous diagnoses, though these did not reach statistical significance.
In patients who completed IVIG treatment, epidermal nerve fiber density increased markedly along with subjective and objective clinical improvement.
Seropositive patients trended toward a higher rate of prior erroneous diagnosis compared to seronegative patients, though this did not reach statistical significance.
Among patients who completed a course of IVIG, both clinical examinations and patient-reported questionnaires showed improvement.
Mean epidermal nerve fiber density increased by 297% in patients who completed IVIG treatment for antibody-associated small fiber neuropathy.

The index patient with clinically and neurophysiologically confirmed small fiber neuropathy was found to carry a heterozygous SCN9A c.2215A>G (p.Ile739Val) variant, a previously reported disease-causing mutation.

Quantitative sudomotor axon reflex testing (QSART) in the index patient showed significantly decreased sweat production in both proximal and distal segments of the right leg, consistent with small fiber/autonomic dysfunction.
Skin biopsy in the index patient demonstrated significantly reduced epidermal nerve fiber density in the distal thigh and distal leg, confirming small fiber neuropathy.

In silico protein modeling of the I739V variant yielded divergent pathogenicity predictions: SIFT predicted the variant tolerated, PolyPhen predicted it probably damaging, and MutationTaster predicted it disease-causing.

The I739V variant is a rare polymorphism with population allele frequencies ranging from 0.0010 (1000 Genomes) to 0.009 (GoNL), and 0.002470 with two homozygotes reported in ExAC/gnomAD without associated clinical data.

Additional heterozygous variants in HINT1 and FAM124B (both typically autosomal recessive disease genes) were detected but, lacking a second variant, are unlikely to be disease-producing in this family.

The patient's father, who paternally transmitted the I739V mutation, has decreased sensitivity to extreme heat and cold and reduced pain sensitivity but no pain symptoms, in contrast to his daughter's pain syndrome, illustrating intrafamilial phenotypic variability.

Prior electrophysiological voltage clamp studies of the I739V mutation demonstrated a gain-of-function effect with increased neuronal hyperexcitability, reduced current threshold, and increased firing frequency in response to depolarizing stimuli.

A prior study of Dutch patients first identified the I739V mutation in a 51-year-old woman with autonomic neuropathy symptoms including dry eyes, dry mouth, orthostatic dysfunction, and joint and muscle pain, with similar complaints in her sister and two sons.
The I739V mutation has also been described in a family presenting with paroxysmal itch.

In a cohort of 7 patients carrying the I739V mutation, 5 developed a painful neuropathy, and some were subsequently diagnosed with diabetes mellitus, suggesting a potential role of this variant in painful diabetic neuropathy.

A next-generation sequencing study of over 400 individuals with peripheral neuropathy found the I739V mutation in about 1% of patients, with little difference in mutation frequency between those with pain versus those without discomfort.

A homozygous 9-bp in-frame deletion in LTBP4 exon 30 (c.3774_3782del, p.Asp1259_Asp1261del) was identified in a 17-month-old girl with autosomal recessive cutis laxa type 1C (ARCL1C), inherited from heterozygous unaffected parents.
RT-PCR analysis of RNA showed no impact of the deletion on splicing, with no exon 30 skipping detected despite in silico prediction of high exon-skipping probability.

AlphaFold-based protein structure prediction indicated that residues Asp1259, Asn1260, and Asp1261 normally form hydrogen bonds important for the calcium-binding motif structure of the EGF-like 14 domain, suggesting the deletion disrupts calcium binding and protein folding.

The LTBP4 variant was classified as likely pathogenic (ACMG class 4) based on two PP and three PM criteria, including absence from gnomAD, predicted protein truncation, and location within the EGF-like 14 functional domain.

The patient's generalized cutis laxa and craniofacial features (periorbital swelling, hypertelorism, long philtrum, depressed nasal bridge, microretrognathia) were consistent with the phenotypic spectrum reported in prior ARCL1C cases.

The patient developed early pulmonary emphysema in both lower lobes with pulmonary artery hypoplasia (-2 to -3 Z-scores) and a bronchogenic cyst, without pulmonary hypertension at the time of reporting.
Doppler echocardiography revealed minimal aortic arch hypoplasia and mild aortic insufficiency, a cardiovascular anomaly the authors state has not previously been reported in ARCL1C patients.

Most previously reported LTBP4 pathogenic variants cause premature termination codons leading to nonsense-mediated decay and absence of LTBP4 protein, disrupting fibulin-5-elastin complex targeting to microfibrils and impairing elastic fiber formation, whereas only three missense variants disrupting conserved cysteine residues in the TB/hybrid domain had previously been reported.
This is reported as the first short in-frame deletion within LTBP4, in contrast to previously described loss-of-function or cysteine-disrupting missense variants.
Sanger sequencing confirmed that both unaffected parents and unaffected siblings were heterozygous carriers of the LTBP4 deletion, consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

The authors note that missense pathogenic variants in the calcium-binding domain of EGF-like domains in FBN1 (Marfan syndrome) and FBN2 (congenital arachnodactyly) support the pathogenic potential of disrupting the same consensus calcium-binding motif, of which the deleted LTBP4 residues (Asp1259-Asn1260-Asp1261) represent the first three amino acids.
The percentage of participants reporting a thermal grill illusion of pain was significantly higher in patients with fibromyalgia or irritable bowel syndrome than in healthy controls.
TGIP intensity and unpleasantness ratings were significantly greater in patients with fibromyalgia or irritable bowel syndrome compared with healthy controls.
TGIP intensity correlated positively with clinical pain intensity in patients with fibromyalgia or irritable bowel syndrome.
TGIP intensity correlated positively with the cold pain threshold measured on the hand in patients with fibromyalgia or irritable bowel syndrome.
The authors propose that TGIP may serve as a clinical marker of central sensitization in patients with nociplastic chronic pain syndromes such as fibromyalgia and irritable bowel syndrome.
TEA increased the number of complete spontaneous bowel movements per week compared with sham-TEA after 4 weeks of treatment.
TEA reduced abdominal pain as measured by the visual analog scale compared with sham-TEA.
TEA reduced overall IBS symptom severity as measured by the Irritable Bowel Syndrome Severity Scoring System compared with sham-TEA.
TEA significantly improved quality of life related to constipation, as shown by decreased Patient Assessment of Constipation Quality of Life scores.
TEA accelerated colon transit compared with sham-TEA, as measured by radiopaque marker studies.
TEA increased the sensory threshold for desire to defecate, indicating reduced rectal hypersensitivity, compared with sham-TEA.
TEA increased the maximum tolerability threshold of rectal sensation compared with sham-TEA.
TEA increased vagal activity compared with sham-TEA.
At the end of treatment, vagal activity (assessed via ECG-derived autonomic measures) was significantly correlated with colonic transit time.
Vagal activity at the end of treatment was also significantly correlated with the number of complete spontaneous bowel movements per week (CSBMs/week).
MSTN protein was detectable in wild type pig hearts but absent in MSTN knockout hearts, confirming loss of function.
MSTN knockout pigs showed a significantly decreased heart-to-body weight ratio compared to wild type pigs.

Morphometric analyses including picrosirius red staining, immunofluorescence, and ultrastructural endomysium thickness showed significantly reduced connective tissue content in MSTN knockout hearts compared to wild type.
Hydroxyproline content, type I collagen (Col1A), and phosphorylated Smad3/Smad3 ratio were significantly lower in MSTN knockout hearts in vivo compared to wild type.
In vitro treatment of cardiac fibroblasts with exogenous active MSTN protein caused overexpression of Col1A and activation of Smad and AKT signaling pathways.
Of 18 patients with a mutation in an LDS-causing gene, 15 had known pathogenic variants, two had variants of unknown significance, and one had a benign variant.
Among patients who underwent proximal ascending aortic replacement, only 2 of 11 required additional aortic operations for arch or descending aortic complications during long-term follow-up.
No surgical or late follow-up mortality was observed among any of the 18 LDS patients in the study.
Among patients who underwent surgery, the median ascending aortic diameter at the time of intervention was 5.0 cm.

The study concludes that LDS patients undergoing proximal aortic replacement have a low long-term risk of arch complications, suggesting routine prophylactic total arch replacement may not be warranted when the arch is nonaneurysmal.
Increased TGF-beta concentrations in bone are proposed as a causative factor impairing bone remodeling in OI mice, and restoring homeostatic levels improves bone strength and volume.
Patients with osteogenesis imperfecta reportedly show approximately three-fold higher TGF-beta concentrations in plasma and bone compared to healthy individuals.
In vivo blockade of TGF-beta signaling with 1D11 improved bone volume fraction and biomechanical strength in a G610C osteogenesis imperfecta mouse model.
The preclinical 1D11 PK/BVF model translated to humans predicts that GC2008 administered at 0.5 mg/kg every 3 months or 2.5 mg/kg every 6 months would produce a 5% increase in bone volume fraction.

A PK/PD model built on Fresolimumab (GC1008) clinical BMD data in OI patients predicts GC2008 doses of 0.4 mg/kg every 3 months or 2 mg/kg every 6 months would yield a 5% increase in bone mineral density.
PBPK modeling predicts that GC2008 doses of 0.35 mg/kg every 3 months or 2.5 mg/kg every 6 months would normalize elevated TGF-beta levels in bone to healthy physiological values in OI patients.
The PBPK model predicted GC2008 distribution to bone at approximately 5% of plasma concentration, consistent with literature reports of ~7% distribution of large molecules to bone.
In OI patients receiving a single dose of Fresolimumab, 1 mg/kg had minimal effect on bone mineral density dynamics, whereas 4 mg/kg produced a more pronounced early increase.

GC2008 is a second-generation human anti-TGF-beta antibody differing from Fresolimumab (GC1008) by a single amino acid substitution (S228P) in the heavy chain, retaining identical CDR sequences and TGF-beta affinity.

Population PK analysis showed Fresolimumab serum PK is best described by a two-compartment model with linear clearance and an estimated half-life of 14 days that did not change with dose, with body weight as the only significant covariate.
In a clinical study of 46 adults with OI, neridronate treatment every 3 months increased spine and hip BMD by 3% and 4.3% respectively in the first year, with further increases in the second year.
In a randomized trial of 79 adults with OI, subcutaneous teriparatide increased lumbar spine aBMD by 6.1% versus 2.8% with placebo, and total hip aBMD by 2.6% versus -2.4% with placebo.

A retrospective analysis found that whole body vibration physiotherapy over 12 months increased areal BMD by ~10% and total body BMD by ~3%, along with improved motor function, in 53 children with OI.
Denosumab, a RANK ligand inhibiting antibody, led to a 19% increase in lumbar areal BMD in 10 children with osteogenesis imperfecta.
TGF-beta signaling regulates bone remodeling by recruiting mesenchymal stem cells to bone resorptive sites to undergo osteoblastic differentiation and form new bone.
Aortic event risk differed significantly among the smooth muscle contraction genes ACTA2, MYLK, and PRKG1.
Aortic event risk differed significantly among the TGF-β pathway genes associated with Loeys-Dietz syndrome (SMAD3, TGFB2, TGFBR1, TGFBR2).
In patients with variants in ACTA2, MYLK, PRKG1, and SMAD3, cumulative incidence of type A aortic dissection was higher than that of elective aneurysm surgery.
In contrast to the other genes, patients with TGFBR2 variants had a lower cumulative incidence of type A aortic dissection than elective aneurysm surgery.
Cumulative incidence of type B aortic dissection was higher for ACTA2, PRKG1, and TGFBR2 gene variants compared with other HTAD genes.
After adjusting for proband status, sex, and recruitment location, specific variants in ACTA2 and TGFBR2 were associated with substantially higher risk of aortic events with childhood onset.
COMPASS-31 dysautonomia symptom scores significantly decreased after CT-guided celiac ganglion block with liposomal bupivacaine.
All patients reported significant reduction in abdominal angina after celiac ganglion block, with the majority achieving complete resolution.
Non-postprandial abdominal pain was significantly reduced after the block, with over half of responders achieving complete resolution.
Functional GI symptom scores for vomiting, constipation frequency, constipation severity, and nausea significantly improved after celiac ganglion block.
CT-guided celiac ganglion block was safe, with only minor adverse events and no major adverse events reported.
Only about 15% of surveyed workers with post-COVID-19 syndrome had returned to work at the time of the survey.
About 53% of workers rated their physical workability as moderate at best following COVID-19.
About 50% of workers rated their psychological workability as moderate at best following COVID-19.

Fatigue was identified as a leading obstacle to workability, alongside the interaction between symptoms and job demands, lack of control over job pressures, inappropriate sickness absence management, and lack of COVID-aware organizational culture.

Respondents advocated self-management support, modified work, flexible co-developed graded return-to-work planning, and improved line management competency as key enablers of post-COVID-19 workability.

The authors propose that maintaining or regaining post-COVID workability should follow a biopsychosocial framework adapted to the fluctuating nature of post-COVID symptoms, involving flexible, regularly reviewed return-to-work planning co-developed by workers and line managers with support from HR and occupational health professionals.

At 500 Hz, the left-ear pure tone audiometry threshold was significantly better (lower) in the Ex COVID group compared to both the Long COVID and No COVID groups, while the right ear showed no such difference.

Transient evoked otoacoustic emission signal-to-noise ratio at 2.8 kHz was significantly lower in the Long COVID group compared to the No COVID control group, suggesting possible subclinical cochlear involvement.
At 4 kHz, the No COVID group showed a numerically higher TEOAE signal-to-noise ratio than both the Long COVID and Ex COVID groups, but this difference did not reach statistical significance.

Across all other tested frequencies (250 Hz to 8 kHz), pure tone audiometry thresholds showed no significant differences between Long COVID, Ex COVID, and No COVID groups, and overall the study found no clinically significant hearing loss attributable to Long COVID.
19 of 42 post-COVID-19 syndrome (PCS) patients with persistent fatigue and exertion intolerance fulfilled the Canadian Consensus Criteria (CCC) for ME/CFS six months after COVID-19.
Most PCS patients who did not meet ME/CFS diagnostic criteria (18 of 23) had exertion intolerance with post-exertional malaise (PEM) lasting less than 14 hours.

Bell disability scores indicated severe functional impairment in both PCS and non-COVID ME/CFS cohorts, with median scores of 40 and 30 (out of 100) respectively, and 50 in the PCS/non-ME_CFS subgroup, indicating most patients needed reduced work hours or were unable to work.
PCS patients who did not fulfill ME/CFS criteria (PCS/non-ME_CFS) reported less fatigue on the Chalder Fatigue Score than non-COVID-19 ME/CFS patients.
PEM frequency and severity strongly discriminated PCS/non-ME_CFS from non-COVID ME/CFS patients, but did not significantly differ between PCS/non-ME_CFS and PCS/ME_CFS patients.

PEM, fatigue, stress intolerance and hypersensitivity to temperature were less severe in PCS/non-ME_CFS compared to non-COVID ME/CFS, and flu-like symptoms were less severe in both PCS cohorts compared to non-COVID ME/CFS after BH correction.

When comparing only the two PCS cohorts, PCS/ME_CFS patients had significantly greater symptom burden for stress intolerance and hypersensitivity to temperature, noise and light than PCS/non-ME_CFS patients.

Most PCS patients (21 moderate, 11 severe of 42) showed autonomic dysfunction on COMPASS-31, with severity not significantly different between PCS/ME_CFS, PCS/non-ME_CFS, and non-COVID ME/CFS cohorts.

Most PCS patients had hand grip strength (maximal and mean force, Fmax1/2 and Fmean1/2) below reference cut-off values for age-matched healthy subjects, consistent with muscle fatigability seen in ME/CFS.
Four patients (3 female, 1 male) with PCS/ME_CFS and one patient with PCS/non-ME_CFS fulfilled diagnostic criteria for postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS).
Orthostatic hypotension was diagnosed in six patients with PCS/ME_CFS (5 female, 1 male) and one patient with PCS/non-ME_CFS.
Mannose-binding lectin (MBL) deficiency, previously found more frequently in ME/CFS than historical controls, was also found more frequently in both PCS cohorts (17% PCS/ME_CFS, 23% PCS/non-ME_CFS).
IL-8 in erythrocytes was above normal range in 37% of PCS/ME_CFS and 48% of PCS/non-ME_CFS patients, suggesting recent inflammation.
CRP was only slightly elevated in two PCS patients, indicating no evidence of ongoing overt systemic inflammation in most patients.

Elevated antinuclear antibodies (ANA, titers 1:160-1:1280) were found in eight PCS patients (predominantly female), suggesting a possible autoimmune mechanism, though anti-dsDNA and ENA were negative and no rheumatological disease was found.
Four patients (two of each PCS group) had elevated anti-thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies with normal TSH and fT3/fT4; three had pre-existing Hashimoto thyroiditis.
Vitamin D deficiency was found in 11% of PCS/ME_CFS and 22% of PCS/non-ME_CFS patients.
Folic acid deficiency was found in 19% of all PCS patients.
NT-proBNP was slightly elevated in three PCS patients despite no evidence of impaired cardiac function.
ACE1 levels were below normal range in 31% of all PCS patients, assessed due to presumed dysregulation of the renin-angiotensin system in PCS.
Hand grip strength parameters showed a significant positive correlation with hemoglobin levels in both PCS/non-ME_CFS and PCS/ME_CFS cohorts, suggesting a role for oxygen supply in muscle fatigue.
In the PCS/non-ME_CFS cohort, Fmax1 (hand grip strength) correlated negatively with erythrocyte IL8 levels.

ME/CFS patients showed significantly greater fibrinaloid microclot burden (ThT-positive amyloid signal) in platelet-poor plasma than healthy controls.
Thrombin-induced fibrin clot networks from ME/CFS plasma showed significantly greater ThT fluorescence (amyloid content) than those from healthy controls.
ME/CFS platelets showed a hyperactivated phenotype with significantly greater spreading (granule release) than healthy control platelets.
Platelet clumping was observed in over half of ME/CFS subjects, with mean clumping scores markedly higher than in healthy controls (who scored zero).

Roughly half of the ME/CFS whole blood samples fell outside normal clinical ranges for R, K, α angle, MA, and MRTG, indicating faster and stronger clot formation consistent with a hypercoagulable tendency.
None of the ME/CFS whole blood samples fell outside the normal clinical range for the TMRTG and TTG thromboelastography parameters.
PPP α angle (clot formation rate) was significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than healthy controls, indicating a hypercoagulable state.
PPP MRTG (maximum rate of thrombus generation) was significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than healthy controls, further supporting a hypercoagulable state.
COVID-19 vaccination status had no discernible effect on the % area of fibrinaloid microclots in either the ME/CFS or control groups, indicating vaccination did not confound the microclot results.
16% of the ME/CFS cohort self-reported comorbid POTS.
16% of the ME/CFS cohort self-reported comorbid fibromyalgia.
4% of the ME/CFS cohort self-reported comorbid mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS).
4% of the ME/CFS cohort self-reported comorbid dysautonomia (and 4% orthostatic hypotension).
The ME/CFS cohort scored highest (most severe) on the post-exertional neuroimmune exhaustion domain of the ICC severity questionnaire, with 60% rating this domain as severe.
The fibrinaloid microclot burden in ME/CFS was notably lower than that previously reported by the same group in acute COVID-19, Long COVID/PASC, and type 2 diabetes.

The degree of hypercoagulability observed in the ME/CFS group was less severe than that previously reported in diabetes, acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, or Long COVID/PASC, and hypercoagulability varied among individual ME/CFS patients.
Among 275 ME/CFS patients, 116 (42%) had pain drawing markings corresponding to a predefined C2 cervical nerve root pain pattern, interpreted as cervicogenic headache.
Patients with a C2 pain pattern had strongly increased odds of reporting dizziness/imbalance compared to patients with no headache (adjusted OR 6.50).
Patients with a C2 pain pattern had increased odds of dizziness/imbalance compared to patients with headache but no C2 pain pattern (adjusted OR 3.15).
Odds of dizziness/imbalance did not differ significantly by sex, age group (<60 vs ≥60), pain intensity, or body pain extent in the adjusted logistic regression model.
Headache without a C2 pain pattern showed a non-significant trend toward higher odds of dizziness/imbalance compared to no headache (adjusted OR 2.13, p=0.16).
Patients with a C2 pain pattern reported significantly higher pain intensity (VAS median 66.5mm) than those with headache without C2 pattern (48.5mm) or no headache (40.0mm).
Patients with a C2 pain pattern reported significantly greater body pain extent (61.4%) than those with headache without C2 pattern (46.25%) or no headache (31.5%).
Patients with a C2 pain pattern reported significantly lower health-related quality of life (EQ-VAS median 26.5mm) than those with no headache (35.0mm).
A quarter (25%) of ME/CFS patients undergoing specialist investigation had documented dizziness or imbalance at their first physician visit.
Interrater agreement for classifying drawings using the standardized C2 pain pattern key was high (96%), with only 12 of 275 drawings requiring consensus discussion.
EAT treatment significantly reduced IL-6 mRNA expression in the epipharyngeal submucosa compared to untreated chronic epipharyngitis patients.
EAT treatment reduced TNFα mRNA expression in the submucosal region of the epipharynx, mirroring the IL-6 decrease.

Double staining showed IL-6 mRNA was mainly co-localized with CD20+ B cells in epipharyngeal submucosal lymphoid tissue, with less expression in T cells and none detectable in macrophages or vascular endothelial cells.
Continuous EAT reduced endoscopic mucosal swelling and induced a temporary whitening phenomenon considered to indicate reduced epipharyngeal inflammation.
Cited prior literature indicates that elevated serum/plasma IL-6 has been implicated in IgA nephropathy, ME/CFS, and Long COVID, motivating the study's focus on epipharyngeal IL-6.
The authors attribute EAT's reduction of submucosal lymphocyte aggregation to fibrotic stroma formation induced by zinc chloride cotton-swab abrasion, as previously reported by the same group.
The review states that chronic inflammation with overproduction of inflammatory cytokines is thought to be a major cause of long COVID symptoms.
Long COVID symptoms are described as similar to those seen in patients with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS).

Vaccination, rehabilitation, and coordinated multidisciplinary care (including behavioral, lifestyle, and integrative approaches) are proposed as management strategies for long COVID by allergist/immunologists working with other specialists.
Moderate to severe pain affects over 60% of children with CFS/ME compared with 3.6%-16.6% of healthy children.
In this qualitative cohort, 12 of the 13 children interviewed experienced pain as part of their CFS/ME.

Children with CFS/ME described pain occurring at multiple body sites, most commonly the back, legs and neck, with some experiencing pain throughout the body and two reporting heightened skin/hair sensitivity.
Physical activity and tiredness were commonly identified triggers or worsening factors for pain in children with CFS/ME.
Two children with headaches reported that auditory and visual stimuli worsened their pain.
Two participants reported that pain was linked to temperature, with worse pain experienced in colder climates.
Pain interfered with children's education, affecting school attendance, concentration and writing ability.
Pain severely limited participation in physical activity and sport, with three children unable to walk at the same pace as peers.
Older children described greater impact of pain on social activities and peer relationships compared with younger children.

The majority of children described a negative impact of pain on mental health, including anxiety, frustration, feeling isolated, and in one severe case panic attacks associated with becoming bed bound.

Nine of thirteen children interviewed had used simple analgesics for pain, with five taking them daily or on most days, and response to analgesics was variable, ranging from helpful to partially effective to not helpful at all.

Of five prior treatment studies in paediatric CFS/ME including pain as an outcome (CBT, self-confrontation method, Lightning Process, low-dose clonidine), no intervention resulted in a significant reduction in pain, although two suggested pain may improve in 'recovered' versus 'non-recovered' patients.
One child experienced severe mood-related side effects secondary to amitriptyline used for pain.
Two teenagers found that non-pharmacological CFS/ME interventions, specifically physiotherapy and osteopathy, worsened their pain.

Children trialled a range of unregulated home treatments for pain including massage, baths, vitamin supplementation, herbal teas, electric blankets, heat packs, acupuncture bands and magnesium tablets, with no treatment resulting in complete resolution of pain.

Ergothioneine has been shown to be beneficial in preventing ischaemia-reperfusion injury, suggesting potential value in chronic diseases exhibiting this mechanism.

Gut microbiome composition predicted the nature and likelihood of PASC (Long COVID) symptoms in one study, and tracked recovery in another.
Autoantibodies directed against actin are described as leading to muscle weakness, contributing to autoimmune pathology in these chronic diseases.
Hyperactivated platelets shed their stored serotonin, which also provides a pro-coagulant surface facilitating platelet complex formation and endothelial binding.

There was an inverse association between serotonin antagonist medication use and mortality in severe COVID-19.

At post-treatment to short-term follow-up, significant improvement in fatigue occurred in 43% of CBT participants versus 20% of controls, a 23-point difference.

At short-term to medium-term follow-up, 59% of CBT participants showed clinically significant improvement in physical functioning versus 45% of controls, and 44% rated themselves globally improved versus 24% of controls.
At short-term to medium-term follow-up, 11% of CBT participants reported global worsening versus 19% of controls, 8 percentage points fewer.
In a post-hoc sensitivity analysis assuming participants lost to follow-up had worsened, global worsening remained lower after CBT (18%) than control (23%).
At post-treatment to medium-term follow-up, 61% of GET participants showed clinically significant improvement in physical functioning versus 38% of controls.
At post-treatment to short-term follow-up, 43% of GET participants rated themselves globally improved versus 17% of controls.

In a sensitivity analysis assuming dropouts had worsened, global worsening remained lower after GET (21%) than control (28%).
When restricting to moderate/strong quality studies, CBT still showed higher fatigue improvement (42%) than control (28%), similar to the main analysis.
Excluding one weak-quality study, CBT physical functioning improvement remained higher than control (65% vs 49%), slightly larger than the main estimate.

Trials comparing higher versus lower resource or intensity CBT, and higher versus lower intensity GET, found no significant differences in fatigue or physical functioning outcomes between the intensity/resource levels.

Two included studies found CBT led to greater increases in employment than control conditions, though the review notes other research shows only modest employment gains and possible discordance between subjective and objective measures.
Nearly all participants experienced a diagnostic delay of several years for ME/CFS, often encountering physicians who resisted making the diagnosis.
Pacing, the method of balancing daily activity to energy levels, was described by interviewees and prior literature as one of very few helpful interventions for ME/CFS.
Being denied sick insurance and declared 'fit for work' precipitated a crisis that most interviewees described as more distressing and harder to cope with than the onset of ME/CFS itself.
Several respondents reported that depressive symptoms were not part of their original ME/CFS clinical picture but emerged after being declared fit for work by the Social Insurance Agency.
Suicidal ideation was spontaneously raised by interviewees in about half of the interviews, without the interviewer introducing the topic.

All interviewees reported that their health deteriorated as a consequence of contacts with and decisions by the Social Insurance Agency (SIA), which undermined the rest and pacing needed to manage ME/CFS.
Comorbid mental illness was common among participants, but interviewees and researchers noted these debuted after the onset of ME/CFS rather than preceding it; comorbid somatic illness was rare.

A subset of participants who reframed their denied-insurance experience as resulting from oppressive politics (often via online peer/political engagement) reported reduced loneliness and improved ability to make sense of their situation.

Participants with sufficient economic means who withdrew from the sick insurance system and adopted a 'philosophy of the present' reported improved subjective wellbeing and acceptance of their ME/CFS.
The paper describes FBN1 mutation on chromosome 15 as the genetic basis of Marfan syndrome, which was excluded in this patient by genetic testing.
Genetic testing ruled out Marfan syndrome in this pediatric patient who presented with joint hypermobility and was initially suspected of having MFS.
Subsequent genetic testing in the same patient ruled out both classical and hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome subtypes.

The authors argue that joint hypermobility was removed from the updated 2010 Ghent Nosology criteria due to perceived lack of specificity for Marfan syndrome pathophysiology, contributing to diagnostic ambiguity in cases like this one.

The authors emphasize that genetic testing should be prioritized alongside or ahead of Ghent Nosology clinical criteria to improve diagnostic accuracy for MFS and to generate appropriate differential diagnoses such as EDS.

The review notes that despite increasing recognition of craniocervical instability by spine surgeons, there is insufficient data supporting proposed radiographic parameters (clivo-axial angle, basion-axial interval, pB-C2) for diagnosing spinal instability in EDS patients.

The review reports a lack of high-quality evidence concerning the efficacy of occipitocervical fixation (OCF) surgery for treating chronic debilitating pain in EDS patients with craniocervical instability.
The previously reported FKBP14 c.362dupC frameshift variant results in complete loss of the FKBP22 protein.
A novel missense FKBP14 variant, c.587A>G; p.(Asp196Gly), also causes complete loss of FKBP22 protein.
A novel start codon variant in FKBP14 (c.2T>G; p.?) was identified in one proband with kyphoscoliotic EDS.

Across the 40 individuals reported to date with FKBP14-related kyphoscoliotic EDS, the consistent clinical features are kyphoscoliosis, generalized joint hypermobility, and congenital muscle hypotonia.
Severe vascular complications occur in 12.5% of individuals with FKBP14-related kyphoscoliotic EDS.
Microcornea, observed in two probands in this study, is reported as a previously unrecognized feature of FKBP14-related kyphoscoliotic EDS.
Immunocytochemistry on dermal fibroblasts from FKBP14-deficient probands showed intracellular retention of types III and VI collagen, a mechanism not previously demonstrated in EDS-FKBP14.
Microcornea was identified as a previously unreported clinical feature in two probands with FKBP14-related kyphoscoliotic EDS.
Both the c.587A>G missense variant and the c.362dupC frameshift variant were shown to cause complete loss of the FKBP22 protein.
Immunocytochemistry on dermal fibroblasts from FKBP14 patients provided the first evidence of intracellular retention of type III and VI collagen.
Scratch wound assays performed on FKBP14-deficient dermal fibroblasts were largely normal, indicating no major impairment in cell migration/wound closure.
Western blot analysis of proteins involved in the unfolded protein response and autophagy did not reveal significant upregulation in dermal fibroblasts from FKBP14 patients.
The paper reports a newly detected gene mutation identified in a patient with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome who also presented with elastosis perforans serpiginosa, a skin manifestation.
Vascular (type IV) Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is caused by mutation in the COL3A1 gene, which encodes type III collagen, leading to vascular fragility.
The article states celiprolol is currently the only medication with potential benefit in preventing cardiovascular events in vascular EDS.
The reported patient with vascular EDS experienced multiple major cardiovascular events including aortic, coronary and carotid dissections and venous and arterial thrombosis.
Definitive diagnosis of vascular EDS is established through genetic testing, and management requires a multidisciplinary team with effective blood pressure control.
One child was falsely alleged by her caregiver to have disabling hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome despite not being hypermobile, and the mother sought a power wheelchair for her.
One child presented with fibromyalgia and an alleged mutation-negative diagnosis of Stickler syndrome, with symptoms reportedly occurring only in her mother's presence.

The index case, who had essentially not eaten for 6 years due to alleged food allergies, developed severe pain, used a wheelchair for ambulation beyond a few blocks, and was alleged to have dysautonomia requiring nighttime oxygen monitoring.
