One child had severe incapacitating intermittent pains and abdominal pain that resulted in unnecessary appendectomy, cholecystectomy, and pancreatectomy.
One child was diagnosed with arthritis that led to foot amputation and reported total body pain.

The authors describe characteristic diagnostic clues to medical child abuse presenting as chronic pain, including an unusual or atypical pattern to the pain, multiple additional atypical symptoms and diagnoses, and a generally well-appearing child.

Perpetrators of medical child abuse are described as over-invested in the child's symptoms, deriving tangible and intangible secondary gain from the child's alleged illnesses, and are able to present the child in a manner that enlists physicians to unwittingly aid in perpetuating the abuse.
Children who are victims of medical child abuse are highly over-medicalized and suffer significant morbidity, including in these cases unnecessary amputation and abdominal surgeries.
The authors note that multiple barriers exist to identifying and reporting medical child abuse to Child Protective Services, which must be recognized and overcome to protect these children.
Whole-exome sequencing identified a novel homozygous CHST14 frameshift deletion, confirmed by Sanger sequencing, in a patient with musculocontractural Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (mcEDS).
The same CHST14 mutation was not detected in 100 healthy controls, supporting its pathogenicity.

CHST14 encodes carbohydrate sulfotransferase 14, which converts chondroitin sulfate to dermatan sulfate; loss-of-function mutation is proposed to decrease dermatan sulfate proteoglycan (DSPG) levels and impair collagen fiber formation.

The patient presented with congenital equinovarus deformity, bilateral claw-shaped hands, binocular blindness from optic nerve atrophy, cholecystolithiasis, bilateral nephrohydrosis, and bilateral renal calculi, consistent with a multisystem musculocontractural EDS phenotype.

The patient developed sequential gastrointestinal perforations (colonic splenic flexure and gastric antrum) complicated by peritonitis and recurrent septic shock, ultimately leading to multiple organ dysfunction and death.

During septic shock following gastrointestinal perforation, laboratory tests showed markedly elevated white blood cell count, procalcitonin, and pro-BNP, indicating severe infection and cardiac injury.
To date, 66 patients from 48 families with mcEDS-CHST14 and five patients from four families with mcEDS-DSE have been reported in the literature.
Prior to this case, only two genes, CHST14 and DSE, had been reported to be associated with musculocontractural EDS.
The authors hypothesize that prolonged bed rest after orthopedic surgery weakened gastrointestinal peristalsis, contributing to secondary intestinal obstruction that worsened intestinal perforation.
The patient had classical EDS type I caused by COL5A mutations, associated with disorganized collagen fibril aggregation typical of the disorder.

A single textured breast implant was found to be surrounded by two independent, physically distinct capsules: an internal capsule tightly adherent to the implant and an external capsule attached to surrounding subcutaneous tissue.
The internal capsule displayed unexpectedly organized, unidirectionally aligned mature collagen with increased cellularity, atypical for the typically disorganized collagen seen in EDS.
Trichrome and Herovici staining showed the internal capsule contained thick fibrous tissue with increased, predominantly mature collagen deposition compared with the external capsule.
Immunofluorescence staining showed significantly increased αSMA-positive myofibroblasts in the internal capsule compared with the external capsule, indicating a high mechanical stress environment.

Immunofluorescence staining revealed significantly higher expression of the inflammatory cytokine MCP1 in the internal capsule compared with the external capsule, linking mechanical stress to inflammatory signaling.

The external capsule showed loosely dispersed, irregular, non-aligned collagen fibers with low myofibroblast and MCP1 expression, consistent with classic disorganized type I EDS collagen architecture.

The authors propose that local mechanical stress from tight implant adherence can override the underlying genetic collagen defect in EDS, producing organized collagen architecture and inflammatory signaling distinct from the disorganized phenotype typical of the disorder.

The patient underwent complete internal and external capsulectomy with exchange to a smooth round 560-cm3 silicone implant, followed by an uncomplicated postoperative course with a 5-day course of Keflex.

Three of 39 females with connective tissue disorder features and negative CTD gene panel testing had an intermediate/gray zone FMR1 CGG repeat expansion (45-54 repeats), a 1:13 ratio significantly higher than the 1:66 ratio reported in a general population newborn screening study.

FMR1 premutation status can reduce FMRP levels, which is important for maintaining extracellular matrix-related proteins including matrix metallopeptidase 9 and elastin, potentially contributing to connective tissue disorder presentation.

Elevated FMR1 mRNA in premutation carriers causes protein sequestration and RNA toxicity, affecting multiple gene families and organ systems and contributing to immune-mediated inflammation seen in connective tissue disorders.
In a survey of 344 FMR1 premutation carrier females (age 19-81), 45% had an immune-mediated disorder, most commonly autoimmune thyroiditis (24%) followed by fibromyalgia (10%).
About one-fifth of FMR1 premutation carrier females had fragile X-associated primary ovarian insufficiency (FXPOI), and one-fourth had chronic muscle pain.

A prior study found an association between FMR1 CGG repeat premutation expansions (66-150 repeats) and connective tissue problems in five females with a hypermobile EDS phenotype, implicating RNA toxicity, mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammation.
The three gray zone females in this study each had two AGG interruptions, consistent with the expected range reported in premutation cohorts (mean 0.7±0.7, range 0-2 in 57 premutation females).

A 26-year-old female with joint hypermobility (Beighton score 7/9), recurrent joint dislocations/subluxations, persistent tachycardia, hypothyroidism, and weekly migraine headaches was found to carry an FMR1 gray zone allele of 51 CGG repeats alongside a normal 20-repeat allele.

A 45-year-old female with lifelong hypermobility, migraine headaches, carpal tunnel syndrome, heart palpitations and syncope, and thin/loose skin was found to carry an FMR1 gray zone allele of 48 CGG repeats alongside a normal 33-repeat allele.

A 44-year-old female presenting with fibromyalgia, tachycardia, migraines, tinnitus, hypertension and joint subluxation—whose two sons had features of POTS—was found to carry an FMR1 gray zone allele of 50 CGG repeats alongside a normal 24-repeat allele.

In the full cohort of 100 patients referred for connective tissue disorder evaluation, 48 of 80 females (60%) had no pathogenic, likely pathogenic, or predicted potentially pathogenic variants identified using a comprehensive next-generation sequencing connective tissue disorder gene panel.
The clinical phenotype of adult FMR1 gray zone allele carriers appears similar to that of premutation carriers, including neurological, molecular and cognitive features.

FMR1 premutations have been reported to cause dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis with enhanced cortisol release, impacting the immune system and promoting inflammation including in the central nervous system.

Isolated mild connective tissue abnormalities such as joint hypermobility, multiple dislocations, easy bruising, and poor wound healing are frequently found in patients with spontaneous cervical artery dissection, occurring in 50-96% of cases.
Formally diagnosed collagen vascular disorders meeting clinical and genetic criteria are found in only 1-5% of spontaneous cervical artery dissection cases.
More than 10% of patients with fibromuscular dysplasia have cervical artery dissections, most commonly involving the carotid arteries.
Close to 40% of patients with spontaneous cervical artery dissection were found to have underlying fibromuscular dysplasia.

CeAD patients with cerebrovascular FMD had more intracranial aneurysms and were more likely to have comorbid migraine compared to CeAD patients without FMD, while preceding minor trauma was inversely associated with cerebrovascular FMD.
Cerebrovascular FMD was identified in 8% of all patients with spontaneous cervical artery dissection in the multicenter IPSYS CeAD cohort study.
Elongated styloid processes, a relatively common anatomic variant, have been implicated as a mechanical cause of cervical artery dissection.
Among 1934 patients in the CADISP-plus international multicenter cohort, only 1.03% had a family history of cervical artery dissection.
In the IPSYS CeAD cohort of 1530 patients, only 1.0% (16 patients) had a first-degree family history of arterial dissection.
Familial spontaneous cervical artery dissection occurs at a younger mean age of onset (38.7 years) than sporadic cases in the general population (42-44 years).

Skin biopsy studies found a high prevalence (over 50%) of connective tissue abnormalities, mainly composite collagen fibril and elastic fiber fragmentation, in patients with sporadic cervical artery dissection.
The rate of hereditary connective tissue disorders confirmed by genetic testing in sporadic CeAD is very low, 0.5-2.0% for vascular EDS (COL3A1) and 0.6-0.9% for Marfan syndrome (FBN1).

Using a next-generation sequencing panel of 11 candidate genes, pathogenic mutations related to arterial connective tissue phenotypes were identified in 4 of 9 Caucasian pedigrees with familial spontaneous CeAD.
Whole-exome sequencing identified CeAD-causing variants in 5 of 17 pedigrees with familial spontaneous cervical artery dissection, underscoring a role for monogenic alterations in familial cases.
A genome-wide association study in 1393 CeAD patients and 14,416 controls found the A allele of PHACTR1 variant rs9349379 was a risk factor for cervical artery dissection.
The same PHACTR1 rs9349379[A] allele was similarly associated with increased risk for fibromuscular dysplasia.
A pooled meta-analysis of 29 GWAS studies (23,285 patients) showed the PHACTR1 rs9349379[A] allele was associated with increased risk of migraine without aura.

A meta-analysis of 4 GWAS (15,420 CAD cases, 15,062 controls) showed the same PHACTR1 rs9349379[A] allele was associated with decreased risk of coronary artery disease, contrasting with its risk-increasing role in CeAD and FMD.
PHACTR1 expression was positively correlated with the homozygous A allele at rs9349379 in healthy subjects' skin macrophages and fibroblasts.

Using induced pluripotent stem cells and CRISPR-Cas9 modification, the rs9349379[G] genotype was found to increase expression of endothelin-1 (ET-1), a potent vasoconstrictor implicated in vascular smooth muscle proliferation.
Higher plasma levels of Big ET-1, the precursor of endothelin-1, were found in healthy subjects homozygous for the rs9349379 G allele.

Recent upper respiratory tract infections, flu, and gastrointestinal infections were more common in patients with spontaneous cervical artery dissection, independent of coughing/sneezing triggers, though the causal mechanism is unclear.

In the IPSYS cohort of 2485 young stroke patients, migraine (particularly migraine without aura) was significantly more common in patients whose stroke was due to cervical artery dissection than those without.
A systematic review and meta-analysis reported that migraine is associated with a twofold increased risk of cervical artery dissection.
Younger age, family history, connective tissue disorders such as EDS type IV, and fibromuscular dysplasia were identified as risk factors for recurrent cervical artery dissection.
The IPSYS CeAD study reported a CeAD recurrence rate of 3.3% at median 34-month follow-up, with cerebrovascular FMD and history of migraine identified as independent predictors of recurrence.

Headache or neck pain is among the most common symptoms after cervical artery dissection, occurring in 65-95% of cases, with headache being the initial manifestation in 47% of internal carotid dissections and 33% of vertebral artery dissections.

In a large observational study comparing internal carotid vs vertebral artery dissection, patients with carotid dissection presented with headache more frequently but were less likely to have neck pain or ischemic stroke.
About one-fourth of patients with cervical artery dissection present with partial Horner's syndrome (miosis and ptosis without anhidrosis), making it the third most common symptom.

Pulsatile tinnitus occurs in 8% of patients with cervical artery dissection, more often with carotid dissections, and is associated with a more favorable clinical course and lower rate of ischemic stroke.

Cranial neuropathies occur predominantly with carotid artery dissections, with 12% of spontaneous carotid dissections presenting isolated or multiple cranial nerve palsies, most commonly involving the hypoglossal nerve.

Compressive cervical radiculopathy, most commonly at the C5-C6 level, or myelopathy from compression, spinal cord ischemia, or subarachnoid hemorrhage can rarely occur secondary to vertebral artery dissection.

Thrombolytic therapy for hyperacute ischemic stroke due to cervical artery dissection has a similar safety profile to thrombolysis for stroke of other etiologies, despite a lower rate of favorable outcomes, and should not be withheld due to CeAD.

Mechanical thrombectomy is safe and efficacious for anterior circulation intracranial large vessel occlusions secondary to cervical artery dissection and should be offered to patients with anterior and posterior circulation LVO and CeAD.
Emergent stenting of the internal carotid artery in tandem occlusion cases leads to more successful reperfusion but 90-day functional outcomes were similar to angioplasty or aspiration alone.

In the CADISS trial, ipsilateral stroke occurred in 2% of the antiplatelet group and 1% of the anticoagulant group, with one serious hemorrhagic complication in the anticoagulant group, and ipsilateral stroke/TIA rate was equal (2.4%) in both groups at 12 months.

The TREAT-CAD trial found the composite primary endpoint occurred more commonly in the aspirin group (23%) than the vitamin K antagonist group (15%), failing to demonstrate non-inferiority of aspirin to VKA.
Data for direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) in cervical artery dissection are limited, though they can be considered in selected cases.
A recent study suggested it may be reasonable to discontinue long-term antithrombotic therapy after the acute period in CeAD patients who have achieved full vascular healing.

Radiologic healing of CeAD occurs mostly within the first three months, with complete healing seen in approximately a third of cases (more commonly in carotid arteries), and 82% of healed cases healed within the first year.
After complete carotid artery occlusion from dissection, recanalization rate increases progressively over time: 16% at one month, 50% at three months, and 60% at 6 and 12 months.

Dissecting pseudoaneurysms were seen in 19% of carotid and 11% of vertebral dissections in one series, and up to 49.3% of CeAD patients in another series; patients with aneurysm formation were more likely to have multiple CeADs, arterial redundancies, migraine, and symptoms.

Most dissecting aneurysms resolve or improve over time: 83% of vertebral artery aneurysms and 54% of carotid artery aneurysms either resolved or improved, and patients with dissecting aneurysms tend to remain asymptomatic.

The risk of recurrent TIA/stroke after CeAD ranges between 0% and 13%, with most recurrent events occurring within the first few weeks after the dissection; multiple dissections, worsening stenosis/occlusion, chronic dissecting aneurysm, and hypertension are associated risk factors.

While recurrent CeAD is rare in most series (<5%), a recent large cohort found recurrence rates as high as 9.2%, with most recurrent events occurring within the first two months; younger age, family history, connective tissue disorders like EDS type IV, and FMD were identified as risk factors.
The IPSYS CeAD study reported a recurrence rate of 3.3% at a median follow-up of 34 months, with cerebrovascular FMD and a history of migraine identified as independent predictors of CeAD recurrence.
Half of CeAD patients suffer from a reduced quality of life, though good functional recovery (mRS 0-2) is achieved in 75-92% of cases and mortality is estimated to be low (<5%).

Functional recovery from ischemic stroke due to CeAD is no different from stroke due to other etiologies when controlled for age and other factors; worse functional outcomes are associated with stroke severity, arterial occlusion, carotid (vs vertebral) involvement, and older age.

Partial Horner's syndrome usually improves with healing of carotid dissection (though its long-term prognosis is not well studied), pulsatile tinnitus typically resolves 2-3 months after injury, and compressive symptoms improve/resolve over months with resolution of the intramural hematoma unless there is significant parenchymal damage.
Nationwide inpatient data revealed that the prevalence of dissection among stroke hospitalizations was approximately 7% among patients aged 18-40.
Spectroscopic analysis of blood after extremely low magnetic field treatment showed increased hemoglobin-oxygen affinity in fibromyalgia patients compared to sham-exposed controls.
Osmotic fragility measurements showed that erythrocytes from magnetic-field-treated fibromyalgia patients had increased elasticity and rehydration compared to sham-exposed controls.
Mid-IR spectral analysis revealed that magnetic field treatment altered the erythrocyte skeleton, with the α-helix component of protein secondary structure becoming dominant.

A graded extremely low magnetic field protocol (0.1 μT to 100 μT at 3.33 μT/min) was applied to fibromyalgia patients and associated with systemic blood changes linked to pain relief, compared to sham-exposed controls.
In an intragroup analysis, the GTT group showed a lower pain score on the VAS at the 60-day time point compared with baseline.
Cumulative pain scores (area under the curve of VAS) across the 6-month follow-up were lower in the GTT group than in the placebo group.
Affective pain scores (AUC) on the McGill Pain Questionnaire-Short Form were lower in the GTT group compared with placebo.
GTT did not significantly change quality of life or functional impact scores compared with placebo, as measured by the FIQ and SF-36.
Serum BDNF levels were higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy individuals at baseline.
Serum IL-10 levels were lower in fibromyalgia patients compared with healthy individuals at baseline.
Serum IL-8 levels did not differ significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy individuals.
After intervention, serum BDNF was lower in the GTT group than in the placebo group.
Serum IL-10 levels did not differ between the GTT and placebo groups after intervention.
Serum IL-8 levels did not differ between the GTT and placebo groups after intervention.
Serum dopamine levels did not differ significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy individuals.
Serum 5-HIAA (serotonin metabolite) levels did not differ significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy individuals.
Serum serotonin levels were lower in fibromyalgia patients compared with healthy individuals.
Serum dopamine levels did not differ between GTT and placebo groups.
Urinary BH4 levels did not differ between GTT and placebo groups.
Serum serotonin levels did not differ between GTT and placebo groups.
Serum 5-HIAA levels did not differ between GTT and placebo groups.
Higher baseline serum BDNF predicted a greater reduction in pain scores over the follow-up, regardless of treatment allocation.
Higher baseline serum 5-HIAA predicted a greater reduction in pain scores over the follow-up, regardless of treatment allocation.
Participants with a history of anxiety disorder showed a greater reduction in pain scores over the follow-up.
Higher baseline serum dopamine was associated with a lower effect of intervention on pain reduction across time.

A mixed ANCOVA model showed a significant overall effect of intervention type on VAS pain scores, while there was no significant time-by-intervention interaction and no significant effect of time alone.
Within the GTT group, cumulative pain scores fell from a pretreatment mean of 7.74 to 5.99 across the six follow-up assessments, a large within-group treatment effect.
Within the placebo group, cumulative pain scores also fell significantly from a pretreatment mean of 8.20 to 7.20, a medium within-group effect, smaller than that seen in the GTT group.
The absolute percentage reduction in pain from baseline was greater with GTT than with placebo, with an absolute mean difference of 16.60 percentage points, a moderate effect size.
The patient's serum tryptase level was elevated during an anaphylactic reaction to intravenous diclofenac, consistent with mast cell activation.
Urinary methylhistamine, a histamine metabolite, was detected at elevated levels approximately 4 hours after symptom onset, supporting the diagnosis of an allergic/anaphylactic reaction.
D-dimer was markedly elevated in the setting of anaphylaxis, reflecting activation of the coagulation cascade by allergic processes rather than pulmonary embolism.

Intravenous diclofenac administered for abdominal pain triggered a severe, life-threatening anaphylactic (Type I hypersensitivity) reaction within minutes in a patient with no prior known drug allergy.

The patient was successfully treated for anaphylaxis with epinephrine, antihistamines, intravenous fluids, oxygen therapy, and hydrocortisone, stabilizing within 24 hours in the ICU with no biphasic or multiphasic recurrence.
Montelukast, a CysLTR1 antagonist used for asthma, inhibited RANKL-induced osteoclast formation and bone damage in an animal model.
VDR-knockout mice show elevated serum IgE concentrations compared to wild-type animals.
Vitamin D reduced IgE generation by B lymphocytes, and a VDR agonist altered the IgE response in a type 1 allergy animal model.
Vitamin D added to monocytes reduced dendritic cell maturation (altered MHC class II expression) and shifted CD4+ T cells toward an IL-10-producing regulatory phenotype.
Vitamin D reduced CD40L-induced inflammation and increased IL-10 generation by CD4+ T cells, expanding FoxP3+/CTLA4+ regulatory T cells.

Increased IL-31 in skin and serum was reported in atopic dermatitis, chronic spontaneous urticaria, contact dermatitis, prurigo nodularis, cutaneous lymphoma, and mastocytosis, correlating with disease severity.
Serum IL-31 was elevated in postmenopausal women with reduced bone mineral density, but did not correlate with the degree of osteoporosis.

In chronic spontaneous urticaria patients, 12 weeks of low- or high-dose vitamin D3 supplementation significantly decreased urticaria severity scores, with a greater reduction at week 6 in the high-dose group, and medication scores decreased in both groups.
A study found a significant difference in blood vitamin D concentrations between chronic spontaneous urticaria subjects and controls.
Allergic sensitization, including to foods, was more frequent in young subjects with 25(OH)D deficiency, but no significant correlation between VD levels and food allergy was found in adults.
Baek et al. reported that reduced vitamin D concentrations may correlate with polysensitization to food allergens.

Calcitriol increased VDR numbers in mast cells, and VDR-Lyn complexes blocked Lyn-MyD88/FcεRI interaction, reducing NF-kB, MAPK activation, Syk phosphorylation, and TNF-α transcription (via reduced RNA Pol II and histone H3/H4 acetylation at the TNF-α promoter), indicating vitamin D deficiency promotes mast cell activation.
Vitamin D increased IL-10 mRNA expression and IL-10 secretion in animal mast cells in vitro.
In a mouse model, skin mast cells expressing VDR (versus VDR-deficient mast cells) were required for mast cell-mediated reduction of chronic UVB-induced skin inflammation.

Mast cells can convert 25OHD3 to 1α,25(OH)2D3 via CYP27B1, and these VD3 derivatives reduce mast cell production of pro-inflammatory mediators in a VDR-dependent manner; topical application of VD3 metabolites reduced skin inflammation, requiring mast cell VDR and CYP27B1.
More than 80% of systemic mastocytosis patients carry a somatic KIT codon 816 point mutation (D816V), which is used as a minor diagnostic criterion.
Osteoporosis prevalence in indolent systemic mastocytosis ranges from 18-28% by WHO criteria, while by ISCD criteria reduced BMD was found in about 9% of women and 28% of men with mastocytosis.

In indolent systemic mastocytosis patients without osteoporosis, over 70% had vitamin D deficiency; after 30 months of vitamin D (plus calcium as needed) supplementation, lumbar spine BMD increased by 2.1%, with no change at the hip, and about 60% still had low VD levels after 30 months.
Reduced vitamin D concentrations may be a risk factor for cutaneous mast cell tumors in dogs.
VDR is expressed in both inflammatory and clonal canine mast cells, but VDR expression recurrence is higher in tumoral mast cells.
Calcitriol showed anti-proliferative activity against canine neoplastic cells, including the C2 cutaneous mast cell tumor cell line.
A study reported a relationship between serum tryptase, osteoprotegerin, and C-terminal telopeptide of type 1 collagen in patients with severe systemic mastocytosis variants.
Mast cells express RANK ligand, which drives osteoclastic activity and contributes to bone resorption and osteoporosis.
In contrast to other mast cell mediators that induce bone loss, histamine has been reported to increase bone growth, leading to osteosclerosis.
Vitamin D binding protein (VDBP) was increased in patients with chronic spontaneous urticaria compared to normal controls.

Sera from patients with chronic spontaneous urticaria stimulated VEGF production in mast cells via the PI3K/Akt/p38 MAPK/HIF-1α axis in an IgE-dependent manner, and vitamin D reduced VEGF production by blocking this pathway.
Reduced vitamin D concentrations may be a risk factor for cutaneous mast cell tumors in dogs.
Calcitriol demonstrated anti-proliferative actions on several canine neoplastic cell lines, including the C2 cutaneous mast cell tumor line.
VDR is broadly expressed in both inflammatory and clonal canine mast cells, but its expression recurrence rate is higher in tumoral mast cells.

The proportion of mast cells expressing CYP24A1 was markedly increased in lesional skin of squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, and actinic keratosis compared to only 0.5-2.9% in non-lesional skin.
In LAD2 mast cells isolated from a patient with mast cell sarcoma/leukaemia, approximately 34% of cells were VDR-positive and 6.5% were CYP24A1-positive.
CYP27A1 was notably expressed in mast cells within basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma lesions.
Contrary to the deficiency hypothesis, increased vitamin D concentrations have also been correlated with increased IgE production, indicating a contradictory dose relationship.
Cairncross et al. found that increased 25(OH)D levels were correlated with a greater risk of food allergy in children.
CD1 wild-type mice treated with high-dose 1α,25(OH)2D3 developed skin inflammation resembling atopic dermatitis, with markedly increased thymic stromal lymphopoietin mRNA levels.
Injection of SVF or ADSCs into HCL-induced interstitial cystitis bladders markedly reduced mast cell infiltration compared to untreated HCL-induced cystitis, as assessed by Toluidine Blue staining.
SVF or ADSCs treatment reduced CD3+ T-cell activation/infiltration in HCL-induced cystitis bladder tissue compared to untreated HCL-induced cystitis.
SVF or ADSCs treatment reduced bladder fibrosis in HCL-induced cystitis compared to untreated HCL-induced cystitis, as assessed by Masson Trichrome staining.
SVF injection into the bladder submucosa showed greater therapeutic efficacy than cultured ADSCs in improving histopathological outcomes of HCL-induced cystitis.
Both SVF cells and cultured ADSCs improved histopathological outcomes of HCL-induced bladder injury in a time-dependent manner.
Tspo-/- mice showed significantly worse posturing scores than Tspo fl/fl mice during DSS-induced colitis (days 5-7).
Tspo-/- mice had significantly worse stool scores (rectal bleeding/diarrhea) than Tspo fl/fl mice during DSS colitis.
Tspo-/- mice lost significantly more body weight than Tspo fl/fl mice from day 4 through day 7 of DSS treatment.
Colon length after 7 days of DSS treatment was significantly shorter (a marker of colitis severity) in Tspo-/- mice compared to Tspo fl/fl mice.
Histopathological quantification showed a greater proximal extent of epithelial ulceration (ratio of affected:total colon length) in Tspo-/- mice than Tspo fl/fl mice.
Krt18 expression, a marker of intestinal epithelial integrity, was significantly downregulated only in Tspo-/- colons after 7 days of DSS-induced colitis, indicating greater epithelial loss.
Baseline Cd34 (mature mast cell marker) expression was significantly elevated in Tspo-/- colons compared to Tspo fl/fl colons, though not different during active colitis.
Mast cell tryptase (Mcp6) expression was significantly elevated at baseline and at all colitis timepoints in Tspo-/- colons compared to Tspo fl/fl colons, indicating increased mast cell activation.
Cd11c (macrophage/dendritic cell marker) expression peaked earlier and was significantly higher at day-4 of colitis in Tspo-/- colons compared to Tspo fl/fl colons.
F4/80 macrophage marker expression increased with colitis progression but showed no significant difference between Tspo-/- and Tspo fl/fl colons.
Mcp1 (macrophage activation marker) expression increased with colitis but was not significantly different between Tspo-/- and Tspo fl/fl colons.

Tnfα expression increased significantly from baseline to day-7 in both genotypes during colitis, but the trend toward higher relative expression in Tspo-/- colons did not reach statistical significance.
Intestinal stem cell markers Lgr5 and Ascl2 showed no baseline expression difference between Tspo-/- and Tspo fl/fl colons.
Epithelial adhesion/permeability regulators Cdh1 and Ndrg2 showed no baseline expression difference between Tspo-/- and Tspo fl/fl colons.
Cyclin D1 (Ccnd1), a Wnt target relevant to cell cycle progression, was significantly decreased at baseline in Tspo-/- colons compared to Tspo fl/fl colons, while cMyc showed no difference.
Baseline Cdx2, an intestinal identity transcription factor regulating immune cell infiltration, was significantly upregulated in Tspo-/- colons compared to Tspo fl/fl colons.
Socs3 expression showed a non-significant trend toward higher baseline expression in Tspo-/- colons compared to Tspo fl/fl colons.
Baseline oxidative-stress-related genes Cd36, Fpn1, Hmox1, and Nrf2 were not significantly different between Tspo-/- and Tspo fl/fl colons.
Acadm, involved in mitochondrial medium-chain fatty acid β-oxidation, was significantly increased at baseline in Tspo-/- colons compared to Tspo fl/fl colons.
Other mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation genes (Cpt1a, Acadl, Hadha) showed no significant baseline expression difference between Tspo-/- and Tspo fl/fl colons.
On gross pathology, Tspo-/- mice showed subjectively more petechiae, ecchymoses, and mucosal ulceration than Tspo fl/fl mice after DSS-induced colitis.
Chronic HDM sensitization abolished the normal habituation pattern of ambulatory activity seen in the open field test, unlike PBS controls who showed typical habituation.

HDM-sensitized mice showed increased time spent in the center zone of the open field after treatment compared with their own pre-treatment baseline, suggesting reduced anxiety-like behavior, while PBS controls showed no such change.

In the light-dark transition test, HDM-sensitized mice lost their normal preference for the dark chamber, spending nearly equal time in light and dark, unlike PBS controls who retained dark preference.
HDM-sensitized mice showed a marked increase in light-dark transition frequency compared to their pre-sensitization baseline, whereas PBS controls did not change.

In the Y-maze novel arm test, chronic HDM-sensitized mice lost preference for the novel arm and spent more time in the familiar arm, indicating impaired spatial memory, whereas PBS controls retained normal novel arm preference.
HDM-sensitized mice showed significantly reduced sucrose preference compared to PBS controls, indicative of anhedonia/depressive-like behavior.
HDM-sensitized mice showed increased immobility time during the last 3 minutes of the tail suspension test compared to PBS controls, suggesting increased depressive-like behavior.
Forced swim test immobility time did not significantly differ between HDM-sensitized and PBS control mice.
Six weeks of intranasal HDM administration caused lung inflammation with increased BAL total cell counts and increased BAL protein concentrations compared to PBS controls.
Lung digest cytokine analysis showed increased Th2 cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13), Th17 cytokine IL-17, and TNF-alpha in HDM-sensitized mice compared to controls.

Serum levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1beta, IL-2, and IFN-gamma, as well as Th2-related cytokines IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13, were significantly elevated in HDM-sensitized mice compared with PBS controls.
Serum VEGF concentrations were significantly elevated in HDM-sensitized mice compared to PBS controls, a factor also linked to blood-brain barrier permeability and depression severity in asthmatics.
Serum TNF-alpha, IL-6 and IL-17 levels were not significantly different between PBS control and HDM-sensitized mice, contrary to the authors' initial hypothesis.

Brain c-Fos protein expression, an indirect marker of neuronal activity and mast cell activation, was significantly increased in HDM-sensitized mice compared with PBS controls, prominently in the periventricular thalamus.
Brain chymase (a mast cell serine protease) protein expression was significantly increased in HDM-sensitized mice compared to PBS controls, indicating mast cell activation in the brain.
Brain Iba-1 (microglial activation marker) expression was not significantly different between HDM-sensitized and PBS control mice, suggesting microglia were not overtly activated.
Brain GFAP (astroglial injury marker) expression was significantly elevated in HDM-sensitized mice compared to PBS controls, indicating astrocyte involvement in the neuroinflammatory response.

No cleaved caspase-3 was detected in brain homogenates of either HDM-sensitized or PBS control mice, and TUNEL staining confirmed the absence of apoptotic cell death, indicating behavioral changes were not due to neuronal apoptosis.
Whole brain digest levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1beta, IL-2, IL-6 and TNF-alpha were not significantly different between HDM-sensitized and PBS control mice.
Brain fractalkine concentrations were significantly elevated in HDM-sensitized mice compared to PBS controls, while serum fractalkine was decreased and lung fractalkine was unchanged.
The relative brain chymase/GAPDH protein ratio was negatively correlated with sucrose preference across individual mice, linking brain mast cell activation to anhedonia severity.
No significant correlations were found between relative c-Fos, Iba-1, or GFAP/GAPDH protein ratios and sucrose preference, unlike the chymase correlation.
Lung c-kit positive mast cell numbers were significantly increased in HDM-sensitized mice compared with PBS controls, confirming mast cell recruitment to inflamed lungs.

Brain c-kit positive mast cell numbers, though extremely low overall, were not significantly different between HDM-sensitized and PBS control mice by flow cytometry, despite mast cell activation markers (chymase, c-Fos) being elevated.
IENFD in dermatomyositis patients was not significantly different from healthy controls, indicating no small-fiber neuropathy in DM skin.
IENFD was significantly reduced in cutaneous lupus erythematosus patients compared with both healthy controls and dermatomyositis patients, indicating small-fiber neuropathy in CLE skin.
Within CLE patients, those with cutaneous neuropathic symptoms (pruritus, pain, or burning) showed significantly lower IENFD than asymptomatic CLE patients.
A significant reduction in IENFD was observed across different anatomic skin locations (face, trunk, limbs) when comparing disease groups to healthy controls.
Epidermal NGF expression was significantly increased in dermatomyositis patients compared with both healthy controls and CLE patients.
Epidermal AREG expression was similar across dermatomyositis, CLE, and healthy control skin.
Epidermal Sema3A expression was significantly decreased in dermatomyositis patients compared with healthy controls and CLE patients.
In cultured primary human keratinocytes, treatment with IL-18 (5 ng/mL) induced increased NGF protein expression, peaking at 18 hours.
In cultured primary human keratinocytes, treatment with IL-31 (300 ng/mL) induced increased NGF protein expression, peaking at 18 hours.
Cutaneous neuropathic symptoms (pruritus, pain, or burning sensation) were reported in 60% of dermatomyositis patients and 31% of CLE patients.
Sudomotor sensor responses to a deep breathing test were very weak or absent in the DPN group, with all controls showing larger responses than DPN participants.
Skin evaporation, measured by the humidity sensor on the toe probe, was lower in the DPN group compared to controls.
Average skin temperature at the toe was higher in the DPN group than in controls.
Sudomotor sensor responses agreed with sensory neurography amplitudes from the sural nerve when measured on the same foot.
The standard monofilament test gave normal (falsely negative) results for two of the five DPN participants, unlike the sudomotor probe.
Mean cutaneous silent period (CSP) latency, a marker of small fiber function, was significantly longer in primary Sjögren's syndrome (pSS) patients than in healthy controls.
Mean CSP duration was significantly shorter in pSS patients compared with healthy controls, consistent with small fiber involvement.
CSP latency and duration did not differ significantly between pSS patients with versus without neuropathic pain features (LANSS) or central sensitization (CSI) profiles.
CSP latency correlated positively and CSP duration correlated negatively with the ESSPRI dryness subscore, indicating worse small fiber function with greater dryness symptoms.
CSP latency correlated positively and CSP duration correlated negatively with the ESSPRI fatigue subscore.
CSP latency correlated positively and CSP duration correlated negatively with the ESSPRI pain subscore.
CSP latency correlated positively and CSP duration correlated negatively with mean ESSPRI score, the strongest correlations observed among clinical parameters.
CSP duration correlated negatively with the SF-36 bodily pain subscore, the only significant SF-36 correlation found.
Longer CSP duration correlated with lower (better) SF-36 bodily pain subscore in pSS patients.
Higher HADS anxiety scores correlated with longer CSP duration in pSS patients, while LANSS and CSI showed no significant correlations.

IBS is characterized by disturbed autonomic balance with reduced vagal tone and reduced parasympathetic nervous system activity compared with healthy individuals, as shown in a recent meta-analysis of resting HRV (HF).
Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) significantly increased normalized HF power (vagal/parasympathetic activity) compared with sham-taVNS in IBS patients.
taVNS significantly reduced IBS symptom severity (IBS-SSS) compared with sham-taVNS.
taVNS significantly reduced VAS pain scores compared with sham-taVNS.
taVNS significantly reduced both anxiety (SAS) and depression (SDS) scores compared with sham-taVNS.
Ear acupressure significantly reduced perceived stress compared with the non-treatment control condition.
In the taVNS study, HF-norm was negatively correlated with pain intensity, indicating that greater parasympathetic activity was associated with lower pain severity.
Quality of life (IBS-QoL) was negatively correlated with pain intensity in the taVNS study.

In the CBT with relaxation study, LF/HF ratio was significantly positively correlated, and HF negatively correlated, with changes in IBS symptoms, anxiety, depression, and stress at 12-week follow-up.
A pilot study of slow diaphragmatic breathing training did not show the expected effect on autonomic tension or IBS symptom severity.
Hand acupuncture (Park and Cha) showed no significant intergroup post-test differences and intra-group tests did not show impact of the intervention on autonomic nervous system changes.
Although Park and Cha did not report intergroup post-test statistics for stress, review authors calculated a moderate effect size showing the intervention group experienced less stress than controls.
Across the six analyzed studies, four (taVNS, ear acupressure, CBT with relaxation, and yoga) showed the expected increase in parasympathetic activity following intervention.
In four of six studies, therapeutic interventions significantly reduced IBS symptoms coinciding with increased parasympathetic activity of the ANS.
Pain severity was measured in three studies, of which two demonstrated a significant decrease in pain in the intervention group.
Anxiety and depression were measured in five studies, with a significant reduction observed after three interventions.

Quasi-experimental studies scored on average 6/9 and randomized controlled trials scored on average 8/13 on JBI critical appraisal checklists, with higher bias risk driven by unclear control of concurrent treatments.

A prior meta-analysis (Wolf et al.) did not confirm the validity of autonomic tone measurements as a biomarker of taVNS efficacy, but that analysis was conducted in healthy people rather than clinical populations with reduced autonomic tone.
A heterozygous FBN1 c.479G>A (p.C160Y) mutation was identified in four affected members of family 1 with Marfan syndrome and ectopia lentis, and was absent in unaffected relatives.
A heterozygous FBN1 c.4049G>A (p.C1350Y) mutation was identified in the proband of family 2 with Marfan syndrome, aortic aneurysm and ectopia lentis, and was absent in her unaffected mother.

Bioinformatic modeling predicted that both cysteine substitutions abolish native disulfide bond formation (C1-C3 for C160Y, C5-C6 for C1350Y), with SIFT and PolyPhen-2 predicting damaging effects on protein structure/function.

3D structural modeling showed the C160Y mutation caused significant conformational changes in the EGF2-cbEGF1 region of fibrillin-1, whereas C1350Y caused only slight structural changes in the cbEGF20-24 region.
DUET stability analysis predicted that both the C160Y and C1350Y mutations destabilize the fibrillin-1 protein structure.
Surface plasmon resonance showed the C160Y mutation did not significantly alter the binding affinity of the fibrillin-1 EGF2-cbEGF1 fragment for LTBP1 (KD 1.53 μM wild-type vs 1.23 μM mutant).

Recombinant fibrillin-1 EGF2-cbEGF1 peptide carrying the C160Y mutation showed markedly increased degradation rate compared with wild-type after trypsin or chymotrypsin digestion, being completely hydrolyzed by 60 min (trypsin) or 30 min (chymotrypsin) while wild-type was only partially hydrolyzed.

The cbEGF20-24 fragment with the C1350Y mutation showed no significant change in proteolytic sensitivity to trypsin but showed decreased thermostability and increased sensitivity to chymotrypsin digestion compared with wild-type.

LC-MS/MS analysis showed that the C160Y and C1350Y mutations altered chymotrypsin cleavage sites (shifted from position 140 to 160 for C160Y region, and a new cleavage site created in the FBN1 K1347-W1354 peptide for C1350Y), and the FBN1 C160-R180 tryptic peptide was absent from mutant degradation products.

Both patients carrying FBN1 cysteine substitutions (C160Y and C1350Y) presented with ectopia lentis, and the C1350Y patient additionally had retinal detachment, consistent with cysteine-replacement mutations causing more severe ocular involvement in Marfan syndrome.
CGRP-immunopositive neurons comprised approximately 19% of myenteric neurons in mouse colon with no significant regional variation between proximal, mid, and distal colon.
CGRP-immunopositive myenteric neuron cell bodies were significantly larger than the average size of all Hu+ myenteric neurons.
Nitric oxide synthase-positive neurons comprised approximately 42% of myenteric neurons overall in mouse colon.
NOS+ neurons represented a lower proportion of myenteric neurons in proximal colon compared to mid and distal colon.
Nearly all myenteric neurons were co-labeled by the pan-neuronal markers Hu and peripherin, with Hu+/peripherin- neurons comprising about 6% and Hu-/peripherin+ cells being rare.
NOS+ myenteric neurons showed regional variation along the colon, with a lower proportion in proximal colon compared to mid and distal colon.
Of 118 putatively multiaxonal (Dogiel type II) neurons identified by peripherin immunoreactivity, all were CGRP-immunopositive, supporting CGRP as a marker of this IPAN-like morphology.
Quantification of total myenteric neuron population was based on Hu+ neurons, totaling 8576 neurons across animals with an average of 1225 ± 239 neurons per animal (n=7).

A 16-year-old girl with longstanding poorly controlled type 1 diabetes presented with a three-year history of recurrent nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain, later diagnosed as severe diabetic gastroparesis.
Gastric emptying scintigraphy using a technetium-99mTc-labeled liquid meal confirmed delayed gastric emptying (gastric meal retention), establishing the diagnosis of diabetic gastroparesis.
Treatment with metoclopramide (starting at 30 mg/day) led to progressive improvement of gastrointestinal symptoms, allowing reintroduction of oral feeding.

Initiation of an advanced hybrid closed loop insulin delivery system (Medtronic MiniMed 780G) achieved prompt improvement of glycemic control, with all glucose metrics meeting recommended clinical targets within three weeks.
Nerve conduction studies revealed peripheral neuropathy affecting mainly the lower limbs, indicating additional diabetic microvascular complication.
Fundus examination revealed early-stage diabetic retinopathy, another microvascular complication co-occurring with the gastroparesis.
Diabetic nephropathy was ruled out, as albuminuria in a 24-hour urine collection was normal.
At three-month follow-up after discharge, the patient had persistent remission of gastrointestinal symptoms, weight gain of 5.9 kg, and improved quality of life.
Within the largest adult T1D clinical registry in the United States, 4.8% of patients had a clinical diagnosis of gastroparesis.
A community-based study found a 10-year cumulative incidence of diabetic gastroparesis of 5% in patients with type 1 diabetes, with greater risk compared to type 2 diabetes.
Cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy, the most prevalent form of diabetic autonomic impairment, affects at least 20% of people with diabetes across all ages.

Diabetic gastroparesis is associated with an increased risk of postprandial hypoglycemia, termed 'gastric hypoglycemia,' due to a mismatch between prandial insulin absorption and delayed postprandial glucose rise.
Lower HbA1c levels have been shown to be associated with reduced gastrointestinal symptoms and faster gastric emptying in diabetic gastroparesis.
Daly et al. reported significant reductions in HbA1c and mean glucose in five adult patients with T1D and gastroparesis using hybrid closed loop systems over one year.
Kaur et al. showed that hybrid closed loop systems had similar effectiveness and safety in adults with T1D and gastroparesis compared to age, sex, and diabetes duration-matched controls.

Mast cell-deficient Kit-W-sh mice showed decreased viral myocarditis severity and cardiac fibrosis and improved cardiac function compared with wild-type mice during CVB3 infection, associated with reduced cardiac Ly6C+ monocyte/macrophage influx.

Mast cell-deficient mice showed slightly higher viral titres than wild-type mice despite reduced myocarditis and fibrosis, suggesting mast cells contribute more to immunopathology than viral clearance.

Reconstitution of mast cell-deficient Wsh mice with bone marrow-derived mast cells decreased viral titre but worsened survival and viral myocarditis severity, confirming a causal pathogenic role for mast cells.
In co-culture, cardiac fibroblasts trigger mast cell degranulation and secretion of CCL2 and TNF-alpha via early production of stem cell factor (SCF).
Mast cell-derived fibrogenic mediators including TNF-alpha stimulate cardiac fibroblasts to increase CCL2, alpha-smooth muscle actin, collagen, and TGF-beta expression, aggravating cardiac fibrosis.
Mast cell- and fibroblast-derived CCL2 are both essential for driving cardiac Ly6C+ monocyte/macrophage influx during CVB3 infection.
Administering recombinant mouse SCF to CVB3-infected mice worsened viral myocarditis by accelerating mast cell accumulation and cardiac influx of Ly6C+ monocytes/macrophages.
Mast cell-derived TNF-alpha stimulated cardiac fibroblasts to increase CCL2, alpha-smooth muscle actin, collagen, and TGF-beta expression, aggravating cardiac fibrosis.
CCL2 produced by both mast cells and fibroblasts was essential for driving cardiac Ly6C+ monocyte/macrophage influx during CVB3 infection.
Cardiac fibroblasts trigger mast cell degranulation and CCL2/TNF-alpha secretion by producing early stem cell factor during initial CVB3 infection.
Probable RBD symptom scores and dysautonomia (SCOPA-AUT) scores were very strongly correlated across the PD cohort.
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension prevalence in the PD cohort increased from 8% at baseline to 13% by year 3.

PD subjects with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension had significantly higher SCOPA-AUT autonomic symptom scores than those without, validating the subjective questionnaire against objective orthostatic vitals.
The proportion of PD subjects reporting dysautonomia symptoms rose from 64% at baseline to 76% by year 3.
The proportion of PD subjects with positive probable RBD symptoms increased from 44% at baseline to 53% by year 3.

Self-reported RBD symptoms were inconsistent over time, with 22% of subjects who reported RBD symptoms early losing them by year 3, more variable than dysautonomia symptom persistence (also 22% loss).

Baseline SCOPA-AUT autonomic symptom scores did not differ between PD subjects taking medications with potential autonomic effects and those who were not, and starting PD medication did not differentially affect the 1-year change in SCOPA-AUT scores.

Mixed-effects modeling showed dysautonomia (total SCOPA-AUT score) had a large, significant effect on progression of motor symptoms, activities of daily living, non-motor symptoms, anxiety, depression, and total MDS-UPDRS score, but not cognition.
Dysautonomia and pRBD showed no significant effect on progression of cognitive impairment (MoCA score), possibly due to the early-stage disease of the cohort.
pRBD alone did not significantly predict symptom progression; only its interaction with dysautonomia significantly correlated with activities-of-daily-living decline (MDS-UPDRS part 2).

Baseline SCOPA-AUT scores did not significantly correlate with DATSCAN (dopamine transporter imaging) progression, consistent with prior literature on poor correlation between DATSCAN and motor sign progression.
Among SCOPA-AUT sub-domains, gastrointestinal, sexual, and pupillomotor symptoms most correlated with progression of motor and non-motor PD symptoms.
PD subjects positive for both dysautonomia and pRBD (DysA+/pRBD+) presented with a more severe pattern of motor and non-motor symptoms than other subgroups.

At baseline, DysA+/pRBD+ subjects had significantly worse dysautonomia, anxiety, depression, RBD score, activities of daily living, and total UPDRS scores than DysA-/pRBD- subjects; H&Y motor score differences only emerged by year 3.

Statistically significant differences between subgroups were more frequent when groups differed in dysautonomia status than when they differed in pRBD status, indicating dysautonomia is the stronger discriminator of PD subtype.
Cognitive symptoms (MoCA score) progressed significantly over time only in the combined DysA+/pRBD+ subgroup, not in the other three subgroups.

Although depression and anxiety scores differed significantly between DysA+/pRBD+ and DysA-/pRBD- groups at baseline and year 3, these mood symptoms did not show significant progression over time within groups.

Unsupervised hierarchical clustering of baseline motor and non-motor symptom scores in the PD cohort revealed four distinct clusters, with one cluster comprising sleep- and autonomic-related symptoms (RBDSQ, SCOPA-AUT, MDS-UPDRS part 1 questions 7-13).
Of 124 Italian Long-COVID care centers surveyed, half were located in northern Italy, with Lombardy alone representing nearly one-fifth of all centers.
Most Long-COVID centers provided outpatient or day-hospital care, with only 5% offering inpatient hospital admission.
Nine percent of Long-COVID centers provided care to pediatric patients.
Access to Long-COVID centers occurred mainly through scheduled follow-up of previously hospitalized patients, primary care referral, and specialist referral.
Nearly half of Long-COVID centers were established early in the pandemic (March-September 2020), but new centers continued to be created through the survey period (March-April 2022).
Almost all Long-COVID centers had defined communication pathways with primary care physicians, but telemedicine and domiciliary care were used by only a minority.
Long-COVID centers followed a mean of 40 patients per month, with 22.3 first visits and 23.5 follow-up visits per month on average.

Long-COVID center coordinators were most commonly specialists in respiratory diseases, infectious disease, or internal medicine, with fewer coordinators from geriatrics, cardiology, pediatrics, or neurology.
The number of specialist competences available at each center was highly heterogeneous, with about 14.5% of centers having only a single specialist (most commonly infectious disease or pulmonology).
Case volume (patients followed, first visits, follow-up visits per month) did not differ significantly between centers with single/dual specialist support versus centers with multiple specialties.
Mean number of patients followed did not differ significantly between centers established early in the pandemic versus those established later.

Most centers used a broad panel of diagnostic tests to support Long-COVID assessment, including blood testing, six-minute walking test, HRCT, ECG, heart ultrasonography, arterial blood gas testing, and spirometry with DLCO.
About half of the centers complemented diagnostic testing with multidimensional, psychological, functional status, quality of life, cognitive, and nutritional assessments.

Centers used a variety of validated instruments: Hamilton scales for psychological evaluation, Barthel/IADL/ADL/SPPB for functional status, MMSE/MoCA for cognition, EQ-5D/SF-36 for quality of life, and MUST/MNA for nutritional assessment.
Automated pupillometry parameters were significantly different in ATTRv patients compared to both pre-symptomatic TTR mutation carriers and healthy controls.
In ATTRv patients, pupillometry findings significantly correlated with disease duration.
Pupillometry findings correlated significantly with Neuropathy Impairment Score (NIS) in ATTRv patients.
Pupillometry findings correlated significantly with Sudoscan measurements from the feet in ATTRv patients, suggesting shared small-fiber autonomic pathology.
Pupillometry findings correlated significantly with quality-of-life impairment as measured by the Norfolk QoL-DN questionnaire in ATTRv patients.

The authors' own study found that post-COVID-19 syndrome is linked to multisystem disease, which helps explain the persistent impairments in health-related quality of life, physical function, and psychological wellbeing seen after COVID-19.
The article highlights that hospital physicians should consider the likelihood of myocarditis in patients presenting with post-COVID-19 syndrome, along with its longer-term implications.
Serum exosome-associated mitochondrial DNA levels were elevated in ME/CFS patients specifically following an exercise challenge, but not at baseline.
Exosomes isolated from ME/CFS patients stimulated significant release of IL-1β from cultured human microglial cells.
The authors propose that microglial activation by serum-derived exosomes may represent a novel pathogenic mechanism and a potential treatment target in ME/CFS.

Serum antibody (IgG) responses against bacterial flagellin peptides, mainly from Lachnospiraceae and related Clostridiales, were significantly overrepresented in patients with severe ME/CFS compared to matched healthy controls.
The overall number of antibody-bound peptides per individual and the Shannon α-diversity of the Ig epitope repertoire did not differ significantly between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
No single peptide in the 244,000-antigen library was significantly differentially bound between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls after false discovery rate correction using Fisher's exact test.
A specific Roseburia inulinivorans flagellin peptide elicited antibody responses in half of ME/CFS patients but only 15% of healthy controls, a 3.3-fold overrepresentation.
On average, antibody responses against overrepresented bacterial flagellins were 2.2-fold more frequent in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls.

Machine learning models trained on antibody repertoire data classified ME/CFS patients from healthy controls with AUC 0.67 (metagenomic antigen subgroup), 0.66 (whole library), and 0.59 (flagellins alone).
Antibody responses against several Bacteroidetes (Bacteroidales) surface and secretion-associated proteins were more frequent in healthy controls than in ME/CFS patients.

Antibody responses against nonflagellin Clostridiales proteins (e.g., toxin A, an adhesin from Blautia obeum, and a Lachnospiraceae MurNAc-LAA domain protein) were underrepresented in ME/CFS patients relative to healthy controls.
Blood creatine kinase concentration was significantly lower in patients with severe ME/CFS than in healthy controls, replicating a prior UKMEB report.
Machine learning classifiers trained solely on conventional blood test results distinguished ME/CFS patients from healthy controls with AUC of 0.80.

Combining flagellin antibody repertoire data with conventional blood tests improved diagnostic classification of ME/CFS to an AUC of 0.85, outperforming blood tests alone (AUC 0.80) or antibody data alone (AUC 0.67).
Adding flagellin antibody response data allowed correct classification of an additional 25% of individuals beyond what conventional blood tests alone achieved.

Anti-Lachnospiraceae flagellin antibody overrepresentation observed in ME/CFS mirrors previously reported findings in Crohn's disease, suggesting a shared microbiota-directed immune signature across the two conditions.
Crohn's disease patients have an increased risk of also developing ME/CFS compared to healthy individuals, as reported in prior literature.
Sequence alignment of the most frequently antibody-bound flagellin peptides revealed a shared conserved motif, suggesting cross-reactive antibody recognition across related bacterial species.
Exercise-induced decrease in M-wave amplitude and lengthening of duration was similar in magnitude between ME/CFS and long-COVID patients.
Digestive problems were significantly less frequent in long-COVID patients compared to ME/CFS patients.
Overall incidence of ME/CFS-defining symptoms was similar between the two groups, with the majority (69-81%) of long-COVID patients meeting ME/CFS symptom criteria.
MHGS was similar between long-COVID and ME/CFS groups but was slightly below the lower limit of normal (300 N) in both.
In both groups, MHGS was positively correlated with maximal cycling exercise power.
M-wave alterations induced by exercise were greater in patients (both long-COVID and ME/CFS) who had higher muscle strength and higher exercise performance.
There was no relationship between the duration of long-COVID illness and the magnitude of M-wave alterations.
Cardiovascular response to exercise (maximal increases in systolic and diastolic blood pressure) did not differ between ME/CFS and long-COVID groups.
Cycling exercise performance was the same in long-COVID and ME/CFS patients, with pedaling always interrupted by fatigue.
Fatigue onset began significantly earlier in ME/CFS patients compared to long-COVID patients, who were assessed close to the acute SARS-CoV-2 infection.
The majority (73%) of ME/CFS patients in this cohort had a history of glandular fever with high anti-Epstein-Barr virus antibody titers preceding fatigue onset.
Mean steps per 24 hours measured by Fitbit decreased with increasing ME/CFS severity across the six-month follow-up.
Mean steps per 24 hours were significantly higher in the second half (days 85-168) compared to the first half (days 1-84) of the six-month observation period.
Baseline mean steps per 24 hours correlated significantly with baseline SF-36 Physical Function score.
Mean steps per 24 hours correlated significantly with baseline SF-36 Social Function score.
Mean steps per 24 hours correlated significantly with baseline DSQ-SF (ME/CFS symptom) score.
DSQ-SF symptom scores correlated significantly with SF-36 Physical Function, SF-36 Bodily Pain, self-reported Function level, and COMPASS-31 sum score.
The Fitbit Charge 3 wrist tracker recorded systematically higher step counts than the validated SenseWear armband, despite significant correlation between the two devices.
COMPASS-31 sum score and its orthostatic intolerance domain were significantly positively associated with increasing ME/CFS severity.
COMPASS-31 orthostatic intolerance domain was negatively correlated with patient age, SF-36 General Health, and self-reported Function level.
Steps per 24 hours and resting heart rate were not significantly correlated over the study period.
Day-to-day variability (coefficient of variation) in steps per 24 hours averaged 47% (range 25-79%) but did not differ significantly by disease severity or baseline SF-36 PF category.

In an exploratory subgroup analysis combining baseline SF-36 PF and DSQ-SF, patients with milder symptoms (n=8) showed markedly larger fluctuations in steps, SF-36 PF, and DSQ-SF across 4-week periods than patients with more severe symptoms (n=19).
SF-36 Mental Health scores remained stable throughout follow-up and were similar to published general-population female norms, in contrast to the other five SF-36 domains which were markedly reduced.
Baseline DSQ-SF symptom scores were similar between mild and moderate severity groups but significantly higher in the severe group.
Continuous Fitbit activity monitoring for 24 weeks was highly feasible in ME/CFS patients, with very little missing data for steps and resting heart rate.

Patient survey feedback (22/27 respondents) indicated most participants found the Fitbit easy to use and an accurate reflection of activity level, while half reported that wearing the tracker influenced their activity behavior.

In the authors' previously published placebo-controlled rituximab trial (RituxME), the placebo group showed a mean 12-point increase in SF-36 Physical Function over 24 months of follow-up despite receiving no active treatment, illustrating substantial natural symptom variation over time in ME/CFS.
In a study by Freitag et al., 45.2% of COVID-19 patients met symptom-specific ME/CFS diagnostic criteria six months after infection.
A multinational study of 3762 COVID-19 patients with persisting symptoms found that 56.8% reported post-exertional malaise, a hallmark ME/CFS symptom.
In a 2009 study using an allostatic load model, the ACE T allele (rs4968591) and TT genotype were more common among ME/CFS patients with high allostatic load scores.
ME/CFS patients with the ACE TT genotype had the highest median CRP, lowest urinary cortisol (in females), and an increasing linear trend in IL-6.
High serum IL-6 levels were detected in more than half of COVID-19 patients.

Higher peripheral blood NK cell numbers were associated with faster SARS-CoV-2 clearance, while lower NK cell numbers correlated with prolonged viral shedding and lower survival in lymphocytopenic patients.
The most consistently replicated immunological finding across ME/CFS studies is significantly reduced NK cell cytotoxic function.
A study of 128 participants found no association between fatigue scores and routine inflammatory markers or serum IL-6/soluble CD25 levels.
Autoantibodies targeting GPCRs including β2- and α1-adrenoreceptors, angiotensin-II AT1-receptors, and muscarinic M2-receptors were found active in post COVID-19 condition patients.

Post-acute sequelae COVID patients with ACE2-specific autoantibodies showed lower soluble ACE2 activity in plasma and increased angiotensin II circulation, potentially driving a proinflammatory state.

In 11 severe COVID-19 patients with neurological symptoms, CSF analysis via lumbar puncture showed elevated autoantibodies against multiple CNS antigens, though no non-neurological control CSF samples were collected.

In 19 mild-to-critical COVID-19 patients with neurological symptoms, CSF levels of neurofilament light chain protein, GFAP, and total tau were elevated and correlated with neurological features and disease severity.
A Swedish cohort of ME/CFS patients showed significantly increased levels of autoantibodies to beta-adrenergic and muscarinic cholinergic receptors.
Genetic screening identified several single nucleotide polymorphisms in the TRPM3 ion channel gene group in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
TRPM3 expression is decreased in NK cells of ME/CFS patients, resulting in impaired calcium influx.
In mild and moderate COVID-19 patients, low serum calcium levels correlated with severe multi-organ injury and changes in IL-6 levels, suggesting low Ca2+ as an indicator of higher severity.

A three-month follow-up study found 55% of COVID-19 patients had neurological symptoms, with increased gray matter volumes in olfactory cortices, hippocampi, insulas, opercular/temporal regions and cingulate gyrus correlating with memory and smell loss.
In children infected with SARS-CoV-2, postinfectious immune-mediated encephalomyelitis-like brain changes were found in 16 of 38 patients, with neural enhancement in 13 and myelitis in 8.

FDG-PET/CT imaging revealed brain hypometabolism in the right parahippocampal gyrus and thalamus in post COVID-19 condition patients, associated with persistent anosmia/ageusia, fatigue, and vascular complications.
In a study of 402 recovered COVID-19 patients, 56% were scored as having psychiatric pathologies after infection.

Fatigue was the most common symptom (46.9%) among 130 surveyed COVID-19 patients, and patients with fatigue were significantly older (53.9 vs 48.5 years) and hospitalized longer, though fatigue was not associated with disease severity.
After applying formal systemic exertion intolerance disease/ME/CFS diagnostic criteria, only 13% of post-COVID patients with fatigue in this cohort met full ME/CFS diagnostic criteria.
Cardiovascular MRI in 100 COVID-19 recovered patients found 78% had ongoing cardiac involvement and 60% had myocardial inflammation.
Diarrhea, the second most common COVID-19 symptom, occurred in up to 70% of patients and was associated with 2.7 times higher odds of longer symptom duration.

COVID-19 patients showed underrepresentation of key commensal gut bacteria (Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Eubacterium rectale, bifidobacteria), associated with altered immunomodulation, with dysbiosis persisting after infection clearance.

Crosstalk between SARS-CoV-2 envelope protein E and BRD4 activates macrophage senescence, and BRD4 signalling has been separately linked to muscle weakness, suggesting a potential mechanistic link to post-exertional malaise.
In contrast to other reports, Sykes et al found no correlation between symptom burden and radiographic or biochemical brain abnormalities, though the study included limited testing.
Naltrexone, a mu-opioid receptor antagonist with anti-inflammatory properties, was found to restore TRPM3 channel function in ME/CFS patients (Cabanas et al.).
Ruan et al. demonstrated a significant difference in serum IL-6 levels between COVID-19 survivors and non-survivors, supporting IL-6 as a lethal risk factor.
Tocilizumab, an anti-IL-6 receptor monoclonal antibody, was tested to minimize inflammation in COVID-19 patients with promising results.

In a three-month follow-up study, 55% of COVID-19 patients had neurological symptoms including higher gray matter volumes in olfactory cortices, hippocampi, insulas, and other regions correlated with memory loss and smell loss.

In children infected by SARS-CoV-2, postinfectious immune-mediated encephalomyelitis-like brain changes were the most frequent neurological finding, occurring in 16 of 38 patients, with neural enhancement and myelitis also observed.

FDG-PET/CT imaging in post COVID-19 condition patients showed brain hypometabolism in the right parahippocampal gyrus and thalamus, associated with persistent anosmia/ageusia, fatigue, and vascular complications.

Autopsy investigations found SARS-CoV-2 RNA and spike proteins concentrated at the brainstem and, in 67% of assessed post-COVID samples, at the olfactory mucosal-neuronal junction, alongside inflammatory responses and neurodegeneration.
IL-6 has been proposed as a potential mediator of long-term neuropsychiatric symptoms in COVID-19 survivors.

In a study of 402 recovered COVID-19 patients, 56% were scored as having psychiatric pathologies, suggested to result from direct CNS viral infection, neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier disruption, HPA axis dysfunction, or psychosocial stressors.
A longitudinal study by Jason et al reported that some post COVID condition patients experienced progressive worsening of neurocognitive symptoms over time.

Among 130 surveyed COVID-19 patients, fatigue was the most common symptom (46.9%), with patients experiencing fatigue being older on average and hospitalized longer, though only 13% met formal ME/CFS diagnostic criteria after adjustment.

Sykes et al reported a lack of correlation between symptom burden and radiographic or biochemical brain abnormalities in COVID-19 patients, suggesting some symptoms may be attributable to biopsychosocial effects.
Cardiovascular MRI in 100 patients recovered from COVID-19 found 78% had ongoing cardiac involvement and 60% had myocardial inflammation.
Evidence of vasculitis (inflammation of blood vessels) has been described in COVID-19 patients, alongside single case reports of palpitations and orthostatic intolerance.
ME/CFS patients have also reported cardiovascular problems including abnormal blood pressure, hypertension, and orthostatic intolerance, similar to those seen in post-COVID-19 patients.
Diarrhea, the second most common COVID-19 symptom (up to 70% of patients), was associated with 2.7 times higher odds of longer symptom duration.

Underrepresentation of key commensal bacteria including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Eubacterium rectale, and bifidobacteria was associated with immunomodulation in COVID-19 patients, with dysbiosis persisting even after infection clearance.
A systematic review found limited evidence that enteric dysbiosis is involved in the pathomechanism of ME/CFS.

Interaction between SARS-CoV-2 envelope (E) protein and host Bromodomain-Containing Protein 4 (BRD4), expressed in the small intestine, was shown to activate macrophage senescence and may relate to muscle weakness, a potential link to PEM in ME/CFS.
Tocilizumab, an anti-IL-6 receptor monoclonal antibody, was tested for minimizing inflammation in COVID-19 with promising results.

In a study of 128 participants, no association was found between fatigue scores and serum IL-6 or soluble CD25 levels, nor with routine inflammatory markers such as leukocyte, neutrophil, lymphocyte counts, NLR, LDH, or CRP.

In severe COVID-19 patients with unclear neurological symptoms, CSF analysis using a large autoantigen panel revealed elevated levels of autoantibodies affecting specific brain targets, though appropriate control CSF samples were not collected.
Elevated levels of neurofilament light chain protein (NFLP), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and total tau in CSF were found in COVID-19 patients with neurological symptoms.

Post COVID-19 patients were found to have ACE2-specific autoantibodies, associated with lower soluble ACE2 activity in blood plasma and increased circulating angiotensin II, potentially enhancing a proinflammatory state.
Active GPCR-targeting autoantibodies, including those against β2- and α1-adrenoreceptors, angiotensin-II AT1-receptors, and muscarinic M2-receptors, were found in post COVID-19 condition patients.

A Swedish cohort of ME/CFS patients showed significantly increased levels of autoantibodies to beta-adrenergic and muscarinic cholinergic receptors, although the pathomechanism of their contribution to ME/CFS is unknown.

The autoantibody-blocking aptamer BC 007, targeting GPCRs, was assessed in an initial two-patient treatment trial for long COVID and is now being tested in a larger placebo-controlled trial (reCOVer).

Dihydropyridine Ca2+ channel blockers such as nifedipine (a TRPM3 agonist) and amlodipine have been suggested as a potentially effective therapeutic approach to reduce mortality in elderly COVID-19 patients.
Naltrexone, a mu-opioid receptor antagonist with anti-inflammatory properties, was found to restore TRPM3 function in ME/CFS patients.
A pilot clinical trial (NCT04604704) was registered to test low-dose naltrexone combined with nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) supplementation for treatment of post COVID-19 condition.

BIO101 (20-hydroxyecdysone), a Mas-receptor activator targeting the ACE2 pathway, is being tested in a clinical trial for management of acute SARS-CoV-2 infection and related complications, purportedly exerting anti-inflammatory, anti-thrombotic, and anti-fibrotic effects.
The post-hospitalisation COVID-19 study (PHOSP-COVID) intends to follow 10,000 patients for one year in the United Kingdom to record post-COVID complications.

The CAPACITY registry initiative in the European Union is collecting follow-up reports on SARS-CoV-2 infected patients from multiple European hospitals, including blood test and imaging biomarker data.
The Chalder Fatigue Scale (CFQ) has been successfully used to assess fatigue in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome, systemic lupus erythematosus, and primary Sjogren's syndrome.

In mouse models, iron deficiency without anemia decreased the activity of respiratory chain complex I, reducing performance of muscle fibers (type I and IIA) that rely on aerobic respiration, but not type IIB fibers.
Iron supplementation in women with iron deficiency without anemia improved maximal oxygen consumption (VO2 max) and muscle performance, leading to decreased perceived fatigue.
A meta-analysis by Greig et al. found that fatigue was initially higher in iron-deficient subgroups and decreased following iron supplementation.
Holm et al. found that both intravenous and oral iron therapy reduced physical fatigue in women with postpartum hemorrhage, with faster improvement in the intravenous group.
In adolescent girls with heavy menstrual bleeding, fatigue measured by the Fatigue Severity Scale was significantly higher than in healthy female controls.

Kocaoz et al. found that lower hemoglobin and ferritin levels among women with heavy menstrual bleeding were associated with increased fatigue and greater difficulty performing daily activities on the SF-36 quality of life scale.

In the FERWON-IDA trial of chronic kidney disease patients with iron deficiency anemia, treatment with either iron isomaltoside/derisomaltoside or iron sucrose reduced fatigue by about 15 points on the FACIT scale from baseline, with faster improvement with iron isomaltoside.
Goldenberg et al. showed no relationship between fatigue and iron deficiency in patients with inflammatory bowel disease who did not have anemia.
Jonefjäll et al. found that low ferritin levels were related to higher fatigue intensity in patients with ulcerative colitis.

The FAIR-HF trial (n=459) in chronic heart failure patients with iron deficiency showed that intravenous iron supplementation significantly improved Patient Global Assessment, NYHA classification, 6-minute walk test, and quality of life scores.
In myelodysplastic syndrome patients, self-reported fatigue levels were found to provide a more accurate assessment of quality of life than hemoglobin levels alone.

Among 224 hospitalized elderly individuals (65-95 years), those with iron deficiency (present in ~50%, mostly functional) showed significantly higher fatigue levels, lower hemoglobin, and higher CRP than those without iron deficiency.
Houston et al. demonstrated a significant impact of iron supplementation on reducing experienced fatigue in iron-deficient elderly patients.

In a case report of a 42-year-old man with genetically confirmed hereditary hemochromatosis, fatigue improved substantially across three validated scales (FAS, CFQ, FSS) over 6 months of venesection treatment.
In 73 children with beta-thalassemia minor, low plasma free and total carnitine levels were found, and supplementation with carnitine and folic acid reduced fatigue and muscle weakness.

Oxidative stress from iron overload inhibits SERCA2 enzyme activity, increasing cytoplasmic calcium in cardiomyocytes, contributing to impaired cardiac relaxation and heart failure with associated fatigue.

Diagnostic thresholds for hereditary hemochromatosis are ferritin >200 ng/mL in premenopausal women or >300 ng/mL in men and postmenopausal women, with transferrin saturation >45%, prompting HFE genetic testing.
Among outpatients with a confirmed COVID-19 diagnosis, the cumulative 2-year incidence of a physician-diagnosed post-COVID syndrome was 14.2%.
6.7% of all patients with confirmed COVID-19 received the post-COVID syndrome diagnosis in two or more separate quarterly billing periods, indicating chronification in a substantial subgroup.

Chronic fatigue syndrome (ICD-10 G93.3) was diagnosed in 1.6% of COVID-19 patients over the 2-year follow-up, substantially higher than the single-diagnosis proportions of 0.6% in the other-respiratory-infection group and 0.3% in the control group.
Persistent dyspnoea was diagnosed in 9.9% of the COVID-19 group over follow-up, substantially higher than comparator groups.
Persistent disturbances of smell or taste were diagnosed in 3.2% of the COVID-19 group over follow-up.
Pulmonary embolism was diagnosed in 0.4% of the COVID-19 group during follow-up, substantially increased relative to comparator groups.
