Mild cognitive impairment (ICD-10 F06.7) incidence was 0.39% in the COVID-19 group, lower than other symptoms but higher than in the other-respiratory-infection group (0.18%) or control group (0.31%).
Treatment incidence of psychological disorders was similar between the COVID-19 group (14.8%) and other-respiratory-infection group (12.8%), with both higher than the control group (9.4%).
Myalgia treatment incidence was similar between the COVID-19 group (3.9%) and other-respiratory-infection group (3.4%), both higher than the control group (2.3%).
Post-COVID syndrome incidence showed a strong age gradient, from 2.6% in children aged 0-11 to 19.0% in adults aged 40-59 years.
Chronic fatigue syndrome diagnosis after COVID-19 was rare in children (0.1%) but substantially more common in the 40-59 age group (2.3%).
Persistent smell/taste disturbance incidence in 12-17 year-olds with COVID-19 (3.4%) was comparable to that seen in young and middle-aged adults.

The systematic review found that patients with chronic fatigue syndrome show an increased risk of developing oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), alongside other systemic conditions such as Fanconi's anemia, xeroderma pigmentosum, dyskeratosis congenita, and post bone marrow transplantation status.
Generalized body pain is reported by more than 90% of patients with hEDS, making it the most prevalent pain type in this population.
Soft-tissue pain is reported by more than 90% of hEDS patients, and neuropathic pain by 68%.
Joint dislocations occur in 78% of hEDS patients.
Fibromyalgia is a common comorbidity in hEDS and hEDS is frequently misdiagnosed as fibromyalgia.
On average it takes 10-12 years from symptom onset to receive a diagnosis of EDS.
A case-control study (De Wandele et al) characterized possible nociplastic pain mechanisms in EDS patients, including abnormal temporal pain summation and altered exercise-induced hypoalgesia.

Only 3 of 8 controlled trials in the Palmer et al systematic review found conservative intervention (exercise-based) statistically more effective than no-treatment controls for syndromic hypermobility.
Multiple RCTs and cohort studies in the Palmer et al review found statistically significant pain reduction from pre-treatment to post-treatment with conservative exercise-based interventions.
A cohort study by Bathen et al did not find a significant decrease in pain from pre-treatment to post-treatment, contrasting with other cohort/RCT findings.

A non-randomized controlled trial (Celletti et al, n=18) found that neurocognitive therapeutic exercises significantly reduced pain, fatigue, kinesiophobia, and disability scores in hEDS patients with chronic low back pain.
In the Demes et al survey, opioids were rated the most helpful pain therapy among statistically significant categories, with 58.9% of participants rating them mostly or extremely helpful.

Despite high usage, most Demes et al survey participants (65.2%) rated antidepressants as rarely or not at all helpful for pain, contrasting with fibromyalgia patients who typically respond to antidepressants.
Most Demes et al survey participants (73.1%) found acetaminophen rarely or not at all helpful for pain control.
NSAIDs were rated slightly better than acetaminophen, with 14% finding them mostly/extremely helpful, but their use may be limited by bleeding risk in EDS.
TENS therapy was perceived as slightly more effective than acetaminophen but still rated rarely/not at all helpful by 46.5% of Demes et al survey participants.
Marijuana use for pain increased with pain severity in the Demes et al survey, from 20.0% in the no-pain group to 50.0% in the very-severe-pain group.
The Demes et al survey found no significant gender differences in average pain intensity between male and female EDS/HSD patients.
In the Arthur et al survey of 1179 EDS patients, opioids (used by 34.1%) were perceived as the most effective pain control method overall, with a mean efficacy score of 3.55.
Physical therapy showed only modest perceived effectiveness (mean 2.81) despite being used by 34.9% of Arthur et al survey participants.
Heat therapy and splints/braces showed moderate perceived effectiveness in the Arthur et al survey, comparable to or slightly better than other non-opioid strategies.
Anti-seizure medications used for chronic pain in EDS showed weak and highly variable perceived efficacy in the Arthur et al survey, in contrast to their typical effectiveness in fibromyalgia.
There was a significant overall group effect on total SQ-CH (hypermobility symptom) scores across FND, ASD, and NC groups.
Patients with functional neurological disorders showed significantly more hEDS/HSD-related symptoms than non-clinical controls on the SQ-CH.
Patients with autism spectrum disorder (without intellectual disability) showed significantly more hEDS/HSD-related symptoms than non-clinical controls on the SQ-CH.
There was no significant difference in hEDS/HSD-related symptom scores between the FND group and the ASD group.
Female participants scored significantly higher than male participants on the hypermobility symptom questionnaire, independent of diagnostic group.
No significant interaction was found between diagnostic group and gender on hypermobility symptom scores.
A substantial proportion of both FND (55%) and ASD (52%) participants scored above the SQ-CH cut-off for hypermobility, compared to a smaller proportion of non-clinical controls (31%).
Mean parent-proxy and child self-report scores did not significantly differ across HRQOL-related survey instruments in pediatric hEDS.
Despite similar group means, there was moderate to strong statistical agreement between parent and child scores on all survey measures.
Despite overall agreement in means, a relatively high proportion of individual parent-child dyads showed disagreement on each survey score.
Half of the 36 parent-child dyads (18) disagreed on at least half of the survey instruments administered.
Body mass index centile and the child's perception of cognitive fatigue were the strongest predictors of parent-child disagreement in total HRQOL score.

Postural control on the MABC-2 significantly improved after 15 days wearing whole-body compressive garments, moving from the 5th to the 37th percentile, but returned to pathological levels 15 days after stopping garment use.
Manual dexterity on the MABC-2 improved only after the compressive garments were discontinued (T3), moving from the 5th to the 75th percentile.
Overall MABC-2 total motor score remained below the 5th percentile (pathological) at baseline, while wearing garments, and after stopping garment use.
Distal gnosopraxis (finger movements) remained subnormal across all time points, showing only a small trend of improvement from -1.13 SD to -0.67 SD.
Distal gnosopraxis for hand movements dramatically improved from -5.29 SD at baseline to +0.09 SD after 15 days wearing compressive garments.

Body schema representation, assessed with the draw-a-man test, improved from a developmental age of 5 years 6 months (nearly 2 years behind chronological age) at baseline to 7 years 5 months and then 8 years 3 months after wearing compressive garments.
Writing and spatial orientation performance did not change with compressive garment use and remained pathological throughout.
Visual perception, assessed with the Frostig test, was in the normal range at baseline and remained normal regardless of garment use.

Interpersonal motor synchronization with an animated tightrope-walker avatar, measured as the correlation between the child's bar angle and the avatar's bar angle, significantly increased after wearing the compressive garments compared to baseline.

Motor coordination, measured as the correlation between the child's bar angle and head axis angle during the tightrope-walker task, remained excellent (>0.9) and unchanged after wearing compressive garments.
The child reported subjective improvement in knee pain while wearing the whole-body compressive garments.
The child had a Beighton score of 6, confirming joint hypermobility consistent with a diagnosis of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome hypermobility type.
The child was found to have polyclonal type II cryoglobulinemia, detected via cryoglobulin testing, alongside cold- and moisture-triggered facial urticaria.

In prior comparative data from the same experimental paradigm across 70 participants, children with ASD showed lower interpersonal synchrony (bar-bar correlation) and motor control performance than both typically developing and DCD groups, and with compressive garments the case-patient's performance moved closer to typically developing controls.

EDS-hypermobility type is strongly associated with coexisting neurodevelopmental difficulties, including motor coordination, communication, and social interrelatedness problems, in line with the ESSENCE framework.
Hypermobile EDS (hEDS) was the most common diagnosed subtype among both adults (63%) and minors (62%), followed by hypermobility spectrum disorder (HSD) (12% adults, 6% minors).
Most adults and minors with EDS/HSD were diagnosed by genetics specialists (46% each), followed by rheumatology (22% adults, 24% minors).
A substantial proportion of adults (16%) and minors (29%) were undergoing evaluation for EDS/HSD without yet having a formal diagnosis at the time of the survey.

Patients with EDS/HSD demonstrated high healthcare utilization, with 693 unique visits across 27 different specialties and over 20 hospitals/clinics reported by 155 adults and 83 minors, and over half attending more than one hospital or clinic for EDS care.
Among adults with EDS/HSD, the most commonly utilized specialty visits were cardiology (12%), neurology (8%), gastroenterology (7%), and emergency medicine (7%).
Among minors with EDS/HSD, the most commonly utilized specialty visits were rheumatology (13%), cardiology (11%), neurology (11%), and genetics (11%).

Of all specialty visits, 13% took place outside the surveyed region, most commonly for neurology (11%) and physical/occupational therapy (10%), predominantly among adults (85 of 92 out-of-region visits).
The majority of respondents (67%) felt their current EDS/HSD medical care needs were not being met, with only 10% feeling their needs were met and 23% uncertain.
87% of respondents indicated it would be beneficial to receive care from a multidisciplinary clinic for EDS/HSD.

The top specialties respondents wanted included in a hypothetical EDS/HSD multidisciplinary clinic were pain management (84%), physical and occupational therapy (84%), rheumatology (82%), cardiology (81%), gastroenterology (76%), and neurology (75%).

Respondents expressed substantial willingness to travel for multidisciplinary EDS/HSD care, with 34% willing to travel 30-60 minutes, 22% 60-120 minutes, 22% more than 120 minutes, and 15% willing to fly.

Although almost 60% of respondents felt primary care would be important in a multidisciplinary team, primary care was poorly utilized compared to emergency department care, which had higher utilization among EDS/HSD patients.

A 36-year-old woman with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (type unknown) developed a 3.9-cm pseudoaneurysm of the proximal anterior tibial artery with a large surrounding hematoma, presenting as a painful anterolateral calf mass without prior trauma.
CT angiography revealed multiple additional fusiform true aneurysms in visceral arteries, the right common femoral artery, and the right peroneal artery, attributed to the patient's underlying EDS.

Endovascular bidirectional embolization of the anterior tibial artery (without coil placement in the pseudoaneurysm sac) resulted in stagnant contrast at procedure end and no residual filling of the pseudoaneurysm on surveillance CT angiography at eight months.

The authors cite literature reporting that endovascular procedure complication rates were as low as 2% in a single-institution retrospective study, compared to 33% for surgical procedures in another retrospective study, supporting a preference for endovascular management in EDS patients with vascular fragility.

A cited literature review of 31 patients with vascular EDS found that only 5 patients presented with symptoms suggestive of EDS prior to their vascular event, indicating vascular events can be the first sign of the disease.
A heterozygous splice-site mutation (c.1347+1G>A) in COL3A1 was identified via PCR and Sanger sequencing, confirming a diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (vEDS, type IV).

The patient presented with acute anterior STEMI due to spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) involving the LAD, left main trunk, and left circumflex branch, diagnosed via coronary angiography and intravascular ultrasound.

Physical examination revealed classic vEDS features including protruding eyes, thin/hyperelastic skin, visible subcutaneous veins, ecchymosis, and increased mobility of the bilateral little finger MCP joints.

The patient had a prior history of organ ruptures (splenic and intestinal rupture requiring splenectomy/partial intestinal resection 20 years prior; liver rupture requiring partial liver resection 4 years prior), consistent with vEDS-related organ fragility.

Postoperative CT imaging showed hemopericardium and abdominal/pelvic findings of intestinal wall swelling, hematocele, retroperitoneal hematocele, and an iliac vascular dissection, indicating multi-site vascular fragility consistent with vEDS.

Emergency PCI with three overlapping drug-eluting stents from LAD to LM plus one stent at the LCX successfully restored TIMI grade 3 flow and achieved hemodynamic stability, but the patient died of sudden cardiac death on day 9 post-procedure.
SCAD is rare in males (~10% of all SCAD cases) compared to females, in whom it accounts for 25% of ACS in women younger than 50; vEDS is even rarer among males with SCAD.
vEDS, caused by mutations in COL3A1 (encoding type III procollagen), is a predisposing condition for SCAD, though only 1-2% of SCAD cases overall are related to inherited connective tissue disorders.

Celiprolol, a third-generation cardioselective beta-1 blocker with beta-2 agonist vasodilatory effect, showed preventive effects on arterial mortality and morbidity in the BBEST clinical trial in EDS patients, though the trial had limitations and beta-blockers carry a theoretical risk of vasospasm exacerbation.

In urine of three siblings with biallelic B3GALT6 pathogenic variants and spondylodysplastic EDS, the non-canonical trisaccharide (pentasaccharide-modified) linkage region of bikunin glycopeptides was increased more than 100-fold relative to the canonical tetrasaccharide (hexasaccharide-modified) form compared to their unaffected mother.

The non-canonical trisaccharide linkage region is present at very low levels (reference range <0.5%) on bikunin in healthy individuals, supporting a substrate-competition model between GalT-II and GlcAT-I enzymes.

Only three chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans (bikunin/AMBP, osteopontin, and CD44 antigen) were identifiable in urine of the affected siblings, compared with 16 different CSPGs identified in the unaffected mother's urine, suggesting reduced overall CSPG abundance in disease.

In one sibling (PIV:1), the non-canonical trisaccharide linkage region was found on a neuropeptide W glycopeptide without comparable amounts of the canonical linkage region, indicating that linkage-region distribution varies by core protein.

In a previously reported b3galt6 knock-out zebrafish model with an EDS-like dysplastic phenotype, chondroitin/dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate disaccharide concentrations were significantly decreased in bone and skin compared to wild-type fish, and the non-canonical linkage region was found only on biglycan and aggrecan.
Exome analysis identified a novel heterozygous FLNA variant (c.4868delG) causing a frameshift/early termination that truncates the C-terminal 983 amino acids of filamin A in the patient.
The patient was found to carry the heterozygous RNF213 c.14429G>A (p.R4810K) variant, a known susceptibility variant for Moyamoya disease, inherited from her father.

Only the patient carrying both the FLNA and RNF213 variants manifested the full symptomatic phenotype (PNH, Ehlers-Danlos-like symptoms, and MMD-like vascular formation), whereas each parent carrying only one variant showed subtle or no phenotype, supporting a two-hit gene interaction model.

Filamin A is normally degraded via RNF213-mediated ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover, but the decreased ligase activity of RNF213 p.R4810K may lead to accumulation of abnormal filamin A protein in cells expressing both variants.

The authors propose that C-terminally truncated filamin A may impair migration of newborn neurons from the periventricular zone to the cortex during development, producing periventricular nodular heterotopia.

The authors propose that in adults, the truncated filamin A may cause flow- or pressure-mediated hypermobility of vascular smooth muscle cells via loss of integrin/ECM anchoring, increasing calcium influx through the Piezo1 mechanosensor channel and driving arterial remodeling and cerebral artery stenosis.
The patient exhibited Ehlers-Danlos-like features including joint hypermobility, ecchymoma of the lower limbs, patellar luxation, spontaneous pneumothorax, and mild aortic regurgitation.
A prior case series described only 1 of 54 patients with Moyamoya disease (a 3-year-old male) as having an FLNA abnormality, suggesting FLNA involvement in MMD may be uncommon.
The RNF213 p.R4810K variant is found in approximately 80% of Japanese patients with Moyamoya disease compared with 1.8% of healthy controls.

Mouse models with Rnf213 genetic deletion or human RNF213 c.14429G>A knock-in alone did not develop abnormal cerebrovascular structures, supporting the two-hit theory that additional genetic or environmental factors are required for Moyamoya disease.

The patient's mother carried the same FLNA variant but not the RNF213 variant, and showed asymptomatic bilateral periventricular nodular heterotopia with normal cerebrovascular structure and no Ehlers-Danlos-like symptoms.
The patient's father carried the heterozygous RNF213 p.R4810K variant but showed no abnormalities on MRI or MRA, without the FLNA variant.

RNF213 also functions as an E3-ubiquitin ligase for itself and other molecules including NFAT, and contributes to lipid metabolism, suggesting other RNF213-related genes could similarly act as second-hits in MMD-like vascular formation.
Using a Beighton score >4 as the cutoff, 37% of school boys screened were found to have generalized joint hypermobility.
Hypermobility prevalence declined with increasing age, from 50% in 7–9 year-olds to 31.8% in 15–17 year-olds.
Growing pains, identified by night pain without daytime symptoms, were present in 4.6% (71/1543) of the boys screened.
6.1% (94/1543) of boys reported recurrent joint, muscle, or back pain/stiffness on screening, unrelated to a specific event.
Obese boys were significantly more likely to complain of musculoskeletal pain than non-obese boys (16.3% vs 4.7%).
The estimated prevalence of juvenile idiopathic arthritis in this cohort of Indian boys was 65 per 100,000.

A boy with difficulty climbing stairs, bilateral sacroiliac tenderness, and elevated inflammatory markers tested HLA-B27 positive and had MRI-confirmed bilateral sacroiliitis, consistent with enthesitis-related arthritis.
A 14-year-old obese boy with limping and hip pain for 4 months was diagnosed on radiographs with slipped capital femoral epiphysis and referred for orthopedic surgery.

A third boy with difficulty climbing stairs and recent back pain had normal ESR, negative HLA-B27, and normal MRI of the SI joints, lumbar spine, and hips, with symptom resolution at 6-month follow-up.
Across all lumbar levels, contraction produced a smaller increase in transversus abdominis (TrA) thickness in hypermobile participants than in controls.
At the L3 lumbar level specifically, contraction produced a smaller increase in TrA thickness in hypermobile participants compared with controls, while no difference was found at L1 or L5.
No group-by-condition interaction was observed for TrA length change during contraction, overall or at any lumbar level.
At L3, contraction produced a greater decrease in external oblique (EO) thickness in hypermobile participants than controls, suggesting relatively better EO function.
No group-by-condition interactions were found for EO thickness overall, at L1, or at L5.
No group-by-condition interactions were observed for internal oblique (IO) thickness change during contraction at any lumbar level.
Trunk flexion muscular endurance was 55% greater in hypermobile participants compared with non-hypermobile controls.
There was no difference between hypermobile and control participants in trunk extension strength, trunk flexion strength, or trunk extension endurance.

Correlations between joint mobility scores (Beighton and BOM) and abdominal muscle thickness/length or trunk strength/endurance tended to be non-existent or weak, making the link between hypermobility severity and muscle function inconclusive.
Baseline participant characteristics (age, height, weight) and resting transversus abdominis cross-sectional area did not differ between hypermobile and control groups.
A considerable proportion of patients with inflammatory rheumatic diseases also fulfill diagnostic criteria for fibromyalgia syndrome, complicating diagnosis and treatment evaluation.
Studies evaluating cardiac autonomic function in FMS patients have found decreased heart rate variability along with sympathetic nervous system dominance.
Some FMS patients exhibit blunted autonomic reactivity, impairing their ability to appropriately respond to unexpected stressors encountered during daily activities.
Studies suggest diminished baroreflex sensitivity is involved in the etiology of fibromyalgia syndrome, given that baroreceptor signals normally inhibit central pain processing.
Increased risk of endothelial dysfunction and arterial stiffness has been shown in FMS patients, attributed to autonomic dysfunction, sympathetic dominance, chronic stress, and pain.
Evidence links fibromyalgia syndrome with an increased risk of atrial and ventricular arrhythmias.
At baseline, people with fibromyalgia had significantly higher HRV Stress Index than healthy controls.
People with fibromyalgia showed significantly higher LF power than healthy controls at baseline, interpreted as increased sympathetic modulation.
People with fibromyalgia showed significantly lower HF power than healthy controls at baseline, interpreted as reduced parasympathetic modulation.
Salivary amylase activity was significantly higher in people with fibromyalgia than in healthy controls at baseline, consistent with sympathetic/adrenergic hyperreactivity.
Salivary catalase activity did not significantly differ between people with fibromyalgia and healthy controls at baseline, despite prior reports of lower blood catalase in FM.
Salivary glutathione peroxidase activity showed no significant differences between fibromyalgia and control groups, nor within groups before/after exercise.
In people with fibromyalgia, maximum HR, mean HR, RR interval and Sample Entropy changed significantly from baseline to immediately after the exercise fatigue protocol.
Salivary flow significantly decreased (by 45.16%) after the exercise fatigue protocol in people with fibromyalgia, suggesting stronger parasympathetic inhibition than in controls.
In healthy controls, maximum HR, mean HR, RR interval, PNS index, SNS index, LF, HF and LF/HF all changed significantly from baseline to after the exercise fatigue protocol.
Salivary catalase activity significantly increased after the exercise fatigue protocol in healthy controls, but not in people with fibromyalgia.

When normalizing post-exercise HRV and salivary biomarker changes to baseline, no significant differences were found between fibromyalgia and healthy control groups in the magnitude of exercise-induced change.

People with fibromyalgia reported significantly higher rating of perceived exertion (RPE) than healthy controls both at baseline and after exercise, and both groups significantly increased RPE after the exercise fatigue protocol.

The exercise-induced increase in maximum heart rate was markedly attenuated in fibromyalgia (6% change) compared to healthy controls (25% change), consistent with chronotropic incompetence linked to dysautonomia.
In women with fibromyalgia, daily physical activity level (Godin Leisure Questionnaire) was not associated with vegetative (autonomic) symptoms or with any of the psychological factors studied.
Pain catastrophizing (PCS) was positively correlated with kinesiophobia (fear of movement) in women with fibromyalgia.
Pain catastrophizing was positively correlated with vegetative (autonomic) symptoms measured by COMPASS-31 in women with fibromyalgia.
Self-efficacy scores were positively correlated with vegetative (autonomic) symptoms in women with fibromyalgia.

The paper notes that postural orthostatic tachycardia is a commonly reported autonomic anomaly in fibromyalgia patients, with heightened sympathetic responses to cold, auditory, and mental stress stimuli.
Women with fibromyalgia have approximately 50% more pelvic floor symptoms (pain, urinary/colorectal dysfunction, pelvic organ prolapse) compared to women without fibromyalgia.
Irritable bowel syndrome and chronic fatigue syndrome are cited as up to three times more prevalent in fibromyalgia patients than in the general population.
The discussion cites studies showing Helicobacter pylori infection is significantly increased in fibromyalgia patients, implicating gut dysbiosis in the disorder.
The discussion cites Gezici's group as reporting a significant reduction in fibromyalgia pain (measured by tender point count) following H. pylori eradication therapy.
The discussion cites altered gut bacterial populations and urinary metabolites (including uncommon monosaccharides sorbose, rhamnose, and tagatose) in fibromyalgia patients.

The discussion cites a study showing that patients with chronic musculoskeletal pain present significant disturbances in circadian blood pressure variation, reflecting HPA axis and autonomic dysregulation.

Fecal microbiome alpha-diversity indices (Shannon, evenness, Faith's phylogenetic diversity, observed OTUs, inverse Simpson, ace, chao1) did not differ significantly between FMS patients and healthy controls.

Beta-diversity, phylum-level and differential taxa abundance analyses (DeSeq2, CCA) revealed no significant or clinically relevant differences in bacterial composition between FMS patients and healthy controls.

Quantitative sensory testing revealed significantly altered thresholds in FMS patients versus healthy controls for cold pain threshold, pressure pain threshold, vibration detection threshold, mechanical detection threshold, mechanical pain threshold, and dynamic mechanical allodynia.
FMS patients had significantly higher depression, anxiety, and stress scores (DASS-G), higher ISR-10 symptom scores, and reduced quality of life (MbFhW) compared to healthy controls.
Significantly more FMS patients were smokers compared to healthy controls.
Gastrointestinal complaints (dyspepsia and esophageal reflux) were reported by a substantial subset of FMS patients but by none of the healthy controls.
FMS patients used various medications (e.g., analgesics, antidepressants, NSAIDs, PPIs) more frequently than healthy controls.
Dietary habits (omnivore/vegetarian/vegan distribution) and calculated nutrition scores did not differ significantly between FMS patients and healthy controls.

Lower cold pain, mechanical detection, and mechanical pain thresholds together with dynamic mechanical allodynia suggest that unmyelinated C-fibers and Aβ-fibers contribute to peripheral pain sensitization in FMS, alongside possible central sensitization.

Individuals with somatic symptom disorder and depressive disorders reported higher self-reported daily stress across the 14-day ambulatory period than healthy controls, with depressive disorder patients reporting the highest levels.

Individuals with somatic symptom disorder (trend) and depressive disorders showed a less pronounced alpha-amylase awakening response than healthy controls, indicating blunted sympathetic reactivity to awakening.
Mean diurnal alpha-amylase activity across the day did not differ between somatic symptom disorder, depressive disorder, and healthy control groups.
The three groups (somatic symptom disorder, depressive disorder, healthy controls) did not differ in cortisol awakening response.
Individuals with somatic symptom disorder and depressive disorders had significantly lower mean diurnal cortisol concentrations across the day compared to healthy controls.
Childhood trauma, measured via the CTQ, did not significantly predict self-reported daily stress levels in individuals with somatic symptom disorder or depressive disorders.
Childhood trauma showed a trend-level effect on the alpha-amylase awakening response, such that individuals with a trauma history had a more pronounced AAR than those without.
Age was directly associated with mean diurnal alpha-amylase activity in the multilevel model.
BMI was negatively associated with mean diurnal cortisol in the multilevel model, while previous-day stress and childhood trauma had no effect.

The three groups (somatic symptom disorder, depressive disorders, healthy controls) did not differ in the amount of childhood trauma experienced, and over half of the total sample reported some form of trauma.

Individuals with somatic symptom disorder showed a trend toward higher somatic symptom load than those with depressive disorders, while individuals with depressive disorders had significantly higher depressive symptom scores than those with somatic symptom disorder.
IgE cross-linking activation of RBL-2H3 mast cells caused intracellular calcium to rise approximately 2-fold at 1 hour and peak at ~5-fold at 2 hours before returning to baseline by 3 hours.
Cellular (intracellular) tryptase level measured by Western blotting showed only marginal increases (~0.3- to 0.4-fold) at all time-points after activation, making it a poor marker.
Average cell size increased marginally (~2.5-fold) after mast cell activation, considered a weak/unreliable marker compared to other assays.
Nucleus/cytoplasm ratio decreased marginally (~0.4- to 0.5-fold) following mast cell activation, indicating limited utility as an activation marker.
β-hexosaminidase release stably and markedly increased (~10-fold) after IgE-mediated activation compared to untreated/sensitized-only controls, supporting its use as a recommended activation marker.
CD63 surface expression, measured by both flow cytometry and immunofluorescence, stably increased ~10-fold after mast cell activation, supporting its use as a recommended marker.
Secreted tryptase level, measured by Western blotting, stably increased ~10-fold after mast cell activation, supporting its use as a recommended marker.
Tryptase expression detected by immunofluorescence stably increased ~10-fold (or became detectable only after activation), supporting its use as a recommended marker of mast cell activation.
Routine mental health crisis screening using the MCAS-R was feasible in outpatient autism clinics, with 80% of youth successfully screened.
The MCAS-R screening results strongly aligned with clinician crisis ratings, correctly classifying 88% of cases.
Twenty percent of youth with autism screened met the cutoff for a mental health crisis, with aggression and self-injurious behaviors being the most common associated behaviors.
Most parents (73%) reported the MCAS-R helped them communicate concerns with the clinician, and few (<6%) found the survey too long or upsetting.
All clinicians (100%) rated the MCAS-R as very helpful for communication and safety concern identification, though 33% noted it sometimes interrupted clinical flow.

In adults and children with eosinophilic esophagitis, mast cell infiltration (mastocytosis) can persist even after eosinophilia resolves, and this persistence correlates with ongoing mucosal abnormalities and symptoms.
Despite treatment for eosinophilic esophagitis, mast cells retain an activated transcriptomic profile.
Mast cells are implicated in contributing to epithelial barrier dysfunction in eosinophilic esophagitis.
Mast cells are implicated in smooth muscle hypertrophy and contraction in eosinophilic esophagitis.
Mast cells are implicated in subepithelial fibrosis in eosinophilic esophagitis.
It remains unclear whether targeting mast cells alone would have therapeutic efficacy to improve tissue damage in eosinophilic esophagitis.
Mast cells, together with eosinophils, serve as a biomarker of mucosal healing in eosinophilic esophagitis.
Pre-treatment of bone marrow-derived mast cells with 2 mM VPA significantly reduced the percentage of degranulated (CD107a+) cells after L. monocytogenes stimulation.
VPA pre-treatment reduced the amount of β-hexosaminidase released by mast cells stimulated with L. monocytogenes.
VPA did not significantly affect L. monocytogenes-induced superoxide anion (ROS) production by mast cells.
VPA decreased TNF release from mast cells stimulated with L. monocytogenes.
VPA decreased IL-6 release from mast cells stimulated with L. monocytogenes.
VPA decreased IL-13 release from mast cells stimulated with L. monocytogenes.
VPA decreased CCL2 release from mast cells stimulated with L. monocytogenes.
Male-derived mast cells (m-BMMC) produced less IL-6 in response to L. monocytogenes than female-derived mast cells (f-BMMC), indicating sex-dimorphic mast cell response.
VPA attenuated L. monocytogenes-induced IL-6 release in male-derived mast cells to a similar magnitude as in female-derived mast cells.
VPA did not significantly decrease surface TLR2 expression on mast cells.
VPA pre-treatment decreased IL-6 and IL-13 production by mast cells stimulated with the TLR2 ligand S. aureus Peptidoglycan (PGN).
VPA pre-treatment decreased IL-6 and IL-13 production by mast cells stimulated with the synthetic TLR2 ligand Pam3CSK4.
VPA reduced mast cell degranulation (β-hexosaminidase release) induced by the TLR2-independent toxin Listeriolysin O.
VPA decreased production of TNF, IL-6, IL-13, and CCL2 by mast cells stimulated with Listeriolysin O.
VPA treatment significantly decreased intracellular Ca2+ mobilization in mast cells stimulated with L. monocytogenes.
VPA decreased NF-κB (p65) phosphorylation in mast cells stimulated with L. monocytogenes.
VPA decreased phosphorylation of ERK 1/2 (MAPK pathway) in mast cells stimulated with L. monocytogenes.
VPA decreased phosphorylation of p38 (MAPK pathway) in mast cells stimulated with L. monocytogenes.
VPA did not affect the total protein expression of p38, ERK1/2, or NF-κB (p50/p65) in mast cells, indicating its effect is on phosphorylation/activation rather than protein synthesis.

The c-KIT inhibitor masitinib is proposed to reduce neuroinflammation by limiting mast cell survival, migration, and degranulation, thereby inhibiting downstream proinflammatory and vasoactive molecular cascades.

Short-term (15 min) exposure of BMMCs to 50-75 μM ursolic acid increased surface phosphatidylserine exposure (annexin V) and propidium iodide staining in a small subset of cells without major toxicity.
Ursolic acid dose-dependently inhibited antigen-induced β-glucuronidase degranulation of BMMCs, with near-complete inhibition at 75 μM and ~50% inhibition at 50 μM.
Ursolic acid did not affect spontaneous (non-antigen-triggered) β-glucuronidase release from BMMCs, supporting the non-toxic nature of the treatment.
Ursolic acid pretreatment significantly inhibited thapsigargin-induced degranulation, which bypasses FcεRI-mediated early signaling steps.
Ursolic acid significantly inhibited the antigen-induced rise in cytoplasmic free calcium ([Ca2+]i) in BMMCs measured by Fura-2 fluorescence.
Ursolic acid significantly reduced extracellular 45Ca2+ uptake induced by antigen or thapsigargin, indicating impaired calcium channel/store-operated calcium entry.
Ursolic acid pretreatment significantly reduced chemotaxis of IgE-sensitized BMMCs specifically toward antigen.
Ursolic acid did not significantly inhibit BMMC chemotaxis toward PGE2 or SCF, indicating a selective effect on antigen-driven chemotaxis rather than general migratory capacity.
In antigen-activated BMMCs, ursolic acid treatment significantly increased TNF-α mRNA levels compared to vehicle-treated activated cells.
Despite increased TNF-α production, ursolic acid-treated and antigen-activated BMMCs released significantly less TNF-α into the supernatant than vehicle-treated activated cells.

Intracellular (total cellular) TNF-α protein, measured by flow cytometry in permeabilized cells, was markedly increased (3.7-fold) in ursolic acid-treated antigen-activated cells versus vehicle-treated activated cells.

Surface-exposed (non-permeabilized) TNF-α was only marginally higher (1.4-fold, not significant) in UA-treated activated cells, indicating reduced secretion is not due to accumulation of pro-TNF-α at the plasma membrane.

Ursolic acid had no effect on FcεRI β subunit tyrosine phosphorylation in nonactivated cells, but in antigen-activated cells it significantly enhanced FcεRI-β tyrosine phosphorylation compared to control.
Ursolic acid significantly enhanced SYK activation-loop phosphorylation (Tyr519/520) in both nonactivated and antigen-activated BMMCs at all time points tested.

Ursolic acid alone enhanced LAT1 tyrosine phosphorylation in nonactivated BMMCs, with no further increase observed after antigen stimulation, unlike vehicle-treated cells which showed increased phosphorylation upon activation.

Ursolic acid alone enhanced LAT2 tyrosine phosphorylation in nonactivated BMMCs, with no further increase observed after antigen stimulation, unlike vehicle-treated cells which showed increased phosphorylation upon activation.
Ursolic acid significantly enhanced PLCγ Tyr783 phosphorylation in both nonactivated and antigen-activated cells at all time intervals tested.
Ursolic acid increased ERK Tyr204 phosphorylation in nonactivated cells but significantly reduced it in antigen-activated cells at all time points, a biphasic dysregulation.
Ursolic acid reduced CBL Tyr700 phosphorylation in nonactivated cells and in cells activated with antigen for 1 minute, but not at later (5-15 min) activation time points.
Ursolic acid increased mTOR Ser2448 phosphorylation in nonactivated cells but reduced it after antigen stimulation compared to vehicle-treated cells.

Ursolic acid did not significantly change phosphorylation of the regulatory LYN kinase tyrosines (Tyr397, Tyr508) in either nonactivated or antigen-activated cells, suggesting the enhanced FcεRI-β phosphorylation was not due to increased LYN activity.
Ursolic acid increased the fraction of tyrosine-phosphorylated LYN, LAT1, and LAT2 localized to detergent-resistant membrane (lipid raft) microdomains.
Short-term ursolic acid treatment did not alter plasma membrane surface cholesterol exposure as measured by filipin staining, unlike methyl-β-cyclodextrin which reduced cholesterol.
Ursolic acid reduced the mobility and patch (aggregate) formation of antibody-crosslinked FcεRI on the BMMC surface, as visualized by confocal microscopy.
Ursolic acid reduced the mobility of antibody-aggregated Thy-1.1 glycoprotein on RBL-2H3 cell surfaces.
FRAP analysis showed ursolic acid significantly reduced lateral diffusion of FcεRI-IgE-FITC complexes, increasing the immobile fraction from 34.4% (vehicle) to 64.0% (UA).
FRAP analysis showed ursolic acid significantly reduced mobility of cholesterol-filipin complexes, increasing the immobile fraction from 43.0% (vehicle) to 73.2% (UA).
UA treatment did not significantly change phosphorylation of the regulatory LYN kinase tyrosines Y397 (activating) or Y508 (inhibitory) in nonactivated or antigen-activated BMMCs.

UA exposure increased the fraction of tyrosine-phosphorylated LYN, LAT1, and LAT2 localized within detergent-resistant membrane (DRM) microdomains in nonactivated cells, and antigen-activated UA-treated cells showed increased phosphorylated LAT1 and LAT2 in DRMs.

Short-term (30 min) UA treatment at 50 μM did not alter plasma membrane surface cholesterol exposure as measured by filipin staining, unlike methyl-β-cyclodextrin which significantly reduced filipin fluorescence.

FRAP analysis showed UA significantly reduced the lateral mobility of FcεRI-IgE-FITC complexes on RBL-2H3 cells, increasing the immobile fraction from 34.4% in vehicle-treated cells to 64.0% in UA-treated cells.
FRAP analysis showed UA reduced the mobility of cholesterol-filipin complexes, with the immobile fraction increasing from 43.0% in control cells to 73.2% in UA-treated cells.
UA pretreatment reduced the mobility and patch formation of antibody-aggregated FcεRI on BMMCs, with less fluorescence detected centrally in UA-treated cells compared to controls.
UA reduced antibody-mediated aggregation/patch formation of the Thy-1.1 glycoprotein in RBL-2H3 cells, indicating decreased mobility of this GPI-anchored plasma membrane protein.
Short-term exposure of BMMCs to UA at concentrations up to 75 μM showed no toxic effect as determined by the trypan blue dye exclusion test.

In a prior mouse model referenced by the authors, oral administration of UA suppressed both IgE-mediated passive cutaneous anaphylaxis and ovalbumin-induced active systemic anaphylaxis at concentrations similar in efficacy to the clinically used drug dexamethasone.
DMF treatment at both 30 and 100 mg/kg significantly increased withdrawal responses to Von Frey mechanical stimulation, reducing allodynia beginning at 24h and through day 5 post-surgery.
DMF at 30 and 100 mg/kg increased paw withdrawal latency in the plantar thermal test, indicating reduced thermal hyperalgesia after surgical incision.
DMF, particularly at 100 mg/kg, notably improved locomotor activity/motor coordination on the rotarod test after PO pain induction from 24h and daily through day 5.
Surgical incision caused inflammatory cell infiltration and interstitial oedema in paw tissue at 7 days, which was significantly reduced by DMF at 30 and 100 mg/kg but not at 10 mg/kg.
No significant morphological changes were observed in lumbar spinal cord histology between sham, PO pain, and DMF-treated groups.
PO pain injured mice showed reduced cytosolic IκB-α expression in hind paw and lumbar spinal cord versus control, and DMF at 100 mg/kg restored IκB-α to basal levels.
Nuclear NF-κB expression was increased in PO pain injured mice compared to sham, and DMF (better at 100 mg/kg) significantly reduced nuclear NF-κB in both hind paw and spinal cord.
IL-18 levels were increased in hind paw and lumbar spinal cord of PO pain animals versus controls, and DMF at 30 and 100 mg/kg strongly reduced tissue IL-18 levels.
IL-1β immunostaining was increased in hind paw and lumbar spinal cord of PO pain mice versus control, and was significantly decreased by DMF at both 30 and 100 mg/kg.
ELISA showed a strong increase in TNF-α in hind paw and lumbar spinal cord of vehicle-treated PO pain mice compared to control, and DMF at both 30 and 100 mg/kg notably reduced TNF-α amount.
IL-4 levels were increased in tissues from PO pain mice compared to control, and DMF at 30 and 100 mg/kg significantly reduced IL-4 quantity.

Seven days after hind paw surgical incision, mast cell number in the paw was significantly increased compared to non-injured controls, and DMF at 30 and 100 mg/kg significantly reduced mast cell infiltration.
No substantial difference in mast cell number was observed in the lumbar spinal cord across sham, PO pain, and DMF-treated groups.

NR2B immunoreactivity was increased in hind paw and lumbar spinal cord 7 days after PO pain induction compared to control, and DMF at 30 and 100 mg/kg significantly reduced NR2B staining in both tissues.
PSD95 positive expression was increased in the PO pain group in hind paw and lumbar spinal cord compared to control, and DMF (better at 100 mg/kg in paw) significantly reduced PSD95 immunoreactivity.

PSD93 and NR1 protein levels were significantly increased in lumbar spinal cord tissue from PO pain mice compared to control, and DMF at 30 and 100 mg/kg significantly reduced both PSD93 and NR1 expression.

Intracellular Ca++ concentration was significantly lower in hind paw and lumbar spinal cord tissue from PO pain mice compared to control, and DMF at both 30 and 100 mg/kg further reduced Ca++ concentration according to the results text (though the discussion describes DMF as increasing Ca++ concentration, an apparent internal inconsistency).
The paper reports absence of skin wrinkling (a sympathetic autonomic reflex, typically induced by water immersion) as a clinical/imaging teaching finding in a patient with small fiber neuropathy.

A spinal cord stimulator was implanted in a patient with bilateral lower extremity small fiber neuropathy refractory to conservative treatments, resulting in 80% pain improvement and improved function/quality of life at 5-month follow-up.

The patient's neuropathic pain was attributed to multiple subtypes of small fiber neuropathy secondary to HIV infection and chemotherapy exposure that had failed conservative management including oral medications, physical therapy, and desensitization techniques.
QST-derived sensory phenotypes do not differ between neuropathy patients with pain and those without pain, undermining their use for stratification.

The patient's combined clinical picture of inherited erythromelalgia (IEM), paroxysmal extreme pain disorder (PEPD), and small fiber neuropathy (SFN) — termed a 'pain triangle phenomenon' — was possibly associated with a variant of uncertain significance, SCN9A c.554G>A.
Genetic testing (SCN9A, SCN10A, SCN11A via MIPs-NGS) identified a gain-of-function SCN9A variant, c.554G>A, that enhances resurgent currents and renders DRG neurons hyperexcitable.
The patient's IENFD was 5.6/mm, which fell within the normal range according to established normative values despite her SFN-like symptoms.
QST using the Levels method showed abnormal warmth sensation in both feet, supporting a diagnosis of small fiber neuropathy.

The pathogenicity of SCN9A c.554G>A is questionable given its relatively high population frequency (0.3% overall, 0.24% European non-Finnish, 1.4% African/African-American in GnomAD v2.1.1) and its presence in healthy heterozygous carriers.
Amitriptyline (up to 25 mg, reduced to 15 mg nightly) produced some pain relief at night but caused nausea and vertigo, and pain intensity remained high enough to limit sleep to 3-4 hours.
Clonidine, initiated to reduce the patient's pain, had no effect.
Laboratory work-up revealed an elevated Vitamin B12 level (>1000 pmol/L), but no other laboratory abnormalities associated with SFN were found.
The patient exhibited dysautonomic symptoms including nighttime hyperhidrosis, hot flashes, palpitations, and occasional constipation alongside her small fiber neuropathy/pain triangle presentation.
Upper limb SSR latency was significantly prolonged in newly diagnosed type 2 DM patients compared with healthy controls.
Lower limb SSR amplitude was significantly reduced in newly diagnosed type 2 DM patients compared with controls.
Resting RR interval variability was significantly lower in the DM patient group than in controls.
Deep inspiration RR interval variability was significantly lower in the DM patient group than in controls.
Within the patient group, resting RRIV values were positively correlated with lower limb SSR amplitude.
Within the patient group, deep inspiration RRIV values were positively correlated with lower limb SSR amplitude.
The RRIV change rate from resting to deep inspiration ((D-R)/R) was significantly lower in DM patients than in controls.

Newly diagnosed type 2 DM patients without diabetic polyneuropathy on standard nerve conduction studies showed abnormal autonomic function tests, indicating standard electrophysiological studies are insufficient to detect early small fiber/autonomic involvement.
The vagus nerve exerts anti-inflammatory effects through both its afferent (HPA axis activation) and efferent (cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway) branches.
Stress increases intestinal permeability and is implicated in the pathogenesis of both inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).

In adults given intravenous CRH to provoke small intestinal permeability, a brief non-invasive transcutaneous auricular VNS reduced CRH-induced paracellular permeability but did not reduce I-FABP release.
Intravenous CRH is known to increase small intestinal permeability in healthy human subjects.
The cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway is mediated by vagally-released acetylcholine binding to α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on macrophages, inhibiting their release of TNFα.

The vagus nerve connects with the splenic sympathetic nerve, whose norepinephrine acts on splenic T-lymphocyte β2 receptors to release ACh, which inhibits splenic macrophage TNFα release via α7nAChR (the non-neuronal cholinergic pathway).

Splenic nerve activity enhances plasma cell production dependent on B-cell responsiveness to ACh via α9nAChR, with CRH-expressing neurons in the amygdala and hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus connected to the splenic nerve.
Ucn3, a selective CRH2 agonist, alters both para- and trans-cellular permeability of differentiated HT-29 and Caco-2 cells partly via disruption of adherens junctions and tight junctions.
Neonatal maternal separation predisposes adult rats to stress-induced mucosal barrier dysfunction, with evidence that CRH acts via CRH2 on cholinergic nerves to induce epithelial barrier dysfunction.
CRH triggers an increase in intestinal paracellular permeability via mast cell-dependent release of TNF-α and proteases, requiring input from the enteric nervous system.
Psychological stress-derived CRH can break established endotoxin tolerance in the intestinal mucosa, leading to clinical or subclinical inflammation associated with IBS and IBD.

Leukocyte infiltration is increased in EGC-ablated bowel segments after injury, and VNS decreases macrophage infiltration after ischemia-reperfusion injury only in segments with intact EGCs, indicating EGCs mediate transmission of vagal anti-inflammatory signals.
VNS protects against burn-induced intestinal injury through activation of enteric glial cells, acting locally at the gut tissue level and independent of splenic cytokine production.

Nicotine, an α7nAChR agonist, prevented intestinal barrier breakdown after severe burn injury by preventing decreased/altered localization of occludin and ZO-1, an effect lost when EGCs were removed from cytokine-stimulated intestinal epithelial cell cultures.

VNS induced increased intestinal GFAP expression, prevented burn-induced intestinal permeability and gut injury, and attenuated the burn-induced increase in intestinal TNFα and TJ proteins (myosin light chain kinase, phosphorylated myosin light chain); protection was lost in vagotomized animals.
In a mouse model of traumatic brain injury, VNS prevented TBI-induced intestinal permeability and injury, significantly reduced intestinal TNFα, and increased enteric glial activity (GFAP).

VNS performed within 90 minutes of burn injury protects the intestinal epithelial barrier, but this protective effect is lost when VNS is administered after 90 minutes, indicating a therapeutic window.
Targeted ablation of enteric glial cells in transgenic mice causes fulminating and fatal jejuno-ileitis, underscoring the essential role of EGCs in gut barrier maintenance.
Epithelial choline acetyltransferase expression is reduced during intestinal inflammation.
Rare variants in genes underlying vascular connective tissue diseases were found in 17.0% of individuals with high-risk SCAD and were significantly enriched compared with gnomAD.
COL3A1 variants showed the strongest enrichment signal among high-risk SCAD individuals compared with gnomAD.
Loeys-Dietz syndrome-associated genes were significantly enriched for rare variants in high-risk SCAD individuals compared with gnomAD.
Rare variants in genes prioritized by SCAD GWAS and arterial eQTL colocalization were enriched in 6.4% of high-risk SCAD individuals compared with gnomAD.
Likely pathogenic or pathogenic variants were identified in 4 individuals, localized to the COL3A1, TGFBR2, and ADAMTSL4 genes.
Unbiased genome-wide aggregated rare variant testing identified novel genetic associations specifically with peripartum SCAD.
The abstract's main text states rats had larger proximal colon villus height-to-width and villus height-to-crypt depth ratios compared with mice.

The abstract's closing summary states mice have a higher villi length-to-width and villi length-to-crypt depth ratio than rat in the proximal colon, opposite to the earlier statement in the same abstract.
Blocking nitric oxide synthase with l-NNA increased the frequency of proximal colonic contractions in both species, but the increase was greater in rats than in mice.
Despite the greater motility response to NOS inhibition in rats, the number of NOS-expressing neurons in the myenteric plexus was similar between rats and mice.
The authors conclude that the rat is a relevant additional animal model for studying how the inhibitory neuronal network of the enteric nervous system regulates gastrointestinal motility.

The infant was found to carry a de novo FBN1 variant (c.3152T>C, p.Phe1051Ser), classified as a variant of unknown significance but considered pathogenic in combination with her phenotype, establishing a diagnosis of Marfan syndrome.
The patient displayed metopic suture craniosynostosis, an atypical finding for Marfan syndrome that overlaps with the craniofacial features typical of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.

The authors propose that abnormal TGF-beta signaling underlies craniofacial abnormalities in patients with MFS, consistent with phenotypic overlap with Loeys-Dietz syndrome caused by TGFBR1/TGFBR2 variants.
Intraoperatively, the patient's dura was thin and fragile and the scalp dermis was weak, friable, and atrophic, with sutures tolerating only minimal tension before pulling through the tissue.
Postoperatively, the patient developed wound dehiscence and a 2x2 cm ulcerated area at the scalp incision, which failed to heal spontaneously and required operative debridement and re-closure.

Classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a collagen structure/processing disorder, is characterized by skin fragility and delayed wound healing, cited as a comparator condition for the wound healing issues seen in this MFS patient.

A retrospective study (Van Camp et al.) of patients with classical EDS and MFS undergoing oral and maxillofacial surgery found no significant difference in postoperative complications compared to the general population, attributed to strict perioperative precautions.

Surgical literature recommends closing dermal wounds in connective tissue disorder patients using at least two layers, leaving sutures in place twice as long as usual, and reinforcing with adhesive tape to reduce postoperative wound complications.
Marfan syndrome has a reported prevalence of 0.02-0.03%, with approximately 25% of cases arising from de novo pathogenic FBN1 variants.

Follow-up echocardiogram revealed mitral valve prolapse, mild-to-moderate mitral valve regurgitation, and mildly dilated aortic sinuses and ascending aorta, consistent with cardiovascular manifestations of Marfan syndrome.
The ADRA1A rs1048101*G allele was found at significantly higher frequency in VVS patients than in controls.
The ADORA2A rs5751876*C allele was significantly more frequent in VVS patients than controls.
The COMT rs4680*G (Val158) allele was significantly more frequent in VVS patients than controls, and this association survived Bonferroni correction.
VVS patients more often carried the ADRA1A rs1048101 G/G genotype than controls.
VVS patients more often carried the ADRB1 rs1801253*G allele (genotypes G/G+C/G) than controls.
VVS patients more often carried the ADORA2A rs5751876 C/C genotype than controls.
VVS patients more often carried the COMT rs4680*G allele (genotypes G/G+A/G) than controls.
No significant differences in allele or genotype frequencies were found between VVS patients and controls for HTR1A rs6295 or NOS3 rs2070744.
A biallelic combination of the NOS3*T allele with the COMT*G allele conferred substantially higher risk of VVS than either allele alone, despite NOS3*T alone showing no association.
A protective biallelic combination of the ADRA1A*A allele with the ADORA2A*T allele was associated with lower VVS risk than either allele alone.

A composite logistic regression model combining ADRA1A, ADRB1, ADORA2A, and COMT variant carriage achieved satisfactory classification performance (AUC=0.64) for distinguishing VVS patients from controls, while single-marker or biallelic models remained poor classifiers (AUC<0.60).
TGFβ treatment suppresses FcεRI transcription and expression on mouse and human mast cells, potentially inhibiting IgE-mediated function.
Recombinant TGFβ suppressed c-Kit expression on human mast cells, and c-Kit signaling normally enhances FcεRI-driven signaling.
In contrast to its suppressive effects elsewhere, TGFβ was shown by Lyons et al. to enhance IgE-mediated IL-13 production in BMMCs cultured with IL-3 alone.

TGFβ effects on IgE-mediated mast cell cytokine production depend on mouse genetic background, suppressing responses in C57BL/6-derived mast cells while enhancing or not affecting responses in 129/SV-derived mast cells, associated with differing baseline Fyn and Stat5B levels.

Antisense TGF-β1 oligonucleotide treatment significantly repressed passive cutaneous anaphylaxis and histamine and TNFα release from mast cells in rats, suggesting endogenous TGFβ normally supports IgE-mediated mast cell functions.
TGFβ suppressed IL-33-mediated cytokine release from BMMCs across four mouse strains and abrogated mast cell-dependent IL-33-induced neutrophil recruitment in vivo.
Recombinant TGFβ treatment reduced IL-3 receptor expression in mature mouse and human mast cells, leading to mitochondrial damage and caspase-mediated apoptosis.

Murine mast cells that differentiated in the presence of TGFβ showed reduced granule formation, degranulation, and cytokine production independent of Smad3, without affecting viability, showing a biphasic developmental effect where TGFβ enhances development in the first 10 days but suppresses it later.

TGFβ induces a mucosal mast cell phenotype marked by Mcpt1 and integrin β7 expression, with the Mcpt1-expressing population showing increased Skil (a TGFβ transcriptional target) during Alternaria-mediated airway inflammation.
Loss of TGFβ specifically in Mcpt5-expressing connective tissue mast cells increased total ovalbumin-specific IgE and augmented OVA-induced anaphylaxis compared to controls.

Mice lacking the TGFβ activator integrin β6 showed reduced Mcpt1 and Mcpt2 expression but increased tryptase expression in small intestinal mast cells, without affecting clearance of the parasite T. spiralis.

Bronchial and transbronchial biopsies from patients with uncontrolled asthma displayed higher numbers of TGFβ-positive mast cells compared to healthy volunteers and asthmatics with well-controlled disease.

Mast cell-derived TGFβ neutralization blocked the ability of bone marrow-derived mast cells co-cultured with naïve T cells to induce Treg differentiation, indicating TGFβ contributes to Treg upregulation.
Human germinal center FOXP3-expressing T cell numbers correlated positively with mast cell numbers.

IL-10 deficient mice displayed decreased Th2 cytokine responses, loss of gastrointestinal mast cell accumulation, and reduced anaphylaxis in a food allergy model, effects reversed by adoptive transfer of IL-10 expressing WT mast cells but not IL-10 deficient mast cells.
IL-10 signaling was shown to promote mir155 expression, which inhibited the phosphatase SOCS1, leading to exaggerated IgE-mediated mast cell signaling and functions.

Recombinant IL-35 suppressed IL-5 and IL-13 production from allergen-stimulated ILC2 cells isolated from pollen-allergic individuals and inhibited allergen-driven effector T cell proliferation ex vivo.

IL-35 producing Tregs were decreased in the circulation of patients with allergic asthma, and naïve T cells from allergic individuals differentiated into IL-35 producing Tregs at a lower frequency than those from healthy controls.

IL-35 suppressed histamine release and mRNA expression of IL-6 and IL-17 from the human mast cell line HMC-1 following PMA/calcium ionophore stimulation, attributed to abrogation of p38, Jnk, and Erk phosphorylation.
Patients with chronic spontaneous urticaria, a mast cell-driven disease, had decreased serum IL-35 levels that returned to normal after treatment.
Intraperitoneal IL-37 injection ameliorated allergic contact dermatitis in mice through inhibition of mast cell IL-33 and IgE-induced function.

IL-33 induces mast cell release of IL-13, IL-5, IL-6, IL-10, TNF, GM-CSF, CXCL8 and CCL1, and stimulates eicosanoid (PGD2, LTC4) secretion, without triggering degranulation, but enhances IgE/antigen-mediated degranulation and cytokine/chemokine production.

Short-term IL-33 exposure enhances IgE/antigen-mediated mast cell degranulation and cytokine production, whereas long-term/chronic exposure suppresses these responses, associated with defective calcium mobilization tied to reduced PLCγ1 phosphorylation and Hck expression (MyD88-dependent) or decreased FcεRI expression.
IL-33 released from damaged skin activated gut ILC2s to produce IL-4 and IL-13, driving expansion of gut mast cells and promoting food-induced anaphylaxis.

In a house dust mite lung allergy model, mast cell-specific IL-33/ST2 signaling was shown to drive lung hyperresponsiveness via increased PGE2 production, as demonstrated using mast cell-deficient mice reconstituted with ST2 knockout versus ST2 wild-type mast cells.

Mast cell-deficient mice lacked liver fibrosis and damage in a bile duct ligation-induced cholestasis model, and cholestasis-related liver damage was shown to be dependent on mast cell-derived TGFβ, since liver damage protection was lost when TGFβ-producing (but not TGFβ-deficient) mast cells were transferred back.

Human and mouse mast cell-derived exosomes carry both active and inactive forms of TGFβ that induce endosomal Smad2/3 signaling in mesenchymal stem cells, suggesting systemic effects of mast cell-derived TGFβ.
The large majority of Long Covid survey respondents described predominantly negative interactions with medical professionals, with only about a fifth reporting mostly positive experiences.
About a third of respondents' negative accounts centered on dismissal of their Long Covid symptom reports by medical professionals, often invoking the term 'gaslighting'.

Nearly 40% of respondents described prolonged diagnostic odysseys, including long referral wait times and inability to find supportive clinicians, exacerbated by lack of confirmatory Covid-19 testing early in the pandemic.
About 41% of respondents cited the lack of available treatment options for Long Covid as a source of perceived medical gaslighting and systemic failure of biomedicine.
Female respondents wrote longer and more negatively-valenced accounts of medical interactions than male respondents.
Respondents infected earlier in the pandemic (2020) described their medical interactions more negatively than those infected in 2021.

A subset of frustrated Long Covid patients turned to complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) providers, whom they perceived as more validating of subjective symptoms than mainstream 'Western' medicine.

Respondents who accessed specialized post-Covid care centers (e.g., Mount Sinai, Johns Hopkins) generally reported better, more validating experiences than in general practice, though effective treatments remained scarce even there.
Prohibitive out-of-pocket costs and inadequate insurance coverage forced some Long Covid patients to end diagnostic and treatment pursuits involuntarily.

One respondent reported being diagnosed with post-Covid POTS and Mast Cell Activation Syndrome (MCAS) at a specialty post-acute Covid clinic, but current treatments had not substantially improved their condition.

The paper notes (citing prior literature, not its own primary data) that Long Covid patient communities have distinguished a subtype symptomatically similar to ME/CFS (extreme fatigue, sleep abnormalities) from a subtype characterized by POTS-like orthostatic tachycardia.
ALS patients scored higher than controls on the total COMPASS-31 autonomic symptom questionnaire.
The gastrointestinal sub-score of the COMPASS-31 was higher in ALS patients than in controls.
The urinary sub-score of the COMPASS-31 was higher in ALS patients than in controls.
Sympathetic skin response amplitude in the hands was lower in ALS patients than in controls.
Sympathetic skin response amplitude in the feet was lower in ALS patients than in controls.
Resting heart rate variability did not differ significantly between ALS patients and controls.
Sweat gland density was lower in ALS patients than controls on skin biopsy stereological analysis.
Semi-quantitative analysis of skin biopsies showed structural damage to autonomic nerve fibers innervating sweat glands in ALS patients compared to controls.
SSR and resting HRV remained stable in the ALS cohort over a one-year follow-up period, indicating a relatively slow rate of autonomic nerve fiber degeneration compared to motor neuron degeneration.
Participants reported significantly worse overall current sleep health (RU-SATED total score) than they recalled having before their COVID-19 diagnosis, with a medium effect size.
Sleep regularity (getting in/out of bed at similar times) was significantly worse currently than pre-COVID, with a small effect size.
Sleep satisfaction was significantly worse currently than pre-COVID, showing the largest effect size among the six RU-SATED dimensions.
Daytime alertness was significantly worse currently than pre-COVID.
Sleep timing (proportion sleeping between 2-4 AM) was significantly worse currently than pre-COVID.
Sleep efficiency (minimal wake after sleep onset) was significantly worse currently than pre-COVID, with the smallest effect size of the six dimensions.
Sleep duration (proportion obtaining 6-8 hours) was significantly worse currently than pre-COVID.
Greater self-reported COVID-19 symptom severity during infection was the strongest independent predictor (besides pre-pandemic sleep) of poorer current sleep health.
A greater number of days since COVID-19 diagnosis was independently associated with poorer current sleep health, contrary to the study's hypothesis.

Having a pre-existing chronic health condition was initially associated with poorer current sleep health, but this association was no longer significant once symptom severity and days since diagnosis were added to the model.
Being in a romantic relationship was initially associated with better sleep health, but this association was no longer significant in the final adjusted model.
Older age was significantly associated with better current sleep health once other covariates including comorbidities and severity were controlled for.
Better pre-pandemic (pre-COVID) sleep health was the strongest predictor of better current sleep health.
Gender and education level were not significantly associated with current sleep health in the regression model.
Sleep health differed significantly by global region, with participants from Latin America and the Caribbean reporting better sleep health than those from North America and from Europe/Central Asia.
Poor current sleep health was associated with a greater number of days elapsed since testing positive for COVID-19, controlling for demographics and global region.
Poor current sleep health was associated with greater COVID-19 symptom severity, controlling for demographics and global region.
Current sleep health and quality of life were significantly associated, such that poorer sleep health corresponded to poorer quality of life, controlling for demographics and global region.

A GWAS of severe COVID-19 patients with respiratory failure found the ABO locus (9q34.2, rs657152) associated with disease, with blood group A conferring highest risk and blood group O highest protection.
Whole-exome sequencing in two pairs of brothers with severe COVID-19 identified X-chromosomal TLR7 loss-of-function variants correlated with impaired type I and II interferon responses.
The missense variant rs12329760 in TMPRSS2, which decreases TMPRSS2 stability and ACE2 binding of the virus, was less frequent in critically ill COVID-19 patients.
HLA-A*11:01, B*51:01, and C*14:02 alleles were identified as the most significant risk alleles predisposing to COVID-19 severity.
A UK GWAS reported the most significant COVID-19 association signals in the OAS1-OAS2-OAS3 gene cluster, DPP9, IFNAR2, and near TYK2.
IFITM3 variants rs12252 and rs6598045 were associated with COVID-19 severity/mortality in several studies, though another study found no significant association for rs12252.
The APOE e4e4 genotype was associated with increased risk of severe COVID-19 compared with the e3e3 genotype, notable because APOE is co-expressed in type II alveolar cells in the lungs.
The minor allele of ACE2 rs2285666, which increases gene expression up to 50%, was reported to affect SARS-CoV-2 infection and case fatality rate.

The ACE I/D polymorphism was correlated with both frequency of SARS-CoV-2 infection and mortality in Caucasians, though it was not associated with infection in a Chinese population, possibly due to differing allele frequencies.
The G allele of GRIK2 rs2247215, a gene involved in glutamatergic transmission, increased the risk of ME/CFS and was supported by gene expression data.
The T allele of NPAS2 rs356653, a circadian rhythm regulator gene, increased the risk of ME/CFS.
A GWAS identified 23 SNPs significant at p<1×10−10 for ME/CFS, with rs12235235 in RECK giving the most significant result, alongside variants in T-cell receptor alpha/delta loci.

Genotyping of 11,000 SNPs in immune and inflammatory pathway genes identified 32 variants associated with ME/CFS, highlighting complement activation, chemokine, cytokine, and toll-like receptor signaling pathways.
TNF -857 TT and CT genotypes were significantly increased and low IFN-gamma producer (A/A) genotypes were significantly decreased in ME/CFS patients; TNF rs1799724 was also significantly associated.
SLC25A15, P4HA1, EBF3, and COX7B2 were significantly associated with ME/CFS in the UK Biobank ME/CFS Cohort.
HLA-C*07:04 and HLA-DQB1*03:03 were associated with ME/CFS, suggesting immune system involvement, though this was not confirmed in all studies.
TCOF1 and THUMPD2 showed more copy number variants in UK Biobank ME/CFS cases than in controls.

Variants rs1866388, rs2918419, rs860458, and rs6188 in NR3C1, a major effector of the HPA axis, were associated with ME/CFS, and seven NR3C1 variants overall were detected as significant biomarkers in an integrated approach.
Longer (L and XL) 5-HTTLPR allelic variants were detected more in ME/CFS patients, supporting a serotonin (5-HT) system dysfunction hypothesis involving lower extracellular 5-HT.
The CCTTT8 allele of NOS2A reduced the risk of ME/CFS by 10-fold, whereas the CCTTT11 allele increased the risk of developing the disease.
The DD genotype of the ACE gene increased the risk of developing ME/CFS eight-fold compared with the II genotype.
Serum ACE levels were found to be elevated in about 80% of patients with ME/CFS.
A study examining AMPD1, CPT2, and PGYM genes found no significant association with chronic fatigue syndrome.
Twenty-one variants harbored in 13 different genes were associated with ME/CFS in one study.

The review identified gene overlap between COVID-19 and ME/CFS genetic association studies, comprising ACE, HLA-A, HLA-C, HLA-DQA1, HLA-DQB1, HLA-DRB1, TIRAP, and TYK2, predominantly involved in immune process regulation, chemokine/cytokine inflammation signaling, T-cell activation, and Toll receptor signaling.
Serum S100A8/A9 (calprotectin) was found increased in COVID-19 patients and significantly associated with symptom severity, but has not yet been measured in ME/CFS samples.
TIRAP has been implicated in activation of both mast cells and microglia, which interact to promote neuroinflammation, and both cell types have been separately implicated in COVID-19 and ME/CFS.

The flavonoid luteolin and its more potent analog tetramethoxyluteolin, formulated in olive pomace oil for oral absorption, inhibit microglia and mast cells, prevent neuroinflammation, are neuroprotective, reduce cognitive dysfunction including brain fog, and have been used successfully in COVID-19 and Long-COVID.

HLA-DRhigh CD11chigh inflammatory monocytes accumulate in mild COVID-19 but are depleted in severe disease, whereas HLA-DRlow, S100A (calprotectin)high monocytes are abundant and drive severe disease.
Bioinformatics intersection of Long COVID-related genes (from GEO/DEG analysis) and ME/CFS-related genes (from CTD, GeneCards, DisGeNET) yielded nine shared genes.
Protein-protein interaction network analysis (STRING/Cytoscape/cytoHubba) identified IL-6, IL-1B, CD8A, TP53, and CXCL8 as the top five hub proteins among the shared genes based on degree centrality.

Gene ontology biological process enrichment of the nine common genes highlighted peptidyl-cysteine S-nitrosylation, leukocyte aggregation, peptidyl-cysteine modification, positive regulation of intrinsic apoptotic signaling, and response to iron ion as top terms.
Molecular function GO enrichment identified RAGE receptor binding, arachidonic acid binding, and icosatetraenoic acid binding as top terms among the common genes.
Cellular component GO analysis showed MHC class I protein complex as a top term, with β2-microglobulin (B2M) noted as an early indicator of COVID-19 disease severity and outcome.

KEGG pathway enrichment of the nine common genes identified IL-17 signaling, AGE-RAGE signaling in diabetic complications, HIF-1 signaling, p53 signaling, and NF-kappa B signaling among the top ten enriched pathways.
IL-17 is proposed as an upstream modulator that drives IL-6 production, and elevated peripheral IL-6 may initiate ME/CFS through neuroinflammation.
A cited study found increased levels of inflammatory cytokines IL-6, IL-10, and TNF-α in ME/CFS patients, indicative of a chronic low-grade systemic inflammatory state.
In infection-triggered ME/CFS, IL-1b release is inversely correlated with soluble CD26 (sCD26) expression, which itself has been linked to health-related quality of life.
A cited autopsy study found a substantial reduction of CD8A in spleen specimens from patients who died of COVID-19.
Higher CXCL8 (IL-8) expression was correlated with greater clinical severity of COVID-19 in cited literature.
A cited study reported that CXCL8 (IL-8) levels showed a 42% decrease in CFS patients compared with control subjects.
In the transcription factor-gene interaction network, SERPINE1 is regulated by 57 TF genes and B2M by 54 TF genes, the two most highly regulated common genes.
Cited evidence indicates all COVID-19 patients, regardless of disease severity, have elevated SERPINE1 levels, contributing to coagulopathy, and SERPINE1 also impedes skeletal muscle regeneration.
In the TF-miRNA coregulatory network, IL-8 (CXCL8) showed the highest transcription factor degree (43) among all nodes.

Among identified microRNAs in the TF-miRNA coregulatory network, hsa-miR-204 showed the highest degree (3), potentially mediating neurotransmitter- and ion channel-related gene expression via non-coding RNAs.

Drug-gene interaction analysis via DSigDB predicted dexamethasone as one of the top candidate drugs interacting with the common Long COVID/ME-CFS genes, proposed to act via HPA axis/glucocorticoid receptor modulation.
Phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (TPA) was predicted as the top candidate drug interacting with the common Long COVID/ME-CFS genes via DSigDB analysis.

Lactacystin, a proteasome-modulating compound predicted as a candidate drug, influences mitochondrial metabolism via ROS and glutathione modulation, mechanisms implicated in sleep homeostasis and CFS development.
Cited literature indicates decreased hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis function in ME/CFS patients, consistent with a hypocortisolism state.
Children and adolescents seropositive for SARS-CoV-2 IgG were more likely to report clustered ME/CFS symptoms than seronegative peers in crude analysis, with the risk attenuating after adjustment.
Substantial fatigue (at least moderate severity, present at least half the time) was more frequently reported by seropositive than seronegative children, with an approximately 2-fold adjusted risk.
Female sex was associated with a significantly higher probability of reporting clustered ME/CFS symptoms than male sex.
Older age (14-17 years) was associated with a significantly higher probability of reporting clustered ME/CFS symptoms compared with younger children (5-13 years).
Preexisting disease was associated with a higher probability of reporting clustered ME/CFS symptoms.

When adjusted models additionally included federal state of the study center, associations of seropositivity with clustered ME/CFS symptoms and substantial fatigue remained similar to the primary adjusted models.

Restricting analysis to children unaware of their prior SARS-CoV-2 infection status substantially reduced the association between seropositivity and both clustered ME/CFS symptoms and substantial fatigue, suggesting recall bias inflated the crude estimates.

Reporting any past respiratory illness since the start of the pandemic was associated with increased risk of severe fatigue independent of SARS-CoV-2 serostatus, with similar effect sizes in seropositive and seronegative groups.

A large German health-insurance cohort study (preprint) found a statistically nonsignificant relative risk for ME/CFS diagnosis (ICD-10 code G93.3) in children with versus without previous COVID-19, consistent with the low risk ratios observed in the present study.
Prior genetic and electrophysiological studies found reduced TRPM3 channel activity and reduced calcium mobilization in ME/CFS patients.

Increased expression of the vasoactive intestinal peptide receptor 2, a neuroprotective factor released in response to high glutamate, has been observed in ME/CFS, consistent with excitotoxicity from excess glutamate.
Compared with controls, ME/CFS patients show additional recruitment of brain areas during cognitive tasks on task fMRI, one of the most frequently reported differences in this condition.

The authors' previous neuroimaging study observed less responsive fMRI signals in ME/CFS, characterized by lower sample entropy and looser coupling to tasks, consistent with delayed neurovascular coupling.
ME/CFS affects an estimated 17 to 24 million people worldwide, with about a quarter of patients housebound due to the illness.
A majority (80%) of ME/CFS patients report difficulty obtaining a diagnosis and are often left distressed by the lack of diagnostic certainty and medical understanding.
