The detergent-based extraction protocol (Protocol 2) yielded significantly more total membrane protein from cultured K562 cells than the ultrasonic/salt-precipitation protocol (Protocol 1) as measured by the Pierce BCA assay.
Protocol 2 also yielded significantly higher total membrane protein from K562 cells than Protocol 1 as measured by the Bio-Rad DC (Lowry) assay.
Protocol 1 (ultrasonic/salt precipitation) failed to yield any detectable protein when applied to isolated primary NK cells, unlike its success in K562 cells.

Protocol 2 successfully extracted membrane protein from NK cells isolated from 5 human donor whole blood samples, with mean yields of 1.641 mg/ml (Pierce BCA) and 1.713 mg/ml (Bio-Rad DC), with no significant difference between the two assay kits.

The Bio-Rad DC (Lowry) protein assay standard curves were less reproducible and more prone to overestimating protein concentration compared with the Pierce BCA assay when used with Protocol 2 buffers.
SDS-PAGE analysis localized TRPM3 membrane protein at the expected monomer molecular weight range (150-200 kDa) in all 10 protein samples extracted using Protocol 2.

Two TRPM3 proteotypic peptides, GANASAPDQLSLALAWNR and QAILFPNEEPSWK, were reliably detected by LC-MRM with multiple co-eluting transitions at consistent retention times in all 10 protein samples from ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.

The TRPM3 peptide SIDFEDITSMDTR, which is absent from some TRPM3 isoforms, showed multiple MRM transitions in only 3 of the 10 protein samples, suggesting potential utility for distinguishing TRPM3 isoforms.
Two additional predicted high-responding TRPM3 peptides, NWSNATCLQLAVAAK and EILMSEPGK, showed only limited MRM transition detection across all 10 samples.

Prior literature cited by the authors indicates TRPM3 ion channel impairment has recently been implicated in ME/CFS, alongside other neurological conditions such as neurodegenerative disease, glaucoma, intellectual disability, and epilepsy.

In a longitudinal multiomics study, plasma cortisol was significantly lower in convalescent COVID-19 individuals who still reported respiratory symptoms 3 months after infection, alongside higher titers of anti-interferon autoantibodies.
A post-mortem study of 40 COVID-19 patients found no cellular damage in the adrenal glands, arguing against direct viral adrenal injury as the cause of Long COVID hypocortisolemia.
In acute COVID-19, 52 patients showed higher diurnal salivary cortisol secretion than age- and sex-matched healthy controls, with unchanged morning levels but elevated evening and nocturnal cortisol.
Serum IL-6 levels were six-fold higher in acute COVID-19 patients than in controls and strongly correlated with nocturnal cortisol hypersecretion.

At 180 days post-infection, nocturnal salivary cortisol in 20 previously studied COVID-19 patients was almost 3-fold lower than during acute illness and comparable to 20 healthy controls; none of these individuals reported Long COVID symptoms.
An exploratory cross-sectional study of 215 individuals found that low plasma cortisol robustly distinguished Long COVID patients from asymptomatic convalescents and healthy uninfected controls.

Among 99 Long COVID participants (68% women), plasma cortisol measured more than 400 days post-infection was almost half that of matched controls, independent of age, sex, sample collection time, and BMI.
Machine learning analysis identified cortisol levels as the single most significant predictor for classifying Long COVID status.
Levels of depression and anxiety were markedly increased in Long COVID patients compared to controls.
Despite hypocortisolemia in Long COVID, ACTH levels were comparable to controls, suggesting an impaired compensatory HPA axis response.

Long COVID participants showed elevated humoral responses against SARS-CoV-2 and Epstein-Barr virus, plus significant differences in plasma IL-6, IL-8, and various chemokines compared with 15 convalescent and 25 healthy controls.

Long COVID patients showed elevated percentages (not absolute numbers) of non-classical monocytes, activated B-cells, IL-4/IL-6-secreting CD4 T cells, and exhausted T-cells (present in 20-30% of patients).
The degree of T-cell exhaustion was significantly associated with increased humoral reactivity to Epstein-Barr virus in Long COVID patients.
The combination of low cortisol, T-cell exhaustion, and augmented Epstein-Barr virus reactivity seen in Long COVID has also been observed in patients with ME/CFS, a post-viral condition.
Patients fulfilling ME/CFS diagnostic criteria account for about 45% of individuals across three separate Long COVID cohorts.

Patients with fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome show relative HPA axis hypo-responsiveness, including significantly lower mean 24-h urinary free cortisol, low diurnal salivary cortisol, and relative adrenal unresponsiveness to exogenous CRH and/or ACTH stimulation compared with normal subjects.

The hypocortisolemia and HPA axis hypoactivation described in Long COVID is reminiscent of the previously described post-SARS 'sickness syndrome' characterized by malaise, anorexia, fatigue, and myalgias.
Addison's disease is associated with immune perturbations, including high IL-6 levels, due to failure of cortisol to appropriately suppress increased secretion of proinflammatory cytokines.
The authors state that ME/CFS is associated with patients being more sedentary and having a reduced breadth of activities, which carries significantly increased cardiovascular and metabolic risk.

The authors note that the NICE guidelines for ME/CFS recommend careful energy management and supportive cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) as treatment options, with CBT linked to increased activity levels and associated health benefit.
Desk work and non-desk work groups did not differ significantly in age, Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire (CFQ) score, total brain volume, total gray matter volume, or total white matter volume.
Regional gray matter volume of the right entorhinal area was significantly lower in the desk work group compared to the non-desk work group.
Regional gray matter volume of the right middle frontal gyrus was significantly higher in the desk work group compared to the non-desk work group.
Regional gray matter volume of the left middle frontal gyrus was significantly higher in the desk work group compared to the non-desk work group.
Regional gray matter volume of the left precentral gyrus medial segment was significantly lower in the desk work group compared to the non-desk work group.
No significant correlations were found between CFQ scores and total white matter volume.
Across all participants, gray matter volume of the right supplementary motor area (SMC) was negatively correlated with CFQ fatigue score.
Across all participants, gray matter volume of the left basal forebrain was positively correlated with CFQ fatigue score.
Across all participants, gray matter volume of the right superior parietal lobule (SPL) was positively correlated with CFQ fatigue score.
In the desk workgroup, gray matter volume of the left frontal operculum was negatively correlated with CFQ fatigue score.
In the desk workgroup, gray matter volume of the right occipital pole was negatively correlated with CFQ fatigue score.
In the desk workgroup, gray matter volume of the right putamen was positively correlated with CFQ fatigue score.
In the desk workgroup, gray matter volume of the left fusiform gyrus was positively correlated with CFQ fatigue score.
In the non-desk workgroup, gray matter volume of the left anterior insula was positively correlated with CFQ fatigue score.
In the non-desk workgroup, gray matter volume of the right anterior insula was negatively correlated with CFQ fatigue score.

Overall stepwise multiple regression models significantly predicted CFQ fatigue scores from regional gray matter volumes, age, and sex for all participants, desk-only, and non-desk-only subgroups, with three, five, and three significant gray matter regions identified respectively.
Participants with hEDS/HSD reported long-term limits in social relations and interactions, with reduced ability to participate in society as they had before, significantly impacting quality of life.

The romantic partner relationship changes dramatically for people with hEDS/HSD, with partners needing to go through a process of acceptance and taking on caregiving roles that affect their own life choices.
Intimate relationships and sexual activity are impacted by pain, fatigue, and risk of joint dislocation, making sex less spontaneous and requiring modified positions or planning.
Asking for and accepting help is very difficult for participants, who prefer to remain independent and often feel guilt or a sense of inferiority when relying on others.
Contact with fellow hEDS/HSD sufferers provided relief, mutual understanding and reduced feelings of loneliness for participants.
Participants reported a decreasing number of activities they could engage in due to physical limitations, leading to loss of hobbies, reduced work capacity, and a sense of lost identity.

Use of assistive devices such as (electric) wheelchairs and e-bikes helped participants conserve energy and maintain social participation, despite being perceived as a public barrier due to visible disability stigma.
Participants used pacing strategies, described by some as the 'spoon theory,' to plan activities according to limited daily energy reserves and avoid symptom flare-ups.
After diagnosis, participants' social networks decreased as acquaintances disappeared while closer friendships remained, and social media became an important tool for maintaining contact.

Participants with children found parenting affected by their physical limitations, often unable to physically play with or lift their children, causing frustration despite efforts to provide a normal childhood.
The large majority of hEDS survey respondents identified joint pain/weakness as one of the most disruptive symptoms of their condition.
A majority of hEDS survey respondents reported having psychiatric conditions.
Participants scored highest on the BNE domain measuring expectations to have psychosocial concerns addressed during a genetic counseling appointment.
Participants also scored highly on the BNE domain reflecting desire for positive feelings after a genetic counseling session.
Participants who had previously undergone genetic counseling reported feeling less uncertain about their hEDS diagnosis compared with those who had not.
Participants who had previously undergone genetic counseling reported a lower need for information about hEDS compared with those who had not.
Most participants did not feel that their doctors were knowledgeable about hEDS.
The vast majority of participants strongly supported a multidisciplinary approach to their hEDS care.
The most commonly used complementary therapies among HSD/EDS patients were physical therapy (82%), massage (68%), yoga (58%), chiropractic (48%), and meditation (43%).

Patients with HSD/EDS reported low overall satisfaction with chronic illness care, with mean PACIC and PACIC 5As summary scores of 2.16 and 2.25 respectively (on presumably a 1-5 scale), indicating suboptimal patient-centered care.
Longer typical doctor visit duration (30 minutes or at least an hour) was associated with significantly higher PACIC scores across all domains compared to 15-minute visits.

Over 95% of respondents agreed or strongly agreed on the importance of the patient-provider relationship and trust, physicians' understanding of complete medical history, and prioritization of physical and emotional safety.
HSD/EDS patients commonly use specialized diets in addition to complementary and integrative health treatments for symptom management.
De Coster et al. reported that temporomandibular joint dysfunction occurs in more than 70% of patients with hypermobile EDS.
Stanitski et al. found that 72% of hEDS patients reported a history of joint dislocation, of which 26% were hip dislocations.
Ainsworth et al. observed shoulder dislocation in 63% and knee dislocation in 57% of hEDS patients.
To and Alexander observed a linear relationship between the length of an exercise intervention and the magnitude of strength gains achieved.
A systematic review by Palmer et al. identified only 11 studies of exercise interventions in EDS/G-HSD, showing benefits for muscle strengthening, proprioceptive acuity, and quality of life.
Autonomic dysfunction (dysautonomia) is a recognized complication of EDS/G-HSD, with symptoms reported in up to 78% of patients and POTS being the most prevalent autonomic profile.

George et al. reported that in an international POTS patient registry, 71% of patients who completed 3 months of exercise training no longer met POTS diagnostic criteria and were considered in remission.
Higher levels of community connectedness have been associated with less pain, more energy, better physical functioning, and fewer limitations in people with chronic disease.
Individuals with EDS/G-HSD frequently present with headache, neck pain, and decreased cervical muscle strength, symptoms hypothesized to be related to craniocervical junction instability (CCJI).
Among 101 patients clinically suspected to have vEDS, heterozygous pathogenic/likely pathogenic COL3A1 variants were identified in 33 patients (32.4%) using an amplification-based NGS panel.

Among 35 index vEDS patients, variant types comprised Gly-substitution missense variants (57.1%), one non-Gly missense substitution (2.9%), splice site alterations (22.9%), nonsense variants (8.6%), in-frame deletions (5.7%), and a multi-exon deletion (2.9%).

A heterozygous nonsense variant c.724C>T:p.Arg242* in COL3A1 was identified in two cousins clinically suspected of LDS/FTAAD who developed ascending aortic dissection, and cultured skin fibroblasts from one patient showed markedly reduced type III collagen production (22.7% of normal).

In Patient 13, mRNA-based direct sequencing of COL3A1 failed to detect a pathogenic variant despite reduced type III collagen production (29.5% of normal), whereas the amplification-based NGS panel successfully identified a heterozygous nonsense variant (c.848T>A:p.Leu283*).

Patient 6 with a heterozygous nonsense COL3A1 variant (c.598C>T:p.Glu200*) developed a right carotid-cavernous sinus fistula requiring repeated coil embolization, with additional dissections of carotid, iliac, and colic arteries.

Patient 19 carried a heterozygous non-Gly missense COL3A1 variant (c.1346G>T:p.Arg449Leu) classified as a VUS, associated with only mildly decreased type III collagen production (78.1% of control) and milder collagen fiber irregularity than a Gly-substitution case, yet with a clinically typical vEDS phenotype including arterial rupture and aneurysms.

A heterozygous multi-exon deletion of COL3A1 exons 24-33 was detected by an Ion AmpliSeq CNV visualization method (the Nishio Method) and confirmed by MLPA in Patient 35, whose skin fibroblasts showed severely reduced type III collagen production (4.5% of control).

In a deceased patient (Patient 12), UDG treatment of FFPE-derived DNA prior to NGS markedly increased sequencing coverage (from 14.7% to 91.2% of COL3A1 at ≥20× depth), enabling detection of a COL3A1 Gly substitution variant (c.763G>T:p.Gly255Trp) that was undetectable with untreated DNA.

Pathogenic COL3A1 Gly-substitution variants were successfully identified from FFPE tissue of two patients (Patients 3 and 12) who had died in their teens from arterial rupture, enabling retrospective molecular diagnosis and family cascade testing.

COL3A1 variants causing haploinsufficiency (nonsense, frameshift, splice-site variants predicted to cause premature termination) are reported in the literature to be associated with extended lifespan and delayed onset of first complication (by nearly 15 years) compared with Gly-substitution dominant-negative variants, though with milder arterial lesions but higher aortic disease prevalence.

Among patients clinically suspected of vEDS, some were found via the NGS panel to instead carry variants in TGFBR1, TGFBR2, or FBN1 (associated with Loeys-Dietz syndrome or Marfan syndrome), demonstrating the panel's value for differential diagnosis among overlapping HCTDs.

Three patients clinically suspected of vEDS were instead found to carry Gly-substitution variants in COL5A1 (classical EDS gene), yet presented with vascular lesions including carotid, splenic, mesenteric, and vertebral artery dissections/aneurysms, illustrating clinical overlap between cEDS and vEDS phenotypes.

The NGS panel reclassified two patients with a clinical diagnosis of LDS/FTAAD or FTAAD as having COL3A1 pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants consistent with vEDS, altering their management and enabling celiprolol therapy and family cascade screening.

Following molecular diagnosis of vEDS via NGS, several patients (Patients 9, 13, and affected relatives) were started on celiprolol therapy as a targeted pharmacologic intervention for vascular complication prevention.

Across 448 EDS patients from 220 studies, 720 vessel-specific aneurysms were reported, with the abdominopelvic region most commonly affected, followed by intracranial, thoracic, extremity, and venous locations.
Among 65 EDS patients with ruptured aneurysms, 27 presented with rupture as their first clinical manifestation of disease.
Of 249 EDS patients systematically evaluated for additional aneurysm sites, 163 were found to have multiple aneurysms rather than a single lesion.
The review found that aneurysm formation in EDS is not restricted to arteries, with involvement also reported in the venous system and cardiac septa.

The qualitative sample of 26 children/adolescents under paediatric rheumatology care included those with JIA (n=16), CIPS/CRPS (n=5), and EDS/hypermobility (n=5), reflecting the diverse chronic musculoskeletal pain conditions managed in this setting.
Rheumatologists were the healthcare professionals seen most frequently (69.23% of participants) and the ones with whom children/adolescents were most likely to discuss pain (53.85%).

Children and adolescents reported that pain was sometimes dismissed or 'brushed off' by healthcare professionals when labeled as 'mechanical pain' rather than disease-related, even though it felt the same and had equivalent functional impact.

Children and adolescents, including a participant with EDS/hypermobility, reported that they sometimes concealed the true extent of their pain from parents, complicating parents' role as proxy reporters to healthcare professionals during consultations.

Formal pain assessment tools such as numeric rating scales (1-10) and body manikins were used across consultations, but participants felt these did not adequately capture temporal fluctuation in pain or allow elaboration.

Participants, including one with EDS/hypermobility, described feeling nervous or scared to report pain due to fear of additional treatments, exercises, or new diagnostic findings ('something else wrong').

Familiarity/rapport with a consistent healthcare professional over time was reported (including by an EDS/hypermobility participant) as a facilitator that made pain conversations easier and enabled tailoring of pain management approaches.

Psychological/mental health impact of chronic pain was reported as under-addressed in consultations; one participant described a 'lightbulb moment' realizing that mental health 'down days' distinct from pain-related days were normal and worth discussing.

Inconsistent 'boom and bust' pacing advice given by healthcare professionals for pain/activity management was perceived by some participants as mismatched with their actual activity level, generating frustration and perceived lack of being believed.

The authors derived a set of practice recommendations for pain communication (e.g., asking about pain every visit, breaking pain into components, exploring parental-involvement preferences, balancing pain talk with non-medical topics, and eliciting patients' own self-management ideas) based on the qualitative themes identified.

Patients with fibromyalgia perceived fewer illusory flashes than healthy controls during sound-induced fission illusion trials, suggesting reduced fission illusion susceptibility consistent with visual cortex hyperexcitability.

The fusion illusion (perceiving fewer flashes when paired with a single beep) was similarly present in both FM patients and healthy controls, with no significant group difference in 2F1B, 3F1B, or 4F1B trials.
The presence of comorbid migraine in FM patients did not significantly affect the fission illusion perception, despite a nonsignificant trend toward further reduction in perceived flashes.
No significant correlations were found between fission illusion perception and clinical severity scores (FIQ, HADS-A, HADS-D) in FM patients.
Medication type (antidepressants, antiepileptics, analgesics, vitamins) did not significantly affect fission or fusion illusion trial results in FM patients.

Among FM patients, 41% (n=17) also had comorbid migraine, with chronic migraine (76.5%) more prevalent than episodic migraine (23.5%), supporting a close relationship between fibromyalgia and chronic migraine.
FIQ, HADS-A, and HADS-D scores were numerically higher in FM patients with comorbid migraine compared to those without, but the difference did not reach statistical significance.

In the Nature sounds group, temporal summation (pain amplification to repeated stimuli) was significantly lower while listening to audio compared to silence, whereas the Music group showed no difference between sessions.
Across both audio conditions combined, there was a non-significant trend toward lower temporal summation during audio listening compared to silence.
Temporal summation was marginally, but not significantly, higher in the Music group compared to the Nature group, suggesting a possible pre-existing sensitization difference between groups.
Mechanical pain tolerance (pressure at which pain was rated >80) did not differ significantly between Music and Nature groups or between Silence and Audio sessions.
There was a non-significant trend for the Nature group to show a greater reduction in heart rate from baseline during listening compared to the Music group.
Heart rate variability (HRV, RMSSD) showed no significant effects of audio group or session.

Participants randomized to the Nature group reported significantly higher anxiety symptoms than those in the Music group at baseline, despite groups being matched on FM symptom severity and musical experience.

Heart rate decreased from baseline to listening and further during pain in both groups; the Music group showed a greater pain-related heart rate decrease during music versus silence, while the Nature group showed a greater pain-related decrease during silence versus nature sounds.
Whole-body cryostimulation (WBC) is currently used to relieve symptoms in fibromyalgia patients according to prior literature.
WBC is also being applied to relieve symptoms of post-Covid syndrome.

WBC acts as a training method for the autonomic nervous system: cold-induced afferent signals converge in the hypothalamic medial preoptic region, triggering efferent reflex cutaneous vasoconstriction and a central blood volume shift that raises central pressure, reducing sympathetic nerve activity via baroreflex activation and shifting cardiac autonomic control toward parasympathetic dominance.
Even remote from the cold stimulation, WBC increases parasympathetic cardiac control, an effect that can persist overnight.

Repeated WBC exposure decreases production of pro-inflammatory and oxidative substances while increasing production of anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidative compounds, minimizing secondary tissue damage.

Impaired autonomic nervous system regulation is frequently observed in cardiovascular disease, subacute stroke, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, obstructive pulmonary conditions and obesity, and autonomic dysfunction is associated with poor functional outcome after subacute stroke and with fatigue in multiple sclerosis.
The review proposes that Post-COVID syndrome (PCS) may progress in association with mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS), driven by hyperinflammation.
MCAS, first reported in 2007, is characterized by allergic and inflammatory disorders with a prevalence of 17%.
IL-6 has been shown to increase mast cell proliferation and induce a more reactive phenotype, suggesting a link between elevated IL-6 levels and MCAS in PCS.
Lung biopsies from COVID-19 patients showed large numbers of activated mast cells compared with healthy controls, linking MCAS development to poor outcomes in severe COVID-19.
A case study reported POTS linked with the development of MCAS in a woman with COVID-19.

SARS-CoV-2 proteins E and N contain a PDZ-binding domain that can activate mast cell GPRX2 receptors, and augmented substance P and neurotensin release also engage GPRX2, providing a proposed mechanism for MCAS development in COVID-19.

Famotidine, acting as an H2 receptor inverse agonist/antagonist, is proposed to reduce endothelial permeability and dysfunction and to decrease histamine- and mast-cell-cytokine-mediated pathology in COVID-19 and PCS-related MCAS.
Zileuton, a 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor, is proposed to inhibit leukotriene synthesis, preventing hyperinflammation in COVID-19 and possibly alleviating MCAS symptoms.
A clinical trial of the H4 receptor blocker JNJ39758979 showed a notable effect in managing different allergic disorders, supporting H4 blockade as a potential MCAS treatment strategy.
Antihistamines are proposed to reduce histamine-dependent T cell perturbations in PCS, suggesting therapeutic benefit against PCS and associated MCAS.

Mast cell stabilizers such as Na-cromoglycate, clarithromycin, and hydrocortisone are proposed to prevent release of histamine and pro-inflammatory cytokines, potentially benefiting both PCS and MCAS.
Butyrate inhibits mast cell activation by inhibiting FcR1-mediated signalling.
Ruxolitinib inhibits mast cell activation by suppressing the JAK1/JAK2 pathway.
A monoclonal antibody against Siglec-8 inhibits airway inflammation via an IgE-independent pathway.
A case report found pirfenidone, a TGF-β1 inhibitor and anti-fibrotic agent, was effective in preventing post-COVID pulmonary fibrosis in a 40-year-old woman with COVID-19 pneumonia.
In a follow-up of 55 COVID-19 survivors, high blood urea nitrogen correlated with radiological abnormalities and high D-dimer correlated with functional pulmonary disorders.

A case-controlled study of 133 recovered COVID-19 patients versus 133 matched controls found flow-mediated dilatation was reduced in COVID-19 survivors, indicating persistent endothelial dysfunction independent of confounders.
A prospective study of 60 COVID-19 survivors versus 39 matched controls found neurological dysfunction in 55% of survivors compared with controls, some correlated with high LDH levels.
A meta-analysis of 20 studies found that delirium at admission was linked to poor neurological outcomes and high mortality in COVID-19 patients.
A retrospective cohort study of 236,379 COVID-19 survivors found that 56% developed various neuropsychiatric conditions within six months, mainly among those requiring ICU admission.
A retrospective study of 143 COVID-19 patients evaluated at 77 days post-onset found low testosterone in 28.7% of male patients, indicating pituitary-testicular axis dysfunction.
A case-control study of 43 COVID-19 patients versus 11 healthy controls found 46.5% had inadequate growth hormone response and 9.3% had low cortisol response, indicating pituitary dysfunction.
B cell activation and production of antiphospholipid autoantibodies were detected in 52% of PCS patients, indicating autoimmune involvement.
Post-COVID POTS is described as caused by an autoimmune reaction to SARS-CoV-2 infection and is more common in women.
Puntman et al. found in a study of 100 COVID-19 survivors that 60% had myocarditis and 78% had other cardiac abnormalities, unrelated to initial COVID-19 severity.
CuInS2/ZnS-PEG quantum dots internalized into human LAD2 mast cells at concentrations of 0-100 μg/mL without reducing cell survival or causing baseline degranulation or IL-8/TNF-α release.
CuInS2/ZnS-PEG QDs significantly inhibited Substance P-induced degranulation and chemotaxis of LAD2 mast cells by suppressing calcium mobilization.
CuInS2/ZnS-PEG QDs significantly inhibited LL-37-induced degranulation and chemotaxis of LAD2 mast cells by suppressing calcium mobilization.
Lower concentrations of CuInS2/ZnS-PEG QDs promoted Substance P-stimulated release of TNF-α and IL-8 from LAD2 mast cells.
Higher concentrations of CuInS2/ZnS-PEG QDs significantly inhibited Substance P-stimulated release of TNF-α and IL-8 from LAD2 mast cells.
CuInS2/ZnS-PEG QDs dose-dependently promoted LL-37-mediated TNF-α release from LAD2 mast cells across the 6.25-100 μg/mL range.
CuInS2/ZnS-PEG quantum dots dose-dependently inhibited LL-37-triggered IL-8 release from LAD2 mast cells at concentrations between 12.5 and 100 μg/mL.
Up to 40% of chronic urticaria patients fail to respond even to high-dose (four-fold) antihistamine therapy.

Addition of tofacitinib significantly improved urticarial activity in four refractory chronic spontaneous urticaria patients and one urticarial vasculitis patient, allowing tapering and discontinuation of cyclosporine or antihistamines.
Tofacitinib is proposed to downregulate inflammatory phenomena associated with mast cells, suggesting a mechanistic role in mast cell-driven urticarial disease.
Mast cells are increased in number and activated within psoriatic skin lesions, contributing to disease-associated inflammation.
Treatment of wild-type mice with the dermcidin-derived peptide DCD(86-103) produced a skin inflammatory reaction accompanied by cytokine release in vivo.
DCD(86-103) directly activated mouse primary mast cells and human LAD2 mast cells, inducing release of inflammatory cytokines in vitro.
The ST2 receptor was identified, via molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and siRNA knockdown, as a key mediator of DCD(86-103)-induced mast cell activation and cytokine release.
TPSAB1 gene expression in bronchial epithelial brushings was significantly higher in eosinophil-high than eosinophil-low COPD patients.
CPA3 gene expression in bronchial epithelial brushings was significantly higher in eosinophil-high than eosinophil-low COPD patients.
CMA1 expression showed only a non-significant trend towards lower expression in eosinophil-high than eosinophil-low COPD patients.

The mast cell bronchial biopsy (MCbb) gene signature was significantly higher in eosinophil-high than eosinophil-low COPD patients in bronchial brushings, remaining significant even after removing TPSAB1 and CPA3.
The IgE-activation mast cell signature (MCIgE) did not differ between eosinophil-high and eosinophil-low COPD patients in bronchial brushings.
The bronchial MCbb signature was strongly positively correlated with the COPD T2 gene signature.
The bronchial MCbb signature correlated with blood eosinophil count, sputum eosinophil count, and tissue eosinophil count.
The bronchial MCbb signature was not associated with IL5 gene expression or FeNO.
TPSAB1, CPA3 expression and the MCbb signature were significantly lower in bronchial brushings of COPD patients using inhaled corticosteroids compared to non-users.

There was no difference in total bronchial subepithelial mast cell numbers, tryptase-only (MT) mast cells, or tryptase+chymase+ (MTC) mast cells between eosinophil-high and eosinophil-low COPD patients on immunofluorescence.
Total mast cell numbers, MT, and MTC in bronchial biopsies were significantly lower in ICS users than non-users.
Tryptase-only (mucosal, MT) mast cells were significantly more numerous than tryptase+chymase+ (connective tissue, MTC) mast cells in both eosinophil-high and eosinophil-low COPD patients.
In sputum, TPSAB1 and CPA3 expression trended higher in eosinophil-high than eosinophil-low COPD patients but did not reach statistical significance.
The sputum MCbb signature was significantly higher in eosinophil-high than eosinophil-low COPD patients and remained significant after removing TPSAB1 and CPA3.
The sputum MCbb signature correlated with blood eosinophils, sputum eosinophils, and IL5 gene expression, but not with FeNO.

The sputum MCIgE signature did not differ between groups and did not correlate with T2 signature or eosinophil counts, supporting that chronic IgE-mediated mast cell activation is not involved in eosinophilic COPD inflammation.

An acute IgE activation mast cell signature (2h IgE sensitisation, 2h FcεR1 activation) was the only one of several in-vitro derived signatures to differ significantly between eosinophil-high and eosinophil-low COPD patients, in both bronchial brushings and sputum.
Intra-epithelial tryptase-positive mast cell numbers, normalised to epithelial thickness or basement membrane length, did not differ between eosinophil-high and eosinophil-low COPD patients.
There were no differences in mast cell gene expression, MCbb signature, or biopsy mast cell numbers between current smokers and ex-smokers.
The SFN-SIQ score was significantly higher in patients meeting Besta criteria for definite pure small fiber neuropathy than in patients without SFN.
The total number of distinct symptoms reported on the SFN-SIQ (graded 0-13) did not significantly differ between patients with and without pure SFN, unlike the weighted severity score.
ROC curve analysis comparing patients with and without definite pure SFN showed the SFN-SIQ score had an AUC of 0.8412, indicating excellent diagnostic discriminative ability.
An SFN-SIQ score cutoff of 6.5, derived from the Youden index, yielded 86% sensitivity and 70% specificity for diagnosing pure SFN, with 73% positive and 68% negative predictive values.
An SFN-SIQ score above 12.5 achieved a positive likelihood ratio of 15.73 (>10), indicating a high likelihood of pure SFN, with 97.73% specificity but only 35.71% sensitivity.
An SFN-SIQ score below 3.5 achieved a negative likelihood ratio of 0.09 (<0.1), indicating a very low likelihood of pure SFN, with 97.62% sensitivity but only 25% specificity.
The SFN-SIQ score significantly negatively correlated with intraepidermal nerve fiber density, such that higher symptom scores were associated with lower nerve fiber density.
The SFN-SIQ score significantly correlated with warm detection threshold measured by quantitative sensory testing.
Of 86 patients with suspected pure SFN and normal nerve conduction studies, 42 (48.8%) met the Besta criteria for definite pure small fiber neuropathy while 44 did not.

In a patient with celiac disease and small fiber neuropathy, electrochemical skin conductance measurements improved after adoption of a gluten-free diet, suggesting reversal or amelioration of the neuropathy.
36.3% of SFN patients had an abnormal (clinically relevant) score on the HADS anxiety and/or depression subscale, with 26.5% abnormal on anxiety and 23.0% abnormal on depression.
A greater number of pain sites was associated with increased odds of a high (abnormal) HADS anxiety subscale score in univariate analysis.
Higher current pain intensity was independently associated with a high (abnormal) HADS anxiety subscale score in the multivariable model.
Higher pain catastrophizing scores (PCS) were strongly and independently associated with a high HADS anxiety subscale score in the multivariable model.
Higher SFN-SIQ (SFN symptom burden, including autonomic complaints) scores were independently associated with a high HADS anxiety subscale score in the multivariable model.
HADS anxiety scores were not correlated with patient age or duration of pain.
Male sex was associated with higher odds of an abnormal HADS depression subscale score compared to females.
A greater number of pain sites was associated with increased odds of a high HADS depression subscale score in univariate analysis.
Higher current pain intensity was independently associated with a high HADS depression subscale score in the multivariable model.
Higher pain catastrophizing scores were strongly and independently associated with a high HADS depression subscale score in the multivariable model.
Higher SFN-SIQ symptom burden scores were independently associated with a high HADS depression subscale score in the multivariable model.
HADS depression scores were not correlated with patient age or duration of pain.

Intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD) on skin biopsy and quantitative sensory testing (QST) abnormalities were not significantly associated with high (abnormal) HADS anxiety or depression subscale scores, indicating objective small-fiber pathology measures do not capture psychiatric comorbidity.
Targeted next-generation sequencing identified a novel missense GLA variant, c.1139C>T (p.Pro380Leu), proposed to be pathogenic and causative of late-onset Fabry disease.
Blood alpha-galactosidase A enzymatic activity was low in this patient, consistent with Fabry disease.
Plasma lyso-Gb3 level was borderline in this patient with late-onset Fabry disease.
Cardiac MRI revealed cardiac fibrosis in the patient with late-onset Fabry disease.
The patient presented with an acute ischemic stroke and brain MRI showed cerebrovascular disease, attributed to Fabry disease.
Skin biopsy demonstrated small fiber neuropathy in the patient without evidence of globotriaosylceramide-3 skin deposits.
The patient exhibited angiokeratomas on the nape and back along with acroparesthesia, classic dermatologic and neuropathic features of Fabry disease.
The patient presented to hospital with an acute ischemic stroke as the initial clinical manifestation prompting diagnostic workup.
Skin biopsy showed small fiber neuropathy but did not reveal the globotriaosylceramide-3 skin deposits typically associated with Fabry disease.
Pain in the throat and chest (ICD-10 R07) was significantly more common in COVID-19 patients than in unmatched non-tested controls, with a very large hazard ratio in those with no prior pain history.
Abdominal and pelvic pain (ICD-10 R10) incidence and hazard ratio were higher in the COVID-19 group than in non-tested controls, regardless of prior pain diagnosis history.
Pain not elsewhere classified (ICD-10 R52) incidence and hazard ratio were higher in the COVID-19 group than in non-tested controls, regardless of prior pain diagnosis history.
Pain associated with micturition (ICD-10 R30) did not show a higher incidence or hazard ratio in the COVID-19 group compared with controls, unlike the other unspecified pain categories.
Headache (ICD-10 G43/G44/R51) was the only idiopathic pain disorder with significantly higher incidence and hazard ratio in the COVID-19 group compared with controls in the entire cohort.
No cases of fibromyalgia (ICD-10 M797) occurred in either the COVID-19 or control group during the 90-day observation period, precluding any comparison.
No cases of temporomandibular joint disorder (ICD-10 K076) occurred in either group during the 90-day observation period, despite the authors' expectation of an association via psychological stress.
In the subgroup with no prior pain-diagnosis history, irritable bowel syndrome incidence and hazard ratio were significantly higher in the COVID-19 group than in controls.
Prescription of opioid medications within 90 days was more frequent in the COVID-19 group than in non-tested controls, used as an indirect indicator of pain.
Antidepressant prescription incidence and hazard ratios did not differ significantly between COVID-19 patients and controls, regardless of prescriber specialty.
Anticonvulsant prescription incidence was higher in the COVID-19 group than in the control group.

When the comparator was changed from non-tested individuals to five alternative control groups with various health conditions (e.g., any hospital visit, hospitalization, URI, fracture, depression), hazard ratios for most unspecified and all idiopathic pain diagnoses were reversed, being less than 1 for the COVID-19 group in all five cohorts except throat/chest pain, indicating these alternative controls had higher pain risk than COVID-19 patients.

In the alternative cohort matched to controls who had visited a hospital for any reason, opioid prescription hazard ratio remained greater than 1 for COVID-19 patients even though most unspecified and idiopathic pain HRs were below 1 in that comparison.
Men with UCPPS had lower mean erectile function scores (worse erectile function) compared to positive controls and healthy controls.
Men with UCPPS had a greater degree of ejaculatory dysfunction (higher Ejaculatory Function Scale scores, indicating worse function) than positive controls and healthy controls.
Depression was associated with erectile dysfunction across all three cohorts (UCPPS, positive controls, and healthy controls) in univariable and multivariable analyses.
Stress was associated with erectile dysfunction across all three cohorts in univariable and multivariable analyses.
Pain was associated with erectile dysfunction across all three cohorts in univariable and multivariable analyses.
Diabetes mellitus was associated with erectile dysfunction across all three cohorts in univariable and multivariable analyses.
Pain in the genitalia was associated with ejaculatory dysfunction in univariable and multivariable analysis.
Pain localized to the genitalia was independently associated with greater ejaculatory dysfunction across the study population.
Greater severity of urinary symptoms was independently associated with worse ejaculatory dysfunction.
Depression was independently associated with greater ejaculatory dysfunction across the combined cohort.
Stress was independently associated with greater ejaculatory dysfunction across the combined cohort.
A history of childhood sexual trauma was independently associated with greater ejaculatory dysfunction across the combined cohort.

A 69-year-old woman with a history of fibromyalgia presenting with chronic abdominal pain, nausea, alternating constipation/diarrhea, and bloating was initially diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome before being found to have sclerosing mesenteritis.

Sclerosing mesenteritis symptoms (chronic abdominal pain, bloating, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, weight loss) are non-specific and mimic more common disorders including irritable bowel syndrome, which can delay diagnosis.
Sclerosing mesenteritis was found in 0.6% of over 7,000 consecutive patients undergoing abdominal CT scans, indicating it is a rare condition.

Studies show conflicting evidence on the association between sclerosing mesenteritis and malignancy, with cancer prevalence ranging from no significant difference to just over half of cases across different case series and case-control studies.
A five-year case-control follow-up study of 166 non-Hodgkin lymphoma patients found a 1.8% prevalence of sclerosing mesenteritis, which was not significantly different from controls.
FDG PET scan does not show increased tracer uptake in sclerosing mesenteritis, making it helpful for excluding underlying neoplasia.
Dual-phase CT scan is the most sensitive imaging tool for sclerosing mesenteritis, showing a 'fat ring or halo sign' and a 'tumor pseudocapsule' as characteristic diagnostic findings.
Corticosteroids have resulted in symptomatic improvement in some patients with sclerosing mesenteritis, though evidence for medical management overall remains unclear from case series data.

The patient with sclerosing mesenteritis subsequently developed cutaneous melanoma and, years later, a follicular/diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with IGH/BCL2 translocation and BCL6 rearrangement, illustrating the debated paraneoplastic association of SM.

Differential gene expression analysis identified 2,446 significantly dysregulated genes in COVID-19 brains and 856 significantly dysregulated genes in AD brains compared with their respective controls, with several shared GO pathways between the two diseases.

Network analysis of COVID-19 brain transcriptomes overlaid on the AD risk gene network showed increased expression of inflammatory cytokines IL-18, CXCL8, and IL-6 receptor, transcription factors STAT3 and KLF4, and the neuroinflammation marker GFAP.

STRING-based hub gene analysis identified CCL2, CXCL8, NF-κB, and STAT3 as key differentially expressed genes with the highest number of protein interactors in the COVID-19 brain dataset, reinforcing evidence of neuroinflammation.
Complement activation markers C4a and C5AR1 were increased in the brains of COVID-19 patients compared with controls.
COVID-19 brains showed decreased expression of the chaperones HSP90AB1, HSP90AA1, and HSPA8, while the tau-related chaperone FKBP5 was increased.
Calcium signaling components CAMKK2 and calbindin, along with the cholecystokinin receptor CCKBR, were all decreased in expression in COVID-19 brains.
COVID-19 brains showed a non-significant increase in gene signatures associated with monocytes, neutrophils, and activated dendritic cells compared with controls.

Viral plaque assays showed no detectable virus in brains of infected 3-month-old mice, but significant viral titers were present in brains of infected 6- and 20-month-old mice, and only at the 18 DPI (not 4 DPI) time point.

qPCR detection of CoV-2 N-protein transcript in olfactory bulb, cortex, and hippocampus was age-dependent, with only 20-month-old mice showing transcript in all three brain regions at 18 DPI and also testing positive in olfactory bulb and hippocampus as early as 4 DPI.

Pro-inflammatory cytokines Il-6, Tnf-α, and Ccl20 were increased in brains of 6- and 20-month-old CoV-2 MA10-infected mice, with the highest expression at 18 DPI in 20-month-old mice; only Il-6 and Tnf-α were significantly increased in 3-month-old mice and only in the olfactory bulb.

Inflammasome genes Nlrp3 and Ifi204 (the mouse IFI16 homolog), along with Il1β, were significantly upregulated in brains of 6- and 20-month-old CoV-2-infected mice but were unchanged in 3-month-old mice.
Active cleaved caspase-1 (p20), indicating inflammasome activation, was increased in all examined brain regions of infected 20-month-old mice.

Five key AD risk genes (FKBP5, IFITM3, IFI16, CR1, C5AR1) were not upregulated in 3-month-old CoV-2-infected mice but were significantly upregulated in 6- and 20-month-old infected mice, with Ifitm3 expression lower in hippocampus than olfactory bulb or cortex.
FKBP5 protein expression increase was confirmed by immunohistochemistry in all CoV-2-infected brain regions.

Nanostring nCounter analysis of infected aged mouse cortex confirmed upregulation of Lgals3, Egfr, C4a, Fkbp5, Gfap, Mapt, Ifitm3, Stat3, C5ar1, and Il6r, and downregulation of Hsp90ab1, Bdnf, and App, mirroring the human COVID-19 brain transcriptomic signature.

Phosphorylated tau (pT231)-positive cells were significantly elevated in olfactory bulb, cortex, and hippocampus of 6- and 20-month-old CoV-2-infected mice, with significantly greater increases in olfactory bulb and cortex of 20-month-old mice compared with 6-month-old mice; no p-tau was seen in mock or 3-month-old infected mice.

Tau oligomers (T22-positive cells), a toxic form of tau, were significantly increased in 6- and 20-month-old CoV-2-infected mice compared with mock, with a further significant increase in 20-month-old mice compared with 6-month-old mice across all brain regions.

p-tau was localized specifically adjacent to CD31+ endothelial cells, and increased von Willebrand factor staining was observed in infected brains, suggesting blood-brain barrier damage and a possible vascular etiology of tau pathology.
Immunohistochemistry showed elevated GFAP (astroglial activation) and IBA1 (microglial activation) expression in olfactory bulb, cortex, and hippocampus of CoV-2-infected mouse brains.

A significantly increased grade of demyelination (MBP staining) was seen in the striatum of infected aged brain tissue, along with significantly increased α-synuclein staining in 6- and 20-month-old infected mice.
The SMAD4-I500V variant retains the ability to dimerize but shows severely compromised transcriptional activity compared to wild-type SMAD4.
SMAD4-I500V acts in a dominant-negative manner on wild-type SMAD4 and on receptor-regulated SMADs, altering transcription of downstream target genes.
SMAD4-I500V impacts the transcription and functional activity of the developmental transcription regulator NKX2-5.
The dominant-negative effect of SMAD4-I500V leads to overall dysregulation of TGF-beta and BMP signaling pathways, underlying Myhre syndrome pathogenesis.
Germline variants causing Myhre syndrome localize at two positions in SMAD4, I500 and R496, with I500 V/T/M substitutions being more commonly identified in affected individuals.
Phenytoin stimulated CCN2 (connective tissue growth factor) synthesis in human gingival fibroblasts.
Phenytoin activated latent TGFβ1 in human gingival fibroblasts.
Phenytoin increased cellular ROS generation in human gingival fibroblasts.
Blocking TGFβ signaling with a TGFβ-neutralizing antibody, the TGFβ receptor kinase inhibitor SB431542, or the Smad3 inhibitor SIS3 completely inhibited phenytoin-induced CCN2 synthesis.

The general antioxidant N-acetylcysteine, the NOX inhibitor diphenylene iodonium, and the specific NOX4 inhibitor plumbagin almost completely suppressed phenytoin-induced ROS generation and latent TGFβ1 activation, indicating NOX4-derived ROS mediate this activation.
Curcumin dose-dependently decreased phenytoin-induced TGFβ1 activation and CCN2 synthesis in human gingival fibroblasts.
Higher total sedentary time was directly associated with greater depressive symptoms in women with fibromyalgia.
Time accumulated in sedentary bouts of 30 minutes or more was directly associated with greater depressive symptoms.
Time accumulated in sedentary bouts of 60 minutes or more was directly associated with greater depressive symptoms.
Associations between sedentary time and depressive symptoms generally remained significant after adjusting for moderate-to-vigorous physical activity and physical fitness.
Higher total sedentary time was directly associated with greater state anxiety in women with fibromyalgia.
Time accumulated in sedentary bouts of 30 minutes or more was directly associated with greater state anxiety.
Time accumulated in sedentary bouts of 60 minutes or more was directly associated with greater state anxiety.
The association between sedentary time and state anxiety disappeared after accounting for physical fitness, suggesting a protective/moderating role of fitness.
MVPA did not modify the associations between sedentary time and depressive symptoms or state anxiety.
The association between sedentary time (total and prolonged bouts) and state anxiety was no longer statistically significant after adjusting for physical fitness.

Physical fitness, but not moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, appeared to modify the associations of sedentary time with depressive symptoms and especially state anxiety, suggesting a protective role of fitness.
The authors suggest that reducing sedentary time and avoiding its accumulation in prolonged periods could be a rehabilitation strategy to reduce depressive symptoms and state anxiety in fibromyalgia.
Quantitative proteomics and biological validation showed elevated CCN2 protein levels in NGLY1-deficient human and mouse cell models compared to control cells.
Functional assays demonstrated over-stimulation of TGF-beta signaling in NGLY1-deficient cells, coinciding with elevated CCN2.
NGLY1-deficient cells show abnormal accumulation of endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (ERAD) substrates.
The authors propose that increased CCN2 and TGF-beta signaling may be linked to microscopic liver fibrosis observed in NGLY1 patients.
Mast cell infiltration in intestinal tissue was significantly increased in the IBS rat model compared to normal controls.
Abdominal massage reduced mast cell counts in IBS rat intestinal tissue, and combining massage with ketotifen further reduced mast cell counts.
IBS induction reduced mitochondrial number and caused swollen morphology with disrupted cristae in intestinal mucosal cells compared to control.
Abdominal massage protected mitochondrial integrity in intestinal mucosa of IBS rats, and this effect was enhanced when combined with the mast cell blocker ketotifen.
TRPV1 mRNA expression was reported as upregulated in the IBS group compared to control, though the difference was not statistically significant.
Abdominal massage significantly attenuated the upregulation of TRPV1 mRNA compared to the IBS group, and addition of a mast cell blocker further reduced TRPV1 expression.
TRPV1 protein, examined by immunofluorescence and localized to the plasma membrane, was highly expressed in the IBS group compared to control.
Abdominal massage suppressed TRPV1 protein expression compared to the IBS group; addition of a mast cell blocker further reduced TRPV1 but not significantly.
Tryptase granule levels in mast cells were significantly higher in the IBS group compared to normal controls.
Abdominal massage significantly reduced tryptase particle levels compared to the IBS group, but adding a mast cell blocker did not further reduce tryptase.
PAR2 protein was upregulated in the IBS group compared to control rats.
PKC (PKCepsilon) protein was upregulated in the IBS group compared to control rats.
Abdominal massage reduced PAR2 and PKCepsilon expression compared to the IBS group, and combining massage with a mast cell blocker further suppressed their expression.
Proteins of the PIP2-PLC downstream signaling axis were upregulated in the IBS group and downregulated upon abdominal massage or mast cell blocker treatment.

Histological analysis showed that abdominal massage restored normal intestinal villous morphology in IBS rats, whereas combining massage with ketotifen paradoxically resulted in swollen mucous membrane and acinar cells.
Red blood cell count differed significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls.
Hematocrit differed significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls and correlated with clinical parameters of fibromyalgia.
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) differed significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls.
Platelet count differed significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls.
Serum creatinine levels differed significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls.
HbA1c levels differed significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls.
ESR values differed significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls and correlated with clinical parameters of fibromyalgia.

ROC analysis indicated that routine laboratory parameters (RBC count, hematocrit, MCHC, platelet count, creatinine, HbA1c, ESR) may assist in differentiating fibromyalgia patients from healthy controls.
Both ME/CFS patients showed approximately 20-fold higher unique CpG-site methylation variability across time points compared to the healthy control.
Fragment-level (multi-CpG) methylation variability scores were higher in both patients than in the control, with the more symptomatic patient showing the highest score.
Patients showed greater methylation variability than the control across gene bodies and CpG islands, but variability was similar across all three individuals at transcription start sites.

Hierarchical clustering of 577 common methylation fragments across all 15 samples grouped samples by individual (patient/control identity) rather than by time point, though intra-individual variation across time points was also visible.

STRING pathway enrichment of genes containing differentially methylated fragments in P1 versus control identified nicotine addiction and morphine addiction pathways, driven by GNAS, CACNA1A and GABRD.

STRING pathway enrichment of genes containing differentially methylated fragments in P2 versus control identified TGF-beta family and Immunoglobulin C-2 type domains, from genes IGSF9B, OPCML, GDF7, CERS1 and LINGO3.
In patient P1, all 17 methylation fragments that correlated strongly with self-reported health scores were hypomethylated during the relapse period compared with recovery periods.
In patient P2, of 14 relapse-correlated methylation fragments, 11 were hypomethylated and 3 were hypermethylated during the relapse period compared with recovery.

The number of genes associated with relapse-correlated methylation fragments was significantly greater in the two patients than in simulated 'relapse' analyses performed on the healthy control's data, supporting that the changes reflect true disease biology rather than random variation.

Genes associated with relapse-related methylation changes in both patients were predominantly linked to immune/inflammatory function, including NF-kappa-B activity, wound healing, cytokine release, and angiogenesis, suggesting an enhanced inflammatory state during relapse.
In patient P2, differential methylation of CXCR1 and CXCR2 during relapse suggested potential activation of the interleukin-8 (IL-8) mediated signalling pathway.

The authors cite prior work indicating IL8 is the gene most differentially expressed between ME/CFS patients and controls, and that IL-8 levels are significantly higher in severely affected ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls or moderately affected patients, supporting their own CXCR1/CXCR2 methylation findings.

In patient P1, a hypomethylated fragment during relapse overlapped the first intron of NLRP7 and an enhancer, alongside other NF-kappa-B-associated genes (COMMD5, LRRC14, TONSL), suggesting increased inflammatory gene regulation during relapse.

In patient P2, differentially methylated fragments associated with TICAM1 and IL17RA, genes involved in positive regulation of cytokine production in inflammatory responses, were identified during relapse.
Several methylation-affected genes in patient P2 during relapse (TMBIM1, SLC11A1, MOSPD2, CXCR2, CXCR1, LRG1) are involved specifically in the neutrophil degranulation pathway.

Seven mitochondrial genes, including ACOT9 (acyl-CoA hydrolysis) and HADHA/HADHB (mitochondrial beta-oxidation of long chain fatty acids), showed relapse-associated methylation changes in patient P1, potentially reflecting reduced mitochondrial function during relapse.

A relapse-associated methylation fragment in patient P2 was located within the last (17th) exon of SEMA6B, a gene involved in peripheral and central nervous system development, overlapping a promoter region and regulatory element clusters with YJU2, PLIN5, and LRG1.
Sleep-related symptoms were identified as a risk factor for suicidal ideation among people with ME/CFS.
Stigma was identified as a risk factor for suicidal ideation among people with ME/CFS.
Disability status was identified as a risk factor for suicidal ideation among people with ME/CFS.
Lower physical functioning was identified as a risk factor for suicidal ideation among people with ME/CFS.
Marital status was identified as a risk (or protective) factor for suicidal ideation among people with ME/CFS.
IKZF2 expression was significantly increased in bedridden (severe) ME/CFS patients compared to non-bedridden patients.
IKZF3 expression was significantly increased in bedridden ME/CFS patients versus non-bedridden patients and was among the genes most associated with bedridden status when controlling for age and sex.
ABCE1, an inhibitor of the antiviral OAS/RNase L pathway, was upregulated in severe (bedridden) ME/CFS cases, suggesting impairment of RNase L antiviral signaling in these patients.
BACH2 expression was significantly increased in bedridden ME/CFS patients compared to non-bedridden patients.
CD3D, a T-cell receptor/CD3 complex gene, was significantly upregulated in bedridden ME/CFS patients relative to non-bedridden patients.
HSPA8 was among the top genes associated with bedridden status in ME/CFS patients, significant even after controlling for age and sex.

In the subset of ME/CFS patients with comorbid autoimmune disease, the six bedridden-associated genes showed even greater differential expression between bedridden and non-bedridden patients than in the overall ME/CFS cohort, suggesting an additive effect of autoimmune comorbidity on fatigue-related gene expression.
Interferon-stimulated genes IFIT1, ISG15, and IFI6 were enriched (upregulated) in female ME/CFS patients compared to males within unsupervised clustering analysis.
APOL6 and SLC2A3 expression was higher in ME/CFS patients aged 55 years and older compared to younger patients.
Thirty percent of ME/CFS participants reported having one or more comorbid autoimmune diseases, compared to 10% of healthy controls.
HHV-6 was detected via qPCR in 7 of 163 CFS blood samples and 1 of 79 control samples, a difference that did not reach statistical significance.
Only one CFS blood sample tested positive for EBV DNA by qPCR, indicating that active EBV infection was rare in this cohort.
Approximately half (49%) of ME/CFS participants reported being housebound or bedridden due to their symptoms.

Seventy-six percent of ME/CFS patients reported a triggering event before disease onset, and 80% of those identified a viral or bacterial infection (e.g., EBV, mononucleosis, flu, H. pylori, pneumonia, strep throat, COVID) as the trigger.

Replicate blood samples collected 3-4 weeks apart from the same participants showed high correlation (Spearman r = 0.86) across all 51 AIP panel genes, supporting reproducibility of the fingerstick gene expression test.

Citing a prior Norwegian clinical trial, B-cell depletion with rituximab (anti-CD20) was reported to produce clinical benefit in about half of ME/CFS patients treated, with symptom improvement delayed 3-7 months after initial B-cell depletion.

A cited case series described three ME/CFS patients (7-10 years disease duration) who had substantial relief of all CFS symptoms after rituximab treatment, lasting until about 40 weeks post-treatment before gradual symptom return.

A cited 2013 study found CFS was associated with an increased risk of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, particularly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, and B-cell NHL not otherwise specified.

Two superordinate themes, 'Lack of knowledge and understanding' and 'Holistic Impact', were identified across carers of youth, young adults, and spouses with ME/CFS, echoing themes found in prior caregiver studies.

The sub-ordinate themes 'Caring Blindly', 'Emotional and physical health cost', and 'Impact on the whole family' were more evident among carers of youth with ME/CFS than among carers of young adults or spouses.

The theme 'Worry for the future' was more prominent among carers of young adults and spouses with ME/CFS compared to carers of youth, plausibly reflecting differences in life stage and time since diagnosis.
IgG autoantibodies against the alpha-2A adrenergic receptor were significantly lower in both PCS/ME/CFS and PCS/non-ME/CFS patients compared with both healthy control groups (HC and PCHC).

Autoantibodies against the beta-2 adrenergic receptor were significantly decreased in both PCS/ME/CFS and PCS/non-ME/CFS relative to HC and PCHC, and ADRB2-Ab was the top-ranked classifier in random forest analysis.

Autoantibodies against the scavenger receptor Stabilin-1 were significantly lower in both PCS groups compared to healthy controls and ranked among the top classifiers of PCS in random forest analysis.
Autoantibodies against the chemokine receptor CXCR3 were significantly reduced in both PCS/ME/CFS and PCS/non-ME/CFS compared to healthy control groups.
Autoantibodies against the muscarinic receptor CHRM5 and nicotinic receptor CHRNA1 were specifically diminished in PCS/ME/CFS patients but not clearly in PCS/non-ME/CFS.
Autoantibodies against the protease-activated receptor F2R/PAR-1 were reduced specifically in PCS/non-ME/CFS patients compared to healthy groups.
MAS1 autoantibody levels were the only AAB found to differ between the two healthy control groups (post-COVID PCHC vs seronegative HC), unlike all other measured AABs.

Total serum IgG concentrations did not differ significantly between PCS patients and control groups, indicating that AAB differences are not explained by global hypogammaglobulinemia or hypergammaglobulinemia.

Regression modeling showed that 13 of the 20 measured autoantibodies were significantly affected by confounders, with 9 influenced by gender, 3 by disease duration, and ADRB1 by both, with a general trend toward higher AAB levels in males and decreasing levels with time since infection.

After adjusting for sex, age and time since infection, PCS/ME/CFS patients had higher levels of CHRM1 and F2R/PAR-1 autoantibodies but lower levels of ADRB1, CHRNA1 and EDNRA autoantibodies compared with PCS/non-ME/CFS patients.

Random forest classification using all 20 measured autoantibody levels distinguished healthy individuals from PCS patients with an AUC of 0.77 and an out-of-bag error rate of 20.34%, with ADRB2-Ab, STAB1-Ab, and ADRA2A-Ab as the top three classifiers.

Spearman correlation networks among the 20 autoantibodies showed altered inter-AAB relationships in PCS patients, including weakened correlation of ADRB2 with ADRB1 and CHRM4 compared with healthy groups, and stronger correlations of CHRM1 with AGTR2/CHRM2 in patients and of EDNRB with BDKRB1 mainly in PCS/ME/CFS.

In PCS/ME/CFS patients, fatigue severity correlated positively with circulating autoantibody levels against AGTR1, EDNRA, BDKRB1, ADRB1/2, and CHRM3/5, all of which were otherwise reduced in this group.

Severity of cognitive symptoms in PCS/ME/CFS patients correlated positively with autoantibody levels against F2R/PAR-1, CXCR3, and STAB1, receptors involved in inflammatory processes rather than vasoconstriction.
Immune symptom severity in PCS/ME/CFS correlated positively with autoantibody levels against EDNRB, BDKRB1, and CHRM5.
In PCS/ME/CFS patients, secretomotor autonomic symptoms (dry eyes, dry mouth) on COMPASS-31 correlated negatively with autoantibody levels against AGTR1, EDNRA, ADRA1A, ADRB1/2, and CHRM3.
ADRB2-Ab and CHRM3-Ab levels correlated with vasomotor (Raynaud) symptoms in PCS/ME/CFS patients on the COMPASS-31 questionnaire.

In PCS/non-ME/CFS patients, gastrointestinal symptoms correlated with MAS1-Ab, gastrointestinal and pupillomotor symptoms correlated with F2R/PAR-1-Ab, and bladder symptoms correlated negatively with ADRA2A- and CHRM2/5-Ab; none of the fatigue/cognitive/immune correlations seen in PCS/ME/CFS were significant in this group.

PCS/ME/CFS patients had significantly worse fatigue (Chalder Fatigue Scale), higher PEM score, greater disability (Bell Disability Scale), and worse physical functioning (SF-36) than PCS/non-ME/CFS patients, though overall symptom severity scores for fatigue, cognitive symptoms, headache, and muscle pain did not differ between groups.

The authors note that a sequence in Epstein-Barr virus with high homology to ADRA2 may induce cross-reactive IgG antibodies, potentially relevant given that EBV reactivation during COVID-19 has been identified as a risk factor for Post COVID Syndrome.
Pooled analysis of 52 studies found the global prevalence of chronic fatigue syndrome among long COVID-19 patients to be 45.2%.
Heterogeneity among the included studies was extremely high (I2=99.7%), prompting use of a random effects model.
Publication bias was found to be statistically significant, indicating the pooled prevalence estimate should be interpreted with caution.
Meta-regression showed that the prevalence of chronic fatigue syndrome among long COVID patients increased with larger sample size and later year of study.
Several cited studies report higher prevalence of post-COVID fatigue among women compared to men, with one study finding fatigue prevalence three times higher in women.
Some studies reviewed did not find a difference in fatigue prevalence between men and women.
Chronic post-COVID-19 fatigue prevalence and severity were reported to be higher among adults than younger age groups, and aging was significantly associated with fatigue in one study.

Hospitalized patients experienced greater severity of chronic post-COVID-19 fatigue than non-hospitalized patients in some studies, and length of hospital stay affected the duration of fatigue, though one study found the opposite pattern.
In a Swedish study of healthcare professionals, 8% of participants reported disturbances in their work life and 15% reported disturbances in their social life due to post-COVID-19 syndrome.
In one cited study, 49% of patients experienced long COVID symptoms and chronic fatigue, and social disability was reported in more than 30% of participants in a study by Lemhofer.
FM patients (total group) showed significantly worse levels of depression, stress, anxiety, pain, fatigue, and fibromyalgia impact compared to healthy reference women.
FM patients showed greater fear and anxiety toward COVID-19 compared to the healthy reference group.
Codiagnosis of CFS in FM patients did not significantly affect levels of depression, stress, state anxiety, or trait anxiety compared to FM-only patients.

FM patients (with or without CFS) who reported habitual physical exercise (HPE) showed significantly better levels of depression, stress, and anxiety compared to sedentary patients, approaching reference group values.
COVID-19 related anxiety did not improve significantly with HPE, although a strong trend toward improvement was observed.
FM patients (both FM-only and FM+CFS) who reported HPE had lower levels of fear of COVID-19 compared to sedentary patients, nearly reaching reference group levels.
Codiagnosis with CFS did not affect quality of life/personal control or pain levels in FM patients, although both parameters were worse than the reference group.
The complete FM+CFS group reported significantly greater fatigue than the complete FM-only group.
FM patients (both with and without CFS) who reported HPE had significantly higher quality of life and personal control scores than sedentary patients, reaching reference group values.
No improvement in fatigue and pain levels was observed in women with FM who reported performing HPE, regardless of CFS codiagnosis.
Only in the FM-only group, HPE had a positive influence on the impact of fibromyalgia on daily life.
A differential effect of CFS codiagnosis was observed only in depression response to exercise: only FM patients without CFS showed improved depression with HPE.
A higher percentage of FM+CFS patients reported performing habitual physical exercise compared to FM-only patients, at a similar rate to the healthy reference group.
Patients with CFS/FM reported significantly more symptoms on the CFS Symptom List (CSL) than healthy controls.
No significant between-group differences were found in temporal summation or conditioned pain modulation (CPM) to cold or heat stimuli.
Serum IFN-γ concentration was significantly lower in patients with CFS/FM compared to healthy controls.
DNA methylation at the third CpG region of the MB-COMT promoter (MB-COMTc) was significantly higher (roughly double) in patients with CFS/FM than in healthy controls.
Mean MB-COMT promoter DNA methylation was significantly higher overall in patients with CFS/FM compared to healthy controls.
Mean S-COMT promoter DNA methylation did not differ significantly between patients with CFS/FM and healthy controls.
Genotype frequencies for the COMT polymorphisms rs4633, rs4818, and rs4680 did not differ significantly between patients with CFS/FM and healthy controls.
COMT haplotypes associated with high enzyme activity showed significantly lower S-COMT promoter DNA methylation than the intermediate-low activity haplotype, across the whole sample.
COMT haplotype was significantly associated with TGF-β expression, with the high-activity haplotype showing lower TGF-β levels than the intermediate-low activity haplotype.

COMT haplotype was significantly associated with CSL symptom severity, with the intermediate-low activity haplotype associated with higher symptom scores than the high-activity haplotype in both patients and controls.
COMT haplotype was significantly associated with cold pain thresholds, with the intermediate-low activity haplotype showing higher cold thresholds than the high-activity haplotype.
COMT haplotype significantly affected conditioned pain modulation to cold stimuli (C-CPM), differing between high- and intermediate-low activity haplotype groups.
No significant associations were found between COMT DNA methylation and cytokine levels, nor between DNA methylation and CSL symptom scores.
Older age was significantly associated with reduced DNA methylation at the MB-COMTb CpG region.
Age and IL-6 concentration were significant predictors of IFN-γ expression, with age negatively associated and IL-6 positively associated with IFN-γ levels.
Neither disease group nor COMT haplotype significantly affected IL-6 concentration.
IFN-γ concentration was significantly positively associated with IL-6 concentration.
Serum TGF-β levels did not differ significantly between patients with CFS/FM and healthy controls.
Serum IL-6 levels showed no statistically significant difference between patients with CFS/FM and healthy controls, though patients trended higher.
TNF-α was not detectable via ELISA in serum samples, precluding analysis of this cytokine, possibly due to sample degradation.

In this cohort of 100 patients with interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome, 31% tested positive for small-fiber polyneuropathy based on skin biopsy intraepidermal nerve fiber density measurement.
Intraepidermal nerve fiber density was below the age- and sex-matched median in 81% of the IC/BPS patients studied.
Chronic fatigue syndrome co-occurrence was significantly more common among SFPN-positive IC/BPS patients (31%) than SFPN-negative patients (10.6%).
SFPN-positive IC/BPS patients reported significantly fewer allergies (37.9%) than SFPN-negative patients (60.6%).
There was no significant difference in bladder capacity or Hunner lesion status between SFPN-positive and SFPN-negative IC/BPS patients.
Pooled data from 26 RCTs showed Chinese herbal medicine (CHM), as adjuvant or monotherapy, significantly decreased FS-14 fatigue scores compared with control groups.
Meta-analysis of nine RCTs showed CHM significantly decreased FAI scores versus control, though the effect was not significant in the subgroup with intervention duration >60 days.
Pooled analysis of five RCTs showed CHM significantly lowered SCL-90 mental state scores compared to control.
Meta-analysis of seven RCTs showed CHM significantly decreased SAS anxiety scores compared to control.
Meta-analysis of six RCTs showed CHM significantly reduced SDS depression scores compared to control.
Pooled data from 24 studies showed CHM significantly decreased overall clinical symptom severity scores compared to control.
Meta-analysis of eight RCTs found CHM significantly elevated IgA levels in CFS patients compared to control.
Meta-analysis of eight RCTs found CHM significantly elevated IgG levels in CFS patients compared to control.
Meta-analysis of eight RCTs found CHM significantly elevated IgM levels in CFS patients compared to control.
Pooled analysis of three RCTs found no significant difference in NK cell levels between CHM-treated and control CFS patients overall.
In a subgroup comparing CHM to placebo, one study showed CHM significantly elevated NK cell levels, in contrast to the null overall pooled result versus WCM.
Pooled clinical effective rate across 79 RCTs was significantly higher with CHM treatment than with control interventions.
Across 14 studies reporting adverse events, CHM caused only mild adverse effects (nausea, dry mouth, indigestion, constipation, fever) with no serious adverse events or deaths reported.
A cited study found that IgA, IgG, and IgM levels are significantly lower in CFS patients compared with healthy subjects, providing rationale for the immune-modulating effect of CHM.
A cited study reported that NK cell activity, CD4+, and CD8+ T cell counts were all significantly reduced in CFS patients.
Among 16 patients diagnosed with EDS, 9 (56.3%) also carried a diagnosis of functional movement disorder (FMD).
Among 190 patients diagnosed with FMD, 16 (8.4%) were also diagnosed with EDS.
In all cases where both diagnoses were present, the diagnosis of EDS preceded the onset and diagnosis of FMD, suggesting EDS may be a prodromal subtype of FMD.
Classical EDS patients with heterozygous COL5A1 or COL5A2 mutations show abnormal corneal thinning and increased corneal steepness.
In a study of 50 classical EDS patients, Villani et al. demonstrated corneal surface irregularity and tear film dysfunction.
In a TNX-deficient EDS cohort, approximately 30% of individuals exhibited recurrent subconjunctival hemorrhages.

Cardiac-valvular EDS is defined by a COL1A2 mutation causing absence of the pro-α2 chain of type I collagen via nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, associated with severe cardiac valvular disease and variable ocular findings such as myopia, strabismus, astigmatism, and blue sclera.

A vascular EDS patient with COL3A1-related type IV EDS developed advanced glaucoma with markedly elevated intraocular pressures (46 and 42 mmHg) and glaucomatous optic atrophy, suggesting type III collagen defects predispose to open angle glaucoma via trabecular meshwork abnormalities.

A vEDS patient developed carotid-cavernous fistula presenting with vision loss, proptosis, conjunctival hyperemia, chemosis, orbital pain, and ocular bruits; embolization attempt resulted in retinal ischemia, endophthalmitis, and fatal aortic rupture.
Ghabriya et al. found hEDS patients reported more dry eye symptoms than controls, with symptom severity correlating with Schirmer test findings.
In a study of 12 hEDS patients, dry eye symptoms were present in 83%, with 46% showing objective findings including punctate epithelial erosions or decreased tear break-up time.

Ho et al. found a higher prevalence of sicca complex (dry eye) in EDS patients with comorbid POTS dysautonomia relative to the general public, hypothesized to result from autonomic dysfunction impairing exocrine/lacrimal gland function.

Gharbiya et al. found approximately 16% of hEDS patients exhibited significant retinal atrophy and choroidal thickening (associated with pathological myopia >-6.0 diopters) compared to 0% of controls.
Mishra et al. found higher rates of myopia (>3.00 diopters) in hEDS patients, with 88% of patients having refractive errors between -3 and +3 diopters.

Chiarelli et al. showed hEDS fibroblasts exhibit dysregulated gene expression of extracellular matrix glycoproteins such as elastin, suggesting matrix dysfunction as a mechanism for ocular findings like myopia.
Recent evidence indicates there is likely no increased risk of angioid streaks in hEDS patients, contradicting earlier literature concern.
Mishra et al. examined 34 hEDS patients and found 68% had abnormal eyelids, with 41% exhibiting excess lid laxity and 24% having prominent horizontal upper lid skin folds.
Gharbiya et al. found minor lens opacities were significantly more prevalent in young adult hEDS subjects compared to controls.
Convergence insufficiency was reported to be common in a case series of EDS patients, with 60% of patients manifesting symptoms affecting near vision tasks (fatigue, nausea, headache).
