Migraine is reported to be more common in hEDS patients, associated with reduced vision from aura and postdromal glare sensitivity/convergence insufficiency.

hEDS patients with poor concussion recovery showed persistent visuomotor complaints (convergence insufficiency, smooth pursuit and saccadic deficiency, glare sensitivity) that in a series of 7 patients led to previously undiagnosed hEDS.
In a review of 49 patients with arthrochalasia EDS (COL1A1/COL1A2 mutations), 3 subjects had blue sclera and 3 had both hypertelorism and epicanthal folds.
Foster et al. reported decreased ADAMTS2 expression in cultured keratoconus cells, linking this dermatosparaxis EDS-causing gene to corneal abnormalities.
Flitcroft et al. implicated ADAMTS2 mutations in myopia in genome-wide association studies.

In a case series of six patients with PLOD1-related kyphoscoliotic EDS, all had microcornea with corneal diameters ranging from 9 to 10.5 mm, versus normal adult diameters of 11.04-12.50 mm (men) and 10.70-12.58 mm (women).
In a case series of eleven kEDS patients, all had corneal thinning, and seven of eleven had experienced spontaneous or minimal-trauma corneal rupture, with one having corneal hydrops.
Presence of blue sclera in Brittle Cornea Syndrome correlates with at least a 33% reduction in central corneal thickness.

Arunrut et al. observed bilateral corneal clouding with unilateral corneal scarring and bilateral inferonasal iris colobomas in a 5-year-old female with a novel missense mutation in B4GALT7, associated with spondylodysplastic EDS.
Musculocontractural EDS caused by CHST14/D4ST1 or DSE mutations, leading to dermatan sulfate deficiency, is associated with microcornea, glaucoma, and refractive error as minor diagnostic criteria.

Almost all individuals (96%) with periodontal EDS (C1R/C1S mutations) reported easy bruising from early childhood, with skin fragility involving periorbita causing dermatochalasis and visual field crowding.

Brain MRI in adults with periodontal EDS has shown white matter abnormalities consistent with underlying small-vessel disease, with patients at risk of transient monocular vision loss requiring stroke workup.
Individuals with hEDS had lower muscle mass than healthy controls.
Individuals with G-HSD had lower muscle mass than healthy controls.
Individuals with hEDS had lower muscle cross-sectional area at the tibia than healthy controls.
Individuals with G-HSD had lower muscle cross-sectional area at the tibia than healthy controls.
Individuals with hEDS had lower cortical bone mineral content at the tibia than healthy controls.
Individuals with G-HSD had lower cortical bone mineral content at the tibia than healthy controls.
Individuals with hEDS had lower cortical bone area at the tibia than healthy controls.
Individuals with G-HSD had lower cortical bone area at the tibia than healthy controls.
Individuals with hEDS had lower muscle density than healthy controls.
Individuals with hEDS had lower muscle density at the lower leg compared to healthy controls.
Individuals with hEDS had lower trabecular bone mineral content (BMC) compared to healthy controls.
Individuals with hEDS had lower trabecular bone mineral density (BMD) compared to healthy controls.
Individuals with G-HSD had a lower stress-strain index (a measure of bone bending strength) compared to healthy controls.
Individuals with G-HSD had a lower periosteal circumference of the tibia compared to healthy controls.
Individuals with G-HSD had a lower endosteal circumference of the tibia compared to healthy controls.

A heterozygous multi-exon deletion spanning exons 2-65 of COL5A1 (almost the entire gene) was identified by MLPA as the cause of classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in the proband after initial NGS sequencing failed to detect a causal variant.

The COL5A1 deletion was inherited from the patient's clinically unaffected father, who harbored the deletion in mosaic form (parental gonosomal mosaicism) at approximately 43% in blood and 30% in skin biopsy DNA.

The multi-exon COL5A1 deletion identified in this patient is absent from control populations in gnomAD structural variants v2.1 and has not been previously reported in ClinVar, LOVD, or HGMD professional 2021.4.
In the LOVD database, only 0.8% (4 of 487) of reported COL5A1 variants are exon-level deletions, indicating that gross deletions are a rare mutation type in classical EDS compared to small variants.
Of 168 reported COL5A2 variants in LOVD, only one (0.6%) is a gross (multi-exon) deletion, similarly indicating that large rearrangements are rare in this gene relative to point mutations.
Haploinsufficiency of collagen V (from loss-of-function COL5A1 variants such as large deletions) is described as an established disease mechanism in classical EDS.
No loss-of-function structural variants in COL5A1 are reported among controls in gnomAD structural variants v2.1, supporting intolerance of the gene to such loss-of-function changes.

A study of 75 classical EDS patients suggested milder multisystem involvement and a more favorable disease course in cEDS compared with other EDS subtypes, consistent with the proband's relatively mild presentation.
In vascular EDS (caused by COL3A1 variants), parental mosaicism has been reported to occur at a rate of 2%-3%, providing a comparator estimate for parental mosaicism prevalence in EDS subtypes.

In a Marfan syndrome cohort of 333 individuals, approximately 5% of assumed de novo cases were caused by parental gonosomal mosaicism, and within this study the first reported case of low-level parental mosaicism for a COL5A1 variant (c.3179G>A, 11% VAF in blood) causing cEDS was described.

A second previously reported case of parental gonosomal mosaicism in cEDS involved a COL5A1 c.1369G>T p.(Glu457*) nonsense variant inherited from a father with an estimated 4.8% variant allele frequency in blood.

In a large trio-based exome sequencing study of 4293 probands with developmental disorders, parental mosaicism was identified in 0.5% of trios, associated with a substantially increased sibling recurrence risk.
Classical EDS can rarely be caused by the specific COL1A1 c.934C>T p.(Arg312Cys) variant, as opposed to the more common COL5A1/COL5A2 variants.
Among 93 mutation-positive cEDS patients, two-thirds of pathogenic COL5A1/COL5A2 variants arose de novo, as reported by Symoens and colleagues.
Nearly half of the EDS cohort (47.9%) showed retinal arterial tortuosity (RAT), either possible or definite, on retinal imaging.
No statistically significant differences in age, sex, or EDS subtype were found between patients with possible/definite RAT and those without RAT.
Hypertension and diabetes mellitus prevalence did not differ significantly between patients with definite RAT and those without RAT, and neither was associated with severe RAT.
Three patients in the cohort with vascular EDS carried COL3A1 mutations confirmed by genetic testing.
One patient with classical EDS in the cohort carried a COL5A1 mutation confirmed by genetic testing.
One patient with myopathic EDS in the cohort carried a COL12A1 mutation confirmed by genetic testing.
Among eyes with definite RAT, the severity distribution was 39.2% mild, 40.2% moderate and 20.6% severe tortuosity, using ROP-like grading criteria.

In patients with definite RAT, first-order arterioles were the most commonly involved vessel type (84.9%), distinct from the macular-predominant pattern seen in familial retinal arterial tortuosity (FRAT).
Over half of patients with possible or definite RAT also showed scattered yellowish-white retinal dots of unclear clinical significance, possibly reflecting a degenerative process related to EDS.

hEDS was the most common subtype in the cohort (69.7%) and is proposed to be associated with abnormal vascular extensibility and connective tissue, which may explain retinal arteriolar tortuosity despite hEDS not being classically linked to major vascular abnormalities.

Skin extensibility has been reported as strongly and linearly associated with, and the most predictive factor for, postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) in patients with hEDS in prior literature cited by the authors.
Inter-grader agreement for the presence/absence of RAT and for RAT severity grading was substantial (Kappa = 0.78 and 0.61, respectively).
Tarlov cysts in EDS are thought to arise from weakening of the epineurium and perineurium caused by defective connective tissue.
The pediatric patient with hypermobile-type EDS was found on investigation to have both a tethered spinal cord and a Tarlov cyst in the distal spinal cord.
Surgical obliteration of Tarlov cysts is reported in the literature to be 80-88% successful with complete postoperative symptom resolution.
After surgical resection of the Tarlov cyst and S1-S2 laminectomy, the patient's urinary and bowel incontinence improved drastically and continued to improve at six months.
Approximately one year after cyst resection, the patient's urinary incontinence recurred up to five times per week, exacerbated by daily activities, along with new lower back pain and numbness.

A second surgery (microsurgical resection of the filum terminale for tethered cord) led to improved mobility, reduced pain, and reduced paresthesia/radiating leg pain, but bowel/bladder incontinence and intermittent nerve pain persisted.
The patient continues to have bowel and bladder incontinence and intermittent nerve pain, currently managed pharmacologically with Tamsulosin, Pregabalin, and Hydromorphone as needed.
A large meta-analysis found a 0.53% incidence of Tarlov cysts in the pediatric population overall, with cysts more prominent in females.
The patient had a past medical history of hypermobile-type EDS (type III) alongside a CPA1 gene mutation.
The authors conclude that this case helps recognize urinary incontinence as a symptom associated with Tarlov cyst development in pediatric EDS patients.
Neurological complications reported in EDS include musculoskeletal pain, fatigue, muscle weakness, dystonia, and paresthesia.

The electronic visual analog scale (e-VAS) showed good agreement with the paper-based VAS (p-VAS) for pain intensity measurement in children and adolescents with HSD/HEDS, with an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.87.
Bland-Altman analysis showed a slight bias with e-VAS scoring on average 0.19 points higher than p-VAS, within acceptable limits of agreement, supporting interchangeable use of the two methods.
Median pain scores differed by only 0.20 between the two VAS platforms among children and adolescents with symptomatic hypermobility.
The study sample was predominantly female, reflecting the reported higher prevalence of hypermobility spectrum disorder/hypermobile EDS among females.

The title reports a newly discovered gene mutation in a case of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome associated with elastosis perforans serpiginosa, but no further detail on the gene, variant, or patient characteristics is available from the title alone.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is caused by autosomal dominant mutation of the COL3A1 gene, which encodes type III collagen.

A postpartum patient with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome presented with spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) of the left anterior descending and obtuse marginal arteries, causing cardiogenic shock.

The patient sustained ischemic rupture of both the anterolateral and posteromedial papillary muscles secondary to the coronary dissection, described as the first reported case of ischemic double papillary muscle rupture in vEDS.
The true prevalence of vEDS is estimated to be at least 1 in 100,000 people, accounting for about 4% of all Ehlers-Danlos syndrome cases.
Unlike classic EDS, vEDS is characterized by increased risk of spontaneous vascular or visceral rupture and notably lacks large-joint hyperextensibility.
Rupture of internal organs such as intestine and muscles has been reported in most vEDS patients by age 40, and peripartum mortality is higher than average in this population.

Percutaneous catheter-guided thrombectomy (Penumbra and FlowTriever devices) was used to treat severe mitral stenosis from a large organized thrombus on a prosthetic mitral valve after anticoagulation failed, reducing the mean transvalvular gradient from 13 to 5 mm Hg.

Surgical mitral valve replacement with a 27 mm porcine bioprosthesis was performed for bilateral papillary muscle rupture, and repeat surgery was avoided for subsequent valve thrombosis due to extreme tissue fragility, with the patient recovering to NYHA class I at 6 months postoperatively.

Traditional Growing Rods (TGR) surgery was used to treat early-onset scoliosis in four patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, with pre-operative Cobb angles of 70-104 degrees corrected via surgery preceded by Halo-gravity traction.
All four EDS patients undergoing TGR treatment for early-onset scoliosis had kyphoscoliosis, indicating a notable spinal deformity phenotype in this population.
The large majority of adult vEDS patients in this national cohort had a documented history of arterial lesions (medium-sized artery and/or aortic).
Medium-sized artery (MSA) lesions were far more common than aortic lesions in this vEDS cohort.
After adjusting for age, patients with dominant-negative COL3A1 variants had a significantly higher prevalence of medium-sized artery lesions than those with haploinsufficiency variants.
Renal artery and supra-aortic trunk lesions were more frequent in patients with dominant-negative COL3A1 variants than in those with haploinsufficiency variants, after age adjustment.

The apparently higher rate of aortic lesions in haploinsufficiency patients compared with dominant-negative patients disappeared once adjusted for age at first arterial lesion, indicating the difference was explained by older age at diagnosis in HI patients rather than genotype.
Digestive events (e.g., colonic perforation) as the first manifestation of vEDS occurred exclusively in patients with dominant-negative COL3A1 variants.

Patients with dominant-negative COL3A1 variants had an earlier onset of their first arterial event than those with haploinsufficiency variants, though this did not translate into earlier molecular diagnosis.
Among the 43 deaths recorded (all in patients with prior arterial lesions), those with dominant-negative variants died at a significantly younger age than those with haploinsufficiency variants.
Carotid intima-media thickness and distensibility were substantially lower than predicted from age-, sex-, and BP-based normative reference values in vEDS patients, similarly across genotypes.
Aortic stiffness (carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity) was higher than expected from normative reference values for age and blood pressure in vEDS patients.

Carotid incremental elastic modulus (intrinsic wall stiffness) was significantly lower (i.e., wall more elastic) in dominant-negative than haploinsufficiency patients, persisting after adjustment for age, sex and blood pressure.

In a logistic regression model for aortic lesion occurrence, older age at first arterial lesion was a significant predictor, male sex showed a non-significant trend, and COL3A1 variant type was not significantly associated.
Female sex was independently associated with a higher risk of supra-aortic trunk lesions in the logistic regression model.
Dominant-negative COL3A1 variants were independently associated with a higher risk of supra-aortic trunk lesions in the logistic regression model.

Patients with aortic lesions had higher unadjusted carotid-femoral PWV, carotid IMT, and elastic modulus than those without, but all these differences disappeared after adjustment for age, indicating age (vascular aging) rather than aortic lesion status per se drives these arterial stiffness changes.

Patients with MSA lesions had significantly higher age-adjusted carotid-femoral PWV and reduced carotid distensibility than those without MSA lesions, with the distensibility difference persisting after further adjustment for sex and blood pressure.

Patients with supra-aortic trunk lesions had a significantly smaller carotid diameter than those without, even after adjustment for age, sex, and mean blood pressure, suggesting a possible developmental anomaly.
The type (rupture/dissection/aneurysm) and anatomical location of aortic lesions were not associated with COL3A1 variant class.
Citing prior work, the authors note that celiprolol selectively reduces carotid elastic modulus and has been shown to significantly reduce cardiovascular events in vEDS patients.
Prevalence of classical cardiovascular risk factors (smoking, overweight, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes) at molecular diagnosis was low and similar between DN and HI variant groups.
Aortic lesions in this vEDS cohort were characterized predominantly as dissections and aneurysms, with rupture being rare, and thoracic and abdominal aorta equally affected.
Patients with haploinsufficiency COL3A1 variants were diagnosed at a significantly older median age than those with dominant-negative variants.

Periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (pEDS), characterized mainly by early-onset periodontitis, is caused by heterozygous mutations (missense, in-frame insertion, deletion) in the C1R gene (15 families) or C1S gene (2 families).
A study identified multiple heterozygous C1S mutations (G962C, T961G, T961A) in an extended family as pathogenic variants underlying pEDS.
In cellular studies, the pEDS-associated C1s mutants Val316del and Cys294Arg were produced as truncated proteins lacking their N-terminal domain.

Structural analyses showed that C1r and C1s interact via an extensive interface encompassing the N-terminal regions of both proteins, suggesting pEDS-causing mutations may disrupt this C1r-C1s binding and/or C1r-C1s-C1q coupling, facilitating aberrant C1s activation.
pEDS-associated mutations lead to constitutive (unregulated) activation of C1r and C1s, driving development of periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Plasma norepinephrine levels are higher in fibromyalgia patients than in the general population.
Dopamine levels are reduced in fibromyalgia patients compared with the healthy population, potentially underlying diffuse pain and discomfort.
Serotonin levels are reduced in fibromyalgia patients compared with the healthy population.
Glutamate contributes to greater central pain sensitization in fibromyalgia.
Cerebrospinal fluid substance P concentration is threefold higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy subjects, contributing to pain modulation.
Fibromyalgia patients have lower nighttime melatonin secretion than healthy subjects, which may contribute to poor sleep, daytime fatigue, and altered pain perception.
Low nighttime melatonin is proposed to intensify nocturnal pain sensation in fibromyalgia.
Brain MRI shows increased sensory activity in the insula during fibromyalgia pain episodes.
Fibromyalgia patients show hypofunctioning of the HPA axis, resulting in relative adrenal insufficiency that may explain fatigue and reduced exercise/muscle performance.
CoQ10 levels are reduced in fibromyalgia and contribute to mitochondrial dysfunction, decreased mitochondrial membrane potential, increased superoxide activity, and lipid peroxidation.
Excessive mitophagy and autophagy are detected in blood mononuclear cells and plasma of fibromyalgia patients, potentially promoting cell injury and oxidative stress.
Lipid peroxidation products positively correlate with fibromyalgia severity as measured by the FIQR.
Reduced functioning of superoxide dismutase, catalase, and NADPH oxidase correlates with pain and fatigue severity in fibromyalgia.
Fibromyalgia subjects show low antioxidative enzyme activity (CAT, GR, GPx) with increased NO and MDA in red blood cell lysate.
Antioxidative enzymes are negatively associated with FIQR severity (functioning, pain, distress, sleep), while lipid peroxidation levels are positively correlated with FIQR.
Elevated serum nitrite, related to NOS activation and NO elevation, is a prooxidant marker linked to pain sensation via the spinal pain pathway in fibromyalgia.
La Rubia et al. found that lower antioxidant enzyme activities may lead to oxidative stress via DNA oxidation and elevated protein carbonyl content, affecting FM patients' health status.
Total antioxidant capacity is diminished in women with fibromyalgia compared to controls.
In a rat reserpine-induced myalgia model, melatonin supplementation prevented myotube deterioration and increased mitochondrial markers and CoQ10 in gastrocnemius muscle.
Melatonin administration in fibromyalgia patients can reduce pain and improve sleep quality, improving overall quality of life.
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy deactivates caspase 3 and 9 and increases Bcl-2 expression, suggesting reduced mitochondrial-induced apoptosis.
In animal models, hyperbaric oxygen therapy reduces lipid peroxidation and prooxidative processes.
Clinical trials show hyperbaric oxygen therapy improves global functioning, reduces pain, provides psychological relief, and normalizes brain activity in fibromyalgia patients.
Combined CoQ10, vitamin D, alpha-lipoic acid, magnesium, and tryptophan supplementation significantly reduced pain after one month and improved quality of life in fibromyalgia patients.
In an RCT by Cordero et al., CoQ10 combined with pregabalin significantly reduced pain and anxiety compared to pregabalin monotherapy in fibromyalgia patients.
A case report found that CoQ10 supplementation reduced oxidative stress markers, improved mitochondrial function, and diminished clinical symptoms in a fibromyalgia patient.
A randomized controlled trial found no significant symptomatic improvement in fibromyalgia patients receiving 50,000 IU of vitamin D weekly for three months.
Wepner et al. found that daily supplementation with 1200 IU or 2400 IU vitamin D for 25 weeks decreased pain sensitization (VAS) and morning fatigue (FIQ) in fibromyalgia patients.
A case series reported that vitamin A supplementation reduced or resolved fibromyalgia symptoms including musculoskeletal pain, fatigue, and depressed mood.
A controlled trial found that daily supplementation with 200 mg vitamin C and 200 mg vitamin E for 8 weeks resulted in pain reduction in fibromyalgia patients.
Nazıroğlu et al.'s controlled clinical pilot study found no significant symptom changes after 12 weeks of daily vitamin C (500 mg) and vitamin E (150 mg) supplementation in fibromyalgia patients.
Daily consumption of 50 mL of olive oil for three weeks improved FIQ score, physical ability, and mental health in 23 fibromyalgia patients.
Olive oil consumption decreased cardiovascular risk factors including lipid profile, inflammatory markers, and thrombosis-related parameters in 15 women with fibromyalgia.
Serum zinc concentration is significantly lower in chronic fatigue syndrome patients, associated with oxidative stress.
Serum zinc levels were substantially lower in 45 female fibromyalgia patients compared to controls (p<0.001).
Zinc deficiency is positively correlated with severity of depression, a key clinical feature of fibromyalgia.
Selenium levels are reduced in fibromyalgia patients, a trace element cofactor for glutathione peroxidase involved in neuroprotection.
In an animal model of fibromyalgia-induced rats, selenium supplementation reduced pain intensity, ROS levels, and lipid peroxidation.
Selenoproteins are necessary for development of parvalbumin-positive GABAergic interneurons, whose dysfunction is implicated in central hyperalgesia in fibromyalgia.
Fibromyalgia patients have significantly reduced serum ferritin levels compared to healthy controls.
Iron deficiency anemia was associated with increased risk of fibromyalgia prevalence in females, replicated by a second study showing higher FM incidence in iron-deficient individuals.
A placebo-controlled trial of ferric carboxymaltose in 80 women with fibromyalgia found improved FIQR and brief pain inventory scores and reduced fatigue after 42 days.
Folic acid has antioxidative properties and is reported to improve immune function and pain sensation in fibromyalgia.
Prooxidative processes induce mast cell activation and systemic macrocytosis in fibromyalgia, with mast cells located near nerve fibers modulating nociception via communication with microglia.

In the reserpine-induced myalgia rat model, combined melatonin and folic acid supplementation restored superoxide dismutase activity and reduced lipid peroxidation more effectively than either agent alone, decreasing pain sensitivity and depression-like behavior.
Serum copper and ceruloplasmin levels were significantly elevated in 45 fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls.
Serum copper, manganese, and aluminum concentrations were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than controls, correlating with FIQR score, tender points, and pain sensation.
In a randomized controlled trial, dietary glutamate significantly increased fibromyalgia symptom severity as assessed by worsening FIQR score.

Vellisca and Latorre found no significant difference in pain severity among 36 female fibromyalgia patients after discontinuing dietary MSG and aspartame for three months, contrasting with earlier case studies suggesting benefit.
Serum taurine levels were increased in fibromyalgia patients but were not significantly associated with clinical severity measured by FIQR.
Larson et al. found a significant relationship between CSF taurine level and tender point index in fibromyalgia patients.
A randomized trial found 12 weeks of Tai Chi and aerobic exercise significantly reduced FIQR scores and improved anxiety, pain, and global assessment in fibromyalgia patients.
A telerehabilitation aerobic exercise program showed similar benefits for Spanish fibromyalgia patients, though oxidative stress markers were not assessed in this study.

Whole-body vibration exercise increased superoxide dismutase activity, reduced catalase activity, decreased iron reduction capacity, and diminished thiobarbituric acid reactive substances in fibromyalgia patients.

Antidepressants such as amitriptyline and SNRIs (duloxetine, mirtazapine, venlafaxine) increase serotonin and norepinephrine, improving sleep and reducing pain and fatigue in fibromyalgia, but do not affect tender point tenderness.
Pramipexole, pregabalin, and gabapentin reduce pain in fibromyalgia, but pregabalin may be less effective overall than SNRIs and may induce more somatic symptoms.
Functional MRI shows fibromyalgia patients have greater neuronal activation in brain pain-processing areas, including the insula, compared to controls.
Fibromyalgia patients show increased functional connectivity between the default mode network and the insula.
Fibromyalgia patients show decreased functional connectivity within the descending pain-modulating system.
The cerebrospinal fluid of fibromyalgia patients contains high levels of the excitatory neurotransmitter substance P.
The cerebrospinal fluid of fibromyalgia patients contains high levels of the excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate.
Nearly half of fibromyalgia patients show objective evidence of peripheral small nerve fiber damage, demonstrated via skin biopsy and corneal confocal microscopy.
In rodent models, stressors such as unpredictable noise or forced swimming induce dorsal root ganglia neuroplasticity and resultant neuropathic pain.
Severe fibromyalgia has been associated with a particular dorsal root ganglia sodium channel gene variant.
IgG passively transferred from fibromyalgia patients into mice induces painful behavior and peripheral denervation, with IgG deposition found exclusively in the dorsal root ganglia.
There is clear evidence of sympathetic autonomic nervous system malfunction in individuals with fibromyalgia.
Fibromyalgia is reported to affect 2-4% of the population.
A systematic review found signs of small fiber damage in about half of FM patients, potentially contributing to pain and autonomic symptoms, though findings were heterogeneous.
Diagnosis in the literature has relied on identifying 18 tender points, with FM defined by pain on digital pressure at 11 or more of these points.
In a study of 86 FM patients, 10 who received myofascial release therapy showed marked improvement in tender points, physical function, and clinical severity that was sustained at six months.

An observational interview study of the Fibromyalgia Self-Management Program (FSMP) found it successfully facilitated behavior change via goal-setting and other self-management techniques over a six-week period.
Multiple systematic reviews conclude that cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an effective approach for chronic pain management in FM.
Higher mindfulness in FM patients was associated with better sleep quality and reduced sleep disturbance, pain, and depression, potentially mediated by these psychological factors.
A mindfulness-based intervention (MBI) in women with FM significantly improved satisfaction with life, positive affect, mental health, and resilience compared to controls.
Mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) added to treatment-as-usual (TAU) achieved a significant reduction in indirect and primary healthcare costs compared to TAU alone in Spanish FM patients.
Central sensitization in FM appears to involve an imbalance of BDNF and inflammatory biomarkers, implicated in pain modulation and hyperalgesia.
In an RCT, attachment-based compassion therapy (ABCT) produced significant improvement in FIQ scores and reduced BDNF, CRP, and a pro-inflammatory composite compared to relaxation therapy (RT).

MAIR (Mindfulness plus Amygdala and Insula Retraining) plus TAU improved functional impairment, clinical severity, and quality of life compared to relaxation therapy, and significantly decreased BDNF levels, though no significant change was found in immune-inflammatory variables.
A systematic review (2007-2011) found aerobic and power training exercise improves fitness, physical function, reduces FM symptoms, and improves quality of life.

A systematic review of exercise programs (dance, water activities, body-mind work, fitness, stretching) found pain reduced 10-44.2% and negative quality-of-life impact reduced 5.3-17.9% after multidisciplinary intervention.
Aerobic exercise and Zumba dancing both significantly improved working memory, motor function, and depressive symptoms in women with FM.

Aquatic physiotherapy plus health education significantly reduced fatigue, improved functional capability, and reduced anxiety, depression, and sleep problems in FM patients, but did not significantly reduce pain.
An exercise trial in adults with FM found a 54% increase in daily step count on the 6-minute walk test, 18% improvement in overall function, and 35% reduction in pain.
Improvements achieved during an exercise-based intervention program were not maintained over time, highlighting the problem of persistent inactivity relapse in FM patients.
A three-year longitudinal study found that a six-month combined training program produced immediate health improvements in women with FM, with benefits maintained for 30 months.
The FDA has approved three drugs specifically for FM treatment: duloxetine, milnacipran, and pregabalin.
